translations.an10.13:1: "These ten, bhikkhus, are fetters. Which ten? Five lower fetters, five higher fetters. Which are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, grasping at precepts and vows, sensual desire, ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: "As far as, bhikkhus, there are beings whether footless or two-footed or four-footed or many-footed, whether with form or formless, whether percipient or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient, the Tathāgata is declared supreme among them, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; so too, bhikkhus, whatever wholesome states there are, all are rooted in diligence, converge on diligence. Diligence is declared supreme among them.
translations.an10.15:2: Just as, bhikkhus, whatever footprints of creatures in the jungle there are, all converge on the elephant's footprint, the elephant's footprint is declared supreme among them, that is, by greatness; so too, bhikkhus, whatever wholesome states there are, all are rooted in diligence, converge on diligence. Diligence is declared supreme among them.
translations.an10.15:3: Just as, bhikkhus, whatever rafters there are of a peaked house, all converge on the peak, incline toward the peak, meet at the peak, the peak is declared supreme among them; so too, bhikkhus, whatever wholesome states there are, all are rooted in diligence, converge on diligence. Diligence is declared supreme among them.
translations.an10.15:7: Just as, bhikkhus, whatever minor kings there are, all are vassals to the wheel-turning king, the wheel-turning king is declared supreme among them; so too, bhikkhus …
translations.an10.15:8: Just as, bhikkhus, whatever light of star-forms there is, all do not amount to a sixteenth part of the moon's light, the moon's light is declared supreme among them; so too, bhikkhus …
translations.an10.15:9: Just as, bhikkhus, in the autumn season when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun rising in the sky radiates, illumines, and shines forth, dispelling all darkness in the sky; so too, bhikkhus …
translations.an10.17:1: "Live with a protector, bhikkhus, not without a protector. It is painful, bhikkhus, to live without a protector. These ten, bhikkhus, are things that provide a protector. Which ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults, undertaking and training in the training rules. This too, bhikkhus, is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.17:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is learned, a bearer of learning, a storehouse of learning, those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings are much learned by him, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated in mind, and well penetrated by view. This too, bhikkhus, is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.17:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good comrades. This too, bhikkhus, is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.18:10: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. 'This bhikkhu is indeed mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago'—senior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed, middle bhikkhus … junior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed. For one who is protected by seniors, protected by middles, protected by juniors, growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.18:11: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is wise, possessing noble penetrative wisdom that leads to the destruction of suffering. 'This bhikkhu is indeed wise, possessing noble penetrative wisdom that leads to the destruction of suffering'—senior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed, middle bhikkhus … junior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed. For one who is protected by seniors … not decline. This too is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.18:2: "Live with a protector, bhikkhus, not without a protector. It is painful, bhikkhus, to live without a protector. These ten, bhikkhus, are things that provide a protector. Which ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous … undertaking and training in the training rules. 'This bhikkhu is indeed virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults, undertaking and training in the training rules'—senior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed, middle bhikkhus … junior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed. For one who is protected by seniors, protected by middles, protected by juniors, growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.18:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good comrades. 'This bhikkhu indeed has good friends, good companions, good comrades'—senior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed, middle bhikkhus … junior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed. For one who is protected by seniors, protected by middles, protected by juniors, growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.18:5: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is easy to admonish, possessing qualities that make one easy to admonish, patient, taking instruction rightly. 'This bhikkhu is indeed easy to admonish, possessing qualities that make one easy to admonish, patient, taking instruction rightly'—senior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed, middle bhikkhus … junior bhikkhus think he should be advised and instructed. For one who is protected by seniors, protected by middles, protected by juniors, growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk is skilled and energetic in whatever various duties there are for spiritual companions, endowed with suitable investigation, capable of doing, capable of organizing. 'This monk is skilled and energetic in whatever various duties there are for spiritual companions, endowed with suitable investigation, capable of doing, capable of organizing'—senior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … junior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is cared for by seniors, cared for by middlings, cared for by juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, monks, a monk is fond of the Dhamma, speaks lovingly, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and higher discipline. 'This monk is fond of the Dhamma, speaks lovingly, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and higher discipline'—senior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … junior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is cared for by seniors, cared for by middlings, cared for by juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the acquisition of wholesome qualities, strong, firm in effort, not casting off the burden in wholesome qualities. 'This monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the acquisition of wholesome qualities, strong, firm in effort, not casting off the burden in wholesome qualities'—senior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … junior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is cared for by seniors, cared for by middlings, cared for by juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick. 'This monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick'—senior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … junior monks think he should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is cared for by seniors, cared for by middlings, cared for by juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.20:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a market town of the Kurus called Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks ….
translations.an10.20:10: And how, monks, is a monk one with tranquilized bodily formations? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. Thus, monks, a monk is one with tranquilized bodily formations.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, monks, is a monk well liberated in mind? Here, monks, a monk's mind is liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion. Thus, monks, a monk is well liberated in mind.
translations.an10.20:2: 'These ten, monks, are noble dwellings in which the noble ones have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell. What ten? Here, monks, a monk is one who has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has one guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has thoroughly searched out desires, has unmixed thoughts, has tranquilized bodily formations, is well liberated in mind, is well liberated by wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, monks, is a monk one who has abandoned five factors? Here, monks, a monk's sensual desire is abandoned, ill will is abandoned, sloth and torpor are abandoned, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, doubt is abandoned. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has abandoned five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, monks, is a monk endowed with six factors? Here, monks, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, is neither elated nor dejected, but dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware. Hearing a sound with the ear … smelling an odor with the nose … tasting a flavor with the tongue … touching a tactile object with the body … cognizing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither elated nor dejected, but dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware. Thus, monks, a monk is endowed with six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk one who has one guard? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has one guard.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, monks, is a monk one who has four supports? Here, monks, a monk uses some things after reflection, endures some things after reflection, avoids some things after reflection, and dispels some things after reflection. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has four supports.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, monks, is a monk one who has dispelled individual truths? Here, monks, for a monk, whatever various individual truths there are of various ascetics and brahmins, such as: 'the world is eternal' or 'the world is not eternal,' 'the world is finite' or 'the world is infinite,' 'the soul and the body are the same' or 'the soul is one thing and the body another,' 'the Tathāgata exists after death' or 'the Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' or 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—all of these are dispelled, well dispelled, cast out, vomited up, abandoned, and relinquished. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has dispelled individual truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, monks, is a monk one who has thoroughly searched out desires? Here, monks, a monk's sensual desire is abandoned, desire for existence is abandoned, desire for the spiritual life is pacified. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has thoroughly searched out desires.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, monks, is a monk one with unmixed thoughts? Here, monks, a monk's sensual thought is abandoned, thought of ill will is abandoned, thought of harming is abandoned. Thus, monks, a monk is one with unmixed thoughts.
translations.an10.24:1: At one time Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetīs at Sahajāti. There Venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friend,' those monks replied to Venerable Mahācunda. Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Just as, friends, a man who is wealthy would claim to be wealthy, who is rich would claim to be rich, who is prosperous would claim to be prosperous. When some need for wealth arose, he would be able to bring forth wealth or grain or silver or gold. They would know him thus: 'This venerable one, being wealthy, claims to be wealthy, being rich, claims to be rich, being prosperous, claims to be prosperous. Why is that? Because when some need for wealth arose, this venerable one was able to bring forth wealth or grain or silver or gold.'
translations.an10.24:2: When a monk, friends, making a claim to knowledge, says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma,' if, friends, greed overcomes and stands over that monk, aversion ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... denigration ... insolence ... miserliness ... evil jealousy ... evil desire overcomes and stands over him, he should be understood thus: 'This venerable one does not understand as one who understands does not have greed; thus greed overcomes and stands over this venerable one; this venerable one does not understand as one who understands does not have aversion ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... denigration ... insolence ... miserliness ... evil jealousy ... evil desire; thus evil desire overcomes and stands over this venerable one.'
translations.an10.24:3: When a monk, friends, making a claim to development, says: 'I am one of developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom,' if, friends, greed overcomes and stands over that monk, aversion ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... denigration ... insolence ... miserliness ... evil jealousy ... evil desire overcomes and stands over him, he should be understood thus: 'This venerable one does not understand as one who understands does not have greed; thus greed overcomes and stands over this venerable one; this venerable one does not understand as one who understands does not have aversion ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... denigration ... insolence ... miserliness ... evil jealousy ... evil desire; thus evil desire overcomes and stands over this venerable one.'
translations.an10.24:5: Just as, friends, a man who is poor would claim to be wealthy, who is without wealth would claim to be rich, who is without prosperity would claim to be prosperous. When some need for wealth arose, he would not be able to bring forth wealth or grain or silver or gold. They would know him thus: 'This venerable one, being poor, claims to be wealthy, being without wealth, claims to be rich, being without prosperity, claims to be prosperous. Why is that? Because when some need for wealth arose, this venerable one was not able to bring forth wealth or grain or silver or gold.'
translations.an10.24:9: When a monk, friends, making a claim to knowledge and making a claim to development, says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma, I am one of developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom,' if, friends, greed does not overcome and stand over that monk, aversion ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... denigration ... insolence ... miserliness ... evil jealousy ... evil desire does not overcome and stand over him, he should be understood thus: 'This venerable one understands as one who understands does not have greed; thus greed does not overcome and stand over this venerable one; this venerable one understands as one who understands does not have aversion ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... denigration ... insolence ... miserliness ... evil jealousy ... evil desire; thus evil desire does not overcome and stand over this venerable one.'
translations.an10.29:1: As far as, monks, Kasi and Kosala extend, as far as King Pasenadi of Kosala's realm extends, King Pasenadi of Kosala is declared supreme. But, monks, even for King Pasenadi of Kosala there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the supreme, how much more toward the inferior.
translations.an10.29:10: Perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally, blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luminosity. Just as the flax flower is blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luminosity, or just as that Banares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luminosity; so too, perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally, blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luminosity; 'Having overcome them, I know, I see,' one becomes percipient thus. This is the fifth base of overcoming.
translations.an10.29:11: Perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally, yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luminosity. Just as the kanikara flower is yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luminosity, or just as that Banares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luminosity; so too, perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally, yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luminosity; 'Having overcome them, I know, I see,' one becomes percipient thus. This is the sixth base of overcoming.
translations.an10.29:12: Perceiving internally formless, one sees externally forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luminosity. Just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luminosity, or just as that Bārāṇasī cloth, burnished on both sides, is red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luminosity; so too, perceiving internally formless, one sees externally forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luminosity; 'mastering them, I know, I see,' one becomes thus perceiving. This is the seventh mastery base.
translations.an10.29:13: Perceiving internally formless, one sees externally forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luminosity. Just as the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luminosity, or just as that Bārāṇasī cloth, burnished on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luminosity; so too, perceiving internally formless, one sees externally forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luminosity; 'mastering them, I know, I see,' one becomes thus perceiving. This is the eighth mastery base. These, bhikkhus, are the eight mastery bases.
translations.an10.29:14: The foremost of these eight mastery bases is this: perceiving internally formless, one sees externally forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luminosity; 'mastering them, I know, I see,' one becomes thus perceiving. There are, bhikkhus, beings who are thus perceiving. But for beings who are thus perceiving, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: These, bhikkhus, are four courses. Which four? Painful course with sluggish direct knowledge, painful course with quick direct knowledge, pleasant course with sluggish direct knowledge, pleasant course with quick direct knowledge—these, bhikkhus, are the four courses.
translations.an10.29:16: The foremost of these four courses is this: pleasant course with quick direct knowledge. There are, bhikkhus, beings who practice thus. But for beings who practice thus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: These, bhikkhus, are four perceptions. Which four? One perceives the limited, one perceives the expanded, one perceives the measureless, one perceives the base of nothingness: 'there is nothing'—these, bhikkhus, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The foremost of these four perceptions is this: one perceives the base of nothingness: 'there is nothing.' There are, bhikkhus, beings who are thus perceiving. But for beings who are thus perceiving, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: As far as, bhikkhus, the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters with their shining, so far extends the thousandfold world. In that thousandfold world there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand Cātumahārājika heavens, a thousand Tāvatiṃsa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tusita heavens, a thousand Nimmānaratī heavens, a thousand Paranimmitavasavattī heavens, a thousand Brahma worlds. As far as, bhikkhus, the thousandfold world-system, the Great Brahmā there is declared foremost. But for the Great Brahmā too, bhikkhus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, bhikkhus, some ascetics and brahmins who declare ultimate purity. The foremost of those declaring ultimate purity is this: having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither perception nor non-perception. They teach the Dhamma for the direct knowledge of that, for its realization. There are, bhikkhus, beings who speak thus. But for beings who speak thus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, bhikkhus, when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, for the most part beings are reborn in the Ābhassara realm. There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, beautiful, remaining there for a long time, for a very long time. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, the Ābhassara devas are declared foremost. But for the Ābhassara devas too, bhikkhus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: These, bhikkhus, are ten kasiṇa bases. Which ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, undivided, measureless; one perceives the water kasiṇa … one perceives the fire kasiṇa … one perceives the air kasiṇa … one perceives the blue kasiṇa … one perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one perceives the red kasiṇa … one perceives the white kasiṇa … one perceives the space kasiṇa … one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, undivided, measureless. These, bhikkhus, are the ten kasiṇa bases.
translations.an10.29:5: This is the foremost, bhikkhus, of these ten kasiṇa bases, that is, the consciousness kasiṇa: one perceives above, below, across, non-dual, boundless. There are, bhikkhus, beings who perceive thus. For beings who perceive thus, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes dispassionate toward that too. Becoming dispassionate toward that, he is detached from the foremost, how much more from what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:6: There are, bhikkhus, these eight bases of mastery. What eight? Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly; 'having mastered them, I know, I see,' one perceives thus. This is the first base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:7: Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, boundless, beautiful or ugly; 'having mastered them, I know, I see,' one perceives thus. This is the second base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:8: Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly; 'having mastered them, I know, I see,' one perceives thus. This is the third base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:9: Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, boundless, beautiful or ugly; 'having mastered them, I know, I see,' one perceives thus. This is the fourth base of mastery.
translations.an10.51:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in the ways of his own mind? Just as, bhikkhus, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of adornment—when examining their own facial reflection in a clear, clean mirror or in a bowl of clear water, if they see there dust or a blemish, they strive to remove that very dust or blemish. But if they do not see there dust or a blemish, they become joyful and satisfied on that account: 'Indeed it is a gain for me, indeed it is clean for me.' So too, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, examination is very helpful in regard to wholesome states: 'Do I dwell much with covetousness or without covetousness, with ill will or without ill will, overcome by sloth and torpor or free from sloth and torpor, restless or not restless, doubtful or one who has overcome doubt, angry or without anger, with defiled mind or with undefiled mind, with agitated body or with unagitated body, lazy or with aroused energy, unconcentrated or concentrated?'
translations.an10.51:4: If, bhikkhus, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus: 'I dwell much with covetousness, with ill will, overcome by sloth and torpor, restless, doubtful, angry, with defiled mind, with agitated body, lazy, unconcentrated,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make an extreme effort, strive, arouse energy, be unrelenting, with mindfulness and full awareness for the abandoning of those very unwholesome states. Just as, bhikkhus, one whose clothes or head were on fire would make an extreme effort, strive, arouse energy, be unrelenting, with mindfulness and full awareness to extinguish that very fire on the clothes or head. So too, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make an extreme effort, strive, arouse energy, be unrelenting, with mindfulness and full awareness for the abandoning of those very unwholesome states.
translations.an10.54:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in the ways of his own mind? Just as, bhikkhus, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of adornment—when examining their own facial reflection in a clear, clean mirror or in a bowl of clear water, if they see there dust or a blemish, they strive to remove that very dust or blemish. But if they do not see there dust or a blemish, they become joyful and satisfied on that account: 'Indeed it is a gain for me, indeed it is clean for me.' So too, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, examination is very helpful in regard to wholesome states: 'Am I one who gains internal serenity of mind, am I not one who gains internal serenity of mind, am I one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom, am I not one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom?'
translations.an10.54:5: But if, bhikkhus, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus: 'I do not gain internal serenity of mind, I do not gain insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make an extreme effort, strive, arouse energy, be unrelenting, with mindfulness and full awareness for the acquisition of those very wholesome states. Just as, bhikkhus, one whose clothes or head were on fire would make an extreme effort, strive, arouse energy, be unrelenting, with mindfulness and full awareness to extinguish that very fire on the clothes or head. So too, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make an extreme effort, strive, arouse energy, be unrelenting, with mindfulness and full awareness for the acquisition of those very wholesome states. Then, at a later time, he becomes one who gains internal serenity of mind and one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, bhikkhus, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus: 'I gain internal serenity of mind, I gain insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu, established in those very wholesome states, should make an effort for the destruction of the taints that is higher and further.
translations.an10.58:1: “Mendicants, if wanderers who follow other paths were to ask you: ‘Reverends, what is the root of all things? What is their origin? What is their arising? What is their meeting place? What is their chief? What is their ruler? What is their best? What is their essence? What is their foundation? What is their culmination?’ How would you answer them?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Well then, mendicants, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an10.59:1: “Therefore, mendicants, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will be cultivated in accordance with the going forth; arisen bad unwholesome qualities will not dominate our minds. Our minds will be cultivated in the perception of impermanence, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of not-self, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of foulness, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of danger, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of what is even and uneven in the world, knowing that, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of existence and non-existence in the world, knowing that, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of arising and passing away in the world, knowing that, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of giving up, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of dispassion, our minds will be cultivated in the perception of cessation’—thus, mendicants, should you train yourselves.
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha:
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant—gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the destruction of craving, cessation, extinguishment.’ This is called the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the entire world? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant lives giving up and not grasping at those attachments, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies in the world. This is called the perception of non-delight in the entire world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-desire for all conditioned phenomena? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant is repelled, ashamed, and disgusted by all conditioned phenomena. This is called the perception of non-desire for all conditioned phenomena.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant—gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, with body straight, and establishes mindfulness right there. Mindful, they breathe in; mindful, they breathe out. Breathing in long, they know: ‘I breathe in long.’ Breathing out long, they know: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, they know: ‘I breathe in short.’ Breathing out short, they know: ‘I breathe out short.’ They train: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out.’ They train: ‘Stilling the bodily formation, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Stilling the bodily formation, I will breathe out.’ They train: ‘Experiencing rapture, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Experiencing rapture, I will breathe out.’ They train: ‘Experiencing bliss, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Experiencing bliss, I will breathe out.’ They train: ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe out.’ They train: ‘Stilling the mental formation, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Stilling the mental formation, I will breathe out.’ They train: ‘Experiencing the mind, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Experiencing the mind, I will breathe out.’ … Gladdening the mind … … Concentrating the mind … … Liberating the mind … … Contemplating impermanence … … Contemplating dispassion … … Contemplating cessation … … They train: ‘Contemplating letting go, I will breathe in.’ They train: ‘Contemplating letting go, I will breathe out.’ This is called mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If you, Ānanda, were to recite these ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it is possible that on hearing these ten perceptions his illness would immediately subside.”
translations.an10.60:2: “Sir, Venerable Girimānanda is sick, suffering, gravely ill. Sir, please go to Venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.” “If you, Ānanda, were to recite ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it is possible that on hearing these ten perceptions his illness would immediately subside.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of foulness, the perception of danger, the perception of giving up, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of non-desire for all conditioned phenomena, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant—gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—reflects thus: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, choices are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus they dwell contemplating impermanence in these five grasping aggregates. This is called the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'The eye is non-self, forms are non-self, the ear is non-self, sounds are non-self, the nose is non-self, odors are non-self, the tongue is non-self, tastes are non-self, the body is non-self, tactile objects are non-self, the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self.' Thus he dwells contemplating non-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of foulness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body from the soles of the feet up and from the tips of the hairs down, enclosed in skin, full of many kinds of impurity: 'There are in this body head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.' Thus he dwells contemplating foulness in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of foulness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'This body is much suffering, much danger. Thus various diseases arise in this body, namely: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, head-disease, ear-disease, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, lip-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach-disease, fainting, dysentery, gripes, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scab, cracked skin, scabies, scurvy, blood, bile, diabetes, scrofula, hemorrhoids. Diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from their combination, diseases arising from change of seasons, diseases arising from improper care, diseases arising from assault, diseases arising from kamma-result; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.' Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire, but abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, and brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will, but abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, and brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of cruelty, but abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, and brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate arisen evil unwholesome states, but abandons them, dispels them, terminates them, and brings them to non-existence. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: “Bhikkhus, a first point of ignorance is not discerned: 'Before this, ignorance was not; afterwards it came to be.' Yet though this is said, it is discerned: 'With this as condition, ignorance.'
translations.an10.61:2: Ignorance, bhikkhus, I say is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? 'The five hindrances' should be the reply. The five hindrances, bhikkhus, I say are with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? 'The three kinds of misconduct' should be the reply. The three kinds of misconduct, bhikkhus, I say are with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of misconduct? 'Lack of restraint of the sense faculties' should be the reply. Lack of restraint of the sense faculties, bhikkhus, I say is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of restraint of the sense faculties? 'Lack of mindfulness and full awareness' should be the reply. Lack of mindfulness and full awareness, bhikkhus, I say is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of mindfulness and full awareness? 'Unwise attention' should be the reply. Unwise attention, bhikkhus, I say is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for unwise attention? 'Lack of faith' should be the reply. Lack of faith, bhikkhus, I say is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of faith? 'Not hearing the good Dhamma' should be the reply. Not hearing the good Dhamma, bhikkhus, I say is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for not hearing the good Dhamma? 'Association with bad people' should be the reply.
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, bhikkhus, association with bad people, when complete, fulfills not hearing the good Dhamma; not hearing the good Dhamma, when complete, fulfills lack of faith; lack of faith, when complete, fulfills unwise attention; unwise attention, when complete, fulfills lack of mindfulness and full awareness; lack of mindfulness and full awareness, when complete, fulfills lack of restraint of the sense faculties; lack of restraint of the sense faculties, when complete, fulfills the three kinds of misconduct; the three kinds of misconduct, when complete, fulfill the five hindrances; the five hindrances, when complete, fulfill ignorance; thus is the nutriment for this ignorance, and thus its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, bhikkhus, when it is raining heavily on a mountain top (…) that water, flowing down according to the slope, fills up the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines; the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines being full fill up the pools; the pools being full fill up the ponds; the ponds being full fill up the streams; the streams being full fill up the rivers; the rivers being full fill up the great ocean, the sea; thus is the nutriment for this great ocean, the sea, and thus its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, bhikkhus, association with good people, when complete, fulfills hearing the good Dhamma; hearing the good Dhamma, when complete, fulfills faith; faith, when complete, fulfills wise attention; wise attention, when complete, fulfills mindfulness and full awareness; mindfulness and full awareness, when complete, fulfills restraint of the sense faculties; restraint of the sense faculties, when complete, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; the three kinds of good conduct, when complete, fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness; the four establishments of mindfulness, when complete, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment, when complete, fulfill knowledge and liberation; thus is the nutriment for this knowledge and liberation, and thus its fulfillment.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the venerable Ānanda approached the venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging cordial and memorable greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Could there be, friend Sāriputta, such an attainment of concentration for a monk that he would not perceive earth in earth, would not perceive water in water, would not perceive fire in fire, would not perceive air in air, would not perceive the base of the infinity of space in the base of the infinity of space, would not perceive the base of the infinity of consciousness in the base of the infinity of consciousness, would not perceive the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, would not perceive the base of neither perception nor non-perception in the base of neither perception nor non-perception, would not perceive this world in this world, would not perceive the other world in the other world; yet he would still be perceiving?”
translations.an10.7:4: “But how, friend Sāriputta, could there be such an attainment of concentration for a monk that he would not perceive earth in earth …pe… yet he would still be perceiving?” “Once, friend Ānanda, I was dwelling right here in Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove. There I entered upon such a concentration that I did not perceive earth in earth, I did not perceive water in water, I did not perceive fire in fire, I did not perceive air in air, I did not perceive the base of the infinity of space in the base of the infinity of space, I did not perceive the base of the infinity of consciousness in the base of the infinity of consciousness, I did not perceive the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, I did not perceive the base of neither perception nor non-perception in the base of neither perception nor non-perception, I did not perceive this world in this world, I did not perceive the other world in the other world; yet I was still perceiving.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Possessed of three qualities, bhikkhus, one is deposited in hell as if brought there. What three? One is immoral, and the stain of immorality is not abandoned in one; one is envious, and the stain of envy is not abandoned in one; one is miserly, and the stain of miserliness is not abandoned in one. Possessed of these three qualities, bhikkhus, one is deposited in hell as if brought there.
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, bhikkhus, in whatever place a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ This, bhikkhus, is the second thing in a bhikkhu that should be remembered as long as he lives.
translations.an3.15:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an3.15:2: “In the past, bhikkhus, there was a king named Sacetana. Then, bhikkhus, King Sacetana addressed the wheelwright: ‘Good wheelwright, in six months from now there will be a battle for me. Can you, good wheelwright, make a new pair of wheels for me?’ ‘I can, your majesty,’ the wheelwright replied to King Sacetana. Then, bhikkhus, the wheelwright completed one wheel in six months and six nights. Then, bhikkhus, King Sacetana addressed the wheelwright: ‘Good wheelwright, in six days from now there will be a battle for me, is the new pair of wheels completed?’ ‘This one wheel, your majesty, was completed in six months and six nights.’ ‘But can you, good wheelwright, complete a second wheel for me in these six days?’ ‘I can, your majesty,’ the wheelwright replied. Then, bhikkhus, the wheelwright completed the second wheel in six days. Taking the new pair of wheels, he approached King Sacetana; having approached, he said to King Sacetana: ‘This new pair of wheels is completed for you, your majesty.’ ‘What is the difference, good wheelwright, between this wheel completed in six months and six nights and this wheel completed in six days? I do not see any difference.’ ‘There is a difference, your majesty. Let your majesty see the difference.’
translations.an3.15:3: Then, bhikkhus, the wheelwright set rolling that wheel which was completed in six days. When set rolling, having gone as far as the impetus of the fabrication carried it, it curled around and fell to the ground. But that wheel which was completed in six months and six nights, when set rolling, having gone as far as the impetus of the fabrication carried it, stood as if fixed on an axle.
translations.an3.15:5: It might be, bhikkhus, that you think: ‘Surely that wheelwright was someone else at that time.’ This should not be seen thus, bhikkhus. I was that wheelwright at that time. At that time, bhikkhus, I was skilled in the bends, faults, and defects of wood. But now, bhikkhus, I am an arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, skilled in the bends, faults, and defects of the body, skilled in the bends, faults, and defects of speech, skilled in the bends, faults, and defects of the mind. Whatever monk or nun, bhikkhus, has not abandoned the bend of the body, the fault of the body, the defect of the body, has not abandoned the bend of speech, the fault of speech, the defect of speech, has not abandoned the bend of the mind, the fault of the mind, the defect of the mind—in this way, bhikkhus, they fall away from this Dhamma and Discipline, just like that wheel completed in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: Whatever monk or nun, bhikkhus, has abandoned the bend of the body, the fault of the body, the defect of the body, has abandoned the bend of speech, the fault of speech, the defect of speech, has abandoned the bend of the mind, the fault of the mind, the defect of the mind—in this way, bhikkhus, they are established in this Dhamma and Discipline, just like that wheel completed in six months and six nights.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is with fear, the wise one is without fear. The fool is with calamity, the wise one is without calamity. The fool is with disaster, the wise one is without disaster. There is no fear for the wise one, bhikkhus, there is no calamity for the wise one, there is no disaster for the wise one.
translations.an3.20:1: “Endowed with three factors, bhikkhus, a trader soon attains greatness and abundance in wealth. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a trader is both discerning and energetic and has good support. And how, bhikkhus, is a trader discerning? Here, bhikkhus, a trader knows a commodity: ‘This commodity, when bought in this way and sold in this way, will have this much cost, this much profit.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a trader is discerning.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a trader energetic? Here, bhikkhus, a trader is skilled in buying and selling commodities. Thus, bhikkhus, a trader is energetic.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, bhikkhus, does a trader have good support? Here, bhikkhus, whatever householders or householders' sons there are who are wealthy, of great wealth, of great possessions, they know of this trader: ‘This good trader is discerning and energetic and is capable of supporting wife and children and giving to us from time to time.’ They invest him with wealth: ‘From this, good trader, make wealth and support wife and children and give to us from time to time.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a trader has good support. Endowed with these three factors, bhikkhus, a trader soon attains greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: So too, bhikkhus, endowed with three qualities a bhikkhu soon attains greatness and abundance in wholesome states. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is both discerning and energetic and has good support. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu discerning? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is discerning.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu energetic? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the burden with regard to wholesome states. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is energetic.
translations.an3.22:1: “Three sick people, bhikkhus, are found existing in the world. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, one sick person, whether obtaining suitable food or not obtaining suitable food, whether obtaining suitable medicine or not obtaining suitable medicine, whether obtaining a suitable attendant or not obtaining a suitable attendant, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: But here, bhikkhus, one sick person, obtaining suitable food and not not obtaining, obtaining suitable medicine and not not obtaining, obtaining a suitable attendant and not not obtaining, recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: There, bhikkhus, the sick person who, obtaining suitable food and not not obtaining, obtaining suitable medicine and not not obtaining, obtaining a suitable attendant and not not obtaining, recovers from that illness—it is for the sake of this sick person, bhikkhus, that sick-person's food is allowed, sick-person's medicine is allowed, sick-person's attendant is allowed. And for the sake of this sick person, bhikkhus, other sick people should be attended to. These, bhikkhus, are the three sick people found existing in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: So too, bhikkhus, three persons similar to sick people are found existing in the world. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, one person, whether obtaining a sight of the Tathāgata or not obtaining a sight of the Tathāgata, whether obtaining hearing of the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining hearing of the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, does not enter the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
translations.an3.22:6: But here, bhikkhus, one person, whether obtaining a sight of the Tathāgata or not obtaining a sight of the Tathāgata, whether obtaining hearing of the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining hearing of the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, enters the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
translations.an3.24:1: “Three persons, bhikkhus, are very helpful to a person. Which three? That person, bhikkhus, in dependence on whom a person has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—this person, bhikkhus, is very helpful to this person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, that person in dependence on whom a person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this person, bhikkhus, is very helpful to this person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, that person in dependence on whom a person, with the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom—this person, bhikkhus, is very helpful to this person. These, bhikkhus, are the three persons who are very helpful to a person.
translations.an3.2:1: “Characterized by action, bhikkhus, is a fool; characterized by action, bhikkhus, is a wise person; wisdom is manifested by its fruits. Endowed with three qualities, bhikkhus, a fool is to be known. With which three? With bodily misconduct, with verbal misconduct, with mental misconduct. Endowed with these three qualities, bhikkhus, a fool is to be known.
translations.an3.2:2: Endowed with three qualities, bhikkhus, a wise person is to be known. With which three? With bodily good conduct, with verbal good conduct, with mental good conduct. Endowed with these three qualities, bhikkhus, a wise person is to be known.
translations.an3.30:4: A person of upside-down wisdom,  unwise, unintelligent;  Even if he goes often  to the presence of the bhikkhus.
translations.an3.30:5: The beginning, middle, and end  of a talk—such a one  Is unable to retain it,  for wisdom is not found in him.
translations.an3.30:6: A person of lap wisdom,  better than that one is said;  Even if he goes often  to the presence of the bhikkhus.
translations.an3.30:8: And a person of widespread wisdom,  better than these is said;  Even if he goes often  to the presence of the bhikkhus.
translations.an3.32:4: “Here, Ānanda, it occurs to a bhikkhu: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Thus, Ānanda, there might be for a bhikkhu such an attainment of concentration that in this conscious body there would be no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit, and externally in all signs there would be no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit; and whatever liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom he dwells in having attained, in which there is no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit, he would dwell in that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.
translations.an3.33:1: Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Sāriputta as he was sitting to one side: “Sāriputta, I could teach the Dhamma briefly; I could teach the Dhamma in detail; I could teach the Dhamma both briefly and in detail; but it is hard to find those who understand.” “It is the time, Blessed One, it is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma briefly, to teach the Dhamma in detail, to teach the Dhamma both briefly and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
translations.an3.33:2: “Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train thus: ‘In this conscious body there will be no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit, and externally in all signs there will be no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit, and whatever liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom one dwells in having attained, in which there is no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit, I will dwell in that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.’ Thus, Sāriputta, should you train.
translations.an3.33:3: But when, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu's I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit are no more in this conscious body, and externally in all signs his I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit are no more, and whatever liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom he dwells in having attained, in which there is no I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit, he dwells in that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom—this, Sāriputta, is called: ‘A bhikkhu has cut off craving, has untied the fetter, and by rightly understanding conceit has made an end of suffering.’ And this, Sāriputta, was said by me in reference to this in the Pārāyana in the Udaya Question:
translations.an3.33:4: ‘Abandoning sensual perceptions, and the dispelling of both kinds of sorrow; the elimination of sloth, and the warding off of remorse.
translations.an3.34:1: “Three, bhikkhus, are the origins for the arising of kamma. Which three? Greed is an origin for the arising of kamma, hatred is an origin for the arising of kamma, delusion is an origin for the arising of kamma.
translations.an3.34:10: Whatever kamma, bhikkhus, is born of non-delusion, originated by non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, arisen from non-delusion—when delusion is gone, that kamma is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
translations.an3.34:11: Just as, bhikkhus, seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, well-sown—suppose a man would burn them with fire, having burned them would make them into ashes, having made them into ashes would winnow them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by a swift-flowing river—thus, bhikkhus, those seeds would be cut off at the root, made like palm stumps, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. So too, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is born of non-greed, originated by non-greed, caused by non-greed, arisen from non-greed—when greed is gone, that kamma is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
translations.an3.34:13: Whatever kamma is born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion in one who is unwise; whether little or much, it is to be experienced right here, no other ground is found.
translations.an3.34:2: Whatever kamma, bhikkhus, is born of greed, originated by greed, caused by greed, arisen from greed—wherever his selfhood is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Where that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, either in this very life, or in rebirth, or in some subsequent way.
translations.an3.34:5: Just as, bhikkhus, seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, well-sown, planted in a good field, in well-prepared soil—suppose the rain god would send down proper showers—thus, bhikkhus, those seeds would come to growth, increase, and abundance. So too, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is born of greed, originated by greed, caused by greed, arisen from greed—wherever his selfhood is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Where that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, either in this very life, or in rebirth, or in some subsequent way.
translations.an3.34:6: Whatever kamma is born of hatred … and whatever kamma, bhikkhus, is born of delusion, originated by delusion, caused by delusion, arisen from delusion—wherever his selfhood is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Where that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, either in this very life, or in rebirth, or in some subsequent way. These, bhikkhus, are the three origins for the arising of kamma.
translations.an3.34:9: Whatever kamma, bhikkhus, is born of non-hatred, originated by non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, arisen from non-hatred—when hatred is gone, that kamma is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
translations.an3.35:3: “Well then, prince, I will ask you about this very thing. Answer as it seems proper to you. What do you think, prince, suppose there were a householder or a householder's son with a peaked house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows shuttered. There would be a couch there spread with a coverlet of wool—quilted, white, embroidered with flowers, spread with a splendid antelope hide, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends; an oil lamp would burn there; and four wives would attend upon him with pleasing and displeasing ways. What do you think, prince, would he sleep happily or not? How does this seem to you?” “He would sleep happily, venerable sir. Among those in the world who sleep happily, he would be one of them.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, prince, would that householder or householder's son be overcome by lust-born fevers, bodily or mental, by which, being burned by lust-born fevers, he would sleep in pain?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.an3.35:8: Always indeed he sleeps happily, the brahmin who is completely extinguished; who is not smeared by sensual pleasures, cooled, without acquisitions.
translations.an3.39:10: Thus dwelling, having known the Dhamma without acquisitions; in health and in youth, and in whatever intoxications with life.
translations.an3.39:2: I had, monks, three palaces—one for the cold season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season. I, monks, having spent the four months of the rainy season in the rainy season palace, being entertained by female musicians, did not descend to the lower palace. And just as, monks, in other households husked rice together with sour gruel is given to slaves, workers, and servants, so indeed, monks, in my father's household rice with meat curry was given to slaves, workers, and servants.
translations.an3.39:3: To me, monks, possessed of such power and with such refinement, this occurred: ‘An uninstructed ordinary person, himself subject to aging, not having gone beyond aging, on seeing another who is old, is repelled, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking himself, [thinking] “I too am subject to aging, not having gone beyond aging. If I, being subject to aging, not having gone beyond aging, on seeing another who is old, were to be repelled, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be proper for me.”’ To me, monks, thus reflecting, whatever intoxication with youth there was in youth, that was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:4: An uninstructed ordinary person, himself subject to sickness, not having gone beyond sickness, on seeing another who is sick, is repelled, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking himself: ‘I too am subject to sickness, not having gone beyond sickness. If I, being subject to sickness, not having gone beyond sickness, on seeing another who is sick, were to be repelled, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be proper for me.’ To me, monks, thus reflecting, whatever intoxication with health there was in health, that was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:5: An uninstructed ordinary person, himself subject to death, not having gone beyond death, on seeing another who has died, is repelled, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking himself: ‘I too am subject to death, not having gone beyond death. If I, being subject to death, not having gone beyond death, on seeing another who has died, were to be repelled, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be proper for me.’ To me, monks, thus reflecting, whatever intoxication with life there was in life, that was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:7: Intoxicated with youth, monks, a monk rejects the training and returns to the lower life. Intoxicated with health, monks, a monk … Intoxicated with life, monks, a monk rejects the training and returns to the lower life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to sickness, subject to aging, and also subject to death; being such by nature, ordinary people are disgusted.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted at that, at living beings of such a nature; that would not be proper for me, dwelling thus.
translations.an3.40:1: “There are, monks, these three governing principles. Which three? Self-governance, world-governance, Dhamma-governance. And what, monks, is self-governance? Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘It was not for the sake of robes that I went forth from the home life into homelessness. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodgings, not for the sake of becoming this or that, did I go forth from the home life into homelessness. But I am oppressed by birth, by aging, by death, by sorrows, by lamentations, by pains, by griefs, by despairs, oppressed by suffering, afflicted with suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’ If I, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in such a way, were to seek sensual pleasures of such a kind, or even worse than those, that would not be proper for me. He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused, unsluggish; mindfulness established, not lost; my body tranquil, not agitated; my mind concentrated, one-pointed.’ Having made himself the governing principle, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This is called, monks, self-governance.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, monks, is Dhamma-governance? Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘It was not for the sake of robes that I went forth from the home life into homelessness. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodgings, not for the sake of becoming this or that, did I go forth from the home life into homelessness. But I am oppressed by birth, by aging, by death, by sorrows, by lamentations, by pains, by griefs, by despairs, oppressed by suffering, afflicted with suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’ ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ There are my fellow celibates who dwell knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and discipline, were to dwell lazy, heedless, that would not be proper for me. He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused, unsluggish; mindfulness established, not lost; my body tranquil, not agitated; my mind concentrated, one-pointed.’ Having made the Dhamma the governing principle, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This is called, monks, Dhamma-governance. These, monks, are the three governing principles.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secrecy in the world for one doing evil deeds; you yourself know, man, whether it is true or false.
translations.an3.40:5: Good indeed, sir, is the witness who despises himself; who conceals evil within himself that exists.
translations.an3.40:6: Deities and Tathāgatas see the fool in the world acting crookedly; therefore one who is self-governed, world-governed, prudent, meditative; Dhamma-governed, living in accordance with the Dhamma, the sage with truth as his striving does not decline.
translations.an3.48:1: “Bhikkhus, relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, great sāl trees grow by three growths. By which three? They grow by branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow by bark and outer bark; they grow by sapwood and heartwood. Bhikkhus, relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, great sāl trees grow by these three growths.
translations.an3.48:2: So too, bhikkhus, relying on a faithful householder, the people inside grow by three growths. By which three? They grow by faith, they grow by virtue, they grow by wisdom. Bhikkhus, relying on a faithful householder, the people inside grow by these three growths.
translations.an3.48:3: Just as a rocky mountain  in a forest grove; Relying on that,  the trees of the forest grow.
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins, old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of life, a hundred and twenty years old by birth, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: “We, Master Gotama, are brahmins, old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of life, a hundred and twenty years old by birth; we have not done what is wholesome, we have not done what is skillful, we have not made a shelter from fear. Let Master Gotama advise us, let Master Gotama instruct us, for our long-term welfare and happiness.”
translations.an3.51:2: “Indeed, brahmins, you are old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of life, a hundred and twenty years old by birth; you have not done what is wholesome, you have not done what is skillful, you have not made a shelter from fear. This world, brahmins, is led on by aging, illness, and death. Thus led on by aging, illness, and death, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and the restraint of mind here—this becomes for the deceased a shelter, a cave, an island, a refuge, and a support.”
translations.an3.51:3: Life is led on, of little span;  For one led on by aging there are no shelters;  Seeing this danger in death,  One should do deeds that lead to happiness.
translations.an3.52:4: Thus the world is ablaze  with aging and death;  One should take out by giving,  what is given is well taken out.
translations.an3.57:2: “Vaccha, those who say: ‘The ascetic Gotama says: “A gift should be given only to me … not to other disciples; what is given to others is not of great fruit”’—they are not speaking what was said by me, but they misrepresent me with what is untrue and baseless. Vaccha, one who prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for three, is a hindrance for three. For which three? He creates an obstacle to the merit of the donor, he creates an obstacle to the gain of the recipients, and previously he himself is hurt and injured. Vaccha, one who prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for these three, is a hindrance for these three.
translations.an3.5:1: “Bhikkhus, one possessing three qualities should be known as a fool. Which three? He asks a question unskillfully, he answers a question unskillfully, and when another answers a question skillfully with well-rounded, well-phrased, polished, well-combined words, he does not approve of it. Bhikkhus, one possessing these three qualities should be known as a fool.
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Saṅgāravo approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Saṅgāravo said to the Blessed One: “We, Master Gotama, are brahmins by name. We sacrifice and cause others to sacrifice. There, Master Gotama, both one who sacrifices and one who causes others to sacrifice—all of them have entered upon a way of making merit that is of many bodies, namely, what is connected with sacrifice. But this one, Master Gotama, who has gone forth from some family or other from the household life into homelessness, tames only himself, calms only himself, makes only himself completely quenched—thus this one has entered upon a way of making merit that is of one body, namely, what is connected with going forth.”
translations.an3.60:10: Here, brahmin, one does not indicate by a sign, but having heard a sound of humans or non-humans or deities, he indicates: ‘Thus is your mind, thus is your mind, thus is your thought.’ Even if he indicates much, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: Here, brahmin, one does not indicate by a sign, nor having heard a sound of humans or non-humans or deities, but having heard the sound of the diffusion of thought of one thinking and examining, he indicates: ‘Thus is your mind, thus is your mind, thus is your thought.’ Even if he indicates much, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: Here, brahmin, one does not indicate by a sign, nor having heard a sound of humans or non-humans or deities, nor having heard the sound of the diffusion of thought of one thinking and examining, but having entered upon a concentration without thought and examination, he knows with mind encompassing mind: ‘As this good man’s mental formations are directed, immediately after this thought he will think such and such a thought.’ Even if he indicates much, it is exactly so, not otherwise. This, brahmin, is called the marvel of indication.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the marvel of instruction? Here, brahmin, one instructs thus: ‘Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, enter upon and dwell in this.’ This, brahmin, is called the marvel of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three marvels. Of these three marvels, brahmin, which marvel appeals to you as more excellent and more sublime?”
translations.an3.60:14: “There, Master Gotama, as to this marvel where one here experiences various kinds of supernormal power …pe… and exercises mastery with the body even as far as the brahmā world—this, Master Gotama, is a marvel where only one who does it experiences it, only one who does it has it. This marvel, Master Gotama, seems to me like a thing of the same nature as magic.”
translations.an3.60:16: But this, Master Gotama, is the wonder that someone here instructs thus: 'Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, and dwell having undertaken this.' This alone, Master Gotama, seems to me superior and more excellent than these three wonders.
translations.an3.60:17: It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous, Master Gotama. How well this has been said by Master Gotama! And we regard Master Gotama as endowed with these three wonders. For Master Gotama experiences various kinds of psychic power ... even as far as the Brahma world he wields bodily control. For Master Gotama, with his mind encompassed by the mind of one absorbed in concentration without thought and examination, understands: 'As this good person's mental formations are directed, immediately after this mind he will think such and such a thought.' For Master Gotama instructs thus: 'Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, and dwell having undertaken this.'
translations.an3.60:18: Surely I have spoken to you, brahmin, by way of question and approach; but nevertheless I will explain to you. For I, brahmin, experience various kinds of psychic power ... even as far as the Brahma world I wield bodily control. For I, brahmin, with my mind encompassed by the mind of one absorbed in concentration without thought and examination, understand: 'As this good person's mental formations are directed, immediately after this mind he will think such and such a thought.' For I, brahmin, instruct thus: 'Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, and dwell having undertaken this.'
translations.an3.60:19: But is there, Master Gotama, any single other monk also endowed with these three wonders, apart from Master Gotama? Not just one hundred, brahmin, not two hundred, not three hundred, not four hundred, not five hundred, but rather more, are the monks endowed with these three wonders. But where, Master Gotama, do those monks dwell now? In this very Sangha of monks, brahmin.
translations.an3.60:2: Well then, brahmin, I will ask you about this very thing. You should answer as seems proper to you. What do you think, brahmin? Here a Tathagata arises in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He speaks thus: 'Come, this is the path, this is the practice, by practicing which I have realized and made known the supreme consummation of the spiritual life; come, you too practice thus, and by practicing thus you too will realize and dwell having attained the supreme consummation of the spiritual life.' Thus this teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly, and these are not just one hundred, not one thousand, not one hundred thousand.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? If this is so, is this practice of merit one that bears fruit for one person or for many persons, that is, in connection with going forth? This too, Master Gotama, if it is so, is a practice of merit that bears fruit for many persons, that is, in connection with going forth.
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: Of these two practices, brahmin, which practice seems to you to be less demanding, less troublesome, with greater fruit and greater benefit? When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to Venerable Ānanda: Just as Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are, these are my venerables, these are my praiseworthy ones.
translations.an3.60:5: A second time Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: I do not ask you thus, brahmin: 'Who are your venerables, who are your praiseworthy ones?' Thus I ask you, brahmin: 'Of these two practices, brahmin, which practice seems to you to be less demanding, less troublesome, with greater fruit and greater benefit?' A second time the brahmin Saṅgārava said to Venerable Ānanda: Just as Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are, these are my venerables, these are my praiseworthy ones.
