translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: Even a third time the brahmin Saṅgārava, when asked a legitimate question by Ānanda, evades it and does not answer. What if I were to release him? Then the Blessed One said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: What, brahmin, was the conversation that arose today among the king's men assembled and sitting together in the royal palace? This, Master Gotama, was the conversation that arose today among the king's men assembled and sitting together in the royal palace: 'Formerly there were fewer monks who displayed psychic wonder of superhuman states, but now there are more monks who display psychic wonder of superhuman states.' This, Master Gotama, was the conversation that arose today among the king's men assembled and sitting together in the royal palace.
translations.an3.60:8: There are, brahmin, these three wonders. What three? The wonder of psychic power, the wonder of mind-reading, and the wonder of instruction. And what, brahmin, is the wonder of psychic power? Here, brahmin, someone experiences various kinds of psychic power: being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged he travels in space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes even the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; he wields bodily control even as far as the Brahma world. This, brahmin, is called the wonder of psychic power.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the marvel of mind-reading? Here, brahmin, someone reads signs thus: 'Thus is your mind, thus is your mind, such is your thought.' And though he reads much, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: 'These four noble truths,' monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins. Thus has this been said. And what is this said in reference to? Depending on the six elements, monks, there is the descent of the embryo; with the descent being, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling. For one who feels, monks, I declare this is suffering, I declare this is the origin of suffering, I declare this is the cessation of suffering, I declare this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, (...) death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering, association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: But when one returns to past deeds as the essence, monks, there is no desire or effort or 'this should be done, this should not be done.' Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and actually found, for those dwelling unmindful and unguarded, there is no personal consistent ascetic statement. This, monks, is my first consistent refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view.
translations.an3.61:8: These, monks, are the three standpoints of sectarians which, when examined, investigated, and discussed by the wise, even having gone to the extreme, settle on inaction.
translations.an3.61:9: But this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins? 'These six elements,' monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins. 'These six sense bases for contact,' monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins. 'These eighteen mental explorations,' monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins. 'These four noble truths,' monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, unstained, blameless, uncensured by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: "Three, monks, are the dangers in which mother and son do not find each other," says the uninstructed ordinary person. Which three? There comes a time, monks, when a great conflagration breaks out. When a great conflagration has broken out, villages are burned, towns are burned, cities are burned. When villages are being burned, towns are being burned, cities are being burned, there mother does not find son, son does not find mother. This, monks, is the first danger in which mother and son do not find each other, says the uninstructed ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:2: Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when a great storm breaks out. When a great storm has broken out, a great flood arises. When a great flood has arisen, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there mother does not find son, son does not find mother. This, monks, is the second danger in which mother and son do not find each other, says the uninstructed ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:3: Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when there is danger, an uprising in the wilderness, with the countryside overrun by the wheel [of an army]. When there is danger, an uprising in the wilderness, with the countryside overrun by the wheel, there mother does not find son, son does not find mother. This, monks, is the third danger in which mother and son do not find each other, says the uninstructed ordinary person. These, monks, are the three dangers in which mother and son do not find each other, says the uninstructed ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:4: But, bhikkhus, these three dangers are spoken of by the uninstructed ordinary person as dangers with mother and child, not dangers without mother and child. What three? There comes a time, bhikkhus, when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire has broken out, villages, towns, and cities burn. When villages, towns, and cities are burning, there comes a time when at some point a mother finds her child, and a child finds its mother. This, bhikkhus, is the first danger spoken of by the uninstructed ordinary person as a danger with mother and child, not a danger without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:5: Furthermore, bhikkhus, there comes a time when a great cloud bursts. When a great cloud has burst, a great flood arises. When a great flood has arisen, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. When villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there comes a time when at some point a mother finds her child, and a child finds its mother. This, bhikkhus, is the second danger spoken of by the uninstructed ordinary person as a danger with mother and child, not a danger without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:6: Furthermore, bhikkhus, there comes a time when there is danger, a disturbance in the forest, and the countryside is overrun by wheel-turning armies. When there is danger, a disturbance in the forest, and the countryside is being overrun by wheel-turning armies, there comes a time when at some point a mother finds her child, and a child finds its mother. This, bhikkhus, is the third danger spoken of by the uninstructed ordinary person as a danger with mother and child, not a danger without mother and child. These, bhikkhus, are the three dangers spoken of by the uninstructed ordinary person as dangers with mother and child, not dangers without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:7: There are, bhikkhus, these three dangers without mother and child. What three? The danger of aging, the danger of illness, the danger of death. A mother, bhikkhus, when her child is aging, does not obtain this: 'I am aging, may my child not age'; nor does a child when its mother is aging obtain this: 'I am aging, may my mother not age'.
translations.an3.62:8: A mother, bhikkhus, when her child is ill, does not obtain this: 'I am ill, may my child not be ill'; nor does a child when its mother is ill obtain this: 'I am ill, may my mother not be ill'.
translations.an3.62:9: A mother, bhikkhus, when her child is dying, does not obtain this: 'I am dying, may my child not die'; nor does a child when its mother is dying obtain this: 'I am dying, may my mother not die'. These, bhikkhus, are the three dangers without mother and child.
translations.an3.63:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Venāgapura. The brahmins and householders of Venāgapura heard: 'It is said that the ascetic Gotama, a Sakyan who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura. And regarding that good Gotama, such a good report has spread: 'Thus that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.' Having realized this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, he makes it known himself. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. It is good to see such arahants.'
translations.an3.63:11: It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous, Master Gotama. Who else but Master Gotama would obtain such a noble high and great bed so easily, without difficulty, without trouble?
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmins and householders of Venāgapura approached the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side, some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, having exchanged greetings and cordial talk, sat down to one side, some raised their joined palms in reverential salutation towards the Blessed One and sat down to one side, some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side, some sat down to one side in silence. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said to the Blessed One:
translations.an3.63:5: There are, brahmin, these three high and great beds that I now obtain easily, without difficulty, without trouble. What three? The divine high and great bed, the brahmā high and great bed, the noble high and great bed. These, brahmin, are the three high and great beds that I now obtain easily, without difficulty, without trouble.
translations.an4.10:10: Beings go wandering on through saṁsāra, going to birth and death; but those who completely understand sensual pleasures, and the bond to existence entirely.
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by the bond of sensual desire, and by the bond of existence as well; bound by the bond of views, led by ignorance.
translations.an4.18:1: Bhikkhus, there are these four non-deviations of course. What four? One does not deviate from course through desire, one does not deviate from course through hatred, one does not deviate from course through delusion, one does not deviate from course through fear—these, bhikkhus, are the four non-deviations of course.
translations.an4.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.1:4: Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation; These principles were understood, by the glorious Gotama.
translations.an4.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāketa in Kāḷaka's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this—
translations.an4.24:2: Whatever, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, and pondered over by the mind—that I know.
translations.an4.24:5: If, bhikkhus …pe… I were to say 'I both know and do not know this,' that too would be just the same.
translations.an4.24:7: Thus, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, having seen what is to be seen, does not conceive the seen, does not conceive the unseen, does not conceive what is to be seen, does not conceive a seer; having heard what is to be heard, does not conceive the heard, does not conceive the unheard, does not conceive what is to be heard, does not conceive a hearer; having sensed what is to be sensed, does not conceive the sensed, does not conceive the unsensed, does not conceive what is to be sensed, does not conceive a senser; having cognized what is to be cognized, does not conceive the cognized, does not conceive the uncognized, does not conceive what is to be cognized, does not conceive a cognizer. Thus, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, being such in regard to all things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, is such. 'And there is no other such one higher or more excellent than that such one,' I say.
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever has been seen, heard, or sensed, Clung to as truth by others; Among those who are self-ensnared, He is not such—would he call another true or false?
translations.an4.28:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages, primeval, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unmixed, and never before mixed, which are not mixed and will not be mixed, which are not repudiated by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe, and he does not engage in a wrong search, an improper search, for the sake of a robe; and if he does not get a robe, he does not become agitated; and if he gets a robe, he uses it without being attached to it, without being infatuated with it, without being bound to it, seeing the danger, understanding the escape; and because of this contentment with any kind of robe, he does not extol himself or disparage others. One who in this regard is skilled, energetic, clearly comprehending, and mindful, is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu established in the primeval, ancient noble lineage.
translations.an4.28:4: “Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu finds delight in development, is devoted to development, finds delight in abandoning, is devoted to abandoning; and because of this delight in development, devotion to development, delight in abandoning, and devotion to abandoning, he does not extol himself or disparage others. One who in this regard is skilled, energetic, clearly comprehending, and mindful, is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu established in the primeval, ancient noble lineage. These, bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages, primeval, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unmixed, and never before mixed, which are not mixed and will not be mixed, which are not repudiated by ascetics and brahmins who are wise.
translations.an4.28:5: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses these four noble lineages, whether he dwells in the eastern direction, he himself overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him; whether he dwells in the western direction, he himself overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him; whether he dwells in the northern direction, he himself overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him; whether he dwells in the southern direction, he himself overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him. For what reason? Because the wise one is a victor over discontent and contentment.
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent does not overcome the wise one, Discontent does not overcome the wise one; The wise one overcomes discontent, For the wise one is a victor over discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels. When possessed by devas and humans, the four-wheeled vehicle rolls on; when possessed, devas and humans soon attain greatness and abundance in wealth. What four? Living in a suitable region, association with good people, right aspiration, and previously done merit—these, bhikkhus, are the four wheels. When possessed by devas and humans, the four-wheeled vehicle rolls on; when possessed, devas and humans soon attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an4.32:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of sympathy. What four? Giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and equality—these, bhikkhus, are the four bases of sympathy.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kind speech, Beneficial conduct here, And equality in matters of Dhamma, In each case as appropriate; These are the bases of sympathy in the world, Like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If these bases of sympathy did not exist, Neither would a mother for the sake of her son Obtain regard or honor, Nor would a father for the sake of his son.
translations.an4.33:1: “Bhikkhus, the lion, king of beasts, emerges from his lair in the evening. Having emerged from his lair, he stretches himself. Having stretched himself, he surveys the four quarters all around. Having surveyed the four quarters all around, he roars a lion's roar three times. Having roared a lion's roar three times, he goes out for the hunt. Now, bhikkhus, when those animals of the animal realm hear the sound of the lion, king of beasts, roaring, for the most part they experience fear, agitation, and terror. Those in holes enter their holes, those in water enter their water, those in forests enter their forests, and birds take to the sky. And those royal elephants that are bound with strong bonds in villages, towns, and capitals, they too, having cut and burst those bonds, frightened, abandoning their dung, flee here and there. So powerful, bhikkhus, is the lion, king of beasts, over the animals of the animal realm, so majestic, so mighty.
translations.an4.33:2: “So too, bhikkhus, when the Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One, he teaches the Dhamma: 'Such is identity, such is the origin of identity, such is the cessation of identity, such is the way leading to the cessation of identity.' Now, bhikkhus, when those devas of long life, beautiful, abounding in happiness, dwelling for a long time in lofty palaces, hear the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part they experience fear, agitation, and terror: 'Alas, sirs, it seems we are impermanent, though we thought ourselves permanent; alas, sirs, it seems we are unstable, though we thought ourselves stable; alas, sirs, it seems we are not eternal, though we thought ourselves eternal. Alas, sirs, it seems we are impermanent, unstable, not eternal, included in identity.' So powerful, bhikkhus, is the Tathāgata over the world with its devas, so majestic, so mighty.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, by direct knowledge, Set rolling the Dhamma wheel, For the world with its devas, The Teacher without rival.
translations.an4.33:4: Identity and its cessation, And the origin of identity; And the noble eightfold path, Going to the stilling of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “There are these four, monks, kinds of supreme confidence. What four? As far as, monks, beings are concerned—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, with form or formless, percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared supreme among them, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Those, monks, who are confident in the Buddha are confident in the supreme. For those confident in the supreme, the supreme result comes to be.
translations.an4.34:2: As far as, monks, conditioned things are concerned, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared supreme among them. Those, monks, who are confident in the Noble Eightfold Path are confident in the supreme. For those confident in the supreme, the supreme result comes to be.
translations.an4.34:3: As far as, monks, conditioned or unconditioned things are concerned, dispassion is declared supreme among them—that is to say, the subduing of intoxication, the elimination of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those, monks, who are confident in the state of dispassion are confident in the supreme. For those confident in the supreme, the supreme result comes to be.
translations.an4.34:4: As far as, monks, communities or groups are concerned, the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared supreme among them—that is to say, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This community of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those, monks, who are confident in the Sangha are confident in the supreme. For those confident in the supreme, the supreme result comes to be. These, monks, are the four kinds of supreme confidence.
translations.an4.34:5: Confident in the supreme, having known the supreme Dhamma, confident in the supreme Buddha, unsurpassed, worthy of gifts.
translations.an4.34:6: Confident in the supreme Dhamma, in the bliss of dispassion, confident in the supreme Sangha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:7: Giving gifts to the supreme, supreme merit increases; supreme life, beauty, glory, fame, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.35:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Vassakāra the brahmin, the minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “By means of four things, Master Gotama, we declare a great man to be of great wisdom. By which four? Here, Master Gotama, he is learned, and he knows the meaning of whatever statements are made: ‘This is the meaning of this statement, this is the meaning of this statement.’ He is mindful, able to remember and recollect what was done and said long ago. And whatever household tasks there are to be done, he is skilled in them, not lazy, endowed with the appropriate means of investigation, able to carry out and arrange them. By these four things, Master Gotama, we declare a great man to be of great wisdom. If Master Gotama approves of me, let Master Gotama approve; if he should reject me, let Master Gotama reject me.”
translations.an4.35:6: He who knows the escape from death for all beings, what is beneficial for gods and humans, and teaches the true Dhamma; seeing and hearing which, many people become confident.
translations.an4.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the highway between Ukkatthā and Setabya. Doṇa the brahmin too was traveling along the highway between Ukkatthā and Setabya. Doṇa the brahmin saw on the Blessed One’s feet wheels with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in all respects; seeing this, he thought: “It is wonderful, it is marvelous! Surely these cannot be the feet of a human being.” Then the Blessed One left the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body upright, and established mindfulness in front of him. Then Doṇa the brahmin, following the Blessed One’s footprints, saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree—confident, inspiring confidence, with senses calmed, mind calmed, having attained the supreme taming and tranquility, tamed, guarded, with restrained senses, a nāga. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.36:2: “Will the venerable one become a god?” “I will not become a god, brahmin.” “Will the venerable one become a gandhabba?” “I will not become a gandhabba, brahmin.” “Will the venerable one become a yakkha?” “I will not become a yakkha, brahmin.” “Will the venerable one become a human being?” “I will not become a human being, brahmin.”
translations.an4.36:4: “Those taints, brahmin, by whose non-abandonment I would become a god—those taints have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, unable to arise again in the future. Those taints, brahmin, by whose non-abandonment I would become a gandhabba … a yakkha … a human being—those taints have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, unable to arise again in the future. Just as, brahmin, a blue lotus, red lotus, or white lotus, born in water, grown up in water, stands above the water untouched by water; so too, brahmin, though born in the world, grown up in the world, I dwell having overcome the world, untouched by the world. Know me, brahmin, as the Buddha.”
translations.an4.37:1: “Possessing four qualities, monks, a monk is incapable of decline, he is in the vicinity of Nibbāna. With what four? Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, guarded as to the doors of the senses, moderate in eating, and devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how, monks, is a monk accomplished in virtue? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, complete in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking the training rules. Thus, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue.
translations.an4.37:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu guarded as to the doors of the sense faculties? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp at its sign or its details. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade him, he practises for its restraint; he guards the eye faculty; he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear … Having smelled an odour with the nose … Having tasted a flavour with the tongue … Having touched a tangible with the body … Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its sign or its details. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade him, he practises for its restraint; he guards the mind faculty; he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is guarded as to the doors of the sense faculties.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu moderate in eating? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reflects wisely when taking food: 'Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for embellishment; but just enough for the maintenance of this body, for its sustenance, for avoiding harm, and for supporting the spiritual life. Thus I shall put an end to old feelings and not arouse new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live at ease.' It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking and sitting during the day; in the first watch of the night he purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking and sitting; in the middle watch of the night he lies down on the right side in the lion's posture, one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, with the perception of getting up; in the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking and sitting. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness. Possessed of these four qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is incapable of decline and is in the vicinity of Nibbāna.
translations.an4.37:6: Established in virtue, a bhikkhu, guarded as to the sense faculties; Moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Thus dwelling ardent, unwearying by day and night; Developing wholesome states, for the attainment of security from bondage.
translations.an4.38:1: “One who has shaken off individual dogmas, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is called 'one whose search is allayed, whose bodily formations are tranquil, one who has withdrawn.' And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has shaken off individual dogmas? Here, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu whatever individual dogmas there are of various ascetics and brahmins, such as: 'The world is eternal' or 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world is finite' or 'The world is infinite,' 'The soul is the same as the body' or 'The soul is one thing and the body another,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death' or 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—all these are shaken off, well shaken off, cut off, vomited up, released, abandoned, and relinquished. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has shaken off individual dogmas.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has withdrawn? Here, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu the conceit 'I am' has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has withdrawn. One who has shaken off individual dogmas, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is called 'one whose search is allayed, whose bodily formations are tranquil, one who has withdrawn.'
translations.an4.38:5: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, together with the search for the spiritual life; Thus clinging to dogmas, speculative views and obsessions.
translations.an4.38:6: For one detached from all passion, liberated by the destruction of craving; The search is relinquished, speculative views are eradicated.
translations.an4.52:1: “These four, bhikkhus, are streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, pleasant. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is possessed of confirmed confidence in the Buddha: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: the Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.' This, bhikkhus, is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, pleasant.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is possessed of confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.' This, bhikkhus, is the second stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, pleasant.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is possessed of confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practising the good way, practising the straight way, practising the true way, practising the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' This, bhikkhus, is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, pleasant.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is possessed of virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, pleasant. These, bhikkhus, are the four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, pleasant.
translations.an4.52:5: One whose confidence in the Tathāgata is unshaken and well established; Whose virtue is excellent, dear to the noble ones and praised.
translations.an4.52:6: Whoever has faith in the Sangha, and upright vision; They are called 'not poor', their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: At one time the Blessed One was traveling on the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Many householders and housewives were also traveling on the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Blessed One stepped off the road and sat down at the root of a certain tree. The householders and housewives saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of a certain tree. Seeing him, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said this to those householders and housewives sitting to one side:
translations.an4.53:10: Both are faithful and generous, restrained and living by the Dhamma; They are a wife and husband who speak lovingly to each other.
translations.an4.53:11: Their wealth is abundant, comfort arises; Enemies are displeased, for both are of equal virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: Householders, there are these four kinds of living together. What four? A wretch lives together with a wretch, a wretch lives together with a goddess, a god lives together with a wretch, a god lives together with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a wretch live together with a wretch? Here, householders, the husband is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, a sexual wrongdoer, a speaker of falsehood, a drinker of liquor, wine, and intoxicants causing heedlessness, immoral, of bad character, living at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of miserliness, abusive and insulting to ascetics and brahmins; and his wife is also a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, a sexual wrongdoer, a speaker of falsehood, a drinker of liquor, wine, and intoxicants causing heedlessness, immoral, of bad character, living at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of miserliness, abusive and insulting to ascetics and brahmins. Thus, householders, a wretch lives together with a wretch.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is immoral, miserly and abusive; The wife is virtuous, generous and free from miserliness; She, a goddess, lives together with a wretch of a husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, generous and free from miserliness; The wife is immoral, miserly and abusive; She, a wretch, lives together with a god of a husband.
translations.an4.5:1: Monks, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world. What four? The person going with the stream, the person going against the stream, the person standing firm, and the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, who stands on dry ground, a brahmin. And what, monks, is the person going with the stream? Here, monks, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and does evil deeds. This is called, monks, the person going with the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, monks, is the person going against the stream? Here, monks, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not do evil deeds, and with pain, with grief, with tearful face, weeping, he lives the complete and pure spiritual life. This is called, monks, the person going against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, monks, is the person standing firm? Here, monks, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes one who attains final Nibbāna spontaneously, not liable to return from that world. This is called, monks, the person standing firm.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, monks, is the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, who stands on dry ground, a brahmin? Here, monks, a certain person, with the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it. This is called, monks, the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, who stands on dry ground, a brahmin. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.
translations.an4.5:5: Whatever people here are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, Not free from lust, enjoying sensual pleasures here; Again and again they go to birth and aging, Obsessed by craving, going with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore let the wise one here be established in mindfulness, Not indulging in sensual pleasures and evil; Even with pain let him abandon sensual pleasures, They call him the person going against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: Whoever has abandoned the five defilements, A fulfilled trainee, not liable to decline; Master of mind, with faculties concentrated, That man is called one standing firm.
translations.an4.62:2: Householder, these four kinds of happiness are to be attained by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures from time to time, on occasion, depending on the occasion. What four? The happiness of having, the happiness of wealth, the happiness of being debtless, the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of having? Here, householder, a clansman has wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. He thinks 'I have wealth acquired by energetic striving' and attains happiness, attains joy. This is called, householder, the happiness of having.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of being debtless? Here, householder, a clansman owes nothing to anyone, whether small or great. He thinks 'I owe nothing to anyone, whether small or great' and attains happiness, attains joy. This is called, householder, the happiness of being debtless.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is possessed of blameless bodily action, possessed of blameless verbal action, possessed of blameless mental action. He thinks 'I am possessed of blameless bodily action, possessed of blameless verbal action, possessed of blameless mental action' and attains happiness, attains joy. This is called, householder, the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness to be attained by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures from time to time, on occasion, depending on the occasion.
translations.an4.62:7: Having known the happiness of being debtless, And the supreme happiness of having; A mortal enjoying the happiness of wealth, From that he sees with wisdom.
translations.an5.23:1: "Monks, there are these five impurities of gold, by which impurities gold when impure is neither soft nor workable nor radiant nor brittle nor properly fit for work. Which five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, zinc— these, monks, are the five impurities of gold, by which impurities gold when impure is neither soft nor workable nor radiant nor brittle nor properly fit for work. But when, monks, gold is freed from these five impurities, that gold is soft and workable and radiant and not brittle, properly fit for work. Whatever kind of ornament one wishes— whether a ring, or earrings, or a necklace, or a golden garland— it serves that purpose for him.
translations.an5.23:2: So too, monks, there are these five impurities of the mind, by which impurities the mind when impure is neither soft nor workable nor radiant nor brittle nor properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. Which five? Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt— these, monks, are the five impurities of the mind, by which impurities the mind when impure is neither soft nor workable nor radiant nor brittle nor properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But when, monks, the mind is freed from these five impurities, that mind is soft and workable and radiant and not brittle, properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. Whatever state realizable by higher knowledge he directs his mind toward for the purpose of realizing by higher knowledge, he becomes capable of realizing it there and then, if the basis is there.
translations.an5.23:3: If he should wish: 'May I wield the various kinds of psychic potency— having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; may I travel through the sky while sitting cross-legged like a bird with wings; may I touch and stroke with my hand the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; may I wield bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma world,' he becomes capable of realizing it there and then, if the basis is there.
translations.an5.23:4: If he should wish: 'With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, may I hear both kinds of sounds— divine and human, whether far or near,' he becomes capable of realizing it there and then, if the basis is there.
translations.an5.23:5: If he should wish: 'May I understand the minds of other beings and persons, having encompassed them with my own mind— may I know a mind with lust as a mind with lust; may I know a mind without lust as a mind without lust; may I know a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; may I know a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; may I know a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; may I know a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; may I know a contracted mind as a contracted mind; may I know a distracted mind as a distracted mind; may I know an exalted mind as an exalted mind; may I know an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; may I know a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; may I know an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; may I know a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; may I know an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; may I know a liberated mind as a liberated mind; may I know an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,' he becomes capable of realizing it there and then, if the basis is there.
translations.an5.25:1: "Monks, right view assisted by five factors has liberation of mind as its fruit and benefit, and liberation by wisdom as its fruit and benefit.
translations.an5.26:1: "Monks, there are these five bases of liberation, where a monk who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute— his unliberated mind becomes liberated, or his unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that he had not attained.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, monks, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a monk, nor does another fellow monk in a position of respect, but he teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it, as he has learned it. In whatever way, monks, a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it, as he has learned it, in just that way he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy is born. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body feels pleasure. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the second basis of liberation, where a monk who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute— his unliberated mind becomes liberated, or his unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, monks, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a monk, nor does another fellow monk in a position of respect, nor does he teach the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it, as he has learned it, but he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it, as he has learned it. In whatever way, monks, a monk recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it, as he has learned it, in just that way he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy is born. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body feels pleasure. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the third basis of liberation, where a monk who dwells heedful, ardent ... he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, monks, for a monk, neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma, nor does a respected fellow monastic, nor does he teach others the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it, nor does he recite the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it, nor does he think over and ponder the Dhamma as he has heard and learned it, examining it with his mind; but rather, he has well grasped, well attended to, well retained, and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom a certain meditation sign. In whatever way, monks, a monk has well grasped, well attended to, well retained, and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom a certain meditation sign, in just that way he experiences the meaning in that Dhamma and experiences the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the fifth liberation ground where, for a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, either the unreleased mind is released, or the unexhausted defilements go to exhaustion, or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that was not attained.
translations.an5.27:1: Develop concentration, monks, measureless, prudent, mindful. For monks developing measureless concentration, prudent, mindful, five knowledges arise personally for them. Which five? 'This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future'—knowledge arises personally for them; 'this concentration is noble and undefiled'—knowledge arises personally for them; 'this concentration is not practiced by inferior persons'—knowledge arises personally for them; 'this concentration is peaceful, sublime, acquired through stillness, attained to singleness, not held in place by forceful suppression'—knowledge arises personally for them; 'mindful indeed I enter this attainment and mindful I emerge from it'—knowledge arises personally for them.
translations.an5.28:1: Monks, I will teach the development of the noble five-factored right concentration. Listen to that, attend well to it, I will speak.
translations.an5.28:10: Just as, monks, a thoroughbred horse standing on level ground at a crossroads, harnessed and with the whip hanging down—then a skilled trainer, a horse-tamer, having mounted it, taking the reins with his left hand and the whip with his right hand, could drive it wherever he wished, bring it back wherever he wished—so too, monks, for a monk who has thus developed and frequently practiced the noble five-factored right concentration, wherever he directs his mind for the realization by higher knowledge of any state realizable by higher knowledge, he becomes capable of realizing it there, when the basis is present.
translations.an5.28:15: If he should wish: 'May I know the passing away and rebirth of beings with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human'... he becomes capable of realizing it there, when the basis is present.
translations.an5.28:7: When, monks, a monk has thus developed and frequently practiced the noble five-factored right concentration, wherever he directs his mind for the realization by higher knowledge of any state realizable by higher knowledge, he becomes capable of realizing it there, when the basis is present.
translations.an5.28:8: Just as, monks, a water jar placed on a stand, full of water to the brim so that a crow could drink from it—then if a strong man were to tip it from wherever, would water come out?
translations.an5.28:9: Just as, monks, on level ground there is a square lotus pond with embankments, full of water to the brim so that a crow could drink from it—then if a strong man were to open the embankment from wherever, would water come out?
translations.an5.2:1: Monks, there are these five powers of a trainee. Which five? The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple is faithful, he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, awakened, blessed.' This, monks, is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, monks, is the power of moral shame? Here, monks, a noble disciple has a sense of shame; he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct; he is ashamed of the attainment of evil, unwholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of moral shame.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, monks, is the power of moral dread? Here, monks, a noble disciple is morally dread; he dreads bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct; he dreads the attainment of evil, unwholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of moral dread.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the burden in regard to wholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses wisdom directed to arising and passing away, noble, penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of a trainee.
translations.an5.30:1: So have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large community of monks and arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala. There the Blessed One dwelt in Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: "The ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is dwelling in Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. Such good report has been spread about that venerable Gotama: 'He is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.' Having realized by his own direct knowledge this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, he makes it known to others. He teaches the Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. It is good to see such arahants." Then, when the night had passed, the brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala, taking abundant food of various kinds, went to the Icchānaṅgala forest grove; having approached, they stood outside the gate, making a loud noise, a great noise.
translations.an5.30:3: "Now let the Blessed One consent, let the Fortunate One consent; now is the time for the Blessed One's consent. Wherever the Blessed One will go now, the brahmins and householders of town and country will incline in that same direction. Just as, sir, when thick drops of rain are falling, the waters flow in accordance with the slope, so too, sir, wherever the Blessed One will go now, the brahmins and householders of town and country will incline in that same direction. Why is that? Because of the Blessed One's virtue and wisdom."
translations.an5.31:1: At one time ... at Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Princess Sumanā said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: So too one accomplished in virtue, a faithful person, surpasses all the stingy people in the world by generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud, thundering, garlanded with lightning, with a hundred peaks, fills the high ground and the low, raining down upon the earth,
translations.an5.31:12: so one accomplished in view, a disciple of the perfectly enlightened one, the wise one surpasses the stingy one in five respects.
translations.an5.31:2: "Here, sir, there might be two disciples of the Blessed One equal in faith, equal in virtue, equal in wisdom—one a giver, one a non-giver. With the breakup of the body, after death, they would be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. But would there be any difference, any distinction between them, sir, when they have become devas?"
translations.an5.31:3: "There would be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said. "That giver, Sumanā, when he has become a deva, surpasses that non-giver in five respects: by divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine glory, and divine authority. That giver, Sumanā, when he has become a deva, surpasses that non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:4: "But if they pass away from there and return to this state of being, would there be any difference, any distinction between them, sir, when they have become human?" "There would be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said. "That giver, Sumanā, when he has become a human, surpasses that non-giver in five respects: by human lifespan, human beauty, human happiness, human glory, and human authority. That giver, Sumanā, when he has become a human, surpasses that non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:5: "But if they both go forth from the household life into homelessness, would there be any difference, any distinction between them, sir, when they have gone forth?" "There would be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said. "That giver, Sumanā, when he has gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in five respects: he mostly uses robes that have been requested, not without request; he mostly uses almsfood that has been requested, not without request; he mostly uses lodgings that have been requested, not without request; he mostly uses medicines and provisions for the sick that have been requested, not without request. And whatever fellow celibates he lives with, they mostly treat him with agreeable bodily conduct, not disagreeable; with agreeable verbal conduct, not disagreeable; with agreeable mental conduct, not disagreeable; and they mostly offer him agreeable things, not disagreeable. That giver, Sumanā, when he has gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:6: "But if they both attain arahantship, would there be any difference, any distinction between them, sir, when they have attained arahantship?" "Here, Sumanā, I do not declare any distinction, that is, in liberation."
translations.an5.31:9: Just as the stainless moon, moving in the sphere of space, surpasses all the hosts of stars in the world by its radiance,
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Mahāvana in the hall with the peaked roof. Then General Sīha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, General Sīha said this to the Blessed One: "Is it possible, sir, for the Blessed One to teach a visible fruit of giving?"
translations.an5.34:2: "It is possible, Sīha," the Blessed One said. "A giver, a donor, Sīha, is dear and agreeable to many people. And that a giver, a donor, is dear and agreeable to many people—this too is a visible fruit of giving.
translations.an5.34:8: The giver is dear, many associate with him; he gains fame and his glory increases; unbewildered, he enters the assembly; the man without stinginess becomes confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore the wise, seeking happiness, dispelling the stain of stinginess, give gifts; they, established long in heaven, having gone to companionship with the devas, delight.
translations.an5.36:1: "Five, monks, are timely gifts. Which five? One gives a gift to a guest; one gives a gift to one setting out on a journey; one gives a gift to a sick person; one gives a gift in a time of famine; one presents first to the virtuous whatever new crops and new fruits there are. These, monks, are the five timely gifts."
translations.an5.36:2: The wise give in time, generous, free from stinginess; given in time to the noble, to the upright, to such as these.
translations.an5.36:3: Purified in mind, his offering is abundant; those who rejoice there, or render service, by that the offering is not diminished—they too are sharers in merit.
translations.an5.37:1: "Food, monks, when given, the giver gives five things to the recipients. Which five? He gives life, he gives beauty, he gives happiness, he gives strength, he gives eloquence. Having given life, he becomes a sharer in life, whether divine or human; having given beauty, he becomes a sharer in beauty, whether divine or human; having given happiness, he becomes a sharer in happiness, whether divine or human; having given strength, he becomes a sharer in strength, whether divine or human; having given eloquence, he becomes a sharer in eloquence, whether divine or human. Food, monks, when given, the giver gives these five things to the recipients."
translations.an5.37:2: The wise one gives life, gives strength, gives beauty, gives eloquence; the intelligent one gives happiness, he attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Just as, monks, a great banyan tree on good ground at a crossroads is a refuge for birds all around; so too, monks, a faithful clansman is a refuge for many people—monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers.
translations.an5.38:3: With branches, leaves, and fruits, firm, a great tree; rooted, endowed with fruit, it is a support for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In a delightful, spacious place, birds resort to it; those seeking shade go to the shade, those seeking fruit to the fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: So too the virtuous, faithful person, of gentle conduct, not arrogant, kind, gentle.
translations.an5.38:6: Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, taintless; fields of merit in the world, they resort to such a person.
translations.an5.41:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika as he was sitting to one side: "Five, householder, are the uses of wealth. Which five? Here, householder, a noble disciple with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, righteously obtained, righteously acquired, makes himself happy, contented, and properly maintains his happiness; he makes his mother and father happy, contented, and properly maintains their happiness; he makes his children, wife, slaves, servants, and workers happy, contented, and properly maintains their happiness. This is the first use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, righteously obtained, righteously acquired, performs the five oblations: the oblation to relatives, the oblation to guests, the oblation to ancestors, the oblation to the king, and the oblation to deities—this is the fourth use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, righteously obtained, righteously acquired, presents to those ascetics and brahmins who are free from intoxication and heedlessness, who have established themselves in patience and gentleness, who tame themselves, calm themselves, and completely liberate themselves—presents to such ascetics and brahmins an elevated offering, one with heavenly result, with happy fruit, leading to heaven. This is the fifth use of wealth. These, householder, are the five uses of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, a noble disciple uses these five uses of wealth and his wealth comes to depletion, he thinks thus: 'I have used the uses of wealth, and my wealth has come to depletion.' Thus he has no remorse. If, householder, a noble disciple uses these five uses of wealth and his wealth increases, he thinks thus: 'I have used the uses of wealth, and my wealth has increased.' Thus he has no remorse in both respects.
translations.an5.41:7: Wealth has been enjoyed, dependents supported, adversities overcome; elevated offerings given, and the five oblations performed; virtuous ones attended upon, restrained spiritual practitioners.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever purpose one might wish for wealth, dwelling at home; that purpose of mine has been achieved, done without regret.
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika as he was sitting to one side:
translations.an5.43:4: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires life to pray for life or to rejoice in life for that reason. For one desiring life, householder, a noble disciple should practice the way leading to life. Practicing the way leading to life, it leads to the acquisition of life. He becomes an obtainer of life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires beauty to pray for beauty or to rejoice in beauty for that reason. For one desiring beauty, householder, a noble disciple should practice the way leading to beauty. Practicing the way leading to beauty, it leads to the acquisition of beauty. He becomes an obtainer of beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires happiness to pray for happiness or to rejoice in happiness for that reason. For one desiring happiness, householder, a noble disciple should practice the way leading to happiness. Practicing the way leading to happiness, it leads to the acquisition of happiness. He becomes an obtainer of happiness, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:7: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires fame to ask for fame or to rejoice in fame or for the sake of fame.  For a noble disciple who desires fame, householder, a practice conducive to fame should be followed.  For him, having followed a practice conducive to fame, it leads to the acquisition of fame.  He becomes one who obtains fame, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Long life, beauty, fame, glory,  Heaven, high birth;  Desiring pleasures,  Superior ones again and again.
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.  Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallikā had died.  Then a certain man went to King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he announced in the king's ear:  "Queen Mallikā, Your Majesty, has died."  When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala sat down miserable, sorrowful, with shoulders drooping, face down, brooding, speechless.
translations.an5.51:3: It is impossible, monks, that a monk, without abandoning these five obstructions, hindrances that overwhelm the mind and weaken wisdom, with weak and feeble wisdom, would know his own good, or know another's good, or know both goods, or realize the superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.  Just as, monks, a mountain river flowing far, with swift current, carrying away all, if a man were to open the outlets on both sides with a plow—thus, monks, the current in the middle of the river would be scattered, dispersed, split apart, and would not flow far, nor swiftly, nor carry away all.  So too, monks, it is impossible that a monk, without abandoning these five obstructions, hindrances that overwhelm the mind and weaken wisdom, with weak and feeble wisdom, would know his own good, or know another's good, or know both goods, or realize the superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain monk went to his own preceptor; having approached, he said this to his own preceptor:  "Just now, venerable sir, my body is as if drugged, the directions are not clear to me, the Dhamma does not occur to me, sloth and torpor overwhelm my mind, I live the spiritual life dissatisfied, and I have doubt about the Dhamma."
translations.an5.56:3: "It is thus, monk, for one who is not guarded in the sense doors, who is not moderate in eating, who is not devoted to wakefulness, who does not reflect on the wholesome states, who does not dwell devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment in the first and last watches of the night, that his body becomes as if drugged, the directions are not clear to him, the Dhamma does not occur to him, sloth and torpor overwhelm his mind, he lives the spiritual life dissatisfied, and he has doubt about the Dhamma.  Therefore, monk, you should train thus:  'I will be guarded in the sense doors, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, reflecting on the wholesome states, I will dwell devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment in the first and last watches of the night.'  Thus, monk, should you train."
translations.an5.56:4: Then that monk, exhorted by the Blessed One with this exhortation, rising from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and departed.  Then that monk, dwelling alone, diligent, ardent, and resolute, not long after—realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed goal of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt in it.  He understood:  "Destroyed is birth, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being."  And that monk became one of the arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: 'It is not only for me that there is alteration and separation from all that is dear and agreeable, but for all beings wherever they come and go, pass away and reappear, there is alteration and separation from all that is dear and agreeable.'  For him, frequently reviewing this, the path is born.  He pursues that path, develops it, and makes it much.  For him, pursuing, developing, and making much that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.57:11: 'I am not the only one who is the owner of actions, heir to actions, born of actions, related through actions, and have actions as refuge; whatever action I shall do—good or evil—I shall be its heir; but all beings wherever they come and go, pass away and reappear, are owners of actions, heirs to actions, born of actions, related through actions, and have actions as refuge; whatever action they shall do—good or evil—they shall be its heir.'  For him, frequently reviewing this, the path is born.  He pursues that path, develops it, and makes it much.  For him, pursuing, developing, and making much that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all intoxication,  Having seen renunciation as secure;  There arose in me energy,  Seeing Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: Then that noble disciple, monks, reflects thus:  'I am not the only one who is subject to aging, not gone beyond aging, but all beings wherever they come and go, pass away and reappear, are subject to aging, not gone beyond aging.'  For him, frequently reviewing this, the path is born.  He pursues that path, develops it, and makes it much.  For him, pursuing, developing, and making much that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.57:8: 'I am not the only one who is subject to illness, not gone beyond illness, but all beings wherever they come and go, pass away and reappear, are subject to illness, not gone beyond illness.'  For him, frequently reviewing this, the path is born.  He pursues that path, develops it, and makes it much.  For him, pursuing, developing, and making much that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an8.13:1: “Monks, endowed with eight qualities, a king's excellent thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, fit for royal use, and is reckoned as a factor of kingship. What eight? Here, monks, a king's excellent thoroughbred horse is well-born on both sides— from the mother's side and from the father's side. It is born in the region where other excellent thoroughbred horses are born. Whatever food is given to it— wet or dry— it eats it carefully without scattering it. It is disgusted at sitting or lying down in urine or feces. It is gentle, pleasant to associate with, and does not agitate other horses. Whatever deceitfulness, craftiness, crookedness, or deviousness it has, it reveals these to the charioteer as they really are, so that the charioteer strives to train them out of it. It is a puller. 'Let these horses pull or not, I will pull here'— it arouses this thought. And when going, it goes by the straight path. It is strong and shows its strength right up to the end of life and death. Monks, endowed with these eight qualities, a king's excellent thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, fit for royal use, and is reckoned as a factor of kingship.
translations.an8.14:1: “Monks, I will teach eight horse-faults and eight horse-defects, eight person-faults and eight person-defects. Listen to this, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.14:2: “And what, monks, are the eight horse-faults and eight horse-defects? Here, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, retreats backward and turns the chariot around from behind. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the first horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, rears up backward, strikes the chariot-pole, and breaks the triple rod. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the second horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, lowering its thigh onto the chariot-rail, crushes the chariot-rail itself. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the third horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, takes a wrong turn and overturns the chariot. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the fourth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, leaps up, raising its forequarters and extending its forelegs. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the fifth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, without heeding the charioteer, without heeding the goad-stick, knocking the bit out of its mouth with its teeth, goes off wherever it wants. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the sixth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, neither goes forward nor retreats, but stands still fixed like a post. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the seventh horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, monks, there is a certain horse-fault who, when told 'Go!' and prodded and urged by the charioteer, drawing in its forelegs and drawing in its hindlegs, sits down right there on all four feet. Such a horse-fault is found here, monks. This, monks, is the eighth horse-defect. These, monks, are the eight horse-faults and eight horse-defects.
translations.an8.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā at the root of the Naḷerupucimanda tree. Then Pahārāda the asura chief approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Pahārāda the asura chief said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.22:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the Vajjian country at Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, you should remember Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma as endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: But, venerable sir, if I were to die before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One declared of me: 'There is no fetter by which Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, being fettered, would return to this world.' This, venerable sir, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These, venerable sir, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities found in me. But I do not know: 'By which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities am I declared by the Blessed One to be endowed?'”
translations.an8.22:12: Then that monk, having received almsfood at the residence of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, having returned from his almsround after the meal, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, approached the residence of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma approached that monk; having approached, having paid homage to that monk, he sat down to one side. The monk said this to the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma, who was sitting to one side: "You, householder, are endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities declared by the Blessed One. What, householder, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities with which you are endowed declared by the Blessed One?"
translations.an8.22:3: "I do not know, venerable sir, with what eight wonderful and marvelous qualities I am endowed declared by the Blessed One. But, venerable sir, listen and attend well; I will speak." "Yes, householder," that monk replied to the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma. The householder Ugga of Hatthigāma said this: "When, venerable sir, I was attending in the elephant grove, I saw the Blessed One from afar for the first time; with just that sight, venerable sir, my mind was inspired, and the intoxication of liquor was abandoned. This, venerable sir, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:4: I, venerable sir, with inspired mind attended upon the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma in progressive order, that is—talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation he made known.
