When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, soft, free from hindrances, uplifted, and inspired, then he revealed the Dhamma teaching special to the Buddhas—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth free from stains would properly take dye, so too in that very seat the dust-free, stainless Dhamma eye arose in me: 'Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing.' I, venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, penetrated the Dhamma, crossed over doubt, abandoned uncertainty, attained self-confidence, become independent of others in the Teacher's teaching, right there went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and undertook the five training rules of the holy life. This, venerable sir, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:5: I had, venerable sir, four young wives. Then I, venerable sir, approached those wives; having approached, I said this to those wives: 'I, sisters, have undertaken the five training rules of the holy life. Whoever wishes may enjoy wealth here and make merit, or go to your own relatives' families. Or if there is a man you prefer, to whom shall I give you?' When this was said, venerable sir, the eldest wife said this to me: 'Give me, master, to such and such a man.' Then I, venerable sir, having summoned that man, taking the wife with my left hand and taking a water vessel with my right hand, presented her to that man. When giving up a young wife, venerable sir, I do not recall any alteration of mind. This, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:6: There are, venerable sir, riches in my family. And they are unreservedly shared with virtuous ones of good character. This, venerable sir, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:7: When, venerable sir, I attend upon a monk; I attend upon him respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma; I listen respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. This, venerable sir, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:8: It is not wonderful, venerable sir, that when the Saṅgha is invited, deities approach and announce: 'Such and such a monk, householder, is liberated in both ways; such and such one is liberated by wisdom; such and such one is a body-witness; such and such one is attained to view; such and such one is liberated by faith; such and such one is a Dhamma-follower; such and such one is a faith-follower; such and such one is virtuous of good character; such and such one is immoral of bad character.' When serving the Saṅgha, venerable sir, I do not recall producing such a thought: 'I will give little to this one, much to this one.' But I, venerable sir, give with an even mind. This, venerable sir, is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:9: It is not wonderful, venerable sir, that deities approach me and announce: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, householder.' When this is said, I, venerable sir, say this to those deities: 'Whether you deities speak thus or do not speak thus, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.' I do not recall, venerable sir, any elation of mind on that account: 'Those deities approach me, or I converse with deities.' This, venerable sir, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.23:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. With what seven? Faithful, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; virtuous, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; conscientious, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; prudent, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; learned, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; generous, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; wise, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī—with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities, monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī." This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, approached the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavī; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached that monk; having approached, having paid homage to that monk, he sat down to one side. The monk said this to Hatthaka of Āḷavī, who was sitting to one side:
translations.an8.23:3: “Friend, the Blessed One has declared that you are endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. What seven? ‘Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful; virtuous … conscientious … prudent … learned … generous … wise, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī.’ Friend, the Blessed One has declared that you are endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.” “Surely, sir, there was no white-clad householder present there?” “There was no white-clad householder present here, friend.” “Good, sir, that no white-clad householder was present there.”
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having received almsfood at Hatthaka of Āḷavī's residence, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, after his meal, when he had returned from his alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī: “Hatthaka, this assembly of yours is large. But how, Hatthaka, do you hold together this large assembly?” “Sir, whatever has been taught by the Blessed One as the four bases of sympathy, by those I hold together this large assembly. Sir, I know: ‘This one should be held together by giving,’ I hold that one together by giving; I know: ‘This one should be held together by kind speech,’ I hold that one together by kind speech; I know: ‘This one should be held together by beneficial conduct,’ I hold that one together by beneficial conduct; I know: ‘This one should be held together by consistency,’ I hold that one together by consistency. And, sir, wealth is found in my family. They think that a poor person should not be listened to in the same way.” “Good, good, Hatthaka. This is the proper way for you to hold together a large assembly. For whatever, Hatthaka, in the past held together a large assembly, all of them held together a large assembly by these four bases of sympathy alone. And whatever, Hatthaka, in the future will hold together a large assembly, all of them will hold together a large assembly by these four bases of sympathy alone. And whatever, Hatthaka, now hold together a large assembly, all of them hold together a large assembly by these four bases of sympathy alone.”
translations.an8.26:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in Jīvaka's Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: “To what extent, sir, is one a lay follower?” “When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; to that extent, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:2: “But to what extent, sir, is a lay follower virtuous?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from killing living beings … from drinking liquor and wine that causes heedlessness; to that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
translations.an8.26:3: “But to what extent, sir, is a lay follower practicing for his own benefit, not for the benefit of others?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower himself is accomplished in faith, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of faith … himself knowing the meaning, knowing the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not encourage others in practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. To that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for his own benefit, not for the benefit of others.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, sir, for a monk with taints destroyed, the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and well-developed. And, sir, because the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and well-developed for a monk with taints destroyed, this too, sir, is a power of a monk with taints destroyed, relying on which power a monk with taints destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, sir, for a monk with taints destroyed, the four bases for spiritual power are developed and well-developed … the five faculties are developed and well-developed … the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and well-developed … the noble eightfold path is developed and well-developed. And, sir, because the noble eightfold path is developed and well-developed for a monk with taints destroyed, this too, sir, is a power of a monk with taints destroyed, relying on which power a monk with taints destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: “Monks, there are these eight causes, these eight conditions for the obtaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life, for its increase, growth, development, and fulfillment when it has been obtained. What eight? Here, monks, a monk dwells in dependence on the Teacher or on a certain fellow monk in a position of respect, where there is established in him intense conscientiousness and concern and respect. This, monks, is the first cause, the first condition for the obtaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life, for its increase, growth, development, and fulfillment when it has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:11: ‘Having heard this Dhamma, this venerable one brings it to fulfillment by means of twofold seclusion—by seclusion of body and by seclusion of mind. Surely this venerable one knows as one who knows, sees as one who sees.’ This quality too leads to affection, respect, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.2:15: ‘When gone to the Saṅgha, this venerable one does not engage in irrelevant talk and excessive talk. He himself speaks on the Dhamma or asks another to do so, and he does not despise noble silence. Surely this venerable one knows as one who knows, sees as one who sees.’ This quality too leads to affection, respect, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.2:2: Dwelling in dependence on that teacher, or on some revered spiritual companion in whom there is sharp sense of moral shame and moral dread, love and respect, he approaches them from time to time and asks and questions them: 'How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones reveal what is hidden, clarify what is obscure, and dispel doubt regarding numerous doubtful matters. This, bhikkhus, is the second cause and condition for obtaining the fundamental spiritual wisdom that has not been obtained, and for the increase, expansion, development and fulfillment of that which has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha, complete in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, training himself in the training rules. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth cause and condition for obtaining the fundamental spiritual wisdom that has not been obtained, and for the increase, expansion, development and fulfillment of that which has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:5: He is learned, a bearer and storehouse of what has been heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which declare the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings are much learned by him, borne in mind, recited verbally, examined with the mind, and well penetrated in view. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth cause and condition for obtaining the fundamental spiritual wisdom that has not been obtained, and for the increase, expansion, development and fulfillment of that which has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:6: He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, strong, firm in effort, not casting off the burden of wholesome states. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth cause and condition for obtaining the fundamental spiritual wisdom that has not been obtained, and for the increase, expansion, development and fulfillment of that which has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:7: He is not talkative, not engaged in pointless talk. He speaks the Dhamma himself or asks another to speak it, and he does not despise noble silence. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh cause and condition for obtaining the fundamental spiritual wisdom that has not been obtained, and for the increase, expansion, development and fulfillment of that which has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:8: He dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling ... such is perception ... such are volitional formations ... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.' This, bhikkhus, is the eighth cause and condition for obtaining the fundamental spiritual wisdom that has not been obtained, and for the increase, expansion, development and fulfillment of that which has been obtained.
translations.an8.2:9: His spiritual companions esteem him thus: 'This venerable one dwells in dependence on the teacher or on some revered spiritual companion in whom there is sharp sense of moral shame and moral dread, love and respect. Surely this venerable one knows as one who knows, sees as one who sees.' This quality too leads to being dear, to being respected, to development, to harmony, and to unity.
translations.an8.30:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṁsumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. Now on that occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Cetīs at Pācīnavaṁsa Grove. Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'This Dhamma is for one of few wishes, not for one of many wishes; for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company; for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; for one of established mindfulness, not for one of confused mindfulness; for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated; for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.'
translations.an8.30:10: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, and become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas that are of the mind, pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, your dwelling at the foot of a tree will seem to you like a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with well-fitting doors and windows shut; thus it will seem to you as you dwell content, for delight, for non-distress, for pleasant dwelling, for entering upon Nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:11: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, and become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas that are of the mind, pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, your bed of straw will seem to you like a couch spread with rugs, blankets, and covers, with a canopy above, with red cushions at both ends; thus it will seem to you as you dwell content, for delight, for non-distress, for pleasant dwelling, for entering upon Nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:12: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, and become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas that are of the mind, pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, your medicine of fermented urine will seem to you like the various medicines of a householder or householder's son, that is to say: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses; thus it will seem to you as you dwell content, for delight, for non-distress, for pleasant dwelling, for entering upon Nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should dwell right here among the Cetīs at Pācīnavaṁsa Grove even during the coming rains retreat.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Blessed One, having given this exhortation to Venerable Anuruddha—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm; even so—disappeared from among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Grove and appeared among the Bhaggas in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "I will teach you, bhikkhus, the eight great thoughts of a great man. Listen …pe… And what, bhikkhus, are the eight great thoughts of a great man? This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one of few wants, not for one of many wants; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is secluded, not for one who is fond of society; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one of established mindfulness, not for one of lapsed mindfulness; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise; this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is fond of and delights in non-proliferation, not for one who is fond of and delights in proliferation.
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Blessed One, having known with his mind the thought process in Venerable Anuruddha's mind—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm; even so—disappeared from among the Bhaggas in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park and appeared before Venerable Anuruddha among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Grove. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Venerable Anuruddha also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to Venerable Anuruddha, who was sitting to one side:
translations.an8.30:22: Then Venerable Anuruddha spent the next rains retreat right there among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Grove. Then Venerable Anuruddha, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, not long after—attained that supreme goal of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: "Destroyed is birth, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being." And Venerable Anuruddha became one of the arahants. Then Venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: "Having understood my thought, the Teacher unsurpassed in the world; with mind-made body, by psychic power he approached.
translations.an8.30:24: As was my thought, so he taught beyond that; the Buddha delighting in non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.
translations.an8.30:3: "Good, good, Anuruddha. It is good, Anuruddha, that you thought this great thought of a great man: 'This Dhamma is for one of few wants, not for one of many wants; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who is fond of society; this Dhamma is for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one of established mindfulness, not for one of lapsed mindfulness; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.' Therefore, Anuruddha, think this eighth great thought of a great man: 'This Dhamma is for one who is fond of and delights in non-proliferation, not for one who is fond of and delights in proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:4: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, with thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion, you will dwell having entered upon the first jhāna.
translations.an8.30:5: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, with the subsiding of thought and examination, with internal confidence and single-mindedness, without thought, without examination, with rapture and happiness born of concentration, you will dwell having entered upon the second jhāna.
translations.an8.30:6: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, with the fading away of rapture, you will dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; which the noble ones declare: 'One is equanimous, mindful, one who lives happily,' having entered upon the third jhāna.
translations.an8.30:7: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and dejection, without pain, without pleasure, with the purification of equanimity and mindfulness, you will dwell having entered upon the fourth jhāna.
translations.an8.39:1: "These eight, bhikkhus, are streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, and agreeable, to welfare and happiness. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. This, bhikkhus, is the first stream of merit …pe… leading to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is the second stream of merit …pe… leading to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. This, monks, is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, sustainer of happiness, tending toward heaven, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, agreeable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy. There are these five great gifts, original gifts, long-standing gifts, traditional gifts, not confused, not previously confused, not to be confused, not to be confused in the future, not despised by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. Which five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from the taking of life. Abstaining from the taking of life, monks, the noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from persecution. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from persecution, he shares in immeasurable freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from persecution. This, monks, is the first great gift, original gift, long-standing gift, traditional gift, not confused, not previously confused, not to be confused, not to be confused in the future, not despised by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. This, monks, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, sustainer of happiness, tending toward heaven, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, agreeable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an8.39:7: having abandoned fermented and distilled intoxicants that cause heedlessness, abstains from fermented and distilled intoxicants that cause heedlessness. Abstaining from fermented and distilled intoxicants that cause heedlessness, monks, the noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, gives freedom from enmity, gives freedom from persecution. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, having given freedom from enmity, having given freedom from persecution, he shares in immeasurable freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from persecution. This, monks, is the fifth great gift, original gift, long-standing gift, traditional gift, not confused, not previously confused, not to be confused, not to be confused in the future, not despised by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. This, monks, is the eighth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, sustainer of happiness, tending toward heaven, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, agreeable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an8.40:1: "The taking of life, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of the taking of life for one reborn as a human is to be short-lived.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of taking what is not given for one reborn as a human is the loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of sexual misconduct for one reborn as a human is enmity with rivals.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of false speech for one reborn as a human is being falsely accused.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of divisive speech for one reborn as a human is the breaking of friendships.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of harsh speech for one reborn as a human is disagreeable sounds.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, monks, when pursued, developed, and cultivated, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, leads to rebirth in the realm of ghosts. The minimum result of idle chatter for one reborn as a human is words that are not authoritative.
translations.an8.6:2: For an uninstructed ordinary person, monks, gain arises and so does loss; fame arises and so does disgrace; blame arises and so does praise; pleasure arises and so does pain. For an instructed noble disciple too, monks, gain arises and so does loss; fame arises and so does disgrace; blame arises and so does praise; pleasure arises and so does pain. What is the difference, monks, what is the distinction, what is the distinguishing factor between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed ordinary person?" "Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, taking refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it."
translations.an8.6:4: Gain too overwhelms his mind and remains, loss too overwhelms his mind and remains, fame too overwhelms his mind and remains, disgrace too overwhelms his mind and remains, blame too overwhelms his mind and remains, praise too overwhelms his mind and remains, pleasure too overwhelms his mind and remains, pain too overwhelms his mind and remains. He welcomes the gain that has arisen, and rebels against the loss; he welcomes the fame that has arisen, and rebels against the disgrace; he welcomes the praise that has arisen, and rebels against the blame; he welcomes the pleasure that has arisen, and rebels against the pain. Being thus possessed by favoring and opposing, he is not freed from birth, from aging and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. I say he is not freed from suffering.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain; these are impermanent among human beings, inconstant, of a nature to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Having known these, the mindful one of excellent wisdom, examines the things of a nature to change; pleasing things do not obsess his mind, nor does displeasing things produce aversion.
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus with reference to Devadatta: "It is good, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects on his own failure. It is good, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects on the failure of others. It is good, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects on his own success. It is good, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects on the success of others. Overcome, bhikkhus, by eight bad qualities, with mind obsessed, Devadatta is destined for the plane of misery, hell, bound for the aeon, irredeemable.
translations.an8.7:2: By which eight? Overcome, bhikkhus, by gain, with mind obsessed, Devadatta is destined for the plane of misery, hell, bound for the aeon, irredeemable. By loss, bhikkhus … by honor, bhikkhus … by dishonor, bhikkhus … by respect, bhikkhus … by disrespect, bhikkhus … by evil desire, bhikkhus … by bad friendship, bhikkhus, with mind obsessed, Devadatta is destined for the plane of misery, hell, bound for the aeon, irredeemable. Overcome, bhikkhus, by these eight bad qualities, with mind obsessed, Devadatta is destined for the plane of misery, hell, bound for the aeon, irredeemable.
translations.an8.7:3: It is good, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu dwells having overcome, having overcome, gain that has arisen, loss that has arisen … honor that has arisen … dishonor that has arisen … respect that has arisen … disrespect that has arisen … evil desire that has arisen … bad friendship that has arisen.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of the devas, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, so too, having vanished among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, appeared before Venerable Uttara on the Mahisavatthu Saṅkheyyaka Mountain at Vaṭajālikā. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached Venerable Uttara; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Uttara and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: "Is it true, venerable sir, that Venerable Uttara teaches the bhikkhus thus: 'It is good, friends, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects on his own failure, it is good, friends, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects on the failure of others … on his own success … on the success of others'?" "It is so, lord of the devas." "But, venerable sir, is this Venerable Uttara's own inspired utterance, or is it the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?" "Then, lord of the devas, I shall give you a simile. For by means of a simile some intelligent people here understand the meaning of what has been said.
translations.an8.8:6: Just as, lord of the devas, there is a great heap of grain not far from a village or town. From there a great crowd of people would carry away grain—in baskets, in packs, in their laps, in their cupped hands. If, lord of the devas, someone approached that great crowd of people and asked: 'From where do you carry this grain?' how, lord of the devas, would that great crowd of people answer correctly?" "'From that great heap of grain, venerable sir'—thus, venerable sir, that great crowd of people would answer correctly." "Just so, lord of the devas, whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. From that, having taken and taken again, we and others speak.
translations.an8.8:7: "It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir, how well this has been spoken by Venerable Uttara: 'Whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. From that, having taken and taken again, we and others speak.' Once, venerable Uttara, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus with reference to Devadatta:
translations.mn108:1: Thus have I heard. At one time Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
translations.mn108:13: "There are, brahmin, ten inspiring qualities declared by that Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In one in whom these qualities are found, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate; having honored, respected, and esteemed, we live in dependence on him. What ten?
translations.mn108:14: Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha, complete in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking and training in the training rules.
translations.mn108:15: He is learned, a bearer and storehouse of what has been heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view.
translations.mn108:17: He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life.
translations.mn108:18: He wields the various kinds of spiritual power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels in space like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes even the sun and moon, so powerful and mighty; he exercises mastery with the body as far as the brahmā world.
translations.mn108:19: With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and human, those that are far as well as near.
translations.mn108:2: Now at that time King Māgadha Ajātasattu Vedehiputta was having Rājagaha restored, fearing King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:20: They understand the mind of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed it with their own mind. They understand a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust', or they understand a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust', or they understand a mind with aversion as 'a mind with aversion', or they understand a mind without aversion as 'a mind without aversion', or they understand a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion', or they understand a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion', or they understand a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind', or they understand a scattered mind as 'a scattered mind', or they understand an exalted mind as 'an exalted mind', or they understand an unexalted mind as 'an unexalted mind', or they understand a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind', or they understand an unsurpassable mind as 'an unsurpassable mind', or they understand a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind', or they understand an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind', or they understand a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind', or they understand an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind'.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, they dwell having realized here and now by their own direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom. These ten inspiring qualities, brahmin, were taught by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In whom we find these qualities, him we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate; having honored, respected, and esteemed him, we live in dependence on him.
translations.mn108:25: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said to Venerable Ānanda: "But where is Master Ānanda dwelling now?" "I am dwelling now at Veḷuvana, brahmin." "But is Veḷuvana delightful, quiet, free from noise, with an atmosphere of solitude, remote from people, suitable for retreat?" "Indeed, brahmin, Veḷuvana is delightful, quiet, free from noise, with an atmosphere of solitude, remote from people, suitable for retreat, as it is guarded and protected by ones such as you." "Indeed, Master Ānanda, Veḷuvana is delightful, quiet, free from noise, with an atmosphere of solitude, remote from people, suitable for retreat, as it is for masters who are meditators, devoted to meditation. Masters are indeed meditators, devoted to meditation. This one time, Master Ānanda, that Master Gotama was dwelling at Vesālī in the Mahāvana in the Gabled Hall. Then, Master Ānanda, I approached the Mahāvana, the Gabled Hall, where that Master Gotama was. And there that Master Gotama spoke about meditation in various ways. That Master Gotama was indeed a meditator, devoted to meditation. And that Master Gotama praised all meditation."
translations.mn108:28: "It seems that Master Gotama criticized meditation, Master Ānanda, and praised what was praiseworthy. Well then, Master Ānanda, let us go now; we have much to do, many duties." "Do now, brahmin, what you think it is time for." Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, having delighted in and approved of what Venerable Ānanda said, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to Venerable Ānanda: "It is too early to walk for alms in Rājagaha. What if I were to approach Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin at his workplace, where Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin is?"
translations.mn108:4: Then Venerable Ānanda approached Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin at his workplace, where Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin was. Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin saw Venerable Ānanda coming in the distance. Having seen him, he said to Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Master Ānanda. Welcome to Master Ānanda. It is long since Master Ānanda made this arrangement, that is, to come here. Let Master Ānanda sit down; this seat is prepared." Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin also, having taken a low seat, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: "Is there, Master Ānanda, even one bhikkhu who is endowed with all those qualities in every way and in all respects with which that Master Gotama was endowed, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?" "There is not, brahmin, even one bhikkhu who is endowed with all those qualities in every way and in all respects with which that Blessed One was endowed, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For that Blessed One, brahmin, was the originator of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was knower of the path, expert in the path, accomplished in the path. And his disciples now dwell following the path, becoming endowed with it afterwards."
translations.mn108:7: "Is there, Master Ānanda, even one bhikkhu who was appointed by that Master Gotama: 'He will be your refuge after my passing away', whom you would now take as your support?" "There is not, brahmin, even one bhikkhu who was appointed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'He will be your refuge after my passing away', whom we would now take as our support."
translations.mn108:9: "But how, Master Ānanda, is there concord when there is no refuge?" "We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; the Dhamma is our refuge."
translations.mn117:10: There, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as 'wrong intention', and one understands right intention as 'right intention'; this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, monks, is wrong intention? Intention of sensual desire, intention of ill will, intention of cruelty—this, monks, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? I say, bhikkhus, right intention is twofold—there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-cruelty: 'this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions'.
translations.mn117:14: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever, bhikkhus, in one of noble mind, of taintless mind, one possessed of the noble path, developing the noble path, is thinking, thought, intention, mental absorption, mental fixity, focusing of the mind, verbal formation—this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: One strives for the abandoning of wrong intention and for the acquisition of right intention: this is one's right effort. One is mindful in abandoning wrong intention, mindful in entering upon and dwelling in right intention: this is one's right mindfulness. Thus these three things run and circle around right intention, namely: right view, right effort, right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: There, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong speech as wrong speech, right speech as right speech: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? I say, bhikkhus, right speech is twofold—there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? Abstinence from false speech, abstinence from divisive speech, abstinence from harsh speech, abstinence from idle chatter—this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:2: “I will teach you, bhikkhus, the noble right concentration with its supports and its requisites. Listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever, bhikkhus, in one of noble mind, of taintless mind, one possessed of the noble path, developing the noble path, is abstinence, desistance, abstention from the four kinds of verbal misconduct—this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: There, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong action as wrong action, right action as right action: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? I say, bhikkhus, right action is twofold—there is, bhikkhus, right action that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; there is, bhikkhus, right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, bhikkhus, is right action that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? Abstinence from killing living beings, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from sexual misconduct—this, bhikkhus, is right action that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:28: There, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, right livelihood as right livelihood: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood? Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain—this, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? I say, bhikkhus, right livelihood is twofold—there is, bhikkhus, right livelihood that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; there is, bhikkhus, right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes a living by right livelihood—this, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:34: There, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? For one of right view, bhikkhus, right intention arises; for one of right intention, right speech arises; for one of right speech, right action arises; for one of right action, right livelihood arises; for one of right livelihood, right effort arises; for one of right effort, right mindfulness arises; for one of right mindfulness, right concentration arises; for one of right concentration, right knowledge arises; for one of right knowledge, right liberation arises. Thus, bhikkhus, the trainee is possessed of eight factors, the arahant is possessed of ten factors. There too, by right knowledge, numerous evil unwholesome states are eliminated and go to the full perfection of development.
translations.mn117:35: There, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? For one of right view, bhikkhus, wrong view is eliminated. And whatever numerous evil unwholesome states originate with wrong view as condition, those too are eliminated for him. With right view as condition, numerous wholesome states go to the full perfection of development. For one of right intention, bhikkhus, wrong intention is eliminated … for one of right speech, wrong speech is eliminated … for one of right action, wrong action is eliminated … for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is eliminated … for one of right effort, wrong effort is eliminated … for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is eliminated … for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is eliminated … for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is eliminated … for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is eliminated. And whatever numerous evil unwholesome states originate with wrong liberation as condition, those too are eliminated for him. And with right liberation as condition, numerous wholesome states go to the full perfection of development.
translations.mn117:36: So, bhikkhus, twenty factors of the wholesome side, twenty factors of the unwholesome side—the great fortyfold Dhamma exposition has been set rolling, irreversible by any ascetic or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: There, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong view as wrong view, and right view as right view—this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong view? 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed, no fruit or result of good and bad actions, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously arisen beings, no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have gone rightly, gone rightly on, who with direct knowledge realize this world and the other world and make it known'—this, bhikkhus, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Right view, bhikkhus, I say is twofold: there is, bhikkhus, right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; there is, bhikkhus, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? 'There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is what is sacrificed, there is fruit and result of good and bad actions, there is this world, there is the other world, there is mother, there is father, there are spontaneously arisen beings, there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have gone rightly, gone rightly on, who with direct knowledge realize this world and the other world and make it known'—this, bhikkhus, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever, bhikkhus, is wisdom, faculty of wisdom, power of wisdom, investigation-of-Dhammas enlightenment factor, right view as path factor, of one with a noble mind, with a taintless mind, one possessed of the noble path, developing the noble path—this is called, bhikkhus, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: One strives for the abandoning of wrong view, for the acquisition of right view—this is one's right effort. Mindfully one abandons wrong view, mindfully one acquires and dwells in right view—this is one's right mindfulness. Thus these three dhammas run and circle around right view, that is: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, in the mansion of Migāra's mother, together with many very well-known elder disciples—Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahākassapa, Venerable Mahākaccāyana, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, Venerable Mahākappina, Venerable Mahācunda, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, and Venerable Ānanda, together with other very well-known elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven enlightenment factors. The seven enlightenment factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, ever mindful he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he understands: 'I breathe in long'; breathing out long, he understands: 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he understands: 'I breathe in short'; breathing out short, he understands: 'I breathe out short.' He trains thus: 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Tranquilizing the bodily formation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Tranquilizing the bodily formation, I will breathe out.'
translations.mn118:19: He trains thus: 'Experiencing rapture, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing rapture, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Experiencing happiness, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing happiness, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Tranquilizing the mental formation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Tranquilizing the mental formation, I will breathe out.'
translations.mn118:2: Now on that occasion elder bhikkhus were instructing and admonishing new bhikkhus. Some elder bhikkhus were instructing and admonishing ten bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were instructing and admonishing twenty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were instructing and admonishing thirty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were instructing and admonishing forty bhikkhus. And those new bhikkhus, being instructed and admonished by the elder bhikkhus, understood a lofty distinction beyond before.
translations.mn118:20: He trains thus: 'Experiencing the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the mind, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Gladdening the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Gladdening the mind, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Concentrating the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Concentrating the mind, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Liberating the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Liberating the mind, I will breathe out.'
translations.mn118:21: He trains thus: 'Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Contemplating fading away, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating fading away, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Contemplating cessation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating cessation, I will breathe out.' He trains thus: 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out.'
translations.mn118:23: And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed, how is it cultivated so that it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: On whatever occasion, monks, a monk breathing in long discerns 'I am breathing in long'; or breathing out long discerns 'I am breathing out long'; or breathing in short discerns 'I am breathing in short'; or breathing out short discerns 'I am breathing out short'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in tranquillizing the bodily formation'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily formation'—on that occasion, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. I say, monks, that this is a certain body among the bodies, namely, in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, monks, on that occasion a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
translations.mn118:25: On whatever occasion, monks, a monk trains thus 'I shall breathe in experiencing rapture'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out experiencing rapture'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in experiencing happiness'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out experiencing happiness'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in tranquillizing the mental formation'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out tranquillizing the mental formation'—on that occasion, monks, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. I say, monks, that this is a certain feeling among the feelings, namely, close attention to in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, monks, on that occasion a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
translations.mn118:26: On whatever occasion, monks, a monk trains thus 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out gladdening the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in concentrating the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out concentrating the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in liberating the mind'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out liberating the mind'—on that occasion, monks, a monk dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. I do not say, monks, that there is mindfulness of breathing for one who is muddle-minded and not fully aware. Therefore, monks, on that occasion a monk dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
translations.mn118:27: On whatever occasion, monks, a monk trains thus 'I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in contemplating fading away'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out contemplating fading away'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in contemplating cessation'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out contemplating cessation'; trains thus 'I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; trains thus 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment'—on that occasion, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. Having seen with wisdom the abandoning of covetousness and grief, he closely looks on with equanimity. Therefore, monks, on that occasion a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
translations.mn118:28: When, monks, mindfulness of breathing has been developed and cultivated in this way, it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: And how, monks, when the four establishments of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated, do they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
translations.mn118:3: Now on that occasion—the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the full-moon night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony—the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the community of monks. Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the community of monks in silence, addressed the monks:
translations.mn118:30: On whatever occasion, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world, on that occasion his mindfulness is established without distraction. On whatever occasion, monks, a monk's mindfulness is established without distraction, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused in the monk; on that occasion the monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of mindfulness goes to the fulfillment of development in the monk.
translations.mn118:31: Dwelling thus mindfully, he examines that state with wisdom, investigates it, makes an examination of it. On whatever occasion, monks, a monk dwelling thus mindfully examines that state with wisdom, investigates it, makes an examination of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena is aroused in the monk; on that occasion the monk develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena goes to the fulfillment of development in the monk.
translations.mn118:33: In one of aroused energy, non-sensual rapture arises. On whatever occasion, monks, non-sensual rapture arises in a monk of aroused energy, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of rapture is aroused in the monk; on that occasion the monk develops the enlightenment factor of rapture; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of rapture goes to the fulfillment of development in the monk.
translations.mn118:34: For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil. On whatever occasion, monks, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil for a monk with a rapturous mind, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of tranquillity is aroused in the monk; on that occasion the monk develops the enlightenment factor of tranquillity; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of tranquillity goes to the fulfillment of development in the monk.
translations.mn118:35: For one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. On whatever occasion, monks, the mind becomes concentrated for one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of concentration is aroused in the monk; on that occasion the monk develops the enlightenment factor of concentration; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of concentration goes to the fulfillment of development in the monk.
translations.mn118:36: They carefully look on with equanimity at that concentrated mind.  At that time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu carefully looks on with equanimity at that concentrated mind, the equanimity enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu at that time, the bhikkhu develops the equanimity enlightenment factor at that time, the equanimity enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu at that time.
translations.mn118:4: “I am committed, bhikkhus, to this practice;  I am committed in mind, bhikkhus, to this practice.  Therefore, bhikkhus, arouse even more energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the acquisition of the unacquired, for the realization of the unrealized.  I will wait right here in Sāvatthī for the Komudī full moon of the fourth month.”
translations.mn118:40: When, bhikkhus, the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and cultivated in this way, they fulfill the seven enlightenment factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how, bhikkhus, are the seven enlightenment factors developed and cultivated so as to fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those senior bhikkhus admonish and instruct the junior bhikkhus even more.  Some senior bhikkhus admonish and instruct ten bhikkhus, some senior bhikkhus admonish and instruct twenty bhikkhus, some senior bhikkhus admonish and instruct thirty bhikkhus, some senior bhikkhus admonish and instruct forty bhikkhus.  And those junior bhikkhus, being admonished and instructed by the senior bhikkhus, know a lofty distinction between before and after.
translations.mn118:9: There are, bhikkhus, in this bhikkhu saṅgha, arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the spiritual life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge— such bhikkhus too, bhikkhus, are in this bhikkhu saṅgha.
translations.mn11:13: In such a Dhamma and Discipline, the confidence in the Teacher is not rightly placed, it is said;  the confidence in the Dhamma is not rightly placed, it is said;  the fulfillment of the precepts is not rightly placed, it is said;  the affection for those who share the same Dhamma is not rightly placed, it is said.  Why is that?  Because, bhikkhus, it is thus in a Dhamma and Discipline that is badly proclaimed, badly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, not proclaimed by a perfectly enlightened one.
translations.mn11:14: But the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, claiming to be one who proclaims the full understanding of all clinging, rightly proclaims the full understanding of all clinging— he proclaims the full understanding of sensual clinging, he proclaims the full understanding of view clinging, he proclaims the full understanding of precept and vow clinging, he proclaims the full understanding of self-doctrine clinging.
translations.mn11:15: In such a Dhamma and Discipline, the confidence in the Teacher is rightly placed, it is said;  the confidence in the Dhamma is rightly placed, it is said;  the fulfillment of the precepts is rightly placed, it is said;  the affection for those who share the same Dhamma is rightly placed, it is said.  Why is that?  Because, bhikkhus, it is thus in a Dhamma and Discipline that is well proclaimed, well expounded, leading out, conducive to peace, proclaimed by a perfectly enlightened one.
translations.mn11:2: “Only here is there a recluse, here a second recluse, here a third recluse, here a fourth recluse;  empty of recluses are the other sects’ doctrines.”  Thus, bhikkhus, you should rightly roar your lion's roar.
translations.mn11:6: These two, bhikkhus, are views— the view of existence and the view of non-existence.  Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, are addicted to the view of existence, have entered into the view of existence, are attached to the view of existence, they are opposed to the view of non-existence.  Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, are addicted to the view of non-existence, have entered into the view of non-existence, are attached to the view of non-existence, they are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, do not understand as it really is the origin and passing away, the gratification, danger, and escape from these two views, they are with lust, with aversion, with delusion, with craving, with clinging, they are unwise, they favor and oppose, they delight in proliferation, they take pleasure in proliferation;  they are not freed from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrows, from lamentations, from pains, from griefs, from despairs;  ‘they are not freed from suffering,’ I say.
translations.mn11:9: These four, bhikkhus, are clingings.  What four?  Sensual clinging, view clinging, precept and vow clinging, self-doctrine clinging.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the grove outside the city to the east.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.  And whatever, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible, this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata's power of the Tathāgata, having which power the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in assemblies, and sets rolling the Brahma wheel.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, with the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it.  And whatever, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, with the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it, this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata's power of the Tathāgata, having which power the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in assemblies, and sets rolling the Brahma wheel.
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta the Licchaviputta had recently left this Dhamma and Discipline.  He was declaring in the assembly at Vesālī:  “The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.  The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of inquiry, arrived at by investigation.  And the purpose for which the Dhamma was taught by him does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.”
translations.mn12:20: These, Sāriputta, are the ten Tathāgata's powers of the Tathāgata, possessing which powers the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in assemblies, and sets rolling the Brahma wheel.
translations.mn12:22: These four, Sāriputta, are the Tathāgata's confidences, possessing which confidences the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in assemblies, and sets rolling the Brahma wheel.  What four?
translations.mn12:23: 'For one claiming to be perfectly enlightened, these things are not fully understood.' There, Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for a recluse or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world to legitimately reproach me. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:24: 'For one claiming to be one whose defilements are destroyed, these defilements are not completely destroyed.' There, Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for a recluse or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world to legitimately reproach me. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:25: 'But those things said to be obstructive, when indulged in are not enough to cause obstruction.' There, Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for a recluse or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world to legitimately reproach me. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:26: 'But for the purpose for which the Dhamma was taught by you, it does not lead out the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.' There, Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for a recluse or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world to legitimately reproach me. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:32: There are these four, Sāriputta, modes of generation. Which four? Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, and spontaneous generation.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born generation? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born breaking out of an eggshell—this, Sāriputta, is called egg-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born generation? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born breaking out of a membrane-bag—this, Sāriputta, is called womb-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born generation? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born in rotting fish or in rotting corpses or in rotting dough or in a cesspool or in a drain—this, Sāriputta, is called moisture-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous generation? Devas, hell-beings, certain human beings, and certain fallen beings—this, Sāriputta, is called spontaneous generation. These, Sāriputta, are the four modes of generation.
translations.mn12:35: There are these five, Sāriputta, destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, human beings, and devas.
translations.mn12:36: I understand, Sāriputta, hell, the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell; and I understand how one practicing accordingly, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell. I understand, Sāriputta, the animal realm, the path leading to the animal realm, and the practice leading to the animal realm; and I understand how one practicing accordingly, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in the animal realm. I understand, Sāriputta, the ghost realm, the path leading to the ghost realm, and the practice leading to the ghost realm; and I understand how one practicing accordingly, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in the ghost realm. I understand, Sāriputta, human beings, the path leading to the human world, and the practice leading to the human world; and I understand how one practicing accordingly, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn among human beings. I understand, Sāriputta, devas, the path leading to the divine world, and the practice leading to the divine world; and I understand how one practicing accordingly, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. I understand, Sāriputta, Nibbāna, the path leading to Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna; and I understand how one practicing accordingly, with the destruction of the defilements, dwells having realized here and now by his own direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.
translations.mn12:4: 'This Sunakkhatta, Sāriputta, is an angry man. And this statement of his was spoken from anger. Intending to speak dispraise, Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta speaks only praise of the Tathāgata. This, Sāriputta, is praise of the Tathāgata when one would say: 'For the purpose for which the Dhamma was taught by him, it leads out the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.'
translations.mn12:43: One who knowing me thus, seeing me thus, would say: 'There is no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones for the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of inquiry as it occurs to him'—without giving up that speech, without giving up that thought, without giving up that view, he will be cast into hell as if brought there. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, concentration, and wisdom would attain final knowledge here and now—so certain is this, Sāriputta, I say: without giving up that speech, without giving up that thought, without giving up that view, he will be cast into hell as if brought there.
translations.mn12:44: I recall, Sāriputta, having lived the holy life complete in four factors—I was one of fierce austerity, of the most fierce austerity; I was one who was rough, of the most extreme roughness; I was one who was scrupulous, of the most extreme scrupulousness; I was one who was secluded, of the most extreme seclusion.
translations.mn12:46: In this, Sāriputta, there was this for me in regard to roughness—dust and dirt accumulated on my body over many years, growing in layers. Just as, Sāriputta, a tinduka tree-trunk has dust and dirt accumulated over many years, growing in layers, so too, Sāriputta, dust and dirt accumulated on my body over many years, growing in layers. And it did not occur to me, Sāriputta: 'Oh, that I might rub off this dust and dirt with my hand, or that others might rub off this dust and dirt with their hand.' Thus too, Sāriputta, it was not for me. This, Sāriputta, was there for me in regard to roughness.
translations.mn12:47: In this, Sāriputta, there was this for me in regard to scrupulousness—I, Sāriputta, moved forward mindfully and moved back mindfully, so much so that even for a drop of water compassion was established in me: 'May I not bring destruction to the small creatures that might be in the path.' This, Sāriputta, was there for me in regard to scrupulousness.
translations.mn12:49: Then, Sāriputta, I went to those cattle-sheds with cows established, with cowherds gone away, and approaching on all fours, I ate whatever dung of young calves and cow-dung there was. And as long, Sāriputta, as my own urine and excrement was not exhausted, I ate that very urine and excrement. This was my, Sāriputta, practice of eating vast filth.
translations.mn12:5: For this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not even have this much confidence in me regarding the Dhamma: 'Thus indeed is that Blessed One an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.'
translations.mn12:50: Then, Sāriputta, I entered and dwelt in a certain dreadful forest grove. There, Sāriputta, that dreadful forest grove was so dreadful that whoever, not free from lust, entered that forest grove, for the most part his hairs would stand on end. Then, Sāriputta, on those nights that were cold, wintry, in the eight-day interval, at the time of snowfall, on such nights I dwelt in the open air by night, in the forest grove by day; in the last month of summer I dwelt in the open air by day, in the forest grove by night. And this verse, Sāriputta, not heard before, occurred to me spontaneously: 'Scorched and frozen, alone in the dreadful forest; Naked, not sitting by fire, the sage intent on search.'
translations.mn12:51: Then, Sāriputta, I made my bed in a charnel ground, resting on the bones of corpses. And, Sāriputta, village boys came up to me and spat on me, urinated on me, threw dirt on me, and stuck sticks in my ears. But I, Sāriputta, do not recall having generated a bad mind towards them. This was my, Sāriputta, dwelling in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are of such view and such opinion: 'Purity comes from food.' They say: 'Let us live on beans.' They eat beans, bean flour, and drink bean water—they consume beans prepared in many ways. But I, Sāriputta, recall eating one bean as food. It might occur to you, Sāriputta: 'The bean must have been large at that time.' But this, Sāriputta, should not be seen thus. The bean was just the same then as it is now. When I, Sāriputta, ate one bean as food, my body reached extreme emaciation. Just as the joints of the eighty-year-old or the black joints, so indeed my limbs and joints became through that little food. Just as the hoof-marks of an ox, so indeed my buttocks became through that little food. Just as a string of beads, so indeed my spinal vertebrae, protruding and sunken, became through that little food. Just as the rafters of an old shed, broken and fallen, so indeed my ribs, broken and fallen, became through that little food. Just as in a deep well the water-star, deep-set and sunken, is seen, so indeed the eye-star, deep-set and sunken, was seen in my eye-sockets through that little food. Just as a bitter gourd, cut unripe, is shriveled and withered by wind and sun, so indeed the skin of my head was shriveled and withered through that little food. Then I, Sāriputta, thinking 'I will rub my belly-skin,' took hold of my spinal vertebrae, and thinking 'I will rub my spinal vertebrae,' took hold of my belly-skin. So much, Sāriputta, was my belly-skin stuck to my spinal vertebrae through that little food. Then I, Sāriputta, thinking 'I will defecate or urinate,' fell right there face down through that little food. Then I, Sāriputta, stroking my limbs with my hand to revive that very body. When I, Sāriputta, stroked my limbs with my hand, rotten roots of hair fell from my body through that little food.
