translations.mn12:56: But by that practice, by that way, by that performance of painful austerities, I did not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why is that? Because I did not attain that noble wisdom which when attained is noble and emancipating, and leads the one who practices in accordance with it to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are of such view and such opinion: 'Purity comes from wandering on.' But that wandering on, Sāriputta, is not easy to find that I have not wandered on before during this long period of time, except with the Pure Abode devas. And if I, Sāriputta, were to wander on with the Pure Abode devas, I would not return again to this world.
translations.mn12:6: For this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not even have this much confidence in me regarding the Dhamma: 'Thus indeed is that Blessed One who experiences various kinds of supernormal power—being one he becomes many, being many he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged he travels in space like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes even the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma world.'
translations.mn12:60: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are of such view and such opinion: 'Purity comes from sacrifice.' But that sacrifice, Sāriputta, is not easy to find that I have not sacrificed before during this long period of time, and that as a king or khattiya anointed on the head, or a brahmin of great wealth.
translations.mn12:61: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are of such view and such opinion: 'Purity comes from fire service.' But that fire, Sāriputta, is not easy to find that I have not served before during this long period of time, and that as a king or khattiya anointed on the head, or a brahmin of great wealth.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: ‘As long as this man is young, a black-haired youth, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, so long is he endowed with the highest keenness of wisdom. But when this man is old, aged, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, then he declines from that keenness of wisdom.’ This should not be seen thus, Sāriputta. I, Sāriputta, am now old, aged, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life; my life has reached eighty years. Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four disciples who were centenarians, centenarian in lifespan, endowed with supreme mindfulness, resolution, and steadfastness, and with the highest keenness of wisdom. Just as, Sāriputta, a skilled archer, trained, practiced, well-practiced, could easily, without difficulty, shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree, so too are they endowed with supreme mindfulness, supreme resolution, supreme steadfastness, and the highest keenness of wisdom. They might ask me questions about the four establishments of mindfulness, taking them up point by point, and I, when asked, would answer them, and they would remember my answers as answered, and would not ask me a second time further. Except for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, except for defecating and urinating, except for dispelling sleepiness and fatigue, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata’s analytical explanation of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata’s ready response to questions would not be exhausted. Then those four disciples of mine, centenarians, centenarian in lifespan, would pass away at the end of a hundred years. Even if you carry me about on a couch, Sāriputta, there would be no change in the Tathāgata’s keenness of wisdom.
translations.mn12:7: For this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have this following of the Dhamma in regard to me: ‘Such is the Blessed One who, with the divine ear element that is purified and surpasses the human, hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.’
translations.mn12:8: For this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have this following of the Dhamma in regard to me: ‘Such is the Blessed One who, with the mind encompassing mind, understands the mind of other beings and other persons—he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind, an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’
translations.mn12:9: There are, Sāriputta, these ten powers of the Tathāgata, possessing which powers the Tathāgata claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Brahma wheel. What ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, student, a certain woman or man is not a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, dwelling, and lighting. By that kamma thus performed, thus undertaken, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. If, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is not reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell, but comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is poor. This, student, is the practice that leads to poverty, that is, not being a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, dwelling, and lighting.
translations.mn135:2: Then the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their kamma, heirs of their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, abiding in their kamma. Kamma divides beings, that is, into inferiority and superiority.
translations.mn135:3: What, Master Gotama, is the cause and condition why, among human beings who are human beings, inferiority and superiority are seen? For, Master Gotama, human beings with short lifespans are seen, and those with long lifespans are seen; those with much illness are seen, and those with little illness are seen; those who are ugly are seen, and those who are beautiful are seen; those who are insignificant are seen, and those who are influential are seen; those who are poor are seen, and those who are wealthy are seen; those of low birth are seen, and those of high birth are seen; those who are unwise are seen, and those who are wise are seen. What, Master Gotama, is the cause and condition why, among human beings who are human beings, inferiority and superiority are seen?
translations.mn135:4: Beings are owners of their kamma, heirs of their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, abiding in their kamma. Kamma divides beings, that is, into inferiority and superiority. I do not understand, Master Gotama, the detailed meaning of this statement spoken in brief by Master Gotama without expounding the detailed meaning. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of this statement spoken in brief by Master Gotama without expounding the detailed meaning. Then, student, listen and attend closely; I will speak. Yes, sir, the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: “Here, student, a certain woman or man is a killer of living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to killing and slaying, showing no mercy to living beings. Because of that deed, thus undertaken and thus performed, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. If, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell, but come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This, student, is the practice leading to short life, that is, being a killer of living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to killing and slaying, showing no mercy to living beings.
translations.mn135:6: But here, student, a certain woman or man, abandoning the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious, merciful, they dwell compassionate to all living beings. Because of that deed, thus undertaken and thus performed, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. If, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, but come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This, student, is the practice leading to long life, that is, abandoning the killing of living beings, abstaining from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious, merciful, dwelling compassionate to all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If, monks, while that clansman is striving, exerting himself, and making effort, those riches do not come to be, he experiences pain and dejection: ‘My effort has been in vain, my striving has been fruitless.’ If, monks, while that clansman is striving, exerting himself, and making effort, those riches do come to be, he experiences pain and dejection in protecting them: ‘How can my riches be neither taken by kings, nor stolen by thieves, nor burned by fire, nor swept away by water, nor taken by unloved heirs?’ While he is guarding and protecting those riches, kings take them, or thieves steal them, or fire burns them, or water sweeps them away, or unloved heirs take them. He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes confused: ‘What I had is now gone.’ This too, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:11: Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, kings quarrel with kings, khattiyas with khattiyas, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders; mother quarrels with son, son with mother, father with son, son with father; brother quarrels with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, friend with friend. Here, having fallen into quarrels, disputes, and arguments, they attack each other with fists, clods, sticks, and knives. Here they undergo death and deadly suffering. This too, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:12: Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, having taken sword and shield, having strung the bow, they charge into battle massed on both sides, with arrows flying and spears flying, with swords flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, their heads are cut off with swords. There they undergo death and deadly suffering. This too, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:13: Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, having taken sword and shield, having strung the bow, they charge into battle with scaling ladders erected, with arrows flying and spears flying, with swords flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, boiling cauldrons are poured over them, crushed by the elephant's foot, their heads are cut off with swords. There they undergo death and deadly suffering. This too, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:15: Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, they engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind. Having engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. This too, monks, is a future danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:16: And what, monks, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not thus understand as it really is the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger in sensual pleasures as danger, and the escape from sensual pleasures as escape—it is impossible that they themselves will fully understand sensual pleasures or will instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, he will fully understand sensual pleasures. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, thus understand as it really is the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger in sensual pleasures as danger, and the escape from sensual pleasures as escape—it is possible that they themselves will fully understand sensual pleasures or will instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, he will fully understand sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:18: And what, monks, is the gratification in forms? Suppose, monks, there is a khattiya maiden or a brahmin maiden or a householder maiden, fifteen or sixteen years of age, not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, not too fair—is she at that time at the height of her beauty and loveliness? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ That happiness and joy that arises conditioned by that beauty and loveliness—this is the gratification in forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, monks, is the danger in forms? Here, monks, one might see that same sister at a later time as eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, bent double, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as she walks, sick, past her youth, with broken teeth, grey and wrinkled, with scanty hair, bald, wrinkled, with blotched limbs. What do you think, monks, has that former beauty and complexion vanished, has the danger become apparent? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then several monks, having dressed in the morning and taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: 'It is too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī; suppose we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?' Then those monks went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects; having exchanged greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to those monks:
translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own urine and excrement, being lifted up by others, being laid down by others. What do you think, monks, has that former beauty and complexion vanished, has the danger become apparent? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister's body thrown into a charnel ground—as a skeleton with flesh and blood, connected by sinews; as a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, connected by sinews; as a skeleton without flesh or blood, connected by sinews; as bones without connection, scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle-bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, here the skull. What do you think, monks, has that former beauty and complexion vanished, has the danger become apparent? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister's body thrown into a charnel ground—bones white like the color of conch shells; bones heaped up, more than a year old; bones rotted away to powder. What do you think, monks, has that former beauty and complexion vanished, has the danger become apparent? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:3: 'The ascetic Gotama, friends, proclaims full understanding of sensual pleasures; we too proclaim full understanding of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama, friends, proclaims full understanding of forms; we too proclaim full understanding of forms. The ascetic Gotama, friends, proclaims full understanding of feelings; we too proclaim full understanding of feelings. What, friends, is the distinction here, what is the difference, what is the divergence between the ascetic Gotama and us—that is, regarding the teaching or the teaching, regarding the instruction or the instruction?'
translations.mn13:30: And what, monks, is the escape from forms? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for forms—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, monks, is the gratification in feelings? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. At that time, monks, when a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both; he feels only a feeling that is not afflicted. I say, monks, that the gratification in feelings is maximum non-affliction.
translations.mn13:36: And what, monks, is the danger in feelings? That feelings are impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those monks neither approved nor disapproved of what those wanderers of other sects said; without approving or disapproving, they rose from their seats and departed: 'We will understand the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
translations.mn13:6: When wanderers of other sects speak thus, monks, they should be spoken to thus: 'But, friends, what is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in forms, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, what is the escape?' When asked thus, monks, wanderers of other sects will not be able to respond, and will further fall into distress. Why is that? Because, monks, it is not their domain. I do not see anyone, monks, in this world with its devas, with its Māra, with its Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, who could satisfy the mind with the explanation of these questions, apart from the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.mn13:8: And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Here, bhikkhus, a clansman makes a living by some craft—whether by accounting, calculation, reckoning, agriculture, trade, cattle-herding, archery, royal service, or by some other craft—exposed to cold, exposed to heat, afflicted by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, dying of hunger and thirst; this too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason.
translations.mn13:9: If, bhikkhus, when that clansman strives and struggles in this way, those riches do not come to success, he sorrows, grieves, and laments, weeps beating his breast and becomes distraught: 'My effort is futile, my striving is fruitless.' This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadhan country and arrived at Rājagaha; he approached Bhaggava the potter; having approached, he said to Bhaggava the potter:
translations.mn140:12: 'One should not be negligent of wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate relinquishment, should train for peace alone'—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is hard, solid, clung-to, that is, head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is hard, solid, clung-to—this is called, bhikkhu, the internal earth element. Now both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, he becomes disenchanted with the earth element, he detaches his mind from the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal water element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, clung-to, that is, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, oil of the joints, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, clung-to—this is called, bhikkhu, the internal water element. Now both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, he becomes disenchanted with the water element, he detaches his mind from the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, clung-to, that is, that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one burns, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, clung-to—this is called, bhikkhu, the internal fire element. Now both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, he becomes disenchanted with the fire element, he detaches his mind from the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, bhikkhu, is the air element? The air element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal air element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, clung-to, that is, winds going up, winds going down, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, clung-to—this is called, bhikkhu, the internal air element. Now both the internal air element and the external air element are simply the air element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, he becomes disenchanted with the air element, he detaches his mind from the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, bhikkhu, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal space element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, clung-to, that is, ear-holes, nose-holes, mouth, that by which one swallows what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted stands, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted passes down to the lower part, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, hollow, hollowed-out, an opening, opened-up, not contacted by flesh and blood, clung-to—this is called, bhikkhu, the internal space element. Now both the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, he becomes disenchanted with the space element, he detaches his mind from the space element.
translations.mn140:2: 'If it is not troublesome to you, Bhaggava, let us stay one night in your dwelling.' 'It is not troublesome to me, venerable sir. There is a wanderer who has already taken up residence here. If he gives permission, stay, venerable sir, as you please.'
translations.mn140:20: Then only equanimity remains, purified, bright, pliable, workable, and radiant. Just as, monk, a skilled goldsmith or goldsmith's apprentice would prepare a furnace, and having prepared the furnace, would stoke it, and having stoked it, would take gold with tongs and put it in the furnace, and from time to time would blow on it, from time to time sprinkle it with water, from time to time look on at it, that gold becomes well-worked, thoroughly worked, cleansed, free of dross, pliable, workable, and radiant, and whatever kind of ornament he wishes to make from it—whether a bracelet, or earrings, or a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves that purpose; so too, monk, then only equanimity remains, purified, bright, pliable, workable, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands 'It is impermanent,' he understands 'It is not clung to,' he understands 'It is not delighted in.' If he feels a painful feeling, he understands 'It is impermanent,' he understands 'It is not clung to,' he understands 'It is not delighted in.' If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands 'It is impermanent,' he understands 'It is not clung to,' he understands 'It is not delighted in.'
translations.mn140:29: 'Let one not be negligent in wisdom, let one preserve truth, let one cultivate relinquishment, let one train only in peace'—thus what was said, this was said in reference to this.
translations.mn140:3: Now at that time a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith in the Blessed One. He was the first to take up residence in that potter's shed. Then the Blessed One approached Venerable Pukkusāti; having approached, he said to Venerable Pukkusāti: 'If it is not burdensome to you, monk, let us dwell in this shed for one night.' 'The potter's shed is cramped, friend. Let the venerable one dwell as he pleases.'
translations.mn140:30: 'Where one stands, the floods of conceiving do not flow; and when the floods of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace'—this was said. In reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:31: 'I am,' monk, is a conceiving; 'I am this' is a conceiving; 'I shall be' is a conceiving; 'I shall not be' is a conceiving; 'I shall be possessed of form' is a conceiving; 'I shall be formless' is a conceiving; 'I shall be percipient' is a conceiving; 'I shall be non-percipient' is a conceiving; 'I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient' is a conceiving. Conceiving, monk, is a disease, conceiving is a boil, conceiving is a dart. By overcoming all conceivings, monk, one is called a sage at peace. And the sage at peace, monk, is not born, does not age, does not die, is not agitated, does not long for. For him, monk, there is nothing whereby he could be born; not being born, how could he age? Not aging, how could he die? Not dying, how could he be agitated? Not being agitated, what could he long for?
translations.mn140:32: 'Where one stands, the floods of conceiving do not flow; and when the floods of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace'—thus what was said, this was said in reference to this. You should remember this, monk, this brief analysis of the six elements by me.'
translations.mn140:33: Then Venerable Pukkusāti thought: 'The Teacher has come to me, the Fortunate One has come to me, the Perfectly Enlightened One has come to me,' and rising from his seat, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One: 'A transgression overcame me, venerable sir, like a fool, like a confused person, like an unskillful one, in that I thought to address the Blessed One with the term 'friend.' May the Blessed One, venerable sir, accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future.' 'Indeed, monk, a transgression overcame you, like a fool, like a confused person, like an unskillful one, in that you thought to address me with the term 'friend.' But since you, monk, see your transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it. For this is growth in the noble discipline, monk, when one sees one's transgression as a transgression and makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and enters upon restraint for the future.'
translations.mn140:34: May I receive the going forth, venerable sir, in the presence of the Blessed One?' 'But do you have a complete bowl and robes, monk?' 'I do not have a complete bowl and robes, venerable sir.' 'Monk, the Tathāgatas do not give the going forth to one without a complete bowl and robes.'
translations.mn140:35: Then Venerable Pukkusāti, having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's words, rising from his seat, paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, departed in search of a bowl and robes. Then while Venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a stray cow deprived him of life.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter's shed, and having prepared a spread of grass on one side, he sat down, cross-legged, having set his body straight, having established mindfulness in front of him. And the Blessed One spent much of the night sitting. Venerable Pukkusāti too spent much of the night sitting. Then the Blessed One thought: 'This clansman conducts himself in an agreeable manner. What if I were to question him?' Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: 'In reference to whom did you go forth, monk? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?' 'There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, a Sakyan, who went forth from the Sakyan clan. And of that Blessed One Gotama this good report has spread abroad: 'Thus indeed is that Blessed One, worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' I went forth in reference to that Blessed One. He is my teacher. I approve of the Dhamma of that Blessed One.' 'But where, monk, does that Blessed One, worthy, perfectly enlightened one, dwell now?' 'There is, friend, in the northern country a city named Sāvatthī. There that Blessed One, worthy, perfectly enlightened one, dwells now.' 'But have you seen that Blessed One before, monk; and having seen him, would you recognize him?' 'I have not seen that Blessed One before, friend; and having seen him, I would not recognize him.'
translations.mn140:6: Then the Blessed One thought: 'This clansman has gone forth out of faith in me. Let me teach him the Dhamma.' Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Pukkusāti: 'Bhikkhu, I will teach you the Dhamma. Listen, pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Venerable Pukkusāti replied. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn140:7: 'This person has six elements, six sense bases, eighteen mental examinations, and four foundations. When one stands there, floods of conceit do not flow; and when floods of conceit do not flow, one is called a silent sage. One should not be negligent in wisdom, should guard the truth, should cultivate relinquishment, and should train for peace alone'—this is the summary of the Analysis of the Elements.
translations.mn146:12: 'Sisters, I have given this simile for the purpose of conveying the meaning. This is the meaning here: 'inner flesh-body,' sisters, is a designation for the six internal sense bases; 'outer skin-body,' sisters, is a designation for the six external sense bases; 'inner tendons, inner sinews, inner bindings,' sisters, is a designation for delight and lust; 'sharp butcher's knife,' sisters, is a designation for this noble wisdom; with this noble wisdom one cuts, severs, carves, and chops the inner defilement, inner fetter, inner binding.
translations.mn146:13: Sisters, there are these seven factors of enlightenment, by the development and cultivation of which a bhikkhu, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. What seven? Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of states... the enlightenment factor of energy... the enlightenment factor of rapture... the enlightenment factor of tranquility... the enlightenment factor of concentration... the enlightenment factor of equanimity, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. These, sisters, are the seven factors of enlightenment, by the development and cultivation of which a bhikkhu, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge.
translations.mn146:14: Then Venerable Nandaka, having advised those bhikkhunis with this exhortation, dismissed them: 'Go, sisters; it is time.' Then those bhikkhunis, having rejoiced in and approved of Venerable Nandaka's words, rose from their seats, paid homage to Venerable Nandaka, and keeping him on their right, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those bhikkhunis, the Blessed One said to them: 'Go, bhikkhunis; it is time.' Then those bhikkhunis, having paid homage to the Blessed One and keeping him on their right, departed.
translations.mn146:3: Now on that occasion the elder bhikkhus were advising the bhikkhunis in turn. Venerable Nandaka did not wish to advise the bhikkhunis in turn. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: 'Whose turn is it today, Ānanda, to advise the bhikkhunis in turn?' 'All have had their turn, venerable sir, to advise the bhikkhunis in turn. Venerable Nandaka, venerable sir, does not wish to advise the bhikkhunis in turn.'
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Nandaka: 'Advise the bhikkhunis, Nandaka; instruct the bhikkhunis, Nandaka; make a Dhamma talk for the bhikkhunis, brahmin.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Venerable Nandaka replied. Having dressed in the morning, he took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, returning from the alms round, he went alone to the Rājakārāma. Those bhikkhunis saw Venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Having seen him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he washed his feet. Those bhikkhunis too paid homage to Venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhunis, Venerable Nandaka said to them:
translations.mn146:5: 'There will be a discussion, sisters. There, those who understand should say 'we understand,' those who do not understand should say 'we do not understand.' And if anyone has any doubt or uncertainty, I should be asked about that: 'Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this; what is the purpose of this?'' 'We are already satisfied and pleased with Venerable Nandaka, venerable sir, in that Venerable Nandaka invites us to ask.'
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'Rāhula's qualities that lead to liberation are mature. Let me lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints.' Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, returning from the alms round, he addressed Venerable Rāhula: 'Take a seat, Rāhula; let us go to the Blind's Grove for the day's abiding.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Venerable Rāhula replied. Having taken a seat, he followed the Blessed One, keeping close behind him.
translations.mn147:2: Now at that time many thousands of deities were following the Blessed One, thinking: "Today the Blessed One will lead the venerable Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints." Then the Blessed One, having plunged into the Blind Men's Grove, sat down on a seat prepared at the root of a certain tree. The venerable Rāhula too, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the venerable Rāhula, who was sitting to one side: "What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir." "Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir." "Is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.mn148:16: This, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the origin of identity—one regards the eye thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self';
translations.mn148:2: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I will make known the holy celibate life that is utterly perfect and pure, that is, the six internal and external sense bases. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: This, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of identity—one regards the eye thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'.
translations.mn148:3: "The six internal sense bases should be understood, the six external sense bases should be understood, the six classes of consciousness should be understood, the six classes of contact should be understood, the six classes of feeling should be understood, the six classes of craving should be understood.
translations.mn148:34: Bhikkhus, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When one is touched by pleasant feeling, one does not delight in it, welcome it, or remain attached to it. The underlying tendency to lust does not underlie that. When one is touched by painful feeling, one does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat one's breast, or fall into confusion. The underlying tendency to aversion does not underlie that. When one is touched by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands as it really is the origin and passing away, the gratification, danger, and escape in regard to that feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that. It is possible, bhikkhus, that by abandoning the underlying tendency to lust in regard to pleasant feeling, by dispelling the underlying tendency to aversion in regard to painful feeling, by eradicating the underlying tendency to ignorance in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, by abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge, one will here and now make an end of suffering.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes dispassionate toward the eye, becomes dispassionate toward forms, becomes dispassionate toward eye-consciousness, becomes dispassionate toward eye-contact, becomes dispassionate toward feeling, becomes dispassionate toward craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be fully understood by direct knowledge? The five aggregates subject to clinging should be said: that is, the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These are the things to be fully understood by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence—these are the things to be abandoned by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight—these are the things to be developed by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be realized by direct knowledge? True knowledge and liberation—these are the things to be realized by direct knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Great Discourse on the Six Sense Bases. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: "Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are, not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is, not knowing and not seeing as it really is whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one becomes enamored with the eye, becomes enamored with forms, becomes enamored with eye-consciousness, becomes enamored with eye-contact, becomes enamored with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For one who dwells thus enamored, attached, confused, seeing gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging increase in the future. And his craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, delighting now here now there—that too increases. For him both bodily torments and mental torments increase; both bodily fevers and mental fevers increase; both bodily burns and mental burns increase. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: For one who dwells thus enamored, attached, confused, seeing gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging increase in the future. And his craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, delighting now here now there—that too increases. For him both bodily torments and mental torments increase; both bodily fevers and mental fevers increase; both bodily burns and mental burns increase. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing the eye as it really is, knowing and seeing forms as they really are, knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, knowing and seeing eye-contact as it really is, knowing and seeing as it really is whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one does not become attached to the eye, does not become attached to forms, does not become attached to eye-consciousness, does not become attached to eye-contact, does not become attached to whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For one who dwells seeing the danger in what is unattracted, unbound, unconfused, the five aggregates subject to clinging go to decline in the future. Craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there—that too is abandoned. Bodily distresses are abandoned, mental distresses are abandoned; bodily fevers are abandoned, mental fevers are abandoned; bodily pariahs are abandoned, mental pariahs are abandoned. He experiences bodily happiness and mental happiness.
translations.mn19:11: Bhikkhus, whatever a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders, his mind inclines in that direction. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders the thought of renunciation, he abandons the thought of sensuality, makes much of the thought of renunciation, his mind inclines to the thought of renunciation. If, bhikkhus, [he thinks about] the thought of non-ill will ... If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders the thought of non-cruelty, he abandons the thought of cruelty, makes much of the thought of non-cruelty, his mind inclines to the thought of non-cruelty.
translations.mn19:12: Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been gathered into the village, a cowherd would guard the cows, and while he is at the root of a tree or in the open air, he needs only to be mindful: 'These are the cows.' So too, bhikkhus, I needed only to be mindful: 'These are the states.'
translations.mn19:13: And, bhikkhus, my energy was aroused without slackening, my mindfulness was established without confusion, my body was tranquil without disturbance, my mind was concentrated one-pointed.
translations.mn19:14: Then, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
translations.mn19:24: This, bhikkhus, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Just as, bhikkhus, there might be a large low-lying marsh in a forest grove, and a great herd of deer would dwell near it. Then a man might appear who is not desirous of their welfare, not desirous of their benefit, not desirous of their security from bondage. He would block up the safe, secure, pleasant path, open up the wrong path, set up a decoy, and station a decoy herdsman. Thus, bhikkhus, that great herd of deer would later meet with calamity and disaster. But then, bhikkhus, to that same great herd of deer a man might appear who is desirous of their welfare, desirous of their benefit, desirous of their security from bondage. He would open up the safe, secure, pleasant path, block up the wrong path, remove the decoy, and eliminate the decoy herdsman. Thus, bhikkhus, that great herd of deer would later meet with growth, increase, and expansion.
translations.mn19:26: This simile, bhikkhus, was made by me to convey the meaning. And here is the meaning: 'large low-lying marsh' is a designation for sensual pleasures. 'Great herd of deer' is a designation for beings. 'Man not desirous of welfare, not desirous of benefit, not desirous of security from bondage' is a designation for Māra the Evil One. 'Wrong path' is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, namely: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. 'Decoy' is a designation for delight and lust. 'Decoy herdsman' is a designation for ignorance. 'Man desirous of welfare, desirous of benefit, desirous of security from bondage' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'Safe, secure, pleasant path' is a designation for the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, bhikkhus, the safe, secure, pleasant path has been opened up by me, the wrong path blocked up, the decoy removed, the decoy herdsman eliminated.
translations.mn19:3: While I was dwelling thus, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a sensual thought arose in me. I understood thus: 'This sensual thought has arisen in me. It leads to my own affliction, to others' affliction, to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, is on the side of anguish, and does not lead to nibbāna.' When I considered: 'It leads to my own affliction,' it subsided; when I considered: 'It leads to others' affliction,' it subsided; when I considered: 'It leads to the affliction of both,' it subsided; when I considered: 'It obstructs wisdom, is on the side of anguish, and does not lead to nibbāna,' it subsided. So I abandoned, removed, and eliminated that sensual thought whenever it arose.
translations.mn19:6: Bhikkhus, whatever a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders, his mind inclines in that direction. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders the thought of sensuality, he abandons the thought of renunciation, makes much of the thought of sensuality, his mind inclines to the thought of sensuality. If, bhikkhus, [he thinks about] the thought of ill will ... If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders the thought of cruelty, he abandons the thought of non-cruelty, makes much of the thought of cruelty, his mind inclines to the thought of cruelty.
translations.mn19:7: Just as, monks, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn when the crops are thick, a cowherd would guard the cattle. He would strike them, push them, restrain them, and hold them back here and there with a stick. What is the reason for that? Because he sees that from that [carelessness] there would be slaughter, bondage, a fine, or blame. So too, monks, I saw the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of unwholesome states, and the benefit of renunciation as purification.
translations.mn19:8: When I, monks, was thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, the thought of renunciation arose in me. I understood thus: 'This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It leads neither to self-affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it is conducive to the growth of wisdom, conducive to non-obstruction, conducive to Nibbāna.' If I were to think and ponder upon this, monks, by night, I would see no danger from that. If I were to think and ponder upon this, monks, by day, I would see no danger from that. If I were to think and ponder upon this, monks, by night and day, I would see no danger from that. But if I were to think and ponder upon this for too long, my body would become tired. When the body is tired, the mind would be disturbed. When the mind is disturbed, it is far from concentration. So I, monks, steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated my mind internally. What is the reason for that? 'So that my mind will not be disturbed.'
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the root of a sāla tree. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: They perceive the Brahmā as Brahmā; having perceived the Brahmā as Brahmā, they conceive themselves as Brahmā, they conceive themselves in Brahmā, they conceive themselves as coming from Brahmā, they conceive 'Brahmā is mine,' they delight in Brahmā. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:11: They perceive the Ābhassara as Ābhassara; having perceived the Ābhassara as Ābhassara, they conceive themselves as Ābhassara, they conceive themselves in Ābhassara, they conceive themselves as coming from Ābhassara, they conceive 'Ābhassara is mine,' they delight in Ābhassara. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:123: Whatever monk, monks, is an arahant with taints destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive himself as earth, he does not conceive himself in earth, he does not conceive himself as coming from earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. What is the reason for that? Because of the destruction of delusion, because of being free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: They perceive the Vehapphala as Vehapphala; having perceived the Vehapphala as Vehapphala, they conceive themselves as Vehapphala, they conceive themselves in Vehapphala, they conceive themselves as coming from Vehapphala, they conceive 'Vehapphala is mine,' they delight in Vehapphala. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:14: They perceive the Abhibhu as Abhibhu; having perceived the Abhibhu as Abhibhu, they conceive themselves as Abhibhu, they conceive themselves in Abhibhu, they conceive themselves as coming from Abhibhu, they conceive 'Abhibhu is mine,' they delight in Abhibhu. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:147: The Tathāgata too, monks, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive himself as earth, he does not conceive himself in earth, he does not conceive himself as coming from earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has been fully understood by the Tathāgata.
translations.mn1:171: The Tathāgata too, monks, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive himself as earth, he does not conceive himself in earth, he does not conceive himself as coming from earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. What is the reason for that? 'Delight is the root of suffering'—thus knowing, 'for what has come to be there is birth, and for what is born there is aging and death.' Therefore, monks, I say 'the Tathāgata has awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment through the complete destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishing of all craving.'
translations.mn1:19: They perceive the seen as seen; having perceived the seen as seen, they conceive themselves as seen, they conceive themselves in the seen, they conceive themselves as coming from the seen, they conceive 'the seen is mine,' they delight in the seen. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:2: 'I will teach you, monks, the root of all things. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: They perceive the heard as heard; having perceived the heard as heard, they conceive themselves as heard, they conceive themselves in the heard, they conceive themselves as coming from the heard, they conceive 'the heard is mine,' they delight in the heard. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:22: They perceive the cognized as cognized; having perceived the cognized as cognized, they conceive themselves as cognized, they conceive themselves in the cognized, they conceive themselves as coming from the cognized, they conceive 'the cognized is mine,' they delight in the cognized. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:23: They perceive unity as unity; having perceived unity as unity, they conceive themselves as unity, they conceive themselves in unity, they conceive themselves as coming from unity, they conceive 'unity is mine,' they delight in unity. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:24: They perceive diversity as diversity; having perceived diversity as diversity, they conceive themselves as diversity, they conceive themselves in diversity, they conceive themselves as coming from diversity, they conceive 'diversity is mine,' they delight in diversity. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:25: They perceive all as all; having perceived all as all, they conceive themselves as all, they conceive themselves in all, they conceive themselves as coming from all, they conceive 'all is mine,' they delight in all. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:27: Whatever monk, monks, is in training, whose mind has not yet attained the goal, who dwells aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, let him not conceive himself as earth, let him not conceive himself in earth, let him not conceive himself as coming from earth, let him not conceive 'earth is mine,' let him not delight in earth. What is the reason for that? I say it is because it should be fully understood.
translations.mn1:3: “Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has no regard for the noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for good persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma— perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, they conceive it to be earth, they conceive it to be in earth, they conceive it to be from earth, they conceive 'earth is mine,' they delight in earth. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood, I say.
translations.mn1:4: They perceive water as water; having perceived water as water, they conceive it to be water, they conceive it to be in water, they conceive it to be from water, they conceive 'water is mine,' they delight in water. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood, I say.
translations.mn1:5: They perceive fire as fire; having perceived fire as fire, they conceive it to be fire, they conceive it to be in fire, they conceive it to be from fire, they conceive 'fire is mine,' they delight in fire. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood, I say.
translations.mn1:51: But also, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge— he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive it to be earth, he does not conceive it to be in earth, he does not conceive it to be from earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because it is fully understood, I say.
translations.mn1:7: They perceive beings as beings; having perceived beings as beings, they conceive them to be beings, they conceive them to be in beings, they conceive them to be from beings, they conceive 'beings are mine,' they delight in beings. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood, I say.
translations.mn1:8: They perceive gods as gods; having perceived gods as gods, they conceive them to be gods, they conceive them to be in gods, they conceive them to be from gods, they conceive 'gods are mine,' they delight in gods. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood, I say.
translations.mn1:9: They perceive Pajāpati as Pajāpati; having perceived Pajāpati as Pajāpati, they conceive him to be Pajāpati, they conceive him to be in Pajāpati, they conceive him to be from Pajāpati, they conceive 'Pajāpati is mine,' they delight in Pajāpati. Why is that? Because it is not fully understood, I say.
translations.mn20:2: “A bhikkhu who is intent on the higher mind, bhikkhus, should from time to time attend to five signs. What five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, bhikkhus, you should bear in mind whatever meaning of my statement you would understand. But whatever meaning of my statement you would not understand, I should be questioned about it in that matter, or else the competent bhikkhus.
translations.mn22:14: I have taught you the Dhamma, bhikkhus, like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. Understanding this, you should abandon even the Dhamma, how much more so what is contrary to the Dhamma.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Could there be, venerable sir, agitation about what is external?” “There could be, bhikkhu”—the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, it occurs to someone: 'Oh, may it have been mine! Oh, it is not mine! Oh, may it be mine! Oh, I do not get it!' He sorrows, grieves, laments, weeps beating his breast, and becomes confused. Thus, bhikkhu, there is agitation about what is external.”
translations.mn22:19: “But, venerable sir, could there be no agitation about what is external?” “There could be, bhikkhu”—the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, it does not occur to someone: 'Oh, may it have been mine! Oh, it is not mine! Oh, may it be mine! Oh, I do not get it!' He does not sorrow, does not grieve, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, and does not become confused. Thus, bhikkhu, there is no agitation about what is external.”
translations.mn22:20: “Could there be, venerable sir, agitation about what is internal?” “There could be, bhikkhu”—the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, someone has such a view: 'The world is the self, I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change; I will remain the same for eternity.' He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all views, standpoints, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies, for the stilling of all formations, for the relinquishing of all attachments, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna. It occurs to him: 'I will be annihilated, I will be destroyed, I will be no more.' He sorrows, grieves, laments, weeps beating his breast, and becomes confused. Thus, bhikkhu, there is agitation about what is internal.”
translations.mn22:23: That, bhikkhus, you should cling to as self-clinging, clinging to which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Do you see, bhikkhus, that self-clinging, clinging to which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair?” “No, venerable sir”. “Good, bhikkhus. I too do not see that self-clinging, clinging to which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.mn22:24: That, bhikkhus, you should rely on as reliance on view, relying on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Do you see, bhikkhus, that reliance on view, relying on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair?” “No, venerable sir”. “Good, bhikkhus. I too do not see that reliance on view, relying on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.mn22:25: If, bhikkhus, there were a self, would there be what belongs to my self?” “Yes, venerable sir”. “If, bhikkhus, there were what belongs to a self, would there be my self?” “Yes, venerable sir”. “Since, bhikkhus, a self and what belongs to a self are not apprehended as true and established, then this standpoint: 'The world is the self, I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change; I will remain the same for eternity'— is not this, bhikkhus, an entirely and completely foolish doctrine?” “How could it not be, venerable sir? It is entirely and completely a foolish doctrine, venerable sir.”
translations.mn22:27: “Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling … whatever perception … whatever volitional formations … whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness,
translations.mn22:29: becoming disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; when liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’
translations.mn22:30: This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has lifted the barrier, who has filled in the moat, who has pulled up the pillar, who is unbarred, a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached.
translations.mn22:31: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has lifted the barrier? Here, bhikkhus, ignorance has been abandoned by a bhikkhu, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has lifted the barrier.
translations.mn22:32: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has filled in the moat? Here, bhikkhus, the round of birth and death leading to renewed existence has been abandoned by a bhikkhu, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has filled in the moat.
translations.mn22:33: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has pulled up the pillar? Here, bhikkhus, craving has been abandoned by a bhikkhu, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has pulled up the pillar.
translations.mn22:34: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu unbarred? Here, bhikkhus, the five lower fetters have been abandoned by a bhikkhu, cut off at the root, made like palm stumps, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is unbarred.
translations.mn22:35: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached? Here, bhikkhus, the conceit ‘I am’ has been abandoned by a bhikkhu, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached.
translations.mn22:38: If, bhikkhus, others honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata in that way, there is no joy, no gladness, no elation of mind for the Tathāgata. If, bhikkhus, others honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata in that way, there is this for the Tathāgata: ‘What was formerly fully understood, it is for that that such acts are done for me.’
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, bhikkhus, if others abuse, revile, scold, and harass you, on that occasion you should not give rise to resentment, ill will, or mental displeasure. Therefore, bhikkhus, if others honor, respect, revere, and venerate you, on that occasion you should not give rise to joy, gladness, or elation of mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, if others honor, respect, revere, and venerate you, on that occasion this should be yours: ‘What was formerly fully understood, it is for that that such acts are done for me.’
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours; having abandoned it, it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.
translations.mn22:42: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks. Thus, bhikkhus, in the Dhamma well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks, those bhikkhus who are arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—for them there is no round for describing.
translations.mn22:43: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks. Thus, bhikkhus, in the Dhamma well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks, those bhikkhus for whom the five lower fetters have been abandoned—all of them are due to appear spontaneously and there attain final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world.
translations.mn22:44: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks. Thus, bhikkhus, in the Dhamma well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks, those bhikkhus for whom the three fetters have been abandoned, with lust, hatred, and delusion attenuated—all of them are once-returners, returning once to this world to make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks. Thus, bhikkhus, in the Dhamma well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks, those bhikkhus for whom the three fetters have been abandoned—all of them are stream-enterers, no longer bound for the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.
translations.mn22:46: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks. Thus, bhikkhus, in the Dhamma well expounded by me, made manifest, opened up, cleared of its husks, those bhikkhus who are Dhamma-followers and faith-followers—all of them have enlightenment as their destination.
translations.mn22:6: “Who indeed, you foolish man, do you understand the Dhamma as taught by me in this way? Have I not, you foolish man, spoken of obstructive things in many ways as obstructive? And indulging in them is sufficient for obstruction. Sensual pleasures have been spoken of by me as having little gratification, much suffering, much trouble, and danger is greater here. Sensual pleasures have been spoken of by me as comparable to a skeleton … comparable to a piece of meat … comparable to a grass torch … comparable to a pit of coals … comparable to a dream … comparable to borrowed goods … comparable to the fruit of a tree … comparable to a slaughterhouse … comparable to a sword stake … comparable to a snake's head, having much suffering, much trouble, and danger is greater here. And yet you, you foolish man, with your own wrong grasp, slander us and destroy yourself, and produce much demerit. That, you foolish man, will be for your harm and suffering for a long time.”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “What do you think, monks, could this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture trainers, be even slightly warm in this Dhamma and Discipline?” “How could he, venerable sir? No, venerable sir.” When this was said, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture trainers, sat silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to reply. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture trainers, was silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to reply, said to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture trainers: “You will be known by this your own evil view. Here I will question the monks.”
translations.mn22:9: It is impossible, monks, that one could indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual pleasures, apart from perceptions of sensual pleasures, apart from thoughts of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn26:10: And what, monks, do you call subject to sorrow? Wife and children, monks, are subject to sorrow, slaves and servants are subject to sorrow, goats and sheep are subject to sorrow, chickens and pigs are subject to sorrow, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to sorrow. Here this one, attached, infatuated, fallen into, being himself subject to sorrow, seeks what is subject to sorrow.
translations.mn26:11: And what, monks, do you call subject to defilement? Wife and children, monks, are subject to defilement, slaves and servants are subject to defilement, goats and sheep are subject to defilement, chickens and pigs are subject to defilement, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to defilement, gold and silver are subject to defilement. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to defilement. Here this one, attached, infatuated, fallen into, being himself subject to defilement, seeks what is subject to defilement. This, monks, is ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: I too, monks, before my enlightenment, when I was still unenlightened but a bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth, sought what is subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, sought what is subject to aging; being myself subject to sickness, sought what is subject to sickness; being myself subject to death, sought what is subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, sought what is subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement, sought what is subject to defilement. Then, monks, this occurred to me: ‘Why do I, being myself subject to birth, seek what is subject to birth, being myself subject to aging … subject to sickness … subject to death … subject to sorrow … being myself subject to defilement, seek what is subject to defilement? Suppose I, being myself subject to birth, having known the danger in what is subject to birth, should seek the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to aging, having known the danger in what is subject to aging, should seek the unaging, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to sickness, having known the danger in what is subject to sickness, should seek the sickness-free, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to death, having known the danger in what is subject to death, should seek the deathless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to sorrow, having known the danger in what is subject to sorrow, should seek the sorrow-free, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to defilement, having known the danger in what is subject to defilement, should seek the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna.’
translations.mn26:14: Then I, monks, at a later time, being still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, having shaved off my hair and beard, and having put on ochre robes, went forth from the home life into homelessness, though my parents wished otherwise, with tearful faces, weeping.
translations.mn26:17: Then I, monks, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, most excellent state of peace, wandering by stages in the Magadhan country, arrived at Uruvelā, the Senānigama. There I saw a delightful stretch of ground, a lovely grove, a flowing river with clear, agreeable, delightful water, with good fords, and villages nearby for alms. Then, monks, this occurred to me: ‘This stretch of ground is indeed delightful, the grove is lovely, the river flows with clear, agreeable, delightful water, with good fords, and villages nearby for alms. This is indeed sufficient for a clansman desiring to strive for striving.’ Then I, monks, sat down right there—‘This is sufficient for striving.’
translations.mn26:21: Then, bhikkhus, having understood Brahmā's request and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha's eye.  Surveying the world with the Buddha's eye, bhikkhus, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to instruct and hard to instruct, and some dwelling seeing fear in blame in the other world, and some not dwelling seeing fear in blame in the other world.  Just as, bhikkhus, in a pond of blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses, some blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, submerged in the water, thrive inside the water; some blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, stand at the level of the water; some blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, rise above the water and stand unsoiled by the water;  even so, bhikkhus, surveying the world with the Buddha's eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to instruct and hard to instruct, and some dwelling seeing fear in blame in the other world, and some not dwelling seeing fear in blame in the other world.
