Then, bhikkhus, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse:  'The doors to the deathless are opened,  Let those with ears release faith;  Foreseeing trouble, I did not speak,  The refined Dhamma among humans, Brahmā.'  Then, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking 'The Blessed One has made an opportunity for teaching the Dhamma,' having paid homage to me, keeping me on his right, disappeared right there.
translations.mn26:25: Upaka the Ājīvaka saw me, bhikkhus, traveling on the road between Gayā and Bodhi.  Having seen me, he said to me:  'Your faculties are serene, friend, your complexion is pure and bright.  For whose sake have you gone forth, friend, or who is your teacher, or whose Dhamma do you delight in?'  When this was said, bhikkhus, I replied to Upaka the Ājīvaka in verses:  'I am one who has conquered all, knower of all,  Unstained by all things;  Having abandoned all, liberated by the destruction of craving,  Having known for myself, whom should I point to?  There is no teacher for me,  None like me is found;  In the world with its devas,  There is no rival for me.  I am an arahant in the world,  I am the unsurpassed teacher;  I alone am perfectly self-enlightened,  Cooled and quenched.  To set rolling the Dhamma wheel,  I go to the city of Kāsi;  In a world blinded,  I shall beat the drum of deathlessness.'  'As you claim, friend, you are worthy to be an infinite victor.'  'Victors like me are those  Who have attained the destruction of the taints;  Evil states are conquered by me,  Therefore, Upaka, I am a victor.'  When this was said, bhikkhus, Upaka the Ājīvaka, saying 'May it be so, friend,' shook his head, took a side road, and departed.
translations.mn26:26: Then, bhikkhus, wandering by stages, I approached the group of five bhikkhus at the Deer Park in Bārāṇasī at Isipatana.  The group of five bhikkhus saw me, bhikkhus, coming from afar.  Having seen me, they agreed among themselves:  'This ascetic Gotama is coming, friend, indulgent, having abandoned the struggle, returned to indulgence.  He should not be greeted, nor should one rise for him; his bowl and robe should not be accepted.  But a seat may be placed, if he wishes he will sit.'  But, bhikkhus, as I approached, the group of five bhikkhus were unable to keep to their agreement.  Some rose to meet me and accepted my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, some set out water for washing the feet.  Yet they addressed me by name and as 'friend.'
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, bhikkhus, I said to the group of five bhikkhus:  'Do you remember, bhikkhus, that I ever previously made such a declaration?'  'No, venerable sir.'  'The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an arahant, perfectly self-enlightened.  Give ear, bhikkhus, the deathless has been attained, I instruct, I teach the Dhamma.  Practicing as instructed, you will not long dwell—having yourselves directly known and realized in this very life that unsurpassed goal of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.'
translations.mn26:29: I was able, bhikkhus, to persuade the group of five bhikkhus.  At one time, bhikkhus, I instructed two bhikkhus, and three bhikkhus went for alms.  What the three bhikkhus brought back from going for alms, that was what the six of us lived on.  At one time, bhikkhus, I instructed three bhikkhus, and two bhikkhus went for alms.  What the two bhikkhus brought back from going for alms, that was what the six of us lived on.
translations.mn26:30: Then, bhikkhus, the group of five bhikkhus, being thus instructed and thus advised by me, being subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to aging … being subject to sickness … being subject to death … being subject to sorrow … being subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna.  And knowledge and vision arose in them:  'Our liberation is unshakeable, this is our last birth, there is no more renewed existence.'
translations.mn26:31: There are, mendicants, these five kinds of sensual stimulation. What five? Sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds known by the ear … Smells known by the nose … Tastes known by the tongue … Touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
translations.mn26:34: Suppose, mendicants, a deer in the wilderness, in a forest grove, goes about confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, and lies down confidently. Why is that? Because it is out of the hunter's range. In the same way, mendicants, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra, who has made him eyeless, who has destroyed Māra's sight, who has gone unseen by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:35: Furthermore, mendicants, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and confidence, and without placing the mind and keeping it connected. This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:36: Furthermore, mendicants, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant remains equanimous, mindful and aware, and experiences bliss with the body. They enter and remain in the third absorption, of which the noble ones declare: 'Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in bliss.' This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:37: Furthermore, mendicants, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the ending of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:38: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:39: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Buddha went to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. Now at that time several mendicants were sitting together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka, engaged in a Dhamma discussion. Then the Buddha stood outside the door waiting for the discussion to end. When he knew the discussion had ended, he coughed and knocked with the latch. The mendicants opened the door for the Buddha. Then the Buddha entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the seat spread out. Seated, the Buddha said to the mendicants: 'Mendicants, what was the discussion you were sitting together for? And what was the discussion that was left unfinished?' 'Venerable sir, the Dhamma discussion we were sitting together for was about the Buddha himself, and then the Buddha arrived.' 'Good, mendicants! It is proper for you as gentlemen who have gone forth in faith from the lay life to homelessness to sit together for a Dhamma discussion. When you gather together, mendicants, you should do one of two things: have a Dhamma discussion or noble silence.
translations.mn26:40: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing at all,' enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:41: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. This is called a mendicant … by the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:5: There are, mendicants, these two kinds of search: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, mendicants, is the ignoble search? Here, mendicants, someone who is himself subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth; himself subject to aging seeks only what is subject to aging; himself subject to sickness seeks only what is subject to sickness; himself subject to death seeks only what is subject to death; himself subject to sorrow seeks only what is subject to sorrow; himself subject to defilement seeks only what is subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, mendicants, do you call subject to birth? Wife and children, mendicants, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These acquisitions, mendicants, are subject to birth. Attached, infatuated, and fallen into this, someone who is himself subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth.
translations.mn27:12: A householder or householder's son or someone born in a good family hears that Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma, they gain faith in the Tathāgata. Possessing that faith, they reflect: 'Living in a house is cramped and dirty, but the life of one gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the spiritual life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?' After some time, abandoning a large or small fortune, abandoning a large or small circle of relatives, they shave off their hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having thus gone forth, he becomes one who has undertaken the training and way of life of the monks, abandoning the killing of living beings, he abstains from killing living beings, with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and merciful, he dwells compassionate to all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given, taking only what is given, expecting only what is given, by means of this pure mode of living he dwells. Abandoning uncelibacy, he is celibate, living apart, abstaining from the village practice of sexual intercourse. Abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech, he is a speaker of truth, one to be relied on, trustworthy, dependable, not a deceiver of the world. Abandoning divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech, having heard something here he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of causing division among these, or having heard something elsewhere he does not repeat it here for the purpose of causing division among those. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided, a promoter of friendships, one who delights in concord, rejoices in concord, delights in concord, he speaks words that promote concord. Abandoning harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech, he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, agreeable, going to the heart, urbane, pleasing and agreeable to many people. Abandoning idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter, he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is factual, speaks on what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline, his words are worth treasuring, timely, well-reasoned, well-defined, connected with the goal. He abstains from injuring seeds and plants, he eats only one meal a day, abstaining from eating at night, outside the proper time, he abstains from dancing, singing, music, and theatrical performances, he abstains from wearing garlands, applying scents, and beautifying himself with ointments and ornaments, he abstains from high and luxurious beds, he abstains from accepting gold and silver, he abstains from accepting raw grain, he abstains from accepting raw meat, he abstains from accepting women and girls, he abstains from accepting male and female slaves, he abstains from accepting goats and sheep, he abstains from accepting fowl and pigs, he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares, he abstains from accepting fields and land, he abstains from running errands and acting as a go-between, he abstains from buying and selling, he abstains from false weights, false metals, and false measures, he abstains from bribery, fraud, cheating, and crooked practices, he abstains from mutilating, killing, binding, robbing, plundering, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to maintain his stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden, so too a monk is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to maintain his stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Possessed of this noble aggregate of moral discipline, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.
translations.mn27:15: On seeing a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unrestrained, bad unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade him, he practices restraint, guards the eye faculty, achieves restraint over the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear … On smelling an odor with the nose … On tasting a flavor with the tongue … On touching a tactile object with the body … On cognizing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unrestrained, bad unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade him, he practices restraint, guards the mind faculty, achieves restraint over the mind faculty. Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself an unblemished happiness.
translations.mn27:16: He is one who acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning, when looking ahead and looking aside, when bending and stretching, when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes, when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, when defecating and urinating, when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Possessed of this noble aggregate of moral discipline, possessed of this noble contentment, possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, possessed of this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded dwelling: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, the open air, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: Having returned from his almsround, after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body straight, and establishing mindfulness before him. Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies his mind from covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Having abandoned dullness and drowsiness, he dwells free from dullness and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending, he purifies his mind from dullness and drowsiness. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly peaceful, he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having gone beyond doubt, unperplexed about wholesome states, he purifies his mind from doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This too is called, brahmin, the footprint of the Tathāgata, the track of the Tathāgata, the path trodden by the Tathāgata. But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was setting out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day with a completely white mule carriage. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar. Having seen the wanderer Pilotika, he said to him: "Well now, where is Master Vacchāyana coming from in the middle of the day?" "Sir, I am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama." "What does Master Vacchāyana think of the ascetic Gotama's proficiency of wisdom—does he seem wise?" "Who am I, sir, who would know the ascetic Gotama's proficiency of wisdom? Indeed, he would be such a one who would know the ascetic Gotama's proficiency of wisdom." "Master Vacchāyana surely praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise." "Who am I, sir, who would praise the ascetic Gotama? Praised as he is, that Master Gotama is supreme among devas and humans." "But what reason does Master Vacchāyana see for having such confidence in the ascetic Gotama?"
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of samādhi. This too is called, brahmin …pe… the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well."
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, of which the noble ones declare: 'Equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily,' he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This too is called, brahmin …pe… the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well."
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This too is called, brahmin, the Tathāgata's footprint, or the Tathāgata's resort, or the Tathāgata's domain. But even so, a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well.'
translations.mn27:3: "Just as, sir, a skilled elephant tracker would enter an elephant forest. He would see in the elephant forest a large elephant's footprint, long in extent and broad across. He would come to the conclusion: 'Indeed, sir, this is a great elephant.' Even so, sir, when I saw in the ascetic Gotama these four footprints, then I came to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well.'
translations.mn27:4: What are the four? Here, sir, I see certain warrior-nobles who are learned, subtle, who have mastered the doctrines of others, sharp as archers. They seem to wander about breaking apart view-creations with their wisdom. They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama, sir, will enter such and such a village or town.' They prepare a question: 'Having approached the ascetic Gotama, we will ask him this question. If he answers us thus when asked, we will refute him in this way. And if he answers us thus when asked, we will refute him in this way too.' They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama, sir, has entered such and such a village or town.' They approach the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, encourages, inspires, and gladdens them with a Dhamma talk. Instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a Dhamma talk, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama a question—how could they refute him? On the contrary, they become the ascetic Gotama's disciples. When, sir, I saw in the ascetic Gotama this first footprint, then I came to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well.'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One all the conversation he had had with the wanderer Pilotika. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: "Brahmin, the simile of the elephant's footprint is not yet complete in detail in this way. But, brahmin, listen to how the simile of the elephant's footprint is complete in detail, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, sir," the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus." "Friend," those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:10: If, friends, while that bhikkhu is recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established, he is stirred by that and becomes agitated: 'It is a loss for me, it is no gain for me; it is bad luck for me, it is no good luck for me, that while I am recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established.' Just as, friends, a daughter-in-law is stirred and becomes agitated upon seeing her father-in-law; so too, friends, if while that bhikkhu is recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established, he is stirred by that and becomes agitated: 'It is a loss for me, it is no gain for me; it is bad luck for me, it is no good luck for me, that while I am recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established.' If, friends, while that bhikkhu is recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome becomes established, he becomes satisfied with that. Even to this extent, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element erupts. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean sinks down a hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, five hundred yojanas, six hundred yojanas, seven hundred yojanas. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean there remains water to the depth of seven palm trees, six palm trees, five palm trees, four palm trees, three palm trees, two palm trees, one palm tree. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean there remains water to the depth of seven men, six men, five men, four men, three men, two men, one man. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean there remains water to the depth of half a man, to the depth of the hips, to the depth of the knees, to the depth of the ankles. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean there is not even water the depth of a finger-joint. For even this external water element, so vast, its impermanence will be evident, its nature of destruction will be evident, its nature of vanishing will be evident, its nature of change will be evident.
translations.mn28:13: What then of this body, clung to by craving, of such brief duration? Rather, there is no 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am' in this.
translations.mn28:14: If, friends, while that bhikkhu is recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome becomes established, he becomes satisfied with that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friends, when the external fire element erupts. It burns villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. Reaching a green field, a road, a rocky area, water, or a delightful piece of ground, it goes out for lack of fuel. There comes a time, friends, when they seek fire with a cock's feather or a strip of sinew. For even this external fire element, so vast, its impermanence will be evident, its nature of destruction will be evident, its nature of vanishing will be evident, its nature of change will be evident. What then of this body, clung to by craving, of such brief duration?
translations.mn28:18-20: Rather, there is no 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am' in this. If, friends, while that bhikkhu is recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Saṅgha thus, equanimity supported by the wholesome becomes established, he becomes satisfied with that. Even to this extent, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:2: Just as, friends, whatever kinds of footprints of jungle creatures there are, all of them are encompassed by the elephant's footprint, and the elephant's footprint is declared to be supreme among them in terms of greatness; so too, friends, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are encompassed by the four noble truths. In which four? In the noble truth of suffering, in the noble truth of the origin of suffering, in the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, in the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friends, when the external air element erupts. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friends, in the last month of the hot season when they seek wind with a palm-leaf fan or a fan, and they do not want even grass in the drip-irrigated fields. For even this external air element, so vast, its impermanence will be evident, its nature of destruction will be evident, its nature of vanishing will be evident, its nature of change will be evident. What then of this body, clung to by craving, of such brief duration? Rather, there is no 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am' in this.
translations.mn28:23: If, friends, others abuse, revile, scold, and torment that bhikkhu, he understands thus: 'This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me. That is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.' He sees that contact is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. His mind, with the elements as its object, leaps forward, settles, becomes steady, and becomes concentrated.
translations.mn28:24: If, friends, others attack that monk with what is disagreeable, unpleasing, and unwelcome—by hand contact, clod contact, stick contact, or knife contact—he understands thus: 'This body is of such a nature that hand contacts impinge upon it, clod contacts impinge upon it, stick contacts impinge upon it, knife contacts impinge upon it. But this was said by the Blessed One in the Simile of the Saw: "Even if, monks, bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, whoever would give rise to a mind of hatred on that account would not be carrying out my teaching." My energy will be aroused and unslackening, mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and unexcited, my mind concentrated and unified. Let hand contacts impinge upon this body, let clod contacts impinge upon it, let stick contacts impinge upon it, let knife contacts impinge upon it. This is the teaching of the Buddhas that is being practiced.'
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friends, when space is enclosed by timber and vines and grass and clay, it comes to be called a house; so too, friends, when space is enclosed by bones and sinews and flesh and skin, it comes to be called form.
translations.mn28:27: If, friends, the internal eye is intact but external forms do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding class of consciousness. If, friends, the internal eye is intact and external forms come into its range, but there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding class of consciousness. But when, friends, the internal eye is intact and external forms come into its range, and there is corresponding engagement, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding class of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: Whatever form there is in one who is thus constituted is included in the form clinging-aggregate; whatever feeling there is in one who is thus constituted is included in the feeling clinging-aggregate; whatever perception there is in one who is thus constituted is included in the perception clinging-aggregate; whatever formations there are in one who is thus constituted are included in the formations clinging-aggregate; whatever consciousness there is in one who is thus constituted is included in the consciousness clinging-aggregate. He understands thus: 'So it seems that there is a coming together, a concurrence, a combination of these five clinging-aggregates. But this was said by the Blessed One: "One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination." These five clinging-aggregates are dependently originated. Whatever desire, attachment, delight, and clinging there is regarding these five clinging-aggregates is the origin of suffering. Whatever removal and abandonment of desire and lust regarding these five clinging-aggregates is the cessation of suffering.' To this extent, friends, much has been done by a monk.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. And what, friends, are the five clinging-aggregates? Namely: the form clinging-aggregate, the feeling clinging-aggregate, the perception clinging-aggregate, the formations clinging-aggregate, the consciousness clinging-aggregate.
translations.mn28:37: the mind is intact but external phenomena do not come into its range and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding class of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element is disturbed. At that time the external earth element disappears. For even this external earth element, so vast, its impermanence will be evident, its nature of destruction will be evident, its nature of vanishing will be evident, its nature of change will be evident. What then of this body, which is clung to by craving, so small and fleeting—'I am' or 'mine' or 'I exist'? Indeed, it is not found there.
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the monks with reference to Devadatta:
translations.mn29:3: Here, monks, some clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith: 'I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; overwhelmed by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.' Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and praise. He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and praise, his purpose is not fulfilled. He does not extol himself or disparage others because of that gain, honor, and praise. He does not become intoxicated, negligent, or fall into negligence because of it. Being heedful, he achieves accomplishment in virtue. He is satisfied with that accomplishment in virtue, his purpose is fulfilled. He extols himself and disparages others because of that accomplishment in virtue: 'I am virtuous, of good character, but these other monks are immoral, of bad character.' He becomes intoxicated, negligent, and falls into negligence because of that accomplishment in virtue; being negligent, he dwells in suffering. Just as, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passing by the heartwood, passing by the sapwood, passing by the bark, cutting off the outer bark, would take it away thinking it was heartwood. A man with good sight, seeing him, would say: 'This good man did not know the heartwood, did not know the sapwood, did not know the bark, did not know the outer bark, did not know the branches and foliage. Thus this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passing by the heartwood, passing by the sapwood, passing by the bark, cutting off the outer bark, has taken it away thinking it was heartwood; and whatever he had to do with heartwood, that purpose of his will not be served.'
translations.mn2:10: And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should not be attended to, which when attended to cause unarisen defilements to arise and arisen defilements to increase? For a bhikkhu who attends to certain things, if unarisen sensual defilement arises, or arisen sensual defilement increases; if unarisen defilement of existence arises, or arisen defilement of existence increases; if unarisen defilement of ignorance arises, or arisen defilement of ignorance increases—these are the things that should not be attended to, which when attended to cause unarisen defilements to arise and arisen defilements to increase. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be attended to, which when attended to cause unarisen defilements not to arise and arisen defilements to be abandoned? For a bhikkhu who attends to certain things, if unarisen sensual defilement does not arise, or arisen sensual defilement is abandoned; if unarisen defilement of existence does not arise, or arisen defilement of existence is abandoned; if unarisen defilement of ignorance does not arise, or arisen defilement of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things that should be attended to, which when attended to cause unarisen defilements not to arise and arisen defilements to be abandoned. By not attending to things that should not be attended to and by attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen defilements do not arise and arisen defilements are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: He attends properly: 'This is suffering,' he attends properly: 'This is the origin of suffering,' he attends properly: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' he attends properly: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' When he attends in this way, three fetters are abandoned: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rites and rituals. These are called, bhikkhus, the defilements to be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Defilements to be Abandoned by Restraint And what, bhikkhus, are the defilements to be abandoned by restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, having properly reflected. For, bhikkhus, whatever defilements of distress and burning might arise for one dwelling unrestrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, for one dwelling restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, those defilements of distress and burning do not exist thus. Having properly reflected, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the ear faculty …pe… restrained with the restraint of the nose faculty …pe… restrained with the restraint of the tongue faculty …pe… restrained with the restraint of the body faculty …pe… restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty. For, bhikkhus, whatever defilements of distress and burning might arise for one dwelling unrestrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, for one dwelling restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, those defilements of distress and burning do not exist thus. For, bhikkhus, whatever defilements of distress and burning might arise for one dwelling unrestrained with restraint, for one dwelling restrained with restraint, those defilements of distress and burning do not exist thus. These are called, bhikkhus, the defilements to be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Having properly reflected, he makes use of almsfood: 'Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for decoration, but just enough for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for keeping it unharmed, for supporting the spiritual life, thinking:
translations.mn2:16: Having properly reflected, he makes use of medicinal requisites for the sick: 'Just enough for the warding off of painful feelings that have arisen, for maximum freedom from affliction.'
translations.mn2:17: For, bhikkhus, whatever defilements of distress and burning might arise for one not making use of them, for one making use of them, those defilements of distress and burning do not exist thus. These are called, bhikkhus, the defilements to be abandoned by using.
translations.mn2:3: I say, bhikkhus, that the destruction of the defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. What, bhikkhus, does one know and what does one see for the destruction of the defilements? Proper attention and improper attention. For one who attends improperly, bhikkhus, unarisen defilements arise and arisen defilements increase; but for one who attends properly, bhikkhus, unarisen defilements do not arise and arisen defilements are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should not be attended to, which when attended to cause unarisen defilements to arise and arisen defilements to increase? For a bhikkhu who attends to certain things, if unarisen sensual defilement arises, or arisen sensual defilement increases; if unarisen defilement of existence arises, or arisen defilement of existence increases; if unarisen defilement of ignorance arises, or arisen defilement of ignorance increases—these are the things that should not be attended to, which when attended to cause unarisen defilements to arise and arisen defilements to increase. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be attended to, which when not attended to cause unarisen defilements not to arise and arisen defilements to be abandoned? For a bhikkhu who attends to certain things, if unarisen sensual defilement does not arise, or arisen sensual defilement is abandoned; if unarisen defilement of existence does not arise, or arisen defilement of existence is abandoned; if unarisen defilement of ignorance does not arise, or arisen defilement of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things that should be attended to, which when not attended to cause unarisen defilements not to arise and arisen defilements to be abandoned.
translations.mn2:7: For him, by attending to things that should not be attended to and by not attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen defilements arise and arisen defilements increase. He attends improperly thus: 'Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?' Or else he is inwardly perplexed about the present thus: 'Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will it go?'
translations.mn2:8: When he attends unwisely in this way, one of six views arises in him. The view 'I have a self' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I have no self' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with self' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I perceive not-self with self' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with not-self' arises in him as true and established; or else he has such a view: 'This self of mine that speaks and feels, that experiences the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions here and there—this self of mine is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will endure as long as eternity.' This, bhikkhus, is called the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the contortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views. Fettered by the fetter of views, bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say he is not freed from suffering.
translations.mn2:9: But, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple—who is a seer of the noble ones, well trained and well practiced in the noble Dhamma, a seer of superior persons, well trained and well practiced in the Dhamma of superior persons—understands what things should be attended to and what things should not be attended to. Understanding thus what things should be attended to and what things should not be attended to, he does not attend to those things that should not be attended to, and he attends to those things that should be attended to.
translations.mn31:10: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, while dwelling thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling?' 'How could it not be so, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, venerable sir, is the superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, the comfortable dwelling, that we have attained while dwelling thus heedful, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.mn31:11-13: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, by surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling?' 'How could it not be so, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, with the subsiding of thought and examination, we enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. By surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, this other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, the comfortable dwelling, has been attained by us.'
translations.mn31:14: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, by surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling?' 'How could it not be so, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, with the fading away as well of rapture, we dwell equanimous and, mindful and fully aware, we experience happiness with the body; that which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily,' we enter and dwell in the third jhāna. By surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, this other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, the comfortable dwelling, has been attained by us.'
translations.mn31:15: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, by surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling?' 'How could it not be so, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, we enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. By surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, this other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, the comfortable dwelling, has been attained by us.'
translations.mn31:16: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, by surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling?' 'How could it not be so, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, by completely surmounting perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' we enter and dwell in the base of infinite space. By surmounting this dwelling, by transcending this dwelling, this other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, the comfortable dwelling, has been attained by us.'
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: Now on that occasion Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood.
translations.mn31:3: Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood. The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming in the distance. Having seen him, he said to the Blessed One: 'Do not enter this park, ascetic. There are three clansmen dwelling here who are devoted to their own good. Do not disturb their comfort.'
translations.mn31:4: Venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper conversing with the Blessed One. Having heard, he said to the park keeper: 'Do not, friend park keeper, keep out the Blessed One. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.' Then Venerable Anuruddha approached Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila; having approached, he said to Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila: 'Come forth, venerable ones, come forth, venerable ones; our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.'
translations.mn31:5: Then Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimila, having gone out to meet the Blessed One, one received his bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, one set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Those venerable ones, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Venerable Anuruddha: "I hope you are keeping well, Anuruddhas, I hope you are comfortable, I hope you are not tired from almsfood?" "We are keeping well, Blessed One, we are comfortable; we are not tired from almsfood, venerable sir."
translations.mn31:6: "But are you living in concord, Anuruddhas, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?" "Surely, venerable sir, we are living in concord with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes." "But how, Anuruddhas, are you living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?"
translations.mn31:9: "Surely, venerable sir, we are dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute." "But how, Anuruddhas, are you dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute?" "Here, venerable sir, whichever of us returns first from the village with almsfood prepares the seats, sets out water for drinking and washing, and sets out the refuse bucket. Whoever returns last from the village with almsfood, if there is leftover food and he wishes, he eats; if he does not wish, he discards it in a place without vegetation or drops it into water without living beings. He puts away the seats, puts away the water for drinking and washing, puts away the refuse bucket, and sweeps the dining hall. Whoever sees a water pot for drinking, a water pot for washing, or a toilet pot empty or vacant, sets it out. If it is beyond his capacity, he invites a companion by a hand signal, and we set it out by lifting with our hands; but, venerable sir, we do not break into speech on that account. And every five days, venerable sir, we sit together for a Dhamma discussion all night long. Thus, venerable sir, we are dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute."
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: "I have confidence in Master Gotama thus: Master Gotama is developed in body and developed in mind." "Surely, Aggivessana, this statement of yours was made casually and without reflection; nevertheless, I will answer you. Since I, Aggivessana, having shaved off my hair and beard and put on the ochre robe, went forth from the home life into homelessness, it is impossible that when a pleasant feeling has arisen, it should invade my mind and remain, or when a painful feeling has arisen, it should invade my mind and remain."
translations.mn36:12: "What could there be, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this occurred to me: 'The household life is crowded, a dusty path; the going forth is like the open air. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.'"
translations.mn36:2: Now on that occasion, in the early morning, the Blessed One had dressed and, taking his bowl and robe, was intending to go into Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Suppose I clench my teeth, press my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and restrain, press, and torment my mind with my mind.' So I, Aggivessana, clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and restrained, pressed, and tormented my mind with my mind. Sweat ran from my armpits. Just as, Aggivessana, a strong man might seize a weaker man by the head or shoulders and restrain, press, and torment him; so too, Aggivessana, when I clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and restrained, pressed, and tormented my mind with my mind, sweat ran from my armpits. And although my energy was aroused and unremitting, my mindfulness was established and unshaken, yet my body was strained and unrelieved because of the painful striving. Such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:26: Some devas, Aggivessana, on seeing me, said: 'The ascetic Gotama has died.' Other devas said: 'The ascetic Gotama has not died, but he is dying.' Other devas said: 'The ascetic Gotama has not died, nor is he dying; the ascetic Gotama is an arahant, for such is the dwelling of an arahant.'
translations.mn36:27: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Suppose I practice complete cutting off of food.' Then devas, Aggivessana, came to me and said: 'Do not practice complete cutting off of food, sir. If you practice complete cutting off of food, sir, we shall infuse divine nutriment through your pores, and you shall be sustained by that.' It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'If I were to claim to be completely fasting, and these devas were to infuse divine nutriment through my pores, and I were to be sustained by that, that would be a lie on my part.' So I, Aggivessana, dismissed those devas, saying: 'Enough.'
translations.mn36:28: Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'What if I were to take food little by little, a palmful at a time, whether bean soup, lentil soup, pea soup, or rice gruel?' So I, Aggivessana, took food little by little, a palmful at a time, whether bean soup, lentil soup, pea soup, or rice gruel. Because I took food little by little, Aggivessana, a palmful at a time, whether bean soup, lentil soup, pea soup, or rice gruel, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation. Just as the joints of the eighty small bones or the joints of the black bones; so too my limbs and joints became just like that through that very insufficient food. Just as the hoofprint of an ox; so too my buttocks became just like that through that very insufficient food. Just as a twisted rope of beads; so too my spinal vertebrae stuck out, bulging and crooked, through that very insufficient food. Just as the rafters of a dilapidated shed fall down, broken and collapsed; so too my ribs fell down, broken and collapsed, through that very insufficient food. Just as in a deep well the water-star at the bottom appears deep, sunken, and dim; so too my eye-stars appeared deep, sunken, and dim in their sockets through that very insufficient food. Just as a bitter gourd, cut while unripe, is shriveled and withered by wind and sun; so too my head-skin was shriveled and withered through that very insufficient food. I, Aggivessana, when intending to touch my belly-skin, grasped my spinal vertebrae, and when intending to touch my spinal vertebrae, grasped my belly-skin, so much so, Aggivessana, that my belly-skin adhered to my spinal vertebrae through that very insufficient food. I, Aggivessana, when intending to defecate or urinate, fell face-down right there through that very insufficient food. I, Aggivessana, soothing this body, rubbed my limbs with my hand. Because I rubbed my limbs with my hand, Aggivessana, rotten roots of hair fell from my body through that very insufficient food.
translations.mn36:29: And people, Aggivessana, having seen me, said: 'The ascetic Gotama is black.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, the ascetic Gotama is brown.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, nor brown, the ascetic Gotama has yellowish skin.' So much so, Aggivessana, that my pure skin color, bright and clear, was destroyed through that very insufficient food.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the Great Wood, the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha coming from afar. Having seen him, he said to the Blessed One: 'This, sir, is Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha coming, a debater, a skilled speaker, well-regarded by many people. He, sir, wishes to disparage the Buddha, wishes to disparage the Dhamma, wishes to disparage the Saṅgha. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would sit down for a moment out of compassion.' The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging courteous and amiable words, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, sharp, severe, acute sensations through striving, this is the utmost, none greater than this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, sharp, severe, acute sensations through striving, this is the utmost, none greater than this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present experience painful, sharp, severe, acute sensations through striving, this is the utmost, none greater than this. Yet by this severe austerity I do not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to awakening?'
translations.mn36:32: Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'Why should I fear that happiness, since it is happiness apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states?' Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'I do not fear that happiness, since it is happiness apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states.'
translations.mn36:34: I, Aggivessana, having eaten coarse food, having gained strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Even such pleasant feeling that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:38: With my mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, free from defilement, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is—one birth, two births ... thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected my manifold past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was the first knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. Even such pleasant feeling that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:4: "There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the development of the body, not the development of mind. For they, Master Gotama, contact painful bodily feeling. Once, Master Gotama, when one was contacted by painful bodily feeling, his thighs would become rigid, his heart would burst, hot blood would gush from his mouth, he would go mad and become mentally unbalanced. His mind, Master Gotama, was subservient to his body, controlled by the body. Why is that? Because of the non-development of mind. But there are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the development of mind, not the development of the body. For they, Master Gotama, contact painful mental feeling. Once, Master Gotama, when one was contacted by painful mental feeling, his thighs would become rigid, his heart would burst, hot blood would gush from his mouth, he would go mad and become mentally unbalanced. His body, Master Gotama, was subservient to his mind, controlled by the mind. Why is that? Because of the non-development of the body. It occurred to me, Master Gotama: 'Surely Master Gotama's disciples dwell devoted to the development of mind, not the development of the body.'"
translations.mn36:40: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their actions ...
translations.mn36:42: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew as it really is: 'This is suffering,' I directly knew as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering,' I directly knew as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' I directly knew as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' I directly knew as it really is: 'These are the taints,' I directly knew as it really is: 'This is the origin of the taints,' I directly knew as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints,' I directly knew as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.'
translations.mn36:43: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: 'It's liberated.' I directly knew: 'Destroyed is rebirth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'
translations.mn36:45: I recall, Aggivessana, teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. And each one of them thinks: 'The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma referring to me alone.' But it should not be seen thus, Aggivessana; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others only for the purpose of making them understand. I, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very talk, establish, settle, unify, and concentrate my mind internally on that same sign of concentration as before, in which I constantly dwell." "This is to be trusted in Master Gotama as is fitting for one who is accomplished and fully enlightened. But does Master Gotama recall sleeping by day?"
translations.mn36:46: "I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after returning from my almsround and having eaten my meal, having spread out my fourfold robe, lying down on my right side, mindful and fully aware, I fell asleep." "But, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins call this a state of delusion." "It is not, Aggivessana, by such that one is deluded or undeluded. But, Aggivessana, listen to how one is deluded and undeluded, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, sir," Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn36:47: "For anyone, Aggivessana, whose taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death have not been abandoned, I call him 'deluded.' For, Aggivessana, by non-abandonment of the taints one is deluded. For anyone, Aggivessana, whose taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, I call him 'undeluded.' For, Aggivessana, by abandonment of the taints one is undeluded. For the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, unable to arise again in the future. Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree whose crown has been cut off is incapable of growing again; so too, Aggivessana, for the Tathāgata the taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, unable to arise again in the future."
translations.mn36:5: "But what, Aggivessana, have you heard as the development of the body?" "It is this—Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla—these, Master Gotama, are naked ascetics, rejecting conventions, licking their hands, not accepting what is brought, not accepting what is specially made, not accepting invitations; they do not accept food from a pot, from a bowl, across the threshold, across a stick, across a pestle; they do not accept food from two people eating together, from a pregnant woman, from a nursing woman, from a woman lying with a man, from where food is advertised, from where a dog waits, from where flies buzz; they do not eat fish or meat, they do not drink liquor, wine, or fermented brew. They keep to one house, one morsel; or two houses, two morsels ... or seven houses, seven morsels. They subsist on one alms, two alms ... seven alms. They take food once a day, twice a day ... once in seven days. Thus they dwell devoted to the practice of taking food at fortnightly intervals."
translations.mn36:6: "But do they, Aggivessana, live on just that much?" "Indeed not, Master Gotama. Sometimes, Master Gotama, they eat excellent food, consume excellent meals, taste excellent flavors, and drink excellent drinks. They say this body gains strength, grows, and becomes fat." "What you, Aggivessana, give up earlier and accumulate later, in this way there is accumulation and depletion of this body. But what, Aggivessana, have you heard regarding the development of mind?" When asked by the Blessed One about the development of mind, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son was not able to respond.
translations.mn36:8: "And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, for an uninstructed ordinary person, pleasant feeling arises. Touched by pleasant feeling, they become greedy for pleasure and fall into greed for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by painful feeling, they sorrow, languish, lament, weep beating their breast, and become confused. For them, Aggivessana, even when pleasant feeling has arisen, it occupies the mind because the body is undeveloped; even when painful feeling has arisen, it occupies the mind because the mind is undeveloped. For anyone, Aggivessana, for whom it is thus on both sides—even when pleasant feeling has arisen, it occupies the mind because the body is undeveloped; even when painful feeling has arisen, it occupies the mind because the mind is undeveloped—in this way, Aggivessana, one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, for an instructed noble disciple, pleasant feeling arises. Touched by pleasant feeling, they do not become greedy for pleasure and do not fall into greed for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by painful feeling, they do not sorrow, do not languish, do not lament, do not weep beating their breast, and do not become confused. For them, Aggivessana, even when pleasant feeling has arisen, it does not occupy the mind because the body is developed; even when painful feeling has arisen, it does not occupy the mind because the mind is developed. For anyone, Aggivessana, for whom it is thus on both sides—even when pleasant feeling has arisen, it does not occupy the mind because the body is developed; even when painful feeling has arisen, it does not occupy the mind because the mind is developed—in this way, Aggivessana, one is developed in body and developed in mind."
translations.mn38:10: "'This has come to be'—for one who doubts, monks, doubt arises"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'Its nutriment is the cause'—for one who doubts, monks, doubt arises"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation'—for one who doubts, monks, doubt arises"? "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:11: "'This has come to be'—monks, for one who sees with right wisdom as it really is, that doubt is abandoned"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'Its nutriment is the cause'—monks, for one who sees with right wisdom as it really is, that doubt is abandoned"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation'—monks, for one who sees with right wisdom as it really is, that doubt is abandoned"? "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:12: "'This has come to be'—monks, are you free from doubt about this"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'Its nutriment is the cause'—monks, are you free from doubt about this"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation'—monks, are you free from doubt about this"? "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:13: "'This has come to be'—monks, has it been well seen with right wisdom as it really is"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'Its nutriment is the cause'—monks, has it been well seen with right wisdom as it really is"? "Yes, venerable sir." "'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation'—monks, has it been well seen with right wisdom as it really is"? "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:14: "If you, monks, were to cling to, cherish, treasure, and appropriate this view thus purified and cleansed, would you, monks, understand the Dhamma taught by me as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping"? "No, venerable sir." "If you, monks, were not to cling to, not cherish, not treasure, and not appropriate this view thus purified and cleansed, would you, monks, understand the Dhamma taught by me as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping"? "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:15: "There are, monks, four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, for the assistance of those seeking to come to be. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: "Good, monks. Thus you say, and I also say—when this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises; that is—with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time a pernicious view like this had arisen in a bhikkhu named Sāti, son of a fisherman: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that runs and wanders through, not another.”
translations.mn38:20: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: “Good, bhikkhus. Thus you too should say, and I also say thus—when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases, that is: with the cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:23: “Now, bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you run back to the past thus: ‘Were we in the past, were we not in the past, what were we in the past, how were we in the past, having been what, what did we become in the past?’” “No, venerable sir.” “Now, bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you run forward to the future thus: ‘Shall we be in the future, shall we not be in the future, what shall we be in the future, how shall we be in the future, having been what, what shall we become in the future?’” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:25: “Good, bhikkhus. I have brought you, bhikkhus, to this Dhamma that is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. This Dhamma is visible here and now, bhikkhus, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise—thus what was said, it was said referring to this.”
translations.mn38:26: There are, bhikkhus, three conditions for the descent of the embryo. Here, the mother and father are joined together, but the mother is not in season, and the gandhabba is not present—in this case there is no descent of the embryo. Here, the mother and father are joined together, and the mother is in season, but the gandhabba is not present—in this case there is no descent of the embryo. But when, bhikkhus, the mother and father are joined together, and the mother is in season, and the gandhabba is present—it is with the concurrence of these three conditions that the descent of the embryo takes place.
translations.mn38:27: Then, bhikkhus, the mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months with much anxiety and heavy burden. Then, bhikkhus, after nine or ten months have passed, the mother gives birth with much anxiety and heavy burden. Then she nourishes the born child with her own blood. For, bhikkhus, mother's milk is called blood in the noble one's discipline.
translations.mn38:28: That boy, bhikkhus, as he grows and his faculties mature, plays with the games that are for boys, such as: the vanka, ghaṭika, mokkhacika, ciṅgulaka, pattāḷhaka, rathaka, and dhanuka.
translations.mn38:39: Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna …pe… the third jhāna …pe… the fourth jhāna.
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus, would this Sāti bhikkhu, son of a fisherman, have even a trace of heat in this Dhamma and Discipline?” “How could he, venerable sir? No, venerable sir.” When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, became silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to respond. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to respond, said to him: “You will be known by this, foolish man, by your own pernicious view. Here I will question the bhikkhus.”
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Do you too understand the Dhamma taught by me as this Sāti bhikkhu, son of a fisherman, does, who by his own wrong grasp both misrepresents us and injures himself and produces much demerit?” “No, venerable sir. For in many ways, venerable sir, has consciousness that is dependently arisen been stated by the Blessed One, that without a condition there is no origination of consciousness.” “Good, good, bhikkhus. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me thus. For in many ways, bhikkhus, has consciousness that is dependently arisen been stated by me, that without a condition there is no origination of consciousness. Yet this Sāti bhikkhu, son of a fisherman, by his own wrong grasp both misrepresents us and injures himself and produces much demerit. That will be for a long time, for that foolish man, for his harm and suffering.”
translations.mn38:9: "Do you see, monks, that 'this has come to be'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Do you see, monks, that 'that is produced by nutriment'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Do you see, monks, that 'with the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation'?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large community of monks when he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold misconduct by way of the mind? Here, householders, someone is covetous, coveting that which belongs to others, that which is another's wealth and property: 'Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!' And they have a mind of ill will and intentions of hate: 'May these beings be killed, or slain, or annihilated, or destroyed, or may they not exist at all!' And they have wrong view, inverted vision: 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings of spontaneous birth; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly, who practice rightly, and who having known and realized for themselves this world and the other world, make it known.' Thus, householders, is there threefold misconduct by way of the mind. Because of such misconduct and wrong conduct, householders, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold good conduct by way of the body? Here, householders, someone, abandoning the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and kindly, they dwell compassionate toward all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, they abstain from taking what is not given. Whatever is another's wealth and property, in village or forest, they do not take with thievish intent as what is not given. Abandoning sexual misconduct, they abstain from sexual misconduct. They do not engage in sexual intercourse with those protected by mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, clan, or by the law, or with those with a husband, with those under punishment, or even with those engaged to be married. Thus, householders, is there threefold good conduct by way of the body.
