translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold good conduct by way of speech? Here, householders, someone, abandoning false speech, abstains from false speech. When summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or a royal court, and asked to bear witness: 'Come, good man, tell what you know,' not knowing, they say, 'I do not know,' or knowing, they say, 'I know,' not seeing, they say, 'I do not see,' or seeing, they say, 'I see.' Thus they do not deliberately speak falsehood for their own sake, for another's sake, or for some trifling material gain. Abandoning divisive speech, they abstain from divisive speech. Having heard something here, they do not repeat it elsewhere to divide these people, or having heard something elsewhere, they do not repeat it here to divide those people. Thus they are a reconciler of those who are divided, a promoter of friendships, one who delights in concord, rejoices in concord, delights in concord, and speaks words that promote concord. Abandoning harsh speech, they abstain from harsh speech. They speak such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, urbane, agreeable to many, pleasing to many. Abandoning idle chatter, they abstain from idle chatter. They speak at the right time, speak what is factual, speak on what is beneficial, speak on the Dhamma and the Discipline; their speech is treasured up, timely, well-reasoned, well-defined, connected with the goal. Thus, householders, is there fourfold good conduct by way of speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold good conduct by way of the mind? Here, householders, someone is not covetous, not coveting that which belongs to others, that which is another's wealth and property: 'Oh, may what belongs to another not be mine!' And they have a mind without ill will and intentions without hate: 'May these beings be free from enmity, affliction, and anxiety, and may they look after themselves happily!' And they have right view, unobstructed vision: 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly, who practice rightly, and who having known and realized for themselves this world and the other world, make it known.' Thus, householders, is there threefold good conduct by way of the mind. Because of such good conduct and right conduct, householders, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If, householders, one practicing good conduct and right conduct should wish: 'Oh, that with the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of the great khattiya families!'—it is possible that with the breakup of the body, after death, they might be reborn in the company of the great khattiya families. And why is that? Because they practice good conduct and right conduct.
translations.mn41:3: Then the brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after cordial and memorable conversation, sat down to one side; some extended their hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. Sitting to one side, the brahmin householders of Sālā said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn41:4: "What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell? And what is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world?"
translations.mn41:43: Householders, if one practicing the Dhamma, practicing rightly, might wish: ‘Oh, may I dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, through the destruction of the taints’; this possibility exists, that he might dwell having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, through the destruction of the taints. Why is that? Because he practices the Dhamma, practices rightly.”
translations.mn41:5: “Householders, it is because of unrighteous conduct, misconduct, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. Householders, it is because of righteous conduct, right conduct, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.”
translations.mn41:6: “We do not understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by Master Gotama without expounding the meaning in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach the Dhamma so that we might understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by Master Gotama without expounding the meaning in detail.” “Then, householders, listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin householders of Sālā replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn41:8: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous conduct, misconduct by body? Here, householders, someone is a killer of living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to killing and slaying, showing no mercy to living beings. And he is a taker of what is not given. Whatever is another's possession, whether in the village or in the forest, that which is not given, considered theft, he takes. And he is an unchaste practitioner. With those protected by mother, protected by father, protected by mother and father, protected by brother, protected by sister, protected by relatives, protected by clan, protected by Dhamma, who have a husband, to whom punishment applies, even with those adorned with garlands—such ones he engages in conduct. Thus, householders, there is threefold unrighteous conduct, misconduct by body.
translations.mn41:9: And how, householders, is there fourfold unrighteous conduct, misconduct by speech? Here, householders, someone is a speaker of falsehood. Having gone to an assembly, a gathering, having gone to the midst of relatives, the midst of a guild, the midst of a royal court, summoned as a witness: ‘Come, good man, say what you know,’ he not knowing says ‘I know,’ knowing says ‘I do not know,’ not seeing says ‘I see,’ seeing says ‘I do not see.’ Thus for his own sake, for another's sake, or for some trifling gain, he speaks falsehood knowingly. And he is a slanderer. Having heard something here, he repeats it elsewhere to divide these people; having heard something elsewhere, he repeats it here to divide those people. Thus he is a divider of the united, an encourager of the divided, delighting in division, rejoicing in division, taking pleasure in division, he speaks words that create division. And he is a harsh speaker. Whatever speech is rough, hard, hurtful to others, offensive, bordering on anger, not conducive to concentration—such speech he speaks. And he is a prattler. He speaks at the wrong time, speaks falsely, speaks what is unbeneficial, speaks contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the discipline. He speaks words that are unfounded, untimely, unconnected, unlimited, unbeneficial. Thus, householders, there is fourfold unrighteous conduct, misconduct by speech.
translations.mn4:20: It occurred to me, brahmin: ‘Why don't I dwell on such nights as are well-known and designated—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—in such lodgings as are awe-inspiring and hair-raising, in park shrines, forest shrines, tree shrines, so that I might see that fear and dread?’ Then, brahmin, after some time, on such nights as are well-known and designated—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—I dwelt in such lodgings as are awe-inspiring and hair-raising, in park shrines, forest shrines, tree shrines. And while I was dwelling there, brahmin, a deer would come, or a peacock would break a branch, or the wind would rustle a heap of leaves; then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Now that fear and dread is coming.’ Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Why do I dwell always expecting fear? Why don't I, as that fear and dread comes to me in whatever form, dispel that fear and dread in that very form?’ Then, brahmin, while I was walking, that fear and dread came to me. I, brahmin, did not stand, did not sit down, did not lie down, until while walking I had dispelled that fear and dread. Then, brahmin, while I was standing, that fear and dread came to me. I, brahmin, did not walk, did not sit down, did not lie down, until while standing I had dispelled that fear and dread. Then, brahmin, while I was sitting, that fear and dread came to me. I, brahmin, did not lie down, did not stand, did not walk, until while sitting I had dispelled that fear and dread. Then, brahmin, while I was lying down, that fear and dread came to me. I, brahmin, did not sit down, did not stand, did not walk, until while lying down I had dispelled that fear and dread.
translations.mn4:22-26: And, brahmin, my energy was aroused without slackening, my mindfulness was established without confusion, my body was tranquil without disturbance, my mind was concentrated and one-pointed. Then, brahmin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thinking and examining, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thinking and examining, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thinking and examining, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and I experienced happiness with the body; that which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily,' I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna. With the abandoning of happiness and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollecting my past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected my manifold past lives.
translations.mn4:28: This, brahmin, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as is the case for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their karma: 'These beings, indeed, endowed with bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, who revile the noble ones, hold wrong view, and undertake wrong view as their karma, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. But these beings, endowed with bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct, who do not revile the noble ones, hold right view, and undertake right view as their karma, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their karma.
translations.mn4:3: It occurred to me too, brahmin, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta: 'Remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest are difficult to endure, seclusion is difficult to achieve, solitude is difficult to enjoy; I suppose the forests snatch away the mind of a monk who has not attained concentration.'
translations.mn4:30: This, brahmin, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as is the case for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: It might occur to you, brahmin: 'Perhaps the ascetic Gotama is still not free from lust, not free from hatred, not free from delusion, and that is why he resorts to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest.' But it should not be seen thus, brahmin. Seeing two benefits, brahmin, I resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest—seeing a pleasant dwelling for myself in this very life, and having compassion for future generations.
translations.mn4:4: It occurred to me, brahmin: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest with impure bodily conduct, it is because of the defect of impure bodily conduct that those venerable ascetics and brahmins summon unwholesome fear and terror. But I do not resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest with impure bodily conduct; I am one of pure bodily conduct. Whatever noble ones of pure bodily conduct resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest, I am one of them.' Seeing this purity of bodily conduct in myself, brahmin, I found greater delight in dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: It occurred to me, brahmin: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest with impure verbal conduct … with impure mental conduct … with impure livelihood, it is because of the defect of impure livelihood that those venerable ascetics and brahmins summon unwholesome fear and terror.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest with impure livelihood; I am one of pure livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: Whatever noble ones of pure livelihood resort to remote jungle-thicket dwellings in the forest, I am one of them.' Seeing this purity of livelihood in myself, brahmin, I found greater delight in dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard—at one time Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in Beluvagāmaka. Now at that time the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakaṇāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business or other.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of infinite space too is fabricated and mentally constructed. Whatever is fabricated and mentally constructed is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing firm in that, ...pe... he attains the supreme security from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing', enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of nothingness too is fabricated and mentally constructed. Whatever is fabricated and mentally constructed is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing firm in that, he reaches the destruction of the taints. If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then through that attachment to the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who will reappear spontaneously and there attain final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is the one thing declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, where, for a bhikkhu dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the undestroyed taints come to destruction, and the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet reached is reached.
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka approached Kukkuṭārāma and a certain bhikkhu; having approached, he paid homage to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to that bhikkhu:
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka, having settled that business in Pāṭaliputta, approached Vesālī, Beluvagāmaka, and Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn52:4: Here, householder, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He reflects thus: 'This first jhāna too is fabricated and mentally constructed. Whatever is fabricated and mentally constructed is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing firm in that, he reaches the destruction of the taints. If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then through that attachment to the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who will reappear spontaneously and there attain final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is the one thing declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, where, for a bhikkhu dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the undestroyed taints come to destruction, and the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet reached is reached.
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects thus: 'This liberation of mind by loving-kindness too is fabricated and mentally constructed. Whatever is fabricated and mentally constructed is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing firm in that, ...pe... he attains the supreme security from bondage.
translations.mn54:18: Just as, householder, there was a charcoal pit deeper than a man's height, full of glowing coals without smoke or flame. Then a man might come along wanting to live, not wanting to die, wanting happiness, averse to suffering. Then two strong men, grabbing him by both arms, would drag him toward the charcoal pit. What do you think, householder, would that man twist his body this way and that?" "Yes, sir." "What is the reason for that?" "Because, sir, that man knows: 'I will fall into this charcoal pit, and as a result I will meet with death or deadly suffering.'" "So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'Sensual pleasures are like a charcoal pit, said by the Blessed One to be full of suffering, full of tribulation, with greater danger in them.' Seeing this thus as it really is with proper wisdom... he develops that same equanimity.
translations.mn54:23: That noble disciple, householder, by relying on this same unsurpassed purity of equanimity and mindfulness, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations... he understands beings as faring according to their kamma.
translations.mn54:24: That noble disciple, householder, by relying on this same unsurpassed purity of equanimity and mindfulness, with the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge.
translations.mn60:10: There, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who are of such a view and such an opinion: 'There is what is given... they proclaim this world and the other world having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge'—it can be expected of them that, having abandoned these three unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct—and having undertaken and practiced these three wholesome states—bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct—they will behave accordingly. What is the reason for that? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in unwholesome states, and they see the benefit in renunciation and the cleansing aspect of wholesome states.
translations.mn60:12: There, householders, a wise person reflects thus: 'If there is another world, then this person, at the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Let it be that there is no other world, let the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; still this person is praised by the wise in this very life as a virtuous person, one of right view, an affirmativist.' If there really is another world, then this person has won on both counts—he is praised by the wise in this very life, and at the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this irrefutable teaching is well undertaken and well practiced, it stands encompassing both sides, it leaves no room for the unwholesome.
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who are of such a view and such an opinion: 'When one acts or causes to act, cuts or causes to cut, burns or causes to burn, grieves or causes to grieve, wearies or causes to weary, trembles or causes to tremble, kills a living being, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, ambushes highways, goes to others' wives, speaks falsely; evil is not done by the doer. Even if someone were to cut up all the beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh with a razor-edged wheel, there is no evil resulting from that, there is no coming of evil. Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and slaughtering, cutting and causing to cut, burning and causing to burn, there is no evil resulting from that, there is no coming of evil. Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is no merit resulting from that, there is no coming of merit. By giving, by taming, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit, there is no coming of merit.'
translations.mn60:14: But of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins are directly contradictory opponents who say thus: 'When one acts or causes to act, cuts or causes to cut, burns or causes to burn, grieves or causes to grieve, wearies or causes to weary, trembles or causes to tremble, kills a living being, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, ambushes highways, goes to others' wives, speaks falsely; evil is done by the doer. Even if someone were to cut up all the beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh with a razor-edged wheel, there is evil resulting from that, there is a coming of evil. Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and slaughtering, cutting and causing to cut, burning and causing to burn, there is evil resulting from that, there is a coming of evil. Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is merit resulting from that, there is a coming of merit. By giving, by taming, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is merit, there is a coming of merit.' What do you think, householders, don't these ascetics and brahmins speak in direct contradiction to each other?" "Yes, sir."
translations.mn60:16: But since there actually is action, the view of one who holds 'there is no action' is his wrong view. Since there actually is action, his thinking 'there is no action' is his wrong thought. Since there actually is action, his speech 'there is no action' is his wrong speech. Since there actually is action, when he says 'there is no action,' he makes himself an opponent of those arahants who teach that there is action. Since there actually is action, when he persuades another that 'there is no action,' that is his persuasion of what is not the true Dhamma. And with that persuasion of what is not the true Dhamma, he praises himself and disparages others. Thus his good conduct was already abandoned in the past, his bad conduct was established—and this wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, persuasion of what is not the true Dhamma, self-praise, and disparagement of others. Thus these many evil unwholesome states arise in him dependent on wrong view.
translations.mn60:17: There, householders, a wise person reflects thus: 'If there is no action, then this good person will make themselves safe with regard to the body at death; if there is action, then this good person will, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. Let it be that there is no action, let it be that those ascetics and brahmins speak the truth; yet still this good person is censured by the wise in this very life as an immoral person, a wrong-view holder, one who holds the doctrine of non-action.' If there is indeed action, then this good person has a double loss: he is censured by the wise in this very life, and with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. Thus this wrong course has been undertaken by this immoral person, it stands having invaded one side, it abandons the good place.
translations.mn60:19: Since there is indeed action, the view 'there is action' is his; that is right view for him. Since there is indeed action, he intends 'there is action'; that is right intention for him. Since there is indeed action, he speaks the word 'there is action'; that is right speech for him. Since there is indeed action, he says 'there is action'; he does not contradict those arahants who hold the doctrine of action. Since there is indeed action, he persuades another 'there is action'; that is right persuasion for him. And with that right persuasion he neither exalts himself nor disparages another. Thus his former immorality is abandoned and good conduct is established—and this right view, right intention, right speech, non-contradiction of the noble ones, right persuasion, non-exaltation of self, and non-disparagement of others. Thus for him many wholesome states arise dependent on right view.
translations.mn60:21: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause, without condition. There is no power, there is no energy, there is no manly strength, there is no manly effort; all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy, bent on fate, chance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.'
translations.mn60:22: Of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition. They say thus: 'There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause, with condition. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause, with condition. There is power, there is energy, there is manly strength, there is manly effort; not all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy, bent on fate, chance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.' What do you think, householders, do not these ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition to each other?
translations.mn60:29: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'There are no formless states at all.'
translations.mn60:30: Of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition. They say thus: 'There are formless states.' What do you think, householders, do not these ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition to each other?
translations.mn60:32: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'There is no cessation of existence at all.'
translations.mn60:35: These four, householders, are persons found existing in the world. Which four? Here, householders, one person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment. Here, householders, one person is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, one person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, one person is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself, not tormenting others, in this very life is hungerless, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, abiding with a self become Brahma.
translations.mn60:36: And what, householders, is the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment? Here, householders, one person is a naked ascetic, one who rejects conventions, one who licks his hands …pe… thus he dwells devoted to the practice of various kinds of torment and torture of the body. This is called, householders, the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment.
translations.mn60:37: And what, householders, is the person who is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, one person is a sheep-butcher, a pig-butcher …pe… or whatever other cruel occupations there are. This is called, householders, the person who is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:38: And what, householders, is the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, one person is a king, a noble anointed king …pe… they too, threatened with punishment, threatened with fear, with tearful faces, weeping, perform services. This is called, householders, the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:39: And what, householders, is the person who is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others; who, not tormenting himself, not tormenting others, in this very life is hungerless, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, abiding with a self become Brahma?
translations.mn60:4: But do you, householders, have any teacher in whom you have acquired reasoned faith?
translations.mn60:5: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who are of such doctrine and view: 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously reborn beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who are faring rightly, practicing rightly, who proclaim this world and the other world having realized them by their own direct knowledge.'
translations.mn60:6: But of these same ascetics and brahmins, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak in direct opposition. They say: 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously reborn beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are faring rightly, practicing rightly, who proclaim this world and the other world having realized them by their own direct knowledge.' What do you think, householders: 'Don't these ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition to each other?'
translations.mn63:8: And why, Māluṅkyaputta, have I not declared this? Because it is not beneficial, not relevant to the fundamentals of the holy life, not leading to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore I have not declared it.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. Whatever is felt there, perceived there, volitionally formed there, cognized there … he is one who does not return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. Whatever is felt there, perceived there, volitionally formed there, cognized there … he is one who does not return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: 'Do you remember, bhikkhus, the five lower fetters as taught by me?' When this was said, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One: 'I remember, venerable sir, the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One.' 'But how, Māluṅkyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?' 'I remember, venerable sir, identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember, venerable sir, doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember, venerable sir, grasping at precepts and vows as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember, venerable sir, sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember, venerable sir, ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. Thus, venerable sir, I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One.'
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.' 'Then, Ānanda, listen and attend closely; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: But, Ānanda, if there were a path, a way by which one could come to know and see and abandon the five lower fetters—it is possible that one could know and see and abandon the five lower fetters by following that path, that way.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, with thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Whatever is felt there, perceived there, volitionally formed there, cognized there—he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a barb, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind toward the deathless element: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing upon that, he attains the destruction of the taints; if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through attachment to the Dhamma, through delight in the Dhamma, with the wasting away of the five lower fetters, he becomes one spontaneously reborn, one who attains final Nibbāna there, one who does not return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: 'May I wield the various kinds of spiritual power—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; may I travel through the sky like a bird while seated cross-legged; may I touch and stroke with my hand even the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; may I wield mastery with the body as far as the brahmā world'—he should fulfill the precepts … one who exhorts in the empty huts.
translations.mn6:15: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I hear both kinds of sounds with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human—divine and human, whether far or near,' he should fulfill the precepts … develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:16: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I understand the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with my own mind—may I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with aversion as a mind with aversion, a mind without aversion as a mind without aversion; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind, an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,' he should fulfill the precepts … develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:2: “Possessed of virtue, monks, dwell possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest faults; train by undertaking the training rules.
translations.mn6:3: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow celibates, respected and esteemed,' he should fulfill the precepts, devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglecting jhāna, possessed of insight, and develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:6: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May whatever relatives and blood relations who have passed away and departed, recollecting me with confident mind, have that be of great fruit and great benefit,' he should fulfill the precepts, devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglecting jhāna, possessed of insight, and develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:7: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be one who overcomes discontent and delight, may discontent not overcome me, may I dwell having overcome again and again whatever discontent has arisen,' he should fulfill the precepts … develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:8: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be one who overcomes fear and dread, may fear and dread not overcome me, may I dwell having overcome again and again whatever fear and dread has arisen,' he should fulfill the precepts … develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:9: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas belonging to the higher mind, pleasant dwellings in this very life,' he should fulfill the precepts … develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kāsi country together with a large community of monks. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
translations.mn70:11: “But because this is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by wisdom by me: 'For some here, while experiencing such neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,' therefore I say 'enter and dwell in such neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.'
translations.mn70:12: I do not say, monks, that for all monks 'diligence is to be done'; nor do I say, monks, that for all monks 'diligence is not to be done.' Those monks who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—for such monks, monks, I say 'diligence is not to be done.' Why is that? Because they have done what is to be done by diligence. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:13: But those monks who are trainees, who have not attained their mind's ideal, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—for such monks, monks, I say 'diligence is to be done.' Why is that? Perhaps these venerable ones, resorting to suitable dwellings, associating with good friends, and balancing their faculties—may realize for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, may dwell in it. Seeing this fruit of diligence for these monks, monks, I say 'diligence is to be done.'
translations.mn70:14: These seven persons, monks, are found existing in the world. What seven? The one liberated in both ways, the one liberated by wisdom, the body-witness, the one attained to view, the one liberated by faith, the Dhamma-follower, the faith-follower.
translations.mn70:15: And what, monks, is the person liberated in both ways? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless ones, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed. This, monks, is called the person liberated in both ways. For this monk, monks, I say 'diligence is not to be done.' Why is that? Because he has done what is to be done by diligence. He is incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:17: And what, monks, is the person who is a body-witness? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless ones, and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. This, monks, is called the person who is a body-witness. For this monk, monks, I say 'diligence is to be done.' Why is that? Perhaps this venerable one, resorting to suitable dwellings, associating with good friends, and balancing his faculties—may realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, may dwell in it. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk, monks, I say 'diligence is to be done.'
translations.mn70:2: "I, bhikkhus, eat without having a meal at night. Eating without having a meal at night, bhikkhus, I perceive freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, you too, bhikkhus, eat without having a meal at night. Eating without having a meal at night, bhikkhus, you too will perceive freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn70:20: And what, bhikkhus, is a person who is a Dhamma-follower? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not dwell having contacted with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless ones; and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed; and he has sufficient confidence in the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata for examination; and he has these qualities, namely—the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom. This is called, bhikkhus, a person who is a Dhamma-follower. I say that for this bhikkhu too there is work to be done with heedfulness. What is the reason for that? It may be that this venerable one, resorting to suitable dwellings, associating with good friends, bringing his faculties to maturity—might dwell having realized for himself with direct knowledge here and now the unsurpassed culmination of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness for this bhikkhu, I say that for him there is work to be done with heedfulness.
translations.mn70:22: I do not say, bhikkhus, that final knowledge is achieved all at once; nevertheless, bhikkhus, final knowledge is achieved by gradual training, gradual activity, gradual practice.
translations.mn70:23: And how, bhikkhus, is final knowledge achieved by gradual training, gradual activity, gradual practice? Here, bhikkhus, one who has faith approaches; approaching, he sits down near; sitting down near, he lends ear; having lent ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he remembers it; he examines the meaning of the remembered Dhamma; as he examines the meaning, the Dhammas become acceptable; when the Dhammas are acceptable, desire arises; when desire has arisen, he makes an effort; having made an effort, he scrutinizes; having scrutinized, he strives; being resolute, he realizes with the body the supreme truth and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom.
translations.mn70:24: So there was no faith, bhikkhus; there was no approaching, bhikkhus; there was no sitting down near, bhikkhus; there was no lending ear, bhikkhus; there was no hearing the Dhamma, bhikkhus; there was no remembering the Dhamma, bhikkhus; there was no examining the meaning, bhikkhus; there was no acceptance of the Dhamma, bhikkhus; there was no desire, bhikkhus; there was no effort, bhikkhus; there was no scrutiny, bhikkhus; there was no striving, bhikkhus. You have gone astray, bhikkhus, you have gone astray by wrong practice. How far, bhikkhus, have these foolish men departed from this Dhamma and Discipline.
translations.mn70:25: There is, bhikkhus, a four-footed explanation that when taught, a wise man would soon understand the meaning. Shall I teach it to you, bhikkhus, will you understand it from me?" "Who are we, venerable sir, who are the knowers of the Dhamma?"
translations.mn70:26: Even if there were a teacher, bhikkhus, who was attached to material things, a recipient of material things, dwelling in connection with material things, such a proposal would not be fitting for him: 'Let it be thus for us, then we would do it; let it not be thus for us, then we would not do it'—how much more then for the Tathāgata who dwells completely detached from material things.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages in the Kāsi country, arrived at a Kāsi village named Kīṭāgiri. There the Blessed One dwelt in the Kāsi village of Kīṭāgiri.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the bhikkhus named Assaji and Punabbasu were resident at Kīṭāgiri. Then several bhikkhus approached the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu; having approached, they said to the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu: "The Blessed One, friends, eats without having a meal at night, and so does the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Eating without having a meal at night, friends, they perceive freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, you too, friends, eat without having a meal at night. Eating without having a meal at night, friends, you too will perceive freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding." When this was said, the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu said to those bhikkhus: "We eat in the evening and in the morning and at the wrong time of day. Eating in the evening and in the morning and at the wrong time of day, we perceive freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Why should we abandon what is visible here and now and pursue what takes time? We will eat in the evening and in the morning and at the wrong time of day."
translations.mn70:7: "Did I not teach you the Dhamma in such a way, bhikkhus, that here for one person, when he experiences a pleasant feeling of such a kind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, while here for another person, when he experiences a pleasant feeling of such a kind, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; here for one person, when he experiences a painful feeling of such a kind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, while here for another person, when he experiences a painful feeling of such a kind, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; here for one person, when he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of such a kind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, while here for another person, when he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of such a kind, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus in a Kuru village named Kammāsadhamma, in the fire-hall of the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Gotama, on a couch of grass.
translations.mn75:10: “But, Māgaṇḍiya, when I was still a householder, endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure, I enjoyed myself with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear … with odors cognizable by the nose … with flavors cognizable by the tongue … with tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. I had three mansions, Māgaṇḍiya—one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer. I, Māgaṇḍiya, dwelling in the rainy-season mansion, entertained myself for the four months of the rains with music provided entirely by women, without coming down from the mansion. Then, at a later time, having truly understood as they really are the origin and passing away, the gratification, danger, and escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned sensual craving, dispelled the fever of sensual passion, and dwelt with a mind inwardly at peace, free from thirst. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, who are devoured by sensual craving, burning with the fever of sensual passion, indulging in sensual pleasures; I do not envy them, I do not delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, which surpasses even divine bliss—delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, I do not delight in that.
translations.mn75:12: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, when I was still a householder, endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure, I enjoyed myself with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear … with odors cognizable by the nose … with flavors cognizable by the tongue … with tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Then, at a later time, having truly understood as they really are the origin and passing away, the gratification, danger, and escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned sensual craving, dispelled the fever of sensual passion, and dwelt with a mind inwardly at peace, free from thirst. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, who are devoured by sensual craving, burning with the fever of sensual passion, indulging in sensual pleasures; I do not envy them, I do not delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, which surpasses even divine bliss—delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, I do not delight in that.
translations.mn75:13: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores and blisters on his body, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a charcoal pit. His friends and companions, his kinsmen and relatives, would bring a physician to treat him. That physician would make medicine for him, and by means of that medicine he would be freed from his leprosy, healthy, happy, independent, able to go where he wishes. He would see another leper with sores and blisters on his body, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a charcoal pit. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that man envy that leper for his charcoal pit or for taking medicine?” “Indeed not, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because, Master Gotama, when there is disease, medicine is to be used; when there is no disease, medicine is not to be used.”
translations.mn75:16: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past sensual pleasures were painful to touch, greatly burning, greatly feverish; in the future sensual pleasures will be painful to touch, greatly burning, greatly feverish; and now in the present sensual pleasures are painful to touch, greatly burning, greatly feverish. But these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, not free from lust for sensual pleasures, devoured by sensual craving, burning with the fever of sensual passion, with impaired faculties, have acquired a perverted perception: ‘sensual pleasures are pleasant.’
translations.mn75:17: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores and blisters on his body, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizes his body over a charcoal pit. In whatever way, Māgaṇḍiya, that leper with sores and blisters on his body, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizes his body over a charcoal pit, in just that way his wounds become more foul-smelling, more stinking, more putrid; and there is just that much satisfaction and pleasure—namely, from scratching his wounds. Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, devoured by sensual craving, burning with the fever of sensual passion, indulge in sensual pleasures. In whatever way, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, devoured by sensual craving, burning with the fever of sensual passion, indulge in sensual pleasures, in just that way their sensual craving increases, and they burn with the fever of sensual passion; and there is just that much satisfaction and pleasure—namely, dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn75:18: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, have you ever seen or heard of a king or royal minister endowed and provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoying sensual pleasures, who, without abandoning sensual craving, without dispelling the fever of sensual desire, dwells or dwelt or will dwell with thirst gone, with mind internally calmed? No indeed, Master Gotama. Good, Māgaṇḍiya. Neither have I seen or heard of a king or royal minister endowed and provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoying sensual pleasures, who, without abandoning sensual craving, without dispelling the fever of sensual desire, dwells or dwelt or will dwell with thirst gone, with mind internally calmed. But rather, Māgaṇḍiya, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell or dwelt or will dwell with thirst gone, with mind internally calmed, all of them, having fully understood as it really is the origin and passing away, the gratification, danger, and escape in the case of sensual pleasures, having abandoned sensual craving and dispelled the fever of sensual desire, dwell or dwelt or will dwell with thirst gone, with mind internally calmed.
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after the meal, returning from the alms-round, he approached a certain forest grove for the day's abiding. Having entered that forest grove, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn75:22: I have such confidence in Master Gotama. Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know health and see Nibbāna. Just as, Māgaṇḍiya, a man blind from birth would not see dark and light forms, would not see blue forms, would not see yellow forms, would not see red forms, would not see crimson forms, would not see what is even and uneven, would not see the stars, would not see the moon and sun. His friends and companions, relatives and kin would bring him to a surgeon. That surgeon would make medicine for him. Through that medicine he would not produce eyes, he would not purify eyes. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would not that doctor be merely a partaker of fatigue and vexation? So it is, Master Gotama. So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna,' you would not know health, you would not see Nibbāna. That would be fatigue for me, that would be vexation for me.
translations.mn75:24: So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna.' You would know health, you would see Nibbāna. With the arising of your eye, the desire and lust in the five aggregates subject to clinging would be abandoned; and this would occur to you: 'For a long time indeed, sir, I have been cheated, deceived, and tricked by this mind. For I was clinging to form, I was clinging to feeling, I was clinging to perception, I was clinging to formations, I was clinging to consciousness. With clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, there is birth; with birth as condition, there is aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be; thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.mn75:25: I have such confidence in Master Gotama. Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat unblind. Then you, Māgaṇḍiya, should associate with good people. When you, Māgaṇḍiya, associate with good people, then you, Māgaṇḍiya, will hear the true Dhamma; when you, Māgaṇḍiya, hear the true Dhamma, then you, Māgaṇḍiya, will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you, Māgaṇḍiya, practice in accordance with the Dhamma, then you, Māgaṇḍiya, will know and see for yourself: These are diseases, tumors, arrows; here diseases, tumors, arrows cease without remainder. With the cessation of my clinging, there is the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease; thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of monks. May I receive the going forth under Master Gotama, may I receive the higher ordination.
translations.mn75:27: One who was formerly of another sect, Māgaṇḍiya, who wishes for the going forth, who wishes for the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline, lives on probation for four months; at the end of four months, if the monks are satisfied, they give the going forth, they give the higher ordination to the state of being a monk. But here individual differences are recognized. If, venerable sir, those formerly of another sect who wish for the going forth, who wish for the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline live on probation for four months, and at the end of four months, if the monks are satisfied, they give the going forth, they give the higher ordination to the state of being a monk; I will live on probation for four years, and at the end of four years, let the satisfied monks give me the going forth, let them give the higher ordination to the state of being a monk.
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-hall of the brahmin Bhāradvāja. The wanderer Māgaṇḍiya saw a grass mat spread in the fire-hall of the brahmin Bhāradvāja. Having seen it, he said to the brahmin Bhāradvāja: "For whom, good Bhāradvāja, is this grass mat spread in your fire-hall? I suppose it is suitable for an ascetic's bed."
translations.mn75:6: The Blessed One heard this conversation between the brahmin Bhāradvāja and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human. Then the Blessed One, in the evening, emerging from seclusion, approached the fire-hall of the brahmin Bhāradvāja; having approached, he sat down on the prepared grass mat. Then the brahmin Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged friendly greetings and courtesies, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Bhāradvāja: "But did you, Bhāradvāja, have any conversation with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya concerning this very grass mat?" When this was said, the brahmin Bhāradvāja, agitated and with hair standing on end, said to the Blessed One: "This is exactly what we wanted to report to Master Gotama. But Master Gotama has spoken of what was unspoken."
translations.mn75:7: And this conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin Bhāradvāja was left unfinished. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-hall of the brahmin Bhāradvāja where the Blessed One was; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged friendly greetings and courtesies, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya:
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyi, five other things by which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, and having honored and respected me, dwell in dependence on me. What five? Here, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me in terms of higher virtue: 'The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue.'
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness. Here, Udāyi, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which my disciples develop the four right strivings. Here, Udāyi, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which my disciples develop the four bases for spiritual power. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to desire and the formations of striving; he develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to energy and the formations of striving; he develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to mind and the formations of striving; he develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to investigation and the formations of striving. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops the faculty of faith leading to peace, leading to awakening; he develops the faculty of energy … he develops the faculty of mindfulness … he develops the faculty of concentration … he develops the faculty of wisdom leading to peace, leading to awakening. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: Now at that time a number of well-known wanderers were staying at the wanderers' park in the Peacocks' Sanctuary, namely, Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which my disciples develop the seven factors of awakening. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of awakening dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release; he develops the investigation-of-phenomena factor of awakening … he develops the energy factor of awakening … he develops the rapture factor of awakening … he develops the tranquility factor of awakening … he develops the concentration factor of awakening … he develops the equanimity factor of awakening dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice, in accordance with which my disciples develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right concentration. And in this case, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge and attainment.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice, in accordance with which my disciples develop the eight liberations. One possessing form sees forms, this is the first liberation; being internally formless, one sees forms externally, this is the second liberation; one is resolved only on the beautiful, this is the third liberation; with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, 'infinite space', this is the fourth liberation; with the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, 'infinite consciousness', this is the fifth liberation; with the complete surmounting of the base of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, 'there is nothing', this is the sixth liberation; with the complete surmounting of the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither perception nor non-perception, this is the seventh liberation; with the complete surmounting of the base of neither perception nor non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling, this is the eighth liberation. And in this case, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge and attainment.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice, in accordance with which my disciples develop the ten kasiṇa bases. One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, non-dual, boundless; one perceives the water kasiṇa … one perceives the fire kasiṇa … one perceives the air kasiṇa … one perceives the blue kasiṇa … one perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one perceives the red kasiṇa … one perceives the white kasiṇa … one perceives the space kasiṇa … one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, non-dual, boundless. And in this case, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge and attainment.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice, in accordance with which my disciples develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He drenches, saturates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Just as, Udāyi, a skilled bathman or his apprentice might pour soap powder into a bronze basin and, sprinkling water, knead it into a ball of soap so that the ball of soap is pervaded by moisture, saturated with moisture, internally and externally suffused with moisture but not dripping; so too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, saturates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a bhikkhu … enters and dwells in the second jhāna. He drenches, saturates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration. Just as, Udāyi, there is a deep lake with a spring, and neither in the eastern direction would there be an outlet for the water, nor in the western direction, nor in the northern direction, nor in the southern direction, and the deva would not from time to time send down proper rainfall; then cool streams of water would well up from that lake itself and drench, saturate, fill, and suffuse that lake with cool water, so that there would be no part of the entire lake that was not suffused with cool water. So too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, saturates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the fading away of rapture … a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the third jhāna. He drenches, saturates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the happiness without rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the happiness without rapture. Just as, Udāyi, in a pond of blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses, some blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, not rising above the water, are nourished while submerged within, and from their tips to their roots they are drenched, saturated, filled, and suffused with cool water, so that there would be no part of all the blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses that was not suffused with cool water; so too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, saturates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the happiness without rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the happiness without rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. He sits suffusing this very body with a mind that is purified and cleansed, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with a mind that is purified and cleansed. Just as, Udāyi, a man might sit covered from the head down with a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body that was not covered with the white cloth; so too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu sits suffusing this very body with a mind that is purified and cleansed, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with a mind that is purified and cleansed. And in this case, many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge and attainment.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "It is too early yet to wander for alms in Rājagaha. What if I were to go to the Moranivāpa wanderers' park where Sakuludāyī the wanderer is?"
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples, with the divine ear element, purified, surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near. Just as, Udāyi, a powerful conch-blower could easily make himself heard in the four quarters; so too, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples, with the divine ear element, purified, surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near. And in this case many of my disciples abide having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples recollect their manifold past abodes, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of contraction, many aeons of expansion, many aeons of contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, of such appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; passing away from there, I was reborn there; there too I was so named, of such a clan, of such appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus with their aspects and particulars they recollect their manifold past abodes. Just as, Udāyi, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to another village, and from that village he might return to his own village; it would occur to him: 'I went from my own village to that village, there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, remained silent thus; from that village I went to that village, there too I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, remained silent thus; from that village I have returned to my own village.' So too, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples recollect their manifold past abodes, that is: one birth … thus with their aspects and particulars they recollect their manifold past abodes. And in this case many of my disciples abide having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples, with the divine eye, purified, surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions: 'These beings, indeed, endowed with bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, revilers of the noble ones, wrong view, undertaking actions based on wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell; but these beings, indeed, endowed with bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct, non-revilers of the noble ones, right view, undertaking actions based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.'
