Thus with the divine eye, purified, surpassing the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions. Just as, Udāyi, there were two houses with doors, and a man with vision standing in between might see people entering and leaving the house, walking and wandering about; so too, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples, with the divine eye, purified, surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn … And in this case many of my disciples abide having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples, with the destruction of the taints, in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge. Just as, Udāyi, on a mountain slope there is a lake, clear, serene, unclouded, and a man with vision standing on the bank might see oysters and shells, gravel and pebbles, and shoals of fish moving and remaining still; it would occur to him: 'This lake is clear, serene, unclouded, and there are these oysters and shells, gravel and pebbles, and shoals of fish moving and remaining still.' So too, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples a practice, by practicing which my disciples, with the destruction of the taints, in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge. And in this case many of my disciples abide having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One went to where Sakuludāyī the wanderer was. Then Sakuludāyī the wanderer said to the Blessed One: "Come, venerable sir; welcome, venerable sir. It is long, venerable sir, since the Blessed One made this opportunity, that is, to come here. Sit, venerable sir; this seat is prepared." The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Sakuludāyī the wanderer too, taking a low seat, sat down to one side. To Sakuludāyī the wanderer, sitting to one side, the Blessed One said: "With what talk were you sitting together just now, Udāyi, and what was the conversation left unfinished among you?"
translations.mn77:7: "But how many qualities do you, Udāyi, see in me, by which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, venerate me, and having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me?"
translations.mn77:9: “‘The ascetic Gotama is one who eats little, and he praises eating little,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, yet, Udāyi, I have disciples who eat a kosā of food, half a kosā of food, a beluva of food, and half a beluva of food. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat with this bowl even when it is full to the brim, or I eat more. ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who eats little, and he praises eating little,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, those of my disciples, Udāyi, who eat a kosā of food, half a kosā of food, a beluva of food, and half a beluva of food, would not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me with this quality, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he praises contentment with any kind of robe,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, yet, Udāyi, I have disciples who are rag-robe wearers, wearers of coarse robes, who, having collected rags from charnel grounds or rubbish heaps or shops, make a robe and wear it. But I, Udāyi, sometimes wear householder robes that are strong, coarse, and made of hemp. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he praises contentment with any kind of robe,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, those of my disciples, Udāyi, who are rag-robe wearers, wearers of coarse robes, who, having collected rags from charnel grounds or rubbish heaps or shops, make a robe and wear it, would not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me with this quality, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he praises contentment with any kind of almsfood,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, yet, Udāyi, I have disciples who are almsfood eaters, who go on continuous almsround, who delight in the practice of gathering scraps, who, having entered the village, do not accept even when invited to a seat. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat at invitations, rice with various curries and various sauces. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he praises contentment with any kind of almsfood,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, those of my disciples, Udāyi, who are almsfood eaters, who go on continuous almsround, who delight in the practice of gathering scraps, who, having entered the village, do not accept even when invited to a seat, would not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me with this quality, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with any kind of lodging,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, yet, Udāyi, I have disciples who dwell at the root of trees, in the open air, who do not enter a roof for eight months. But I, Udāyi, sometimes dwell in gabled houses, plastered inside and out, protected from the wind, with bolted doors and closed windows. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with any kind of lodging,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, those of my disciples, Udāyi, who dwell at the root of trees, in the open air, who do not enter a roof for eight months, would not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me with this quality, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he praises seclusion,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me, yet, Udāyi, I have disciples who are forest dwellers, dwellers in remote lodgings, who have entered and dwell in forest wilderness lodgings, remote lodgings, who come to the midst of the Sangha every fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But I, Udāyi, sometimes dwell crowded with monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, ascetics, and disciples of ascetics. ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he praises seclusion,’ if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me. Those of my disciples, Udāyi, who are forest dwellers, dwellers in remote lodgings, who have entered and dwell in forest wilderness lodgings, remote lodgings, who come to the midst of the Sangha every fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, would not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me with this quality, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me. Thus, Udāyi, my disciples do not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me with these five qualities, and having honored and respected me, dwell depending on me.
translations.mn7:11: ‘As far as my heart is concerned, it is given up, vomited out, let go, abandoned, and renounced,’ he gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, gains joy connected with the Dhamma; for one who is joyful, rapture arises, for one with rapture in mind the body becomes tranquil, with a tranquil body he feels pleasure, for one who is happy the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will.
translations.mn7:17: He understands: 'There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, and there is an escape beyond this perception.'
translations.mn7:18: For one knowing thus, seeing thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensuality, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy celibate life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' This, monks, is called: 'A monk bathed with the inner bathing.'
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja said to the Blessed One: 'Does Master Gotama go to the Bāhukā river to bathe?' 'What, brahmin, is the Bāhukā river? What will the Bāhukā river do?' 'It is agreed to be auspicious, Master Gotama, the Bāhukā river among many people; it is agreed to be meritorious, Master Gotama, the Bāhukā river among many people; and from the Bāhukā river many people wash away evil deeds done.'
translations.mn7:2: Just as, monks, a cloth that is soiled and stained: whatever dye the dyer might dip it in—whether blue, yellow, red, or magenta—it would take the dye badly and be impure in color. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth. Even so, monks, when the mind is defiled, an unhappy destination is to be expected. Just as, monks, a cloth that is clean and bright: whatever dye the dyer might dip it in—whether blue, yellow, red, or magenta—it would take the dye well and be pure in color. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth. Even so, monks, when the mind is undefiled, a happy destination is to be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja with verses: 'Bāhukā and Adhikakka, Gayā and Sundarikā too, Sarasvatī and Payāga, and also the Bāhumatī river; though a fool may plunge in constantly, one of dark deeds is not purified. What will Sundarikā do, what Payāga, what the Bāhukā river; a hostile man of evil deeds, it will not purify him of evil deeds. For the pure there is always the Phaggunā, for the pure there is always the Uposatha, for the pure of pure deeds, the vow is always fulfilled; bathe here, brahmin, bring safety to all beings. If you do not speak falsely, if you do not harm living beings, if you do not take what is not given, believing, without stinginess; what will you do going to Gayā, for your Gayā is right here.'
translations.mn7:3: And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed are a defilement of the mind; ill will is a defilement of the mind; anger is a defilement of the mind; hostility is a defilement of the mind; contempt is a defilement of the mind; insolence is a defilement of the mind; envy is a defilement of the mind; avarice is a defilement of the mind; deceit is a defilement of the mind; fraud is a defilement of the mind; obstinacy is a defilement of the mind; presumption is a defilement of the mind; conceit is a defilement of the mind; arrogance is a defilement of the mind; vanity is a defilement of the mind; negligence is a defilement of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: he is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.'
translations.mn7:7: he is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kuru country with a large Sangha of monks when he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika, a market town of the Kurus.
translations.mn82:11: Then Raṭṭhapāla's friends went to Raṭṭhapāla's parents; having approached, they said to Raṭṭhapāla's parents: 'Mother, father, this young man Raṭṭhapāla is lying right there on the bare ground:
translations.mn82:13: Raṭṭhapāla the clansman received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he received the full ordination. Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he pleased with the venerable Raṭṭhapāla who had newly gone forth, who had been fully ordained for half a month, set out on a walking tour towards Sāvatthī. Walking by stages, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One dwelt at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.
translations.mn82:14: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapālo, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, not long after attained that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and dwelt having realized it directly through his own higher knowledge. He knew: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being." And the venerable Raṭṭhapālo became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapālo, having risen from his seat, having paid homage to the Blessed One, having circumambulated him, having packed up his dwelling place, taking his bowl and robe, set out on a walking tour towards Thullakoṭṭhika. Walking by stages, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There the venerable Raṭṭhapālo dwelt at Thullakoṭṭhika in King Korabya's deer park. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapālo, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. Walking for alms from house to house in Thullakoṭṭhika, he approached his own father's house.
translations.mn82:17: Now at that time the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was having the middle hall plastered. The venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father saw the venerable Raṭṭhapālo coming in the distance. Having seen him, he said this: "By these shavelings, these ascetics, our only dear and beloved son was made to go forth." Then the venerable Raṭṭhapālo at his own father's house received neither alms nor a refusal; on the contrary, he received only abuse.
translations.mn82:18: Now at that time a slave woman of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relatives was about to throw away some stale porridge. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapālo said this to that slave woman: "If, sister, that is to be thrown away, pour it here into my bowl." Then that slave woman of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relatives, while pouring that stale porridge into the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, noticed a sign of his hands and feet and his voice. Then that slave woman approached the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother; having approached, she said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother: "Please, lady, you should know: 'The young master Raṭṭhapālo has arrived.'" "If, dear, you speak the truth, I give you your freedom." Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother approached the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father; having approached, she said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father: "Please, householder, you should know: 'Raṭṭhapāla the clansman, it is said, has arrived.'"
translations.mn82:19: Now at that time the venerable Raṭṭhapālo was eating that stale porridge leaning against a certain wall. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father approached the venerable Raṭṭhapālo; having approached, he said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapālo: "Is it really so, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you will eat stale porridge? Dear Raṭṭhapāla, should you not go to your own home?" "Whence, householder, is there a home for us who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We went to your, householder, home; there we received neither alms nor a refusal; on the contrary, we received only abuse." "Come, dear Raṭṭhapālo, let us go home." "Enough, householder, I have done my meal business for today." "Then, dear Raṭṭhapālo, consent to a meal for tomorrow." The venerable Raṭṭhapālo consented in silence.
translations.mn82:20: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, having understood the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's consent, approached his own home; having approached, having had a large pile of gold and silver prepared, having covered it with mats, he addressed the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives: "Come, daughters-in-law, adorn yourselves with whatever adornment you were adorned with when formerly you were dear and beloved to Raṭṭhapāla the clansman."
translations.mn82:21: Then, when that night had passed, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father had excellent food, hard and soft, prepared in his own home and announced the time to the venerable Raṭṭhapālo: "It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready."
translations.mn82:22: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapālo, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, approached his own father's home; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father had that pile of gold and silver uncovered and said this to the venerable Raṭṭhapālo: "This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother's wealth, another is your father's, another your grandfather's. It is possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, to enjoy wealth and make merit. Come you, dear Raṭṭhapāla, having returned to the low life, enjoy wealth and make merit." "If you, householder, would do as I say, having loaded this pile of gold and silver on carts, having had it conveyed, you should sink it in the middle of the current of the river Gaṅgā. Why is that? Because, householder, from that cause there will arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair for you."
translations.mn82:23: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives, each taking him by the feet, said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: "What are those nymphs like, dear sir, for whose sake you practice the holy life?" "We do not practice the holy life, sisters, for the sake of nymphs." "The venerable Raṭṭhapāla addresses us by the term 'sisters'"—and they fainted and fell right there.
translations.mn82:24: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: "Householder, if food is to be given, give it; do not trouble us." "Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready." Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father personally served and satisfied the venerable Raṭṭhapāla with excellent food. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having eaten and put away his bowl, standing right there, recited these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having recited these verses while standing, approached King Koravya's Deer Park; having approached, he sat down for the day's abiding at the root of a certain tree.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Koravya addressed the deer-stalker: "Clear the Deer Park, my good deer-stalker; we will go to see the beautiful ground." "Yes, your majesty," the deer-stalker replied to King Koravya, and while clearing the Deer Park he saw the venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting for the day's abiding at the root of a certain tree. Having seen him, he approached King Koravya; having approached, he said to King Koravya: "Your Deer Park is clear, your majesty. There is here a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the foremost family in this very Thullakoṭṭhita, whom you have often praised; he is sitting for the day's abiding at the root of a certain tree." "Well then, my good deer-stalker, enough of the park for today. Now we will attend upon the venerable Raṭṭhapāla."
translations.mn82:28: Then King Koravya, having said "Let all the food that has been prepared there be distributed," had excellent carriages yoked, and mounting an excellent carriage, set out from Thullakoṭṭhita with excellent carriages in royal majesty to see the venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Going as far as the carriage could go, he dismounted from the carriage and approached the venerable Raṭṭhapāla on foot with a large retinue; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Raṭṭhapāla. After exchanging polite and courteous greetings, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Koravya said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: "Let the venerable Raṭṭhapāla sit on the elephant rug." "Enough, great king; you sit down. I am sitting on my own seat." King Koravya sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, King Koravya said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: "There are these four kinds of loss, Master Raṭṭhapāla, by which some people here, having shaved off hair and beard and put on ochre robes, go forth from the home life into homelessness. What four? Loss through aging, loss through illness, loss of wealth, loss of relatives.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita approached the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, sat down to one side; some extended their hands in reverential salutation towards the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, roused, inspired, and gladdened them with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: These, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are the four kinds of loss by which some people here, having shaved off hair and beard and put on ochre robes, go forth from the home life into homelessness. These are not present for Master Raṭṭhapāla. What did the venerable Raṭṭhapāla know or see or hear that he went forth from the home life into homelessness?"
translations.mn82:35: "There are, great king, four Dhamma summaries pointed out by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, which I, having known and seen and heard, went forth from the home life into homelessness. What four?
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the foremost family in that very Thullakoṭṭhita, was sitting in that assembly. Then it occurred to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy while living in a home to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness."
translations.mn82:6: Then Raṭṭhapāla the clansman, not long after the Thullakoṭṭhika brahmins and householders had left, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla the clansman said to the Blessed One: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy while living in a home to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. I wish, venerable sir, having shaved off my hair and beard and put on the ochre robes, to go forth from the home life into homelessness. May I receive the going forth, venerable sir, in the presence of the Blessed One, may I receive the full ordination. Let the Blessed One ordain me." "But have you, Raṭṭhapāla, obtained your parents' permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness?" "I have not, venerable sir, obtained my parents' permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness." "The Tathāgatas, Raṭṭhapāla, do not ordain one who has not obtained his parents' permission." "I will act, venerable sir, in such a way that my parents will give me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness."
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Opāsāda. There the Blessed One dwelt near Opāsāda in the Deva Wood, the Sāla Grove, to the north of Opāsāda.
translations.mn95:10: Then Caṅkī the brahmin went with a large group of brahmins to the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had exchanged cordial and memorable words, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: Now on that occasion the Blessed One was sitting having exchanged some cordial and memorable words with very aged brahmins. Now on that occasion a brahmin student named Kāpaṭhika was sitting in that assembly—youthful, newly tonsured, sixteen years old, master of the three Vedas with their vocabularies, liturgy, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, he was as learned as possible in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man. He kept interrupting the conversation of the very aged brahmins conversing with the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One rebuked Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student: "Do not let Master Bhāradvāja keep interrupting the conversation of the very aged brahmins conversing with each other. Let Master Bhāradvāja wait until the end of the conversation." When this was said, Caṅkī the brahmin said to the Blessed One: "Do not rebuke Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student, Master Gotama. Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student is a clansman, Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student is very learned, Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student is wise, Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student is a good speaker, and Kāpaṭhika the brahmin student is capable of discussing this matter with Master Gotama."
translations.mn95:2: Now on that occasion Caṅkī the brahmin was dwelling at Opāsāda, a populous place, with grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal benefice given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal gift, a brahmin's fief.
translations.mn95:20: When he examines him and sees that he is purified from states that cause delusion; then he places faith in him, and having placed faith, he approaches him, and having approached, he pays respect to him, and paying respect, he gives ear, and giving ear, he hears the Dhamma, and hearing the Dhamma, he remembers it, and remembering, he examines the meaning of the remembered Dhamma, and as he examines the meaning, the Dhammas become acceptable to him through his reflection, and when there is acceptance of the Dhamma through reflection, zeal is born, and with zeal born, he strives, and having strived, he weighs the matter, and having weighed the matter, he strives resolutely, and with resolute striving he realizes with the body the supreme truth and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom. To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is discovery of truth, to this extent one discovers truth, to this extent we describe discovery of truth; but not yet is there the arrival at truth."
translations.mn95:33: "But, Master Gotama, what quality is very helpful for approaching? We ask Master Gotama about the quality that is very helpful for approaching." "Faith, Bhāradvāja, is very helpful for approaching. If faith did not arise, one would not approach. Because faith arises, one approaches. Therefore faith is very helpful for approaching."
translations.mn95:5: Now on that occasion Caṅkī the brahmin had gone up to the upper terrace for his midday rest. Caṅkī the brahmin saw the Opāsāda brahmins and householders leaving Opāsāda in groups and crowds and heading north toward the Deva Wood, the Sāla Grove. Having seen this, he addressed his attendant: "Why, good attendant, are the Opāsāda brahmins and householders leaving Opāsāda in groups and crowds and heading north toward the Deva Wood, the Sāla Grove?"
translations.mn9:11: But, friends, what is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? There are, friends, these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking to become. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. With the arising of craving there is the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of craving there is the cessation of nutriment, and this noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment, thus understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, he abandons the underlying tendency to lust in all respects, removes the underlying tendency to aversion, abolishes the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am,' abandons ignorance and arouses knowledge, and makes an end of suffering in this very life—to this extent too, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has come to this true Dhamma."
translations.mn9:15: But what, friend, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering—in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering—this, friend, is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friend, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there, that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence—this, friend, is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friend, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, its giving up, relinquishing, release, and non-attachment—this, friend, is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friend, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this noble eightfold path, that is, right view …pe… right concentration—this, friend, is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: 'Right view, right view,' friend, it is said. To what extent, friend, does a noble disciple have right view, whose view is straight, who is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has come to this true Dhamma? We would come from afar, friend, to learn the meaning of this statement from the Venerable Sāriputta. It would be good if the Venerable Sāriputta would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard the Venerable Sāriputta, the monks will remember it. Then, friend, listen, pay close attention, I will speak. Yes, friend, those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: Good, friend, those monks, having approved and agreed with what the Venerable Sāriputta said, asked him a further question: Could there be, friend, another way by which a noble disciple has right view, whose view is straight, who is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has come to this true Dhamma?
translations.mn9:3: When, friend, a noble disciple understands what is unwholesome and understands the root of what is unwholesome, understands what is wholesome and understands the root of what is wholesome—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple has right view, whose view is straight, who is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has come to this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: But what, friend, is unwholesome, what is the root of what is unwholesome, what is wholesome, what is the root of what is wholesome? Killing living beings, friend, is unwholesome, taking what is not given is unwholesome, sexual misconduct is unwholesome, false speech is unwholesome, divisive speech is unwholesome, harsh speech is unwholesome, idle chatter is unwholesome, covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, wrong view is unwholesome—this, friend, is called unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friend, is the root of what is unwholesome? Greed is the root of what is unwholesome, hatred is the root of what is unwholesome, delusion is the root of what is unwholesome—this, friend, is called the root of what is unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friend, is the root of what is wholesome? Non-greed is the root of what is wholesome, non-hatred is the root of what is wholesome, non-delusion is the root of what is wholesome—this, friend, is called the root of what is wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: But what, friend, is the taint, what is the origin of the taint, what is the cessation of the taint, what is the path leading to the cessation of the taint? There are these three taints, friend: the taint of sensual pleasures, the taint of existence, the taint of ignorance. With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of the taint, with the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of the taint, this noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of the taint, that is, right view …pe… right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands what is unwholesome, thus understands the root of what is unwholesome, thus understands what is wholesome, thus understands the root of what is wholesome, he, having abandoned the underlying tendency to greed entirely, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am,' having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, becomes one who makes an end of suffering in this very life—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple has right view, whose view is straight, who is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has come to this true Dhamma.
translations.sn1.10:2: Those who dwell in the forest, peaceful ones living the spiritual life, eating a single meal—by what does their complexion become clear?
translations.sn1.10:3: They do not sorrow over the past, nor do they yearn for the future; they maintain themselves with the present—by that their complexion becomes clear.
translations.sn1.17:1: Hard to practice and hard to endure, the spiritual life is difficult for the unskilled; there are many obstacles there, where the fool founders.
translations.sn1.17:2: How long would one practice the spiritual life if one does not restrain the mind? One would founder at every step, following the dictates of thoughts.
translations.sn1.17:3: Like a turtle withdrawing its limbs into its shell, a monk should withdraw his thoughts of mind; independent, not harming another, fully extinguished, he would find fault with no one.
translations.sn1.18:1: Is there any person in the world restrained by conscience, who awakens to blame, like a good horse to the whip?
translations.sn1.18:2: Those who are restrained by conscience, few in number, who always live mindfully, having reached the end of suffering, they live evenly amidst the uneven.
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then a certain devatā, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that devatā said to the Blessed One: How did you cross the flood, dear sir? Without standing still, friend, and without struggling, I crossed the flood. But how, dear sir, did you cross the flood without standing still and without struggling? When, friend, I stood still, then I sank; when, friend, I struggled, then I was swept away. Thus, friend, without standing still and without struggling, I crossed the flood.
translations.sn1.1:2: At long last I see a brahmin fully extinguished, without standing still, without struggling, who has crossed over clinging in the world.
translations.sn1.1:3: This is what that devatā said. The Teacher approved. Then that devatā, thinking The Teacher has approved me, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on her right, and disappeared right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: So have I heard. Once the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Hot Springs Monastery. Then Venerable Samiddhi rose at the crack of dawn and went to the hot springs to wash his limbs. Having washed his limbs in the hot springs and come out, he stood in one robe drying his limbs. Then a certain deity, who in the far gone night had lit up the entire hot springs with a glorious appearance, approached Venerable Samiddhi; and standing in the air, addressed him in verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “You beg, monk, without eating; you do not beg after eating; Eat, monk, and then beg, lest the time pass you by.”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings who perceive what can be told, established in what can be told; Without fully understanding what can be told, they come under the yoke of Death.
translations.sn1.20:21: Having fully understood what can be told, they do not conceive of a speaker; For that does not exist for them, by which they could be spoken of; If you understand, speak, spirit.”
translations.sn1.20:22: “Venerable sir, I do not understand the detailed meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One.”
translations.sn1.20:23: “He who thinks himself equal, superior, or inferior, would dispute on that account; Unshaken in the three modes of conceit, he does not think 'I am equal' or 'superior'; If you understand, speak, spirit.”
translations.sn1.20:25: “He abandoned reckoning, did not conceive of conceit, Cut off craving here in name and form; That one with the knot cut, untroubled, without longing, Seeking, they do not find; Gods and humans here or beyond, Or in heavens in all abodes.
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time, the time is hidden and not seen; Therefore I beg without eating, lest the time pass me by.”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, standing on the earth, said to Venerable Samiddhi: “You are young, monk, gone forth in the prime of life, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not given to the pleasures of the senses. Enjoy, monk, human pleasures; do not abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what is subject to time.”
translations.sn1.20:5: “Friend, I do not abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what is subject to time. I abandon, friend, what is subject to time to pursue what is visible here and now. For pleasures subject to time have been described by the Blessed One as full of suffering, full of trouble, with greater danger in them. This Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.”
translations.sn1.20:6: “But how, monk, have pleasures subject to time been described by the Blessed One as full of suffering, full of trouble, with greater danger in them? How is this Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “I, friend, am new, recently gone forth, newly come to this Dhamma and Discipline. I am not able to explain it in detail. That Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is staying at Rājagaha in the Hot Springs Monastery. Go to that Blessed One and ask about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should remember it.”
translations.sn1.20:8: “It is not easy, monk, for us to approach that Blessed One, as he is surrounded by other powerful deities. If you, monk, would go to that Blessed One and ask about this matter, we too would come to hear the Dhamma.” “So be it, friend.” Venerable Samiddhi, having assented to that deity, approached the Buddha; and having approached, paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Samiddhi said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.21:2: “As if touched by a sword, as if his head were on fire; A mindful monk should wander to abandon sensual desire.”
translations.sn1.21:3: “As if touched by a sword, as if his head were on fire; A mindful monk should wander to abandon identity view.”
translations.sn1.25:1: “He who is a monk, an arahant, accomplished, With defilements destroyed, bearing his final body; He might say 'I speak,' he might say 'They speak of me.'”
translations.sn1.25:2: “He who is a monk, an arahant, accomplished, With defilements destroyed, bearing his final body; He might say 'I speak,' he might say 'They speak of me'; Skilled, having understood the world's conventions, He would use such expressions merely as conventions.”
translations.sn1.25:3: “He who is a monk, an arahant, accomplished, With defilements destroyed, bearing his final body; Would that monk, resorting to conceit, Say 'I speak,' say 'They speak of me'?”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one whose conceit is abandoned there are no knots, All knots of conceit are destroyed; That wise one has transcended the conceit 'I am,' He might say 'I speak.'
translations.sn1.25:5: He might say 'They speak of me,' Skilled, having understood the world's conventions; He would use such expressions merely as conventions.”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain deity, who in the far gone night had lit up the entire Jeta's Grove with a glorious appearance, approached the Buddha; and having approached, paid homage to the Buddha and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.2:5: “Through the destruction of delight in existence, Through the destruction of perception and consciousness, Through the cessation and stilling of feelings; Thus, friend, I know; The release, the liberation, the seclusion of beings.”
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then several deities of the Satullapa host, who in the far gone night had lit up the entire Jeta's Grove with a glorious appearance, approached the Buddha; and having approached, paid homage to the Buddha and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity recited this verse in the presence of the Buddha:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is a person's partner, If unfaithfulness does not stand in the way; Fame and renown come to him, And he goes to heaven, abandoning the body.”
translations.sn1.36:4: “Let one abandon anger, let one abandon conceit, Let one transcend every fetter; Not clinging to name and form, Nothing is attached to the one who owns nothing.”
translations.sn1.36:5: “The foolish people of little wisdom Pursue negligence; The wise one guards heedfulness As the greatest treasure.
translations.sn1.36:6: Do not pursue negligence, Do not be intimate with sensual delight; For the heedful one meditating Attains the highest happiness.”
translations.sn1.38:1: So have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. Now on that occasion the Blessed One's foot had been cut by a stone splinter. Severe pains were occurring to the Blessed One—bodily feelings that were painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable; yet the Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed. Then the Blessed One spread out his outer robe folded in four and lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by vows and rules, practicing rough austerity for a hundred years; their minds are not rightly liberated, of inferior nature, they do not cross to the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: For one who desires conceit there is no taming here, there is no silence for one who is not concentrated; one dwelling alone in the forest, heedless, would not cross beyond the realm of Death.
translations.sn1.38:12: Having abandoned conceit, well concentrated, of good mind, completely liberated in every respect; one dwelling alone in the forest, heedful, would cross beyond the realm of Death.
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred deities of the Satullapa host, with the radiance of their beauty illuminating the entire Maddakucchi, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity uttered this inspired utterance in the presence of the Blessed One: "The ascetic Gotama is indeed a nāga; like a nāga, he endures bodily feelings that have arisen—painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable—mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed."
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity uttered this inspired utterance in the presence of the Blessed One: "The ascetic Gotama is indeed a lion; like a lion, he endures bodily feelings that have arisen—painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable—mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed."
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity uttered this inspired utterance in the presence of the Blessed One: "See the well-developed concentration and the well-liberated mind, neither bent forward nor bent back, not kept in check by forceful suppression. Who would think to surpass such a human nāga, human lion, human thoroughbred, human bull, human burden-bearer, human tusker, except through not seeing him?"
translations.sn1.38:9: The five Vedas with a hundred branches, brahmins practicing austerity; their minds are not rightly liberated, of inferior nature, they do not cross to the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:1: So have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then a certain deity, with the radiance of its beauty illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, it paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.41:4: Giving yields happiness, not giving does not yield that; thieves steal it, kings confiscate it, fire burns it, it is lost.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then in the end one leaves behind this body along with one's possessions; knowing this, the wise should enjoy and give; having given and enjoyed according to one's ability, one goes blameless to heaven.
translations.sn1.42:1: What is the giver of strength? What is the giver of beauty? What is the giver of happiness? What is the giver of sight? And who is the giver of all? Tell me this when asked.
translations.sn1.42:2: Food is the giver of strength, clothing is the giver of beauty; a vehicle is the giver of happiness, a lamp is the giver of sight.
translations.sn1.42:3: And one who gives a dwelling is the giver of all; one who teaches the Dhamma is also the giver of the deathless.
translations.sn1.51:1: What is good even to old age? What is good when established? What is the jewel of people? What is hard for thieves to take?
translations.sn1.51:2: Virtue is good even to old age, faith is good when established; wisdom is the jewel of people, merit is hard for thieves to take.
translations.sn1.55:1: What gives birth to a person? What runs around for him? What has a being entered into saṁsāra? What is his great fear?
translations.sn1.55:2: Craving gives birth to a person, his mind runs around for him; a being has entered into saṁsāra, suffering is his great fear.
translations.sn1.56:1: What gives birth to a person? What runs around for him? What has a being entered into saṁsāra? From what is one not liberated?
translations.sn1.56:2: Craving gives birth to a person, his mind runs around for him; a being has entered into saṁsāra, from suffering one is not liberated.
translations.sn1.57:1: What gives birth to a person? What runs around for him? What has a being entered into saṁsāra? What is his destination?
translations.sn1.57:2: Craving gives birth to a person, his mind runs around for him; a being has entered into saṁsāra, kamma is his destination.
translations.sn1.59:1: What is a person's companion? What instructs him? Delighting in what is a mortal liberated from all suffering?
translations.sn1.59:2: Faith is a person's companion, wisdom instructs him; a mortal delighting in Nibbāna is liberated from all suffering.
translations.sn1.62:1: By what is the world led? By what is it dragged around? Of what single thing do all come under the power?
translations.sn1.62:2: By mind the world is led, by mind it is dragged around; of mind, a single thing, all come under the power.
translations.sn1.63:2: By craving the world is led, by craving it is dragged around; of craving, a single thing, all come under the power.
translations.sn1.64:1: By what is the world fettered? By what does it wander? By the abandoning of what is Nibbāna spoken of?
translations.sn1.64:2: By delight the world is fettered, by thinking it wanders; by the abandoning of craving, Nibbāna is spoken of.
translations.sn1.65:1: By what is the world bound? By what does it wander? By the abandoning of what does one cut all bonds?
translations.sn1.65:2: By delight the world is bound, by thinking it wanders; by the abandoning of craving, one cuts all bonds.
translations.sn1.69:1: By what is the world bound? By the removal of what is one liberated? By the abandoning of what does one cut all bonds?
translations.sn1.69:2: By desire the world is bound, by the removal of desire one is liberated; by the abandoning of desire, one cuts all bonds.
translations.sn1.71:2: Having cut what does one sleep happily? Having cut what does one not sorrow? Of what single thing, Gotama, do you approve the slaying?
translations.sn1.71:3: Having cut anger one sleeps happily, having cut anger one does not sorrow; of anger, O deity, with its poisoned root and honeyed tip; the noble ones praise its slaying, for having cut it one does not sorrow.
translations.sn1.73:1: What wealth here is best for a person? What well-practiced brings happiness? What is indeed sweeter than tastes? How living is life called best?
translations.sn1.73:2: “Faith is the best wealth here for a person, The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness; Truth indeed is the sweetest of tastes, They call the wisdom-life the best life.”
translations.sn1.7:2: “Those whose qualities are not thoroughly understood, Are led astray by the doctrines of others; They are asleep, they do not wake up, It is time for them to wake up.”
translations.sn1.7:3: “Those whose qualities are thoroughly understood, Are not led astray by the doctrines of others; They are fully awakened, rightly knowing, They walk evenly amidst the uneven.”
translations.sn1.8:2: “Those whose qualities are badly confused, Are led astray by the doctrines of others; They are asleep, they do not wake up, It is time for them to wake up.”
translations.sn1.8:3: “Those whose qualities are not confused, Are not led astray by the doctrines of others; They are fully awakened, rightly knowing, They walk evenly amidst the uneven.”
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas: ‘Do not be displeased, dear sirs, with this devaputta. This devaputta, dear sirs, when formerly a human being, undertook faith in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata, undertook virtue, undertook learning, undertook generosity, undertook wisdom. Having undertaken faith in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata, having undertaken virtue, having undertaken learning, having undertaken generosity, having undertaken wisdom, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world, in companionship with the Tāvatiṃsa devas. He surpasses the other devas in beauty and glory.’ Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, pleasing the Tāvatiṃsa devas, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: Therefore the wise one should cultivate Faith and virtue, confidence and vision of the Dhamma; Remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.”
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is delightful ground?”
translations.sn11.15:2: “Parks, shrines, forest shrines, Well-made lotus ponds; They are not worth a sixteenth part Of delightful ground for humans.
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove. There … he said this: “Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a certain yakkha, ugly and deformed, was sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the devas. There, bhikkhus, the Tāvatiṃsa devas found fault with it, complained about it, and criticized it: ‘It is wonderful indeed, sirs, it is marvelous indeed, sirs, that this ugly, deformed yakkha is sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the devas.’ In whatever way, bhikkhus, the Tāvatiṃsa devas found fault with it, complained about it, and criticized it, in that same way that yakkha became more beautiful, more lovely, and more pleasing.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, approached that anger-eating yakkha; having approached, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having placed his right knee on the ground, having extended his hands in reverential salutation towards that anger-eating yakkha, he announced his name three times: ‘I am, dear sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, I am, dear sir, Sakka, lord of the devas.’ In whatever way, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, announced his name, in that same way that yakkha became more ugly and more deformed. Having become more ugly and more deformed, he vanished right there. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, sitting in his own seat, pleasing the Tāvatiṃsa devas, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4: ‘My mind is not easily struck, Nor am I easily drawn by praise; I am not angry for long, Anger does not persist in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: When angry I do not speak harshly, Nor do I proclaim the Dhamma; I restrain myself, Seeing my own good.’”
translations.sn11.24:2: “These two, bhikkhus, are fools. One who does not see a fault as a fault, and one who does not accept a fault declared in accordance with the Dhamma— these, bhikkhus, are two fools. These two, bhikkhus, are wise. One who sees a fault as a fault, and one who accepts a fault declared in accordance with the Dhamma— these, bhikkhus, are two wise ones.
translations.sn11.24:3: Once upon a time, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, pleasing the Tāvatiṃsa devas in the Sudhammā assembly hall, on that occasion recited this verse:
translations.sn11.24:4: ‘Let anger be your master, Do not grow old with friends; Do not blame the blameless, Do not speak divisively; Then anger, like a mountain, Will crush the evil person.’”
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you cannot recollect me, then recollect the Dhamma: “The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.” For, bhikkhus, when you recollect the Dhamma, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there will be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, then recollect the Saṅgha: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing straight, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing rightly, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing properly, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals— this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” For, bhikkhus, when you recollect the Saṅgha, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there will be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: What is the reason for this? Because, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, fearless, unterrified, undaunted, not fleeing.’” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:
translations.sn11.3:13: “Whether in the forest, at the root of a tree, Or in an empty dwelling, bhikkhus; Recollect the Fully Enlightened One, There will be no fear for you.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you cannot recollect the Buddha, The chief of the world, the bull of men; Then recollect the Dhamma, Leading out, well taught.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, Leading out, well taught; Then recollect the Saṅgha, The unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: Thus for those recollecting the Buddha, The Dhamma and the Saṅgha, bhikkhus; Fear or terror, Or hair-raising will not be.”
translations.sn11.3:2: "Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a battle between the devas and asuras was imminent. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa:
translations.sn11.3:3: 'If, dear sirs, fear, terror, or hair-raising should arise in those devas gone to battle, you should look up at my banner at that time. For when you look up at my banner, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there is, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look up at my banner, then you should look up at the banner of Pajāpati, king of devas. For when you look up at the banner of Pajāpati, king of devas, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there is, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: Why is that? For Sakka, bhikkhus, lord of the devas, is not free from lust, not free from hatred, not free from delusion; he is fearful, terrified, frightened, a runaway.
translations.sn11.3:9: But I, bhikkhus, say this: 'If fear, terror, or hair-raising should arise in you, bhikkhus, gone to the wilderness, gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty hut, you should recollect me at that time: "Such is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One." For when you, bhikkhus, recollect me, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there is, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:12: He acts for the welfare of both, of himself and of the other; knowing the other is provoked, the mindful one becomes calm.
translations.sn11.5:14: When Sakka, lord of the devas, had spoken these verses, the devas applauded, the asuras were silent. Then, bhikkhus, the retinue of devas and asuras said this: 'The verses spoken by Vepacitti, lord of asuras, are accompanied by punishment, accompanied by weapons—thus quarrel, thus dispute, thus conflict. The verses spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, are unaccompanied by punishment, unaccompanied by weapons—thus no quarrel, thus no dispute, thus no conflict. Victory to Sakka, lord of the devas, by well-spoken words.' Thus, bhikkhus, victory was to Sakka, lord of the devas, by well-spoken words.
translations.sn11.5:2: 'Fools would break out even more if there were no one to restrain them; therefore the wise should restrain the fool with severe punishment.'
translations.sn11.5:3: When Vepacitti, lord of asuras, had spoken this verse, the asuras applauded, the devas were silent. Then, bhikkhus, Vepacitti, lord of asuras, said to Sakka, lord of the devas: 'Speak, lord of the devas, a verse.' When this was said, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: 'This alone, I think, is the restraint of the fool: knowing the other is provoked, the mindful one becomes calm.'
translations.sn11.5:5: When Sakka, lord of the devas, had spoken this verse, the devas applauded, the asuras were silent. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to Vepacitti, lord of asuras: 'Speak, Vepacitti, a verse.' When this was said, bhikkhus, Vepacitti, lord of asuras, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: 'This alone, by patience, I see a fault, Vāsava: when the fool thinks, "This one endures out of fear for me," the dullard climbs upon one who runs away all the more, like a cow.
translations.sn11.5:8: 'Let him think or not, "This one endures out of fear for me"; there is no higher good than patience, for one whose highest good is one's own good.
translations.sn12.11:1: Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park ... "These four, bhikkhus, are nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the assistance of those seeking to become. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the assistance of those seeking to become.
translations.sn12.12:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. "These four, bhikkhus, are nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the assistance of those seeking to become. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the assistance of those seeking to become."
translations.sn12.15:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Kaccānagotta said this to the Blessed One: "'Right view, right view,' it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is there right view?"
translations.sn12.15:2: "This world, Kaccāna, is for the most part dependent on a duality—on existence and non-existence. For one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no non-existence in the world. For one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no existence in the world. This world, Kaccāna, is for the most part shackled by engagement, clinging, and adherence. But one does not approach, does not cling, does not adhere to that engagement, that mental fixation, that resolve and underlying tendency: 'This is my self.' 'Suffering is what arises, suffering is what ceases'—one does not doubt, does not waver; knowledge alone is one's support here. To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous and amiable greetings, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One: "We would like to ask the venerable Gotama about a certain point, if the venerable Gotama would give us the opportunity to answer the question." "This is not the right time for a question, Kassapa; we have entered among the houses."
translations.sn12.17:5: “‘The one who acts is the one who experiences,’ Kassapa, saying this from the beginning, ‘suffering is self-made,’ this approaches eternalism. ‘One acts, another experiences,’ Kassapa, saying this when one is afflicted by feeling, ‘suffering is made by another,’ this approaches annihilationism. Without approaching either of these extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, sir! Excellent, sir! Just as, sir, one might set upright what had been overturned … or would say ‘Let those with eyes see forms’; so too the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma and the Sangha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, may I receive the full ordination.”
translations.sn12.17:7: “Kassapa, one who formerly belonged to another sect and wishes for the going forth, wishes for the full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline, lives on probation for four months. At the end of four months, bhikkhus whose minds are satisfied give him the going forth and the full ordination to the state of being a bhikkhu. But I recognize individual differences.”
translations.sn12.18:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous and meaningful greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: “‘That feeling is the one who feels,’ Timbaruka, saying this from the beginning, ‘pleasure and pain is self-made,’ I do not say thus. ‘Feeling is one thing, the one who feels is another,’ Timbaruka, saying this when one is afflicted by feeling, ‘pleasure and pain is made by another,’ I do not say thus. Without approaching either of these extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.19:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for the fool hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thus come to be. So there is this body and name-and-form externally: thus this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact and the six sense bases; touched by these, or by any one of them, the fool experiences pleasure and pain.
translations.sn12.19:2: Bhikkhus, for the wise one hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thus come to be. So there is this body and name-and-form externally: thus this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact and the six sense bases; touched by these, or by any one of them, the wise one experiences pleasure and pain.
translations.sn12.19:3: Here, bhikkhus, what is the difference, what is the distinction, what is the distinguishing factor between the wise one and the fool?” “Our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, sir, the Blessed One as their guide, the Blessed One as their resort. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
translations.sn12.19:5: “Bhikkhus, the ignorance by which the fool is obstructed and the craving with which he is fettered—by which this body has come to be—that ignorance of the fool has not been abandoned and that craving has not been exhausted. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the fool has not lived the holy life rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, when the body breaks up, the fool is one who goes to a body; being one who goes to a body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. ‘He is not freed from suffering,’ I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, bhikkhus, is the source of craving? ‘Feeling’ should be said … ‘contact’ should be said … ‘the six sense bases’ should be said … ‘name-and-form’ should be said … ‘consciousness’ should be said … ‘formations’ should be said. Formations, bhikkhus, I say are with source, not without source. And what, bhikkhus, is the source of formations? ‘Ignorance’ should be said.
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as source are formations, with formations as source is consciousness, with consciousness as source is name-and-form, with name-and-form as source are the six sense bases, with the six sense bases as source is contact, with contact as source is feeling, with feeling as source is craving, with craving as source is clinging, with clinging as source is becoming, with becoming as source is birth, with birth as source is suffering, with suffering as source is faith, with faith as source is joy, with joy as source is rapture, with rapture as source is tranquility, with tranquility as source is happiness, with happiness as source is concentration, with concentration as source is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, with knowledge and vision of things as they really are as source is disenchantment, with disenchantment as source is dispassion, with dispassion as source is liberation, with liberation as source is the knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:7: Just as, bhikkhus, when rain falls heavily on a mountaintop, the water flows down according to the slope and fills up the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines; filled up, they fill the pools; the pools fill the lakes; the lakes fill the streams; the streams fill the rivers; and the rivers fill the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then in the evening, the Venerable Bhūmija emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged courteous and meaningful greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhūmija said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: Or, Ānanda, when there is the body, pleasure and pain arises internally with bodily volition as condition. Or, Ānanda, when there is speech, pleasure and pain arises internally with verbal volition as condition. Or, Ānanda, when there is mind, pleasure and pain arises internally with mental volition as condition, and with ignorance as condition.
translations.sn12.25:11: One personally, Ānanda, fabricates that bodily formation, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arises internally. Or others, Ānanda, fabricate that bodily formation, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arises internally. Or one mindfully, Ānanda, fabricates that bodily formation, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arises internally. Or one mindlessly, Ānanda, fabricates that bodily formation, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arises internally.
translations.sn12.25:2: “There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be self-made. But there are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be other-made. There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be both self-made and other-made. But there are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be neither self-made nor other-made, but arisen by chance. Here, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One say, how does he declare it, so that when we answer we would be speaking in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is contrary to fact, and would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who is a fellow-Dhamma-holder would find anything to criticize in our statement?”
translations.sn12.25:3: “Conditioned by contact, friend, pleasure and pain has been declared by the Blessed One. Conditioned by what? Conditioned by contact. Speaking thus, one would be speaking in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is contrary to fact, and would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who is a fellow-Dhamma-holder would find anything to criticize in one's statement.
translations.sn12.25:4: Therein, friend, as to those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be self-made, that too is conditioned by contact. And as to those … and as to those … and as to those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be neither self-made nor other-made, but arisen by chance, that too is conditioned by contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: Therein, friend, as to those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be self-made, it is impossible that they would experience anything apart from contact. And as to those … and as to those … and as to those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma, who declare pleasure and pain to be neither self-made nor other-made, but arisen by chance, it is impossible that they would experience anything apart from contact.”
translations.sn12.25:6: Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.25:7: “Good, good, Ānanda, as Sāriputta would answer correctly. Conditioned by contact, Ānanda, pleasure and pain has been declared by me. Conditioned by what? Conditioned by contact. Speaking thus, one would be speaking in accordance with what I have said, and would not misrepresent me with what is contrary to fact, and would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who is a fellow-Dhamma-holder would find anything to criticize in one's statement.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, bhikkhus, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention—this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. This is called form. Thus this is name and this is form. This, bhikkhus, is called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? These six, bhikkhus, are the classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, bhikkhus, is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, bhikkhus, are the formations? These three, bhikkhus, are the formations: bodily formation, verbal formation, mental formation. These, bhikkhus, are called formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, not knowing the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is existence? These three, bhikkhus, are existences: sensual existence, form existence, formless existence. This, bhikkhus, is called existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? These four, bhikkhus, are clingings: sensual clinging, view clinging, rules-and-vows clinging, self-doctrine clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: “This was said, Sāriputta, in the Pārāyana in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.31:2: ‘Those who have comprehended the Dhamma, and the many trainees here; Their wise conduct, I ask, tell me, O venerable ones.’
translations.sn12.31:3: How, Sāriputta, is the meaning of this brief statement to be seen in detail?” When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta was silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: “Do you see, Sāriputta, ‘This has come to be’?” “‘This has come to be,’ venerable sir, one sees as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen as it really is with correct wisdom ‘This has come to be,’ one is practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be. One sees as it really is with correct wisdom ‘Its nutriment has come to be.’ Having seen as it really is with correct wisdom ‘Its nutriment has come to be,’ one is practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding the nutriment of what has come to be. One sees as it really is with correct wisdom ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation.’ Having seen as it really is with correct wisdom ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation,’ one is practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation. Thus, venerable sir, one is a trainee.
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, sir, is one with things fully understood? 'This has come to be'—seeing this with right wisdom as it really is. Seeing with right wisdom as it really is that 'this has come to be', one becomes liberated by non-clinging through dispassion, fading away, and cessation regarding what has come to be. 'Its nutriment is the cause of its coming to be'—seeing this with right wisdom as it really is. Seeing with right wisdom as it really is that 'its nutriment is the cause of its coming to be', one becomes liberated by non-clinging through dispassion, fading away, and cessation regarding the nutriment as cause of coming to be. 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation'—seeing this with right wisdom as it really is.
