Seeing with right wisdom as it really is that 'with the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation', one becomes liberated by non-clinging through dispassion, fading away, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation. Thus, sir, is one with things fully understood. So, sir, regarding what was stated in the Pārāyana in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.35:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. 'With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, there are formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.' When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: 'What, sir, is aging-and-death, and whose is this aging-and-death?' 'Not a valid question,' said the Blessed One. 'Whoever would say,
translations.sn12.35:2: What, sir, is birth, and whose is this birth?' 'Not a valid question,' said the Blessed One. 'Whoever would say,
translations.sn12.35:3: What, sir, is existence, and whose is this existence?' 'Not a valid question,' said the Blessed One. 'Whoever would say,
translations.sn12.35:4: What, sir, are formations, and whose are these formations?' 'Not a valid question,' said the Blessed One. 'Whoever would say,
translations.sn12.35:5: But, bhikkhu, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever there is of this writhing, this contorting, this fidgeting—
translations.sn12.35:7: But, bhikkhu, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever there is of this writhing, this contorting, this fidgeting—
translations.sn12.38:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. 'Whatever, bhikkhus, one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one has a tendency toward, this becomes a basis for the maintenance of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of future renewed existence. When there is future renewed existence, future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.38:2: If, bhikkhus, one does not intend and does not plan, but still has a tendency toward, this becomes a basis for the maintenance of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of future renewed existence. When there is future renewed existence, future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.44:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. 'The origin and the passing away of the world, bhikkhus, I will teach you. Listen to this, attend carefully, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: "And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world."
translations.sn12.44:3: Dependent on the ear and sounds … dependent on the nose and odors … dependent on the tongue and tastes … dependent on the body and tactile objects … dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling … with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: "And what, bhikkhus, is the passing away of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the passing away of the world."
translations.sn12.46:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous greetings and conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: "What then, Master Gotama, does one act and one experience?" "'One acts and one experiences,' brahmin, this is one extreme."
translations.sn12.46:3: "But what then, Master Gotama, does one act and another experience?" "'One acts and another experiences,' brahmin, this is the second extreme. Without approaching either of these extremes, brahmin, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.51:10: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent, he understands it as not clung to, he understands it as not delighted in. If he feels a painful feeling, he understands it as impermanent, he understands it as not clung to, he understands it as not delighted in. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent, he understands it as not clung to, he understands it as not delighted in. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
translations.sn12.51:11: Feeling a feeling limited by the body, he understands: 'I feel a feeling limited by the body.' Feeling a feeling limited by life, he understands: 'I feel a feeling limited by life.' He understands: 'With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; bodily remains will be left behind.'
translations.sn12.51:12: Just as, bhikkhus, a man might remove a hot pot from a potter's kiln and place it on level ground. There whatever heat there was would subside right there, and the potsherds would be left behind. So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu feeling a feeling limited by the body understands: 'I feel a feeling limited by the body.' Feeling a feeling limited by life, he understands: 'I feel a feeling limited by life.' He understands: 'With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; bodily remains will be left behind.'
translations.sn12.51:13: "What do you think, bhikkhus, would a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed perform a meritorious formation, or a demeritorious formation, or an imperturbable formation?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.51:14: "But with all formations non-existent, with the cessation of formations, would consciousness be discerned?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.51:2: "To what extent, bhikkhus, would a bhikkhu examine so as to be completely committed to the complete destruction of suffering?" "Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it." "Then, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.51:3: "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu examines thus: 'This manifold, various suffering that arises in the world, aging-and-death; what is the source of this suffering, what is its origin, from what is it born, from what does it come to be? When what exists does aging-and-death come to be, when what does not exist does aging-and-death not come to be?' Examining thus, he understands thus: 'This manifold, various suffering that arises in the world, aging-and-death, this suffering has birth as its source, birth as its origin, is born from birth, comes to be from birth. When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; when there is no birth, aging-and-death does not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands aging-and-death, he understands the origin of aging-and-death, he understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and he understands the way of practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, and he practices in accordance with that, he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma; this, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is completely committed to the complete destruction of suffering, to the cessation of aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then further, examining, he examines thus: 'But this birth, what is its source, what is its origin, from what is it born, from what does it come to be? When what exists does birth come to be, when what does not exist does birth not come to be?' Examining thus, he understands thus: 'Birth has existence as its source, existence as its origin, is born from existence, comes to be from existence. When there is existence, birth comes to be; when there is no existence, birth does not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands birth, he understands the origin of birth, he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the practice leading to the cessation of birth, and he practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma; this, monks, is called a monk who is practicing in all respects for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, investigating further, he investigates: 'But what is the cause of existence … what is the cause of this clinging … what is the cause of this craving … feeling … contact … but what is the cause of this six sense bases … but what is this name-and-form … but what is this consciousness … but what is the cause of these formations, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their source; when what exists do formations exist, when what does not exist do formations not exist?' Investigating thus, he understands: 'Formations have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, ignorance as their source; when ignorance exists, formations exist, when ignorance does not exist, formations do not exist.'
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands formations, he understands the origin of formations, he understands the cessation of formations, and he understands the practice leading to the cessation of formations, and he practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma; this, monks, is called a monk who is practicing in all respects for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of formations.
translations.sn12.51:9: When, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person, overwhelmed by ignorance, forms a meritorious formation, consciousness goes to what is meritorious. When he forms a demeritorious formation, consciousness goes to what is demeritorious. When he forms an imperturbable formation, consciousness goes to what is imperturbable. But, monks, when a monk's ignorance has been abandoned and knowledge has arisen, with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, he forms neither a meritorious formation, nor a demeritorious formation, nor an imperturbable formation. Not forming, not intending, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he is not agitated, not being agitated he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'
translations.sn12.52:2: Just as, monks, a great mass of fire burning with ten, twenty, thirty, or forty loads of wood might burn. There a man might from time to time throw in dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood. Thus, monks, that great mass of fire, with that fuel, with that sustenance, would burn for a long time. So too, monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things subject to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.52:3: For one who dwells contemplating danger in things subject to clinging, monks, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:2: Just as, monks, a great tree. Whatever roots of it go downwards, whatever go across, all of those carry the sap upwards. Thus, monks, that great tree, with that food, with that sustenance, would stand for a long time. So too, monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things subject to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:3: For one who dwells contemplating danger in things subject to clinging, monks, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park …
translations.sn12.61:2: But that which, monks, is called mind, or intellect, or consciousness, there an uninstructed ordinary person is not able to become disenchanted, not able to become dispassionate, not able to become liberated. Why is that? Because, monks, for a long time this has been held to, appropriated, and grasped by the uninstructed ordinary person as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' Therefore there an uninstructed ordinary person is not able to become disenchanted, not able to become dispassionate, not able to become liberated.
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better, monks, if an uninstructed ordinary person took this body of four great elements as self, rather than the mind. Why is that? Because, monks, this body of four great elements is seen standing for one year, standing for two years, standing for three years, standing for four years, standing for five years, standing for ten years, standing for twenty years, standing for thirty years, standing for forty years, standing for fifty years, standing for a hundred years, or standing even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple carefully attends to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—that is, with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the origination of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.62:3: There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple carefully attends to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' With contact as basis that is to be felt as pleasant, bhikkhus, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same contact that is to be felt as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose with contact as basis that is to be felt as pleasant—ceases, it subsides. With contact as basis that is to be felt as painful, bhikkhus, painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that same contact that is to be felt as painful, the corresponding feeling—the painful feeling that arose with contact as basis that is to be felt as painful—ceases, it subsides. With contact as basis that is to be felt as neither painful nor pleasant, bhikkhus, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same contact that is to be felt as neither painful nor pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose with contact as basis that is to be felt as neither painful nor pleasant—ceases, it subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, bhikkhus, from the rubbing together and striking together of two sticks, heat is generated and fire is produced. From the separation and disjunction of those same two sticks, the corresponding heat ceases, it subsides; so too, bhikkhus, with contact as basis that is to be felt as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same contact that is to be felt as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose with contact as basis that is to be felt as pleasant—ceases, it subsides …pe… with contact as basis that is to be felt as painful … with contact as basis that is to be felt as neither painful nor pleasant, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same contact that is to be felt as neither painful nor pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose with contact as basis that is to be felt as neither painful nor pleasant—ceases, it subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, bhikkhus, would those people eat food for the sake of play, or for the sake of intoxication, or for the sake of ornamentation, or for the sake of decoration? 'No, venerable sir.' 'Would not those people eat food just for the sake of crossing over the desert?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'So too, bhikkhus, I say that gross nutriment is to be seen thus. When, bhikkhus, gross nutriment is fully understood, the five cords of sensual pleasure are fully understood. When the five cords of sensual pleasure are fully understood, there is no fetter by which the fettered noble disciple might return again to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, bhikkhus, is contact-nutriment to be seen? Suppose, bhikkhus, a cow without hide were to stand leaning against a wall. Creatures dependent on the wall would devour it. If it stood leaning against a tree, creatures dependent on the tree would devour it. If it stood leaning against water, creatures dependent on water would devour it. If it stood leaning against space, creatures dependent on space would devour it. For whatever that cow without hide stands leaning against, creatures dependent on that would devour it. So too, bhikkhus, I say that contact-nutriment is to be seen thus. When, bhikkhus, contact-nutriment is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further for the noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, bhikkhus, is mental-volition-nutriment to be seen? Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a pit of glowing embers, deeper than a man's height, full of embers without flame and without smoke. Then a man would come who wants to live, who does not want to die, who wants happiness and dislikes pain. Then two strong men, having grabbed him by both arms, would drag him to that pit of embers. Then, bhikkhus, that man's desire would be far away, his wish would be far away, his aspiration would be far away. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that man would think: 'I will fall into this pit of embers, and because of that I will meet with death or death-like suffering.' So too, bhikkhus, I say that mental-volition-nutriment is to be seen thus. When, bhikkhus, mental-volition-nutriment is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further for the noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: If, bhikkhus, there is lust, delight, and craving in gross nutriment, consciousness is established and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is descent of name-and-form. Where there is descent of name-and-form, there is growth of formations. Where there is growth of formations, there is future production of renewed existence. Where there is future production of renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is with sorrow, with anguish, with despair.
translations.sn12.64:4: Suppose, monks, a dyer or painter, with dye or lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder, and a well-smoothed plank, wall, or cloth, might create the form of a woman or a man, complete in all its parts. So too, monks, if there is lust, delight, and craving for solid food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of future renewed existence. Where there is the production of future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is with sorrow, with grief, with despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: If, monks, there is no lust, no delight, no craving for solid food, consciousness does not become established there and does not grow. Where consciousness does not become established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations. Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of future renewed existence. Where there is no production of future renewed existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, I say that is without sorrow, without grief, without despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Suppose, monks, a peaked house or a peaked hall had a window to the north, south, or east. When the sun rises, where would its rays become established? In the western wall, venerable sir. If, monks, there were no western wall, where would they become established? On the earth, venerable sir. If, monks, there were no earth, where would they become established? In water, venerable sir. If, monks, there were no water, where would they become established? They would not become established, venerable sir. So too, monks, if there is no lust, no delight, no craving for solid food ...
translations.sn12.65:1: At Sāvatthī. Before, monks, my awakening, when I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, this occurred to me: This world has fallen into hardship, in that it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn. Yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging-and-death. When will the escape from this suffering be discerned, from aging-and-death? Then, monks, this occurred to me: When what exists does aging-and-death come to be; by what condition does aging-and-death come to be? Then, monks, through proper attention, there was for me a breakthrough by wisdom: When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.65:3: Then, monks, this occurred to me—this consciousness turns back from name-and-form, it does not go beyond. It is to this extent that one may be born, age, die, pass away, or be reborn, that is, consciousness with name-and-form as condition; name-and-form with consciousness as condition; the six sense bases with name-and-form as condition; contact with the six sense bases as condition ... thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. Origin, origin—thus, monks, regarding things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose in me, wisdom arose in me, understanding arose in me, light arose in me.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then, monks, this occurred to me: When what does not exist does consciousness not come to be; with the cessation of what is there the cessation of consciousness? Then, monks, through proper attention, there was for me a breakthrough by wisdom: When there is no name-and-form, consciousness does not come to be; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn12.65:6: Then, monks, this occurred to me—this path to awakening has been discovered by me, that is, with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact ... thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. Cessation, cessation—thus, monks, regarding things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose in me, wisdom arose in me, understanding arose in me, light arose in me.
translations.sn12.65:7: Suppose, monks, a man walking through a forest wilderness saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of the past. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, inhabited by people of the past, complete with parks, groves, ponds, and walls, delightful. Then, monks, that man would inform a king or royal minister: May you know, sir—I, walking through a forest wilderness, saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of the past, and I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, inhabited by people of the past, complete with parks, groves, ponds, and walls, delightful. Sir, have that city restored. Then, monks, that king or royal minister would have that city restored. That city would then in time become prosperous and flourishing, populous, filled with people, grown and expanded. So too, monks, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by perfectly awakened ones of the past.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: Monks. Venerable sir, those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: Do you examine internally, monks, the internal? When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: I examine internally, venerable sir, the internal. But how, monk, do you examine internally the internal? Then that monk explained. As that monk explained, he did not satisfy the Blessed One's mind.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "It is the time, Blessed One; it is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to give a detailed analysis. Having heard the Blessed One, the monks will remember it." "Then, Ānanda, listen and attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, examining further, he examines in detail: 'But where does this craving arise when it arises, where does it settle when it settles?' Examining thus, he knows this—whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasing, it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles. And what in the world is agreeable and pleasing? The eye in the world is agreeable and pleasing, it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles. The ear in the world is agreeable and pleasing …pe… the nose in the world is agreeable and pleasing … the tongue in the world is agreeable and pleasing … the body in the world is agreeable and pleasing … the mind in the world is agreeable and pleasing, it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles.
translations.sn12.66:6: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, in the past regarded what is agreeable and pleasing in the world as permanent, regarded it as pleasant, regarded it as self, regarded it as healthy, regarded it as secure—they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased clinging. Those who increased clinging increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not liberated from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrow, from lamentation, from pain, from grief, from despair; 'they were not liberated from suffering,' I say.
translations.sn12.66:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, in the future will regard what is agreeable and pleasing in the world as permanent, will regard it as pleasant, will regard it as self, will regard it as healthy, will regard it as secure—they will increase craving. Those who will increase craving will increase clinging. Those who will increase clinging will increase suffering. Those who will increase suffering will not be liberated from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrow, from lamentation, from pain, from grief, from despair; 'they will not be liberated from suffering,' I say.
translations.sn12.66:8: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, now regard what is agreeable and pleasing in the world as permanent, regard it as pleasant, regard it as self, regard it as healthy, regard it as secure—they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase clinging. Those who increase clinging increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not liberated from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrow, from lamentation, from pain, from grief, from despair; 'they are not liberated from suffering,' I say.
translations.sn12.67:1: On one occasion Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous and meaningful conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said this to Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, is aging-and-death self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance?" "Friend Koṭṭhika, aging-and-death is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance. But rather, with birth as condition there is aging-and-death."
translations.sn12.67:2: "Friend Sāriputta, is birth self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance?" "Friend Koṭṭhika, birth is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance. But rather, with existence as condition there is birth."
translations.sn12.67:4: "Friend Sāriputta, is consciousness self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance?" "Friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance. But rather, with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness."
translations.sn12.67:5: Just now we understand Venerable Sāriputta's statement thus: 'Friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor neither self-made nor other-made but arisen by chance. But rather, with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form.'
translations.sn12.67:7: So, friend Sariputta, how should the meaning of this statement be understood? Now then, friend, I will make a simile for you. For it is through a simile that some intelligent people understand the meaning of what is said. Just as, friend, two sheaves of reeds might stand leaning against each other, so too, friend, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact ... thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. If, friend, someone were to pull one sheaf of reeds, the other would fall; if someone were to pull the other sheaf, the one would fall. So too, friend, with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact ... thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.67:8: It is wonderful, friend Sariputta; it is marvelous, friend Sariputta. So well was this spoken by Venerable Sariputta. And we approve of this statement spoken by Venerable Sariputta with these thirty-six grounds.
translations.sn12.68:13: Then is Venerable Narada an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed? Friend, as the cessation of existence is nibbana has been well seen by me as it really is with right wisdom, yet I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. Just as, friend, on a desert road there might be a well, but without rope or water-bucket. Then a man might come, overcome by heat, exhausted by heat, tired, thirsty. He would look at that well. He would have the knowledge there is water, yet he would not live having touched it with his body. So too, friend, as the cessation of existence is nibbana has been well seen by me as it really is with right wisdom, yet I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.
translations.sn12.68:6: Then is Venerable Musila an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed? When this was said, Venerable Musila was silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's Park. There ... The great ocean, monks, advancing, advances the great rivers; the great rivers advancing, advance the small rivers; the small rivers advancing, advance the great pools; the great pools advancing, advance the small pools. So too, monks, ignorance advancing, advances volitional formations; volitional formations advancing, advance consciousness; consciousness advancing, advances name-and-form; name-and-form advancing, advances the six sense bases; the six sense bases advancing, advance contact; contact advancing, advances feeling; feeling advancing, advances craving; craving advancing, advances clinging; clinging advancing, advances existence; existence advancing, advances birth; birth advancing, advances aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rajagaha on Mount Vulture Peak at the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Now on that occasion the Blessed One was honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, worshipped; he was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and provisions for the sick. The Sangha of monks was also honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, worshipped; it was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and provisions for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, not respected, not esteemed, not venerated, not worshipped; they were not recipients of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and provisions for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:10: But do you, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, abide having touched with your body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless? No indeed, friend.
translations.sn12.70:11: Then here the venerable ones have this explanation but no attainment of these things; how is this for us, friend? We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susima.
translations.sn12.70:12: I do not understand the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by these venerable ones. It is good if these venerable ones would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by these venerable ones. Whether you would understand, friend Susima, or whether you would not understand, we are liberated by wisdom.
translations.sn12.70:13: Then Venerable Susima rose from his seat, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Venerable Susima reported to the Blessed One all that conversation he had had with those monks. Susima, first there is knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma; afterwards, knowledge of nibbana.
translations.sn12.70:14: I do not understand, Lord, the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One. It is good, Lord, if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One. Whether you would understand, Susima, or whether you would not understand, first there is knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma; afterwards, knowledge of nibbana.
translations.sn12.70:16: Therefore, Susima, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling there is ... all feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever perception ... whatever volitional formations there are ... all volitional formations should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever consciousness there is ... all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, Susīma, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, becomes disenchanted with feeling, becomes disenchanted with perception, becomes disenchanted with volitional formations, becomes disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. With liberation, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'
translations.sn12.70:18: 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death,' Susīma, do you see thus? 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'With existence as condition, birth,' Susīma, do you see thus? 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'With clinging as condition, existence,' Susīma, do you see thus? 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'With craving as condition, clinging,' Susīma, do you see thus? 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'With feeling as condition, craving … With contact as condition, feeling … With the six sense bases as condition, contact … With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases … With consciousness as condition, name-and-form … With volitional formations as condition, consciousness … With ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' Susīma, do you see thus? 'Yes, venerable sir.'
translations.sn12.70:2: Now on that occasion the wanderer Susīma was dwelling at Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers. Then the assembly of wanderers said to the wanderer Susīma: 'Come, friend Susīma, live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Having learned the Dhamma, you should teach it to us. Having learned that Dhamma, we will teach it to the householders. Thus we too will be respected, esteemed, honored, venerated, and revered, and will obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and provisions for the sick.' 'Yes, friends,' the wanderer Susīma replied to his assembly. Having consented, he approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Susīma said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Friend Ānanda, I wish to live the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.'
translations.sn12.70:21: But do you, Susīma, knowing and seeing thus, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near? 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn12.70:25: But do you, Susīma, knowing and seeing thus, dwell having contacted with the body those liberations that are peaceful and immaterial, transcending forms? 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn12.70:27: Then Venerable Susīma fell with his head at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me, in that I was so foolish, so muddled, so unskillful as to go forth as a Dhamma-thief in this well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future.'
translations.sn12.70:3: Then Venerable Ānanda, taking the wanderer Susīma, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, this wanderer Susīma says thus: "Friend Ānanda, I wish to live the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline."' 'Then, Ānanda, let Susīma go forth.' The wanderer Susīma received the going forth under the Blessed One, he received the full ordination.
translations.sn12.70:5: But do you, venerable sirs, knowing and seeing thus, wield various kinds of spiritual power: having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and vanish; you go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; you dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; you walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, you travel in space like a bird; with your hand you touch and stroke the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; you exercise mastery with the body as far as the brahmā world? 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:6: But do you, venerable sirs, knowing and seeing thus, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near? 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:7: But do you, venerable sirs, knowing and seeing thus, understand the minds of other beings and persons, having encompassed them with your own mind? You understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust; you understand a mind without lust as a mind without lust; you understand a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; you understand a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; you understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; you understand a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; you understand a contracted mind as a contracted mind; you understand a distracted mind as a distracted mind; you understand an exalted mind as an exalted mind; you understand an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; you understand a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; you understand an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; you understand a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; you understand an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; you understand a liberated mind as a liberated mind; you understand an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind? 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:8: But do you, venerable sirs, knowing and seeing thus, recollect your manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus you recollect your manifold past abodes with their modes and details? 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:9: “But do you, venerable ones, knowing and seeing thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘These beings, endowed with bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, who revile the noble ones, hold wrong view, and take up wrong view as their action, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell; but these beings, endowed with good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, good mental conduct, who do not revile the noble ones, hold right view, and take up right view as their action, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, in a heavenly world’—do you thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: Now on one occasion Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. Now on that occasion Venerable Ānanda was wandering on tour in the Southern Hills together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Sharp moral shame and moral dread will be established in me towards the elders, the new ones, and those of middle standing.’ Thus, Kassapa, should you train.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Whatever Dhamma I hear that is connected with what is wholesome, having made that a bone, having attended to it mentally, having engaged with it with the whole mind, with ear set, I will listen to the Dhamma.’ Thus, Kassapa, should you train.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Mindfulness of the body connected with pleasure will not be abandoned by me.’ Thus, Kassapa, should you train.
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, having instructed me with this exhortation, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. For seven days, friend, I ate almsfood as a debtor; on the eighth day final knowledge arose.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Blessed One stepped down from the road and went to a certain tree root. Then I, friend, having spread out my rag-robe patchwork cloak fourfold, said to the Blessed One: ‘Here, venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit; this will be for my long-term welfare and happiness.’ The Blessed One, friend, sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to me: ‘Soft is this rag-robe patchwork cloak of yours, Kassapa.’ ‘May the Blessed One accept my rag-robe patchwork cloak, venerable sir, out of compassion.’ ‘But will you wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes, Kassapa?’ ‘I will wear the Blessed One’s worn-out hempen rag-robes, venerable sir.’ So I, friend, gave my rag-robe patchwork cloak to the Blessed One. But I took up the Blessed One’s worn-out hempen rag-robes.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, friend, having destroyed the taints, dwell having personally realized in this very life with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom; one might think to cover a seven-jeweled or eight-jeweled elephant with a palm leaf, so whoever might think to cover my six direct knowledges.”
translations.sn16.11:2: Now on that occasion thirty of Venerable Ānanda’s pupils, bhikkhus who were companions in the holy life, had rejected the training and reverted to the lower life, most of them being youths. Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered on tour in the Southern Hills as long as he wished, went to Rājagaha, to the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary, to Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda as he was sitting to one side: “For how many reasons, friend Ānanda, was the rule of three robes laid down by the Blessed One for families?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “For three reasons, venerable Kassapa, was the rule of three robes laid down by the Blessed One for families—for the restraint of ill-behaved persons, for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus, so that those of evil wishes might not split the Saṅgha by taking up a faction, and for compassion towards families. These, venerable Kassapa, are the three reasons for which the rule of three robes was laid down by the Blessed One for families.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “Then why do you, friend Ānanda, wander on tour with these new bhikkhus who are unguarded in their sense faculties, immoderate in eating, and not devoted to wakefulness? You seem to be wandering about destroying crops, you seem to be wandering about destroying families. Your assembly is breaking up, friend; your new pupils are falling away. This youth does not know moderation.”
translations.sn16.11:6: The bhikkhunī Thullanandā heard: “It seems that Venerable Mahākassapa has disparaged Venerable Ānanda the Wise as a youth.”
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, displeased, uttered a displeased utterance: “Why does Venerable Mahākassapa, who was formerly of another sect, think to disparage Venerable Ānanda the Wise as a youth?” Venerable Mahākassapa heard the bhikkhunī Thullanandā speaking this speech.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: "Indeed, friend Ānanda, Thullanandā the bhikkhunī has spoken rashly without reflection. Since I, friend, having cut off my hair and beard and put on the ochre robes, went forth from the home life into homelessness, I do not recall acknowledging any other teacher except the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Formerly, friend, while I was still a householder, this occurred to me: 'Confined is the household life, a path of dust; the going forth is like open air. It is not easy for one dwelling at home to lead the holy life completely perfect, completely pure, polished like a conch shell. Let me then cut off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.' So, friend, at a later time, having made a patchwork cloak of rags, with those in the world who are arahants as my inspiration, having cut off my hair and beard and put on the ochre robes, I went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.sn16.13:2: Just as, Kassapa, gold does not disappear as long as no counterfeit of gold has arisen in the world. But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of gold arises in the world, then gold disappears. So too, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear as long as no counterfeit of the true Dhamma has arisen in the world. But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.
translations.sn16.13:4: These five, Kassapa, are things that lead to the decline and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers dwell without respect and without deference towards the Teacher; they dwell without respect and without deference towards the Dhamma; they dwell without respect and without deference towards the Saṅgha; they dwell without respect and without deference towards the training; they dwell without respect and without deference towards concentration—these, Kassapa, are the five things that lead to the decline and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahākassapa. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahākassapa: "It is said, friend Kassapa, that one without ardor, without fear of wrongdoing, is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme security from bondage; but one with ardor, with fear of wrongdoing, is capable of enlightenment, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the supreme security from bondage."
translations.sn16.2:3: And how, friend, is one without fear of wrongdoing? Here, friend, a bhikkhu does not fear: 'Unarisen evil unwholesome states arising in me would lead to harm'; he does not fear: 'Arisen evil unwholesome states not being abandoned in me would lead to harm'; he does not fear: 'Unarisen wholesome states not arising in me would lead to harm'; he does not fear: 'Arisen wholesome states ceasing in me would lead to harm.' Thus, friend, one is without fear of wrongdoing. Thus, friend, one without ardor, without fear of wrongdoing, is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme security from bondage.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how, friend, is one with ardor? Here, friend, a bhikkhu arouses ardor: 'Unarisen evil unwholesome states arising in me would lead to harm'; he arouses ardor: 'Arisen evil unwholesome states not being abandoned in me would lead to harm'; he arouses ardor: 'Unarisen wholesome states …' Thus, friend, one is with ardor.
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard … at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Venerable Mahākassapa: "You are old now, Kassapa, and these heavy hempen rag-robes that you wear are burdensome. Therefore, Kassapa, you should wear householder robes, accept invitations, and dwell close to me."
translations.sn21.10:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. Now on that occasion a certain bhikkhu named Thera was a lone dweller and a speaker in praise of lone dwelling. He enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, sits alone in seclusion, and resorts to walking meditation alone. Then several bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: "Here, venerable sir, a certain bhikkhu named Thera is a lone dweller and a speaker in praise of lone dwelling."
translations.sn21.10:3: "There is this, Thera, lone dwelling, I do not say there is not. But, Thera, listen to how lone dwelling is completely fulfilled in detail, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," … "And how, Thera, is lone dwelling completely fulfilled in detail? Here, Thera, whatever is past is abandoned, whatever is future is relinquished, and desire and lust for present acquisitions of selfhood are well subdued. Thus, Thera, lone dwelling is completely fulfilled in detail."
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus." "Friend," those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: "Here, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: 'Noble silence, noble silence is said. What is noble silence?' Then, friends, it occurred to me: 'Here a bhikkhu, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, with the settling and unification of mind within, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of samādhi. This is called noble silence.' So, friends, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, with the settling and unification of mind within, without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of samādhi. While I was dwelling in this dwelling, perceptions and attention accompanied by applied thought arose in me.
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus." "Friend," those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: "Here, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: 'Is there anything in the world with regard to which change and alteration would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair in me?' Then, friends, it occurred to me: 'There is nothing in the world with regard to which change and alteration would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair in me.'"
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary, in one dwelling. Then Venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, approached Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. After exchanging polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said this to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: "Your faculties are serene, friend Moggallāna; your facial complexion is pure and bright. Surely Venerable Mahāmoggallāna dwelt today in a peaceful dwelling?" "I dwelt today, friend, in a coarse dwelling. But I had a Dhamma discussion." "But with whom did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma discussion?" "I had a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One, friend." "But the Blessed One is far away, friend; he is now dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by psychic power, or did the Blessed One approach Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by psychic power?" "I did not approach the Blessed One by psychic power, friend, nor did the Blessed One approach me by psychic power. But as far as the Blessed One is, so far my divine eye and divine ear element became purified. And as far as I am, so far the Blessed One's divine eye and divine ear element became purified." "But how did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One?"
translations.sn21.3:3: "Here, friend, I said this to the Blessed One: 'One who has aroused energy, one who has aroused energy, venerable sir, is said. How, venerable sir, is one who has aroused energy?' When I had said this, friend, the Blessed One said this to me: 'Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused—let skin, sinews, and bones remain, let the flesh and blood in the body dry up, as long as what is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion has not been attained, there will be no stopping of energy. Thus, Moggallāna, is one who has aroused energy.' Thus, friend, I had a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One."
translations.sn21.3:6: Only Sāriputta in wisdom, in virtue and in peace; whichever bhikkhu has gone to the far shore, he would be supreme in these."
translations.sn21.6:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya coming from afar. Having seen him, he addressed the bhikkhus: "Do you see, bhikkhus, this bhikkhu coming, ugly, unsightly, hunchbacked, one whom the bhikkhus despise?" "Yes, venerable sir." "This bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is one of great psychic power and great majesty, and that attainment is not easy to achieve which this bhikkhu has not already achieved. He dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge here and now the unsurpassed culmination of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness." The Blessed One said this … the Teacher:
translations.sn21.6:2: Swans, herons, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer; all are afraid of the lion, there is no equality in body.
translations.sn21.8:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One's cousin, having dressed in pressed and ironed robes, having anointed his eyes, having taken a shiny bowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. The Blessed One said this to Venerable Nanda who was sitting to one side: "This does not become you, Nanda, a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith—that you should dress in pressed and ironed robes, anoint your eyes, and carry a shiny bowl. This becomes you, Nanda, a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith—that you should be a forest dweller, an almsfood eater, a rag-robe wearer, and dwell without concern for sensual pleasures." The Blessed One said this … the Teacher:
translations.sn21.8:2: When shall I see Nanda, a forest dweller, a rag-robe wearer, subsisting by gleaning alms, without concern for sensual pleasures?"
translations.sn21.9:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One's first cousin's son, approached the Blessed One; having approached, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side, miserable, dejected, shedding tears. Then the Blessed One said this to Venerable Tissa: "Why are you sitting to one side, miserable, dejected, shedding tears?" "Because, venerable sir, the bhikkhus have stabbed me all around with verbal daggers." "Then you, Tissa, are a speaker but not one who endures speech; that, Tissa, is not proper for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, that you are a speaker but not one who endures speech. This, Tissa, is proper for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness: that you would be both a speaker and one who endures speech."
translations.sn22.100:2: "Have you seen, bhikkhus, a painting called a painting?" "Yes, venerable sir." "That painting too, bhikkhus, called a painting is made by the mind. That painting too, bhikkhus, is even more variegated than the mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, one should constantly examine one's own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, by hatred, by delusion.' By mental defilement, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; by mental purification, beings are purified."
translations.sn22.100:3: "I do not see, bhikkhus, any other single group so variegated as the creatures of the animal realm. Those creatures too, bhikkhus, of the animal realm are made variegated by the mind. Those creatures too, bhikkhus, of the animal realm are even more variegated than the mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, one should constantly examine one's own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, by hatred, by delusion.' By mental defilement, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; by mental purification, beings are purified."
translations.sn22.101:1: At Sāvatthī. "For one who knows, for one who sees, bhikkhus, I say, there is the destruction of the taints, not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see. What, bhikkhus, does one know, what does one see, for there to be the destruction of the taints? 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling ... such is perception ... such are formations ... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness'—it is in this way, bhikkhus, that for one who knows, for one who sees, there is the destruction of the taints."
translations.sn22.101:2: For a bhikkhu dwelling without devotion to development, bhikkhus, even if there arises this wish: 'Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints by non-clinging,' yet his mind is not liberated from the taints by non-clinging. Why is that? 'Because of non-development' should be said. Because of non-development of what? Because of non-development of the four establishments of mindfulness, because of non-development of the four right strivings, because of non-development of the four bases for spiritual power, because of non-development of the five faculties, because of non-development of the five powers, because of non-development of the seven factors of enlightenment, because of non-development of the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Just as, bhikkhus, a hen might have eight or ten or twelve eggs, but she had not sat on them properly, had not warmed them properly, had not developed them properly. Even if there arose in that hen this wish: 'Oh, that my chicks might break out of the eggshell with their foot claws or beaks and hatch safely,' yet those chicks would be unable to break out of the eggshell with their foot claws or beaks and hatch safely. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the hen's eight or ten or twelve eggs had not been sat on properly, had not been warmed properly, had not been developed properly. So too, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu dwelling without devotion to development, even if there arises this wish: 'Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints by non-clinging,' yet his mind is not liberated from the taints by non-clinging. Why is that? 'Because of non-development' should be said. Because of non-development of what? Because of non-development of the four establishments of mindfulness ... pe ... the eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṃsumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the deer park. Then the householder Nakula's father approached the Blessed One; having approached, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Nakula's father said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.1:10: He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. He is obsessed with the notion 'I am feeling, feeling is mine.' For one obsessed with the notion 'I am feeling, feeling is mine,' that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of that feeling, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:11: He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. He is obsessed with the notion 'I am perception, perception is mine.' For one obsessed with the notion 'I am perception, perception is mine,' that perception changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of that perception, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:12: He regards formations as self, or self as possessing formations, or formations as in self, or self as in formations. He is obsessed with the notion 'I am formations, formations are mine.' For one obsessed with the notion 'I am formations, formations are mine,' those formations change and become otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of those formations, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:13: He regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. 'I am consciousness, consciousness is mine'—he is obsessed with this. For one obsessed with 'I am consciousness, consciousness is mine,' when that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. Thus, householder, he is sick in body and sick in mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one sick in body but not sick in mind? Here, householder, a noble disciple who has heard much, who sees the noble ones, who is skilled in the noble Dhamma, who is trained in the noble Dhamma, who sees good persons, who is skilled in the good persons' Dhamma, who is trained in the good persons' Dhamma—he does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. 'I am form, form is mine'—he is not obsessed with this. For one not obsessed with 'I am form, form is mine,' when that form changes and becomes otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.
translations.sn22.1:2: 'I, venerable sir, am old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, come to the last stage. My body is afflicted, constantly troubled. And I, venerable sir, am one who sees the impermanence of the Blessed One and the mind-pleasing monks. May the Blessed One exhort me, may the Blessed One instruct me, for my long-term welfare and happiness.'
translations.sn22.1:3: 'So it is, householder, so it is. This body, householder, is afflicted, wrapped up in a shell. For one who carries around this body, whoever might claim even a moment of health, what is that except folly? Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: 'Though my body is afflicted, my mind shall be unafflicted.' Thus, householder, should you train.'
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakula's father, having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. When he was seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to the householder Nakula's father: 'Your faculties are serene, householder; your facial complexion is pure and bright. Did you hear the Dhamma talk from the Blessed One today?'
translations.sn22.1:7: But did it not occur to you, householder, to ask the Blessed One further: 'To what extent, venerable sir, is one sick in body and sick in mind, and to what extent is one sick in body but not sick in mind?' 'We would have come from afar, venerable sir, to Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if it would occur to Venerable Sāriputta himself to explain the meaning of this statement.'
translations.sn22.1:8: 'Then, householder, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' the householder Nakula's father replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.1:9: And how, householder, is one sick in body and sick in mind? Here, householder, an uninstructed ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, who is unskilled and untrained in the noble Dhamma, who has not seen good persons, who is unskilled and untrained in the good persons' Dhamma—he regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. 'I am form, form is mine'—he is obsessed with this. For one obsessed with 'I am form, form is mine,' when that form changes and becomes otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.22:2: And who, monks, is the burden-carrier? The person, so it is said. This venerable one of such name, such clan—this, monks, is called the burden-carrier.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, monks, is the taking up of the burden? This craving for further becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, that is, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for being, craving for non-being. This, monks, is called the taking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, monks, is the laying down of the burden? The remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. This, monks, is called the laying down of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:6: 'The five aggregates are indeed burdens, the person is the burden-carrier; taking up the burden is suffering in the world, laying down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in the Sakyan town named Devadaha. Then several monks who were going to the western lands approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: 'We wish, venerable sir, to go to the western lands, to take up residence in the western lands.'
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friends, by undertaking and dwelling in unwholesome states one would dwell at ease in this very life, without trouble, without fever, without distress, and with a good destination expected after the breakup of the body, after death, then the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But because, friends, by undertaking and dwelling in unwholesome states one dwells in suffering in this very life, with trouble, with fever, with distress, and with a bad destination expected after the breakup of the body, after death, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:2: 'But have you, monks, taken leave of Sāriputta?' 'No, venerable sir, we have not taken leave of Venerable Sāriputta.' 'Take leave, monks, of Sāriputta. Sāriputta, monks, is wise, a helper of the monks, a companion in the holy life.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One, in a certain thicket of rose-apple trees. Then those bhikkhus, having approved and agreed with what the Blessed One said, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping their right sides towards him, and approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging cordial and memorable words, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, we wish to go to the outlying country, to take up residence in the outlying country. The Teacher has given his consent."
translations.sn22.2:5: "Even from afar, friends, we would come to Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement." "Then, friends, listen and attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One …pe… and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute." "Bhikkhu, whatever one clings to, by that one is measured; whatever one is measured by, that is called 'mine.' Whatever one does not cling to, by that one is not measured; whatever one is not measured by, that is not called 'mine.'" "Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Fortunate One!"
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantis at Kuraraghara on Steep Mountain. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: "Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One in the Māgaṇḍiya Question in the Aṭṭhakavagga:
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one not satiated with sensual pleasures? Here, householder, a certain person is not rid of lust for sensual pleasures, not rid of desire, not rid of affection, not rid of thirst, not rid of fever, not rid of craving for sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, one is not satiated with sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one satiated with sensual pleasures? Here, householder, a certain person is rid of lust for sensual pleasures, rid of desire, rid of affection, rid of thirst, rid of fever, rid of craving for sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, one is satiated with sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, is one given to preferring? Here, householder, a certain person thinks: 'May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling in the future, may I be of such perception in the future, may I be of such formations in the future, may I be of such consciousness in the future.' Thus, householder, one is given to preferring.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, is one a maker of quarrelsome speech with people? Here, householder, a certain person makes such speech: 'You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. What do you understand of this Dhamma and Discipline? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. What should have been said first you said last; what should have been said last you said first. What is consistent for me is inconsistent for you. Your thesis is overturned. You are refuted; get out of that if you can.' Thus, householder, one is a maker of quarrelsome speech with people.
translations.sn22.3:17: Having abandoned home, resorting to the homeless state, Not making intimacies in the village, the sage; Satiated with sensual pleasures, not given to preferring, How would he make quarrelsome speech with people?
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, is one resorting to home? One bound by attachment to and obsession with form-cognizance, householder, is called 'resorting to home.' Sound-cognizance …pe… odour-cognizance … taste-cognizance … tactile-cognizance … mental-cognizance. One bound by attachment to and obsession with mental-cognizance, householder, is called 'resorting to home.' Thus, householder, one is resorting to home.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, is one intimate in the village? Here, householder, a certain person dwells in association with householders, sharing their happiness and sorrow, happy when they are happy, sorrowful when they are sorrowful, and he involves himself in their affairs when they arise. Thus, householder, one is intimate in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, is one not intimate in the village? Here, householder, a bhikkhu dwells without association with householders, not sharing their happiness or sorrow, not happy when they are happy, not sorrowful when they are sorrowful, and he does not involve himself in their affairs when they arise. Thus, householder, one is not intimate in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins perceive various kinds of self, all perceive the five aggregates subject to clinging, or a certain one among them. What five?
