Here, bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for good persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, perceives form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. Perceives feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus this perception and the notion 'I am' have not vanished in him. When, bhikkhus, the notion 'I am' has not vanished, there is descent of the five sense faculties—eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty. There is, bhikkhus, mind, there are mental phenomena, there is the element of ignorance. Touched by feeling born of contact with ignorance, bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling thinks 'I am'; thinks 'I am this'; thinks 'I will be'; thinks 'I will not be'; thinks 'I will be with form'; thinks 'I will be formless'; thinks 'I will be percipient'; thinks 'I will be non-percipient'; thinks 'I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient.'
translations.sn22.48:1: At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, I will teach the five aggregates and the five aggregates subject to clinging. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever kind of form there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the form aggregate. Whatever kind of feeling … whatever kind of perception … whatever kind of formations, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine … this is called the formations aggregate. Whatever kind of consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the consciousness aggregate. These are called, bhikkhus, the five aggregates.
translations.sn22.53:1: At Sāvatthī. "Clinging, bhikkhus, one is unliberated; without clinging, one is liberated. If, bhikkhus, consciousness were to stand, it would stand with form as its support, with form as its object, with form as its foundation, with delight as its infusion, and it would grow, increase, and expand. With feeling as its support … with perception as its support … with formations as its support, bhikkhus, consciousness would stand, it would stand with formations as its object, with formations as its foundation, with delight as its infusion, and it would grow, increase, and expand.
translations.sn22.53:2: If anyone, bhikkhus, should say thus: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will make known the coming, going, passing away, rebirth, growth, increase, or expansion of consciousness'—this is not possible.
translations.sn22.54:2: With form as its support, bhikkhus, consciousness would stand, it would stand with form as its object, with form as its foundation, with delight as its infusion, and it would grow, increase, and expand. With feeling as its support, bhikkhus, consciousness would stand … with perception as its support, bhikkhus, consciousness would stand … with formations as its support, bhikkhus, consciousness would stand, it would stand with formations as its object, with formations as its foundation, with delight as its infusion, and it would grow, increase, and expand.
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: 'Were there not, would there not be for me; it will not be, nor will it be for me'—resolving thus, a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters." When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "But how, venerable sir, resolving 'Were there not, would there not be for me; it will not be, nor will it be for me'—would a bhikkhu cut off the lower fetters?"
translations.sn22.55:10: But how, venerable sir, knowing what, seeing what, is there immediately the destruction of the taints?" "Here, bhikkhu, an uninstructed ordinary person is frightened in a frightening situation. This fear, bhikkhu, of the uninstructed ordinary person: 'Were there not, would there not be for me; it will not be, nor will it be for me.'
translations.sn22.55:4: He does not understand as it really is: painful form is 'painful form' … painful feeling … painful perception … painful formations … painful consciousness is 'painful consciousness.'
translations.sn22.55:5: He does not understand as it really is: non-self form is 'non-self form,' non-self feeling is 'non-self feeling,' non-self perception is 'non-self perception,' non-self formations are 'non-self formations,' non-self consciousness is 'non-self consciousness.'
translations.sn22.55:6: He does not understand as it really is: conditioned form is 'conditioned form,' conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned formations … conditioned consciousness is 'conditioned consciousness.' He does not understand as it really is: form will cease … feeling will cease … perception will cease … formations will cease … consciousness will cease.
translations.sn22.55:8: He understands as it really is: impermanent form is 'impermanent form.' Impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent formations … impermanent consciousness is 'impermanent consciousness.' Painful form … painful consciousness … non-self form … non-self consciousness … conditioned form … conditioned consciousness is 'conditioned consciousness.' He understands as it really is: form will cease. Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness will cease.
translations.sn22.55:9: With the cessation of form, with the cessation of feeling, with the cessation of perception, with the cessation of formations, with the cessation of consciousness—it is thus, bhikkhu, that resolving 'Were there not, would there not be for me; it will not be, nor will it be for me'—a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters." "'Resolving thus,' venerable sir, 'a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters.'
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? These six, bhikkhus, are the classes of consciousness—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called, bhikkhus, consciousness. With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness. This noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.56:14: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, having directly known consciousness thus, having directly known the origin of consciousness thus, having directly known the cessation of consciousness thus, having directly known the way leading to the cessation of consciousness thus, are practicing for disenchantment with consciousness, for dispassion towards it, for its cessation, they are practicing well. Those who are practicing well are grounded in this Dhamma and Discipline.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? Form, I directly knew; the origin of form, I directly knew; the cessation of form, I directly knew; the way leading to the cessation of form, I directly knew. Feeling … Perception … Volitional formations … Consciousness, I directly knew; the origin of consciousness, I directly knew; the cessation of consciousness, I directly knew; the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, I directly knew.
translations.sn22.56:5: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, having directly known form thus …pe… having directly known the way leading to the cessation of form thus, are liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form, they are well liberated. Those who are well liberated are consummate ones. For consummate ones, there is no round for describing.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Sāvatthī. 'One skilled in seven cases, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who investigates in three ways is called in this Dhamma and Discipline a consummate one, one who has lived the holy life, an ultimate person. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in seven cases? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, understands the way leading to the cessation of form; understands the gratification of form, understands the danger of form, understands the escape from form; understands feeling … perception … volitional formations … understands consciousness, understands the origin of consciousness, understands the cessation of consciousness, understands the way leading to the cessation of consciousness; understands the gratification of consciousness, understands the danger of consciousness, understands the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, bhikkhus, are volitional formations? These six, bhikkhus, are classes of volition—volition regarding forms …pe… volition regarding mental phenomena. These are called, bhikkhus, volitional formations. With the arising of contact there is the arising of volitional formations; with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of volitional formations. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations, that is, right view …pe… right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: Whatever pleasure and joy arises in dependence on consciousness—this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, subject to change—this is the danger of consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, having directly known consciousness thus, having directly known the origin of consciousness thus, having directly known the cessation of consciousness thus, having directly known the way leading to the cessation of consciousness thus; having directly known the gratification of consciousness thus, having directly known the danger of consciousness thus, having directly known the escape from consciousness thus, are liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of consciousness, they are well liberated. Those who are well liberated are consummate ones. For consummate ones, there is no round for describing. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is skilled in seven cases.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, bhikkhus, is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. This is called, bhikkhus, form. With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of form; with the cessation of nutriment there is the cessation of form. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of form, that is, right view …pe… right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:5: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, having directly known form thus, having directly known the origin of form thus, having directly known the cessation of form thus, having directly known the way leading to the cessation of form thus; having directly known the gratification of form thus, having directly known the danger of form thus, having directly known the escape from form thus, are liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form, they are well liberated. Those who are well liberated are consummate ones. For consummate ones, there is no round for describing.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, bhikkhus, is feeling? These six, bhikkhus, are classes of feeling—feeling born of eye-contact …pe… feeling born of mind-contact. This is called, bhikkhus, feeling. With the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling; with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of feeling. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, that is, right view …pe… right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:7: Whatever pleasure and joy arises in dependence on feeling—this is the gratification of feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, subject to change—this is the danger of feeling. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Sāvatthī. 'The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form, and is called the Perfectly Enlightened One. The bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, who is liberated by wisdom, is liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form, and is called liberated by wisdom.
translations.sn22.58:3: The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of perception … of volitional formations … of consciousness, and is called the Perfectly Enlightened One. The bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, who is liberated by wisdom, is liberated by non-clinging through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of consciousness, and is called liberated by wisdom.
translations.sn22.59:10: Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.sn22.59:7: “Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.5:11: He does not delight in consciousness, does not approve of it, does not cling to it. For one who does not delight in consciousness, does not approve of it, does not cling to it, the delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight, clinging ceases … thus there comes to be the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of form, what is the origin of feeling, what is the origin of perception, what is the origin of formations, what is the origin of consciousness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights, approves, and clings.
translations.sn22.5:3: What does he delight in, approve of, and cling to? He delights in form, approves of it, and clings to it. For one who delights in form, approves of it, and clings to it, delight arises. That delight in form is clinging. With clinging as condition, there is existence; with existence as condition, there is birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: He delights in feeling … he delights in perception … he delights in formations … he delights in consciousness, approves of it, and clings to it. For one who delights in consciousness, approves of it, and clings to it, delight arises. That delight in consciousness is clinging. With clinging as condition, there is existence; with existence as condition, there is birth; with birth as condition … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: What does he not delight in, not approve of, not cling to? He does not delight in form, does not approve of it, does not cling to it. For one who does not delight in form, does not approve of it, does not cling to it, the delight in form ceases. With the cessation of delight, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases … thus there comes to be the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.60:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Mahāvana in the hall with the peaked roof. Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One … and having sat down to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: “Pūraṇa Kassapa, venerable sir, says thus: ‘There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause, without condition.’ What does the Blessed One say about this?”
translations.sn22.60:3: “There is, Mahāli, a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause, with condition. There is, Mahāli, a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause, with condition.”
translations.sn22.60:4: “But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings; how are beings defiled with cause, with condition?”
translations.sn22.60:5: “For if, Mahāli, this form were exclusively painful, accompanied by pain, penetrated by pain, not penetrated by pleasure, beings would not become attached to form. But because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, penetrated by pleasure, not penetrated by pain, therefore beings become attached to form; being attached, they become bound; being bound, they become defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings; thus beings are defiled with cause, with condition.
translations.sn22.60:8: For if, Mahāli, this consciousness were exclusively painful, accompanied by pain, penetrated by pain, not penetrated by pleasure, beings would not become attached to consciousness. But because, Mahāli, consciousness is pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, penetrated by pleasure, not penetrated by pain, therefore beings become attached to consciousness; being attached, they become bound; being bound, they become defiled. This too, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings. Thus too beings are defiled with cause, with condition.”
translations.sn22.60:9: “But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings; how are beings purified with cause, with condition?” “For if, Mahāli, this form were exclusively pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, penetrated by pleasure, not penetrated by pain, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because, Mahāli, form is painful, accompanied by pain, penetrated by pain, not penetrated by pleasure, therefore beings become disenchanted with form; being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; being dispassionate, they are purified. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings. Thus beings are purified with cause, with condition.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ As far as there are abodes of beings, as far as the highest existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world, that is, the arahants.”
translations.sn22.76:4: “Happy indeed are the arahants,  craving is not found in them;  The conceit ‘I am’ has been cut off,  the net of delusion torn apart.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates,  seven who practice the true Dhamma;  Praiseworthy are the good persons,  sons of the Buddha, born of his breast.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven treasures,  trained in the three trainings;  The great heroes wander about,  having abandoned fear and terror.
translations.sn22.76:8: Endowed with the ten factors,  great elephants, concentrated;  These indeed are the best in the world,  craving is not found in them.
translations.sn22.76:9: The knowledge of the trainee has arisen,  this is the final body;  The essence of the holy life,  in this there is no dependence on another.
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. "Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, recollect their manifold past abodes in recollection, all of them recollect the five aggregates subject to clinging, or a certain one among them. Which five? 'Such was my form in the past'—thus, bhikkhus, in recollecting one recollects form. 'Such was my feeling in the past'—thus, bhikkhus, in recollecting one recollects feeling. 'Such was my perception … 'Such were my volitional formations … 'Such was my consciousness in the past'—thus, bhikkhus, in recollecting one recollects consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:10: 'Now I am devoured by consciousness. In the past too I was devoured by consciousness in just the same way, just as I am now devoured by present consciousness. If I were to delight in future consciousness, in the future too I would be devoured by consciousness in just the same way, just as I am now devoured by present consciousness.' Having reflected thus, he becomes indifferent to past consciousness; he does not delight in future consciousness; and for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness, he practises accordingly.
translations.sn22.79:7: There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: 'Now I am devoured by form. In the past too I was devoured by form in just the same way, just as I am now devoured by present form. If I were to delight in future form, in the future too I would be devoured by form in just the same way, just as I am now devoured by present form.' Having reflected thus, he becomes indifferent to past form; he does not delight in future form; and for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form, he practises accordingly.
translations.sn22.80:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha's Park. Then the Blessed One, having dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus for some reason, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, returning from the alms round, he approached the Great Wood for the day's abiding. Having plunged into the Great Wood, he sat down for the day's abiding at the root of a Beluva sapling.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Blessed One consented by silence. Then Brahmā Sahampati, having understood the Blessed One's consent, having paid homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, disappeared right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then the Blessed One, emerging from seclusion in the evening, approached the Nigrodha's Park; having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that those bhikkhus, appearing respectful, would approach me one by one. Those bhikkhus too, appearing respectful, approached the Blessed One one by one; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. To those bhikkhus who had sat down to one side, the Blessed One said this:
translations.sn22.80:6: "This, bhikkhus, is the lowest among livelihoods, that is, alms-gathering. This, bhikkhus, is a term of abuse in the world: 'You alms-gatherer wander about with a bowl in hand.' And yet, bhikkhus, sons of good family take it up for a good reason, on account of a good reason; not driven by kings, not driven by thieves, not on account of debt, not from fear, not for the sake of livelihood; but [thinking] 'We are beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an ending of this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.'
translations.sn22.80:7: Thus, bhikkhus, has this son of good family gone forth. And he is covetous, with fierce passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will and intentions of corruption, muddle-minded, without clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, with unrestrained faculties. Just as, bhikkhus, a firebrand from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends, smeared with dung in the middle, finds no firewood in the village, finds no firewood in the forest. Such a one, bhikkhus, I say is like this person: failed in the enjoyments of the householder, and not fulfilling the purpose of the ascetic life.
translations.sn22.80:9: These two, bhikkhus, are views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: 'Is there anything in the world that I could cling to without fault?' He understands thus: 'There is nothing in the world that I could cling to without fault. For if I should cling, I would cling only to form, only to feeling, only to perception, only to volitional formations, only to consciousness. For me, from clinging as condition, there would be existence; from existence as condition, birth; from birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair would arise. Thus would be the origin of this entire mass of suffering.'
translations.sn22.81:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita's Park. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kosambī, after the meal, returning from the alms round, having packed away his own resting place himself, taking bowl and robe, without informing his attendants, without taking leave of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, set out on tour alone, without a companion.
translations.sn22.81:10: He does not regard form as self, does not regard feeling as self, does not regard perception … does not regard volitional formations … does not regard consciousness as self; yet he has such a view: 'That self, that world, I will become permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change after death.' That, bhikkhus, is an eternalist view, which is a volitional formation. That volitional formation—what is its source … Thus too, bhikkhus, for one who knows and sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs without delay.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages, arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One dwelt at Pālileyyaka at the root of the Bhaddasāla tree. Then several bhikkhus approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. After exchanging courteous and amiable words, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to Venerable Ānanda: "It has been long since we, friend Ānanda, have heard a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One face to face; we wish, friend Ānanda, to hear a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One face to face."
translations.sn22.82:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in Migāramātu's Mansion, together with a large bhikkhu saṅgha. Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the full-moon night, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the bhikkhu saṅgha.
translations.sn22.82:10: "What, venerable sir, is the gratification in form, what is the danger, what is the escape; what is the gratification in feeling ... what is the gratification in perception ... what is the gratification in formations ... what is the gratification in consciousness, what is the danger, what is the escape?" "Whatever happiness and joy, bhikkhu, arises in dependence on form—this is the gratification in form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form. Whatever happiness and joy arises in dependence on feeling ... in dependence on perception ... in dependence on formations ... whatever happiness and joy arises in dependence on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness." "Good, venerable sir," that bhikkhu said, and having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's statement, he asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: "How, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see so that in this conscious body and in all external signs, the conceit 'I am,' the conceit 'mine,' and the underlying tendency to conceit do not occur?" "Whatever form, bhikkhu, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—one sees all form as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Whatever feeling ... whatever perception ... whatever formations ... whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—one sees all consciousness as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' It is, bhikkhu, when one knows thus, when one sees thus, that in this conscious body and in all external signs, the conceit 'I am,' the conceit 'mine,' and the underlying tendency to conceit do not occur."
translations.sn22.82:12: Now on that occasion a certain bhikkhu had this thought: "So it seems, sir, that form is non-self, feeling ... perception ... formations ... consciousness is non-self; how then do actions done by what is non-self affect oneself?" Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in that bhikkhu's mind, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.82:13: "It is possible, bhikkhus, that some foolish person here, unknowing and unseeing, with a mind obsessed by craving, might think to go beyond the Teacher's teaching. 'So it seems, sir, that form is non-self, feeling ... perception ... formations ... consciousness is non-self. How then do actions done by what is non-self affect oneself?' You have been trained by me through questioning, bhikkhus, in regard to this and that in these and those things.
translations.sn22.82:4: "What, venerable sir, is the root of these five aggregates subject to clinging?" "These five aggregates subject to clinging, bhikkhu, have desire as their root." ... "Is clinging, venerable sir, the same as these five aggregates subject to clinging, or is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging?" "Clinging, bhikkhu, is not the same as these five aggregates subject to clinging, nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging; rather, the desire and lust there is the clinging in regard to that." "Good, venerable sir," that bhikkhu ... asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: "Could there be, venerable sir, diversity in desire and lust for the five aggregates subject to clinging?" "There could be, bhikkhus," the Blessed One said: "Here, bhikkhu, it occurs to someone: 'May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling in the future, may I be of such perception in the future, may I be of such formations in the future, may I be of such consciousness in the future.' Thus, bhikkhu, there could be diversity in desire and lust for the five aggregates subject to clinging." "Good, venerable sir," that bhikkhu ... asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: "What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the form aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the formations aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate?" "The four great elements, bhikkhu, are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the designation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the formations aggregate. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate." "Good, venerable sir," that bhikkhu ... asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: “But sir, how does identity view come about?” “Here, mendicant, an uneducated ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen good persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of good persons. They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form. They regard feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. That’s how identity view comes about.” “Good, sir,” said that mendicant … and asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: “But sir, how does identity view not come about?” “Here, mendicant, an educated noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen good persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of good persons. They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form. They don’t regard feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. That’s how identity view does not come about.” “Good, sir,” said that mendicant … and asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Ānanda addressed the mendicants: “Reverends, mendicants!” “Reverend,” they replied. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn22.83:3: “Reverend Ānanda, suppose a woman or man—young, youthful, and fond of adornments—examines their own facial reflection in a clean bright mirror or a bowl of clear water. They’d look at it with attachment, not without attachment. In the same way, reverend Ānanda, one has the notion ‘I am’ because of attachment to form, not without attachment. One has the notion ‘I am’ because of attachment to feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, not without attachment.
translations.sn22.84:10: “Tissa, this simile was made by me to convey a meaning. And this is the meaning here: ‘A man who is unskilled in the path’ is a term for an ordinary person. ‘A man who is skilled in the path’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. ‘A fork in the road’ is a term for doubt. ‘The left path’ is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view … wrong immersion. ‘The right path’ is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion. ‘A dense forest grove’ is a term for ignorance. ‘A large marshy swamp’ is a term for sensual pleasures. ‘A steep cliff’ is a term for anger and distress. ‘Level, delightful ground’ is a term for extinguishment. Take delight, Tissa, take delight! I will advise you, I will support you, I will instruct you.”
translations.sn22.84:5: “Good, good, Tissa! That’s how it is. When one has not rid oneself of desire for choices, when one has not rid oneself of desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for consciousness, then with the breakup of that consciousness, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn22.84:6: “Good, good, Tissa! That’s how it is. When one has not rid oneself of desire for consciousness. What do you think, Tissa? When one has rid oneself of desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, then with the breakup of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.85:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time a mendicant named Yamaka had the following harmful view: “As I understand the teaching taught by the Buddha, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and does not exist after death.”
translations.sn22.85:10: “What do you think, reverend Yamaka? Do you regard the Realized One as form … feeling … perception … choices … consciousness?” “No, reverend.”
translations.sn22.85:11: “What do you think, reverend Yamaka? Do you regard the Realized One as that which is without form … without feeling … without perception … without choices … without consciousness?” “No, reverend.” “But reverend Yamaka, when the Realized One is not apprehended in this very life as real and truly existing, is it appropriate for you to declare: ‘As I understand the teaching taught by the Buddha, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and does not exist after death’?”
translations.sn22.85:12: “Reverend Sāriputta, formerly, when I was ignorant, I did have such a harmful view. But now that I’ve heard the teaching from Venerable Sāriputta, I’ve given up that harmful view and understood the teaching.”
translations.sn22.85:16: They don’t truly understand impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’. They don’t truly understand impermanent feeling as ‘impermanent feeling’. They don’t truly understand impermanent perception as ‘impermanent perception’. They don’t truly understand impermanent choices as ‘impermanent choices’. They don’t truly understand impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness’.
translations.sn22.85:19: They don’t truly understand conditioned form as ‘conditioned form’. They don’t truly understand conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned choices … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness’.
translations.sn22.85:20: They do not truly understand murderous form as 'murderous form'. They do not truly understand murderous feeling as 'murderous feeling' … murderous perception as 'murderous perception' … murderous formations as 'murderous formations'. They do not truly understand murderous consciousness as 'murderous consciousness'.
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach, cling to, and assert form as 'my self'. They approach, cling to, and assert feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as 'my self'. For them, these five clinging aggregates, approached and clung to, lead to long-term harm and suffering.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand impermanent form as 'impermanent form'. They truly understand impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent formations … impermanent consciousness as 'impermanent consciousness'.
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand selfless form as 'selfless form'. They truly understand selfless feeling … selfless perception … selfless formations … selfless consciousness as 'selfless consciousness'.
translations.sn22.85:5: When those bhikkhus were unable to dissuade Venerable Yamaka from that evil view, then those bhikkhus rose from their seats and approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu named Yamaka has arisen with such an evil view: "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that an arahant bhikkhu, when the body breaks up, is annihilated and destroyed, and does not exist after death." May Venerable Sāriputta approach Yamaka the bhikkhu out of compassion.' Venerable Sāriputta consented in silence. Then Venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, approached Venerable Yamaka; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Yamaka … and sat down to one side. Venerable Sāriputta, having sat down to one side, said to Venerable Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: 'Is it true, friend Yamaka, that such an evil view has arisen in you: "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that an arahant bhikkhu, when the body breaks up, is annihilated and destroyed, and does not exist after death"?' 'Yes, friend, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that an arahant bhikkhu, when the body breaks up, is annihilated and destroyed, and does not exist after death.'
translations.sn22.85:9: 'What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?' 'No indeed, friend.' 'Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?' 'No indeed, friend.' 'In feeling … apart from feeling … in perception … apart from perception … in formations … apart from formations … in consciousness do you regard the Tathāgata?' 'No indeed, friend.' 'Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from consciousness?' 'No indeed, friend.'
translations.sn22.86:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Now at that time Venerable Anurādha was dwelling in a forest hut not far from the Blessed One. Then a number of wanderers of other sects approached Venerable Anurādha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Anurādha. After exchanging polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anurādha: 'Friend Anurādha, that Tathāgata, the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest, when declaring, declares him in these four positions: "The Tathāgata exists after death," or "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"?'
translations.sn22.86:10: 'What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form … feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?' 'No indeed, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.86:11: 'What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard that which is formless … without feeling … without perception … without formations … without consciousness as the Tathāgata?' 'No indeed, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.86:12: 'But here, Anurādha, with the Tathāgata not being found in truth and reality even in this life, is it proper for you to declare: "Friend, that Tathāgata, the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest, when declaring, declares him apart from these four positions—'The Tathāgata exists after death' … 'does not exist' … 'both exists and does not exist' … 'neither exists nor does not exist after death"?' 'No indeed, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, Venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers of other sects: 'Friend, that Tathāgata, the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest, when declaring, declares him apart from these four positions: "The Tathāgata exists after death," or "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death."' When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anurādha: 'This bhikkhu must be newly ordained, recently gone forth, or else he is an elder who is foolish and incompetent.' Then those wanderers of other sects, having disparaged Venerable Anurādha with the charge of being new and the charge of being foolish, rose from their seats and departed.
translations.sn22.86:3: Then, not long after those wanderers of other sects had departed, it occurred to Venerable Anurādha: 'If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me further questions, how should I answer so that I would be one who speaks in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, would answer in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate criticism of my position could be found?'
translations.sn22.86:8: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:9: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?” “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as in feeling …pe… as apart from feeling …pe… as in perception … as apart from perception … as in formations … as apart from formations … as in consciousness … as apart from consciousness?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.89:10: “Just as, friends, the scent of a blue lotus, or a red lotus, or a white lotus. If someone were to say: ‘The scent of the stalk,’ or ‘the scent of the color,’ or ‘the scent of the filaments,’ would he be speaking rightly?” “No, friend.” “Then how, friends, would he answer rightly?” “‘The scent of the flower,’ friend, would be the right answer.” “Even so, friends, I do not say ‘I am’ with regard to form, nor do I say ‘I am’ apart from form. I do not say ‘I am’ with regard to feeling … perception … formations … consciousness, nor do I say ‘I am’ apart from consciousness. Yet, friends, although ‘I am’ is found in me regarding the five clinging-aggregates, I do not regard [anything] as ‘this is what I am.’
translations.sn22.89:11: “Although, friends, for a noble disciple the five lower fetters have been abandoned, still there remains in him the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am,’ the underlying tendency ‘I am’ that is not uprooted regarding the five clinging-aggregates. Then later he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five clinging-aggregates—‘such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ As he dwells contemplating rise and fall in these five clinging-aggregates, whatever conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ underlying tendency ‘I am’ that remained in him regarding the five clinging-aggregates, that too is uprooted.
translations.sn22.89:12: “Just as, friends, a cloth is soiled and stained. Its owners give it to a washerman. The washerman rubs it with salt, lye, or cow dung, and rinses it in clean water. Although that cloth becomes clean and bright, still there remains the smell of salt, lye, or cow dung that is not uprooted. The washerman gives it back to the owners. They put it in a casket scented with fragrance. Whatever smell of salt, lye, or cow dung that remained, that too is uprooted. Even so, friends, although for a noble disciple the five lower fetters have been abandoned, still there remains in him the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am,’ the underlying tendency ‘I am’ that is not uprooted regarding the five clinging-aggregates. Then later he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five clinging-aggregates. ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ As he dwells contemplating rise and fall in these five clinging-aggregates, whatever conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ underlying tendency ‘I am’ that remained in him regarding the five clinging-aggregates, that too is uprooted.”
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the senior monks said to Venerable Khemaka: “We did not ask Venerable Khemaka in order to trouble him, yet Venerable Khemaka was able to explain, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and make plain the Blessed One’s instruction in detail. Thus has Venerable Khemaka explained, taught, proclaimed, established, revealed, analyzed, and made plain the Blessed One’s instruction in detail.”
translations.sn22.90:1: At one time several senior monks were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then in the evening Venerable Channa emerged from seclusion and, taking a key, went from dwelling to dwelling to the senior monks and said: “May the venerable senior monks exhort me, may they instruct me, may they give me a Dhamma talk so that I might see the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the senior monks said to Venerable Channa: “Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.”
translations.sn22.90:3: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: “I too think thus: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’ Yet my mind does not launch out upon, gain confidence in, settle on, or resolve upon the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Agitation and clinging arise; the mind turns back: ‘Then what is my self?’ But one who sees the Dhamma does not think thus. Who might teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma?”
translations.sn22.90:4: Then Venerable Channa thought: "This Venerable Ānanda is dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita's Park, praised by the Teacher and esteemed by wise fellow monks; Venerable Ānanda is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I could see the Dhamma; and I have such confidence in Venerable Ānanda. Let me approach Venerable Ānanda." Then Venerable Channa, having packed away his dwelling place, taking his bowl and robe, went to Kosambī, to Ghosita's Park, to Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda …pe… and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Channa said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn22.90:8: "Even by this much we are satisfied with Venerable Channa; indeed, Venerable Channa has made it known, has cut the bar. Apply your mind, friend Channa, listen; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma." Then Venerable Channa, just by that much, arose with lofty rapture: "I am capable of understanding the Dhamma."
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. "I do not dispute with the world, monks; the world disputes with me. A proponent of Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world. Whatever is not agreed upon in the world by the wise, I too say 'it is not.' Whatever is agreed upon in the world by the wise, I too say 'it is.'
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, monks, is agreed upon in the world by the wise, which I say 'it is'? Form, monks, is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is agreed upon in the world by the wise; I too say 'it is.' Feeling is impermanent …pe… consciousness is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is agreed upon in the world by the wise; I too say 'it is.' This, monks, is agreed upon in the world by the wise; I too say 'it is.'
translations.sn22.94:4: There is, monks, in the world a worldly phenomenon, which the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully understands; having fully awakened to and fully understood it, he explains it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, elucidates it.
translations.sn22.94:7: One who, monks, when being thus explained, taught, proclaimed, established, disclosed, analyzed, elucidated by the Tathāgata, does not know and does not see—what can I do for that person, monks, a fool, an ordinary person, blind, without eyes, unknowing, unseeing?
translations.sn22.95:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayujjhā on the bank of the river Gaṅgā. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.95:10: As one reflects upon it, as one examines it thoroughly; It appears hollow and empty, to one who sees it thoroughly.
translations.sn22.95:11: Concerning this body, taught by the one of vast wisdom; Abandonment of three things, see form as discarded.
translations.sn22.95:12: Life, heat, and consciousness, when they abandon this body; Then it lies cast away, food for others, without consciousness.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuum, this illusion that fools prattle about; This murderer has been declared, no essence is found here.
translations.sn22.95:2: "Suppose, monks, this river Gaṅgā were carrying along a great lump of foam. A man with good eyesight would see it, reflect upon it, and examine it thoroughly. To him, seeing it, reflecting upon it, and examining it thoroughly, it would appear hollow, it would appear empty, it would appear without essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in a lump of foam? So too, monks, whatever form there is, past, future, or present …pe… whether far or near, a monk sees it, reflects upon it, and examines it thoroughly. To him, seeing it, reflecting upon it, and examining it thoroughly, it appears hollow, it appears empty, it appears without essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in form?
translations.sn22.95:3: Suppose, monks, in the autumn, when it is raining in large drops, a water bubble arises and ceases on the water. A man with good eyesight would see it, reflect upon it, and examine it thoroughly. To him, seeing it, reflecting upon it, and examining it thoroughly, it would appear hollow, it would appear empty, it would appear without essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in a water bubble? So too, monks, whatever feeling there is, past, future, or present …pe… whether far or near, a monk sees it, reflects upon it, and examines it thoroughly. To him, seeing it, reflecting upon it, and examining it thoroughly, it appears hollow, it appears empty, it appears without essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in feeling?
translations.sn22.95:4: Suppose, monks, in the last month of the hot season, at midday, a mirage shimmers. A man with good eyesight would see it, reflect upon it, and examine it thoroughly. To him, seeing it, reflecting upon it, and examining it thoroughly, it would appear hollow, it would appear empty …pe… for what essence, monks, could there be in a mirage? So too, monks, whatever perception …pe…
translations.sn22.95:5: Suppose, monks, a man seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, taking a sharp axe, would enter a forest. There he would see a great banana tree, straight, fresh, without sprouts. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut it at the top; having cut it at the top, he would peel away the layers of sheaths. Peeling away the layers of sheaths, he would not even find sapwood, let alone heartwood. A man with good eyesight would see it, reflect upon it, and examine it thoroughly. To him, seeing it, reflecting upon it, and examining it thoroughly, it would appear hollow, it would appear empty, it would appear without essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in a banana tree? So too, monks, whatever formations there are, past, future, or present …pe… whether far or near, a monk sees them, reflects upon them, and examines them thoroughly. To him, seeing them, reflecting upon them, and examining them thoroughly, they appear hollow, they appear empty, they appear without essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in formations?
translations.sn22.95:6: Suppose, monks, a magician or a magician's apprentice were to display a magic trick at a crossroads. A man with good eyesight would see it, observe it, and properly investigate it. To him, seeing it, observing it, and properly investigating it, it would appear empty, it would appear hollow, it would appear insubstantial. For what essence, monks, could there be in a magic trick? In the same way, monks, whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present … or far or near—a monk sees it, observes it, and properly investigates it. To him, seeing it, observing it, and properly investigating it, it appears empty, it appears hollow, it appears insubstantial. For what essence, monks, could there be in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing thus, monks, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated' … he understands: 'There is no further becoming in this state of existence.'
translations.sn22.95:9: Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a banana tree, and consciousness is like a magic trick—so taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: "Is there, venerable sir, any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever? Is there, venerable sir, any feeling … any perception … any formations … any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever?" "There is not, monk, any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever. There is not, monk, any feeling … any perception … any formations … any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever."
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Blessed One, taking up a small clod of cow dung in his hand, said to that monk: "Even this much, monk, of personal existence is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will not remain the same forever. If, monk, even this much of personal existence were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this holy life would not be discerned for the complete destruction of suffering. But because, monk, even this much of personal existence is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the holy life is discerned for the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.sn22.96:3: In the past, monk, I was a king, a khattiya, anointed. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī as the royal capital. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace as the foremost. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand pinnacled halls, with the Great Pinnacled Hall as the foremost. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand couches, made of ivory, of heartwood, of gold, with woolen coverings, woven covers, embroidered covers, with deer-hide coverings on top, with red cushions at both ends. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold, with gold banners, covered with gold nets, with the royal elephant Uposatha as the foremost. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold, with gold banners, covered with gold nets, with the royal horse Valāhaka as the foremost. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with gold, with gold banners, covered with gold nets, with the chariot Vejayanta as the foremost. While I was that king, monk, that anointed khattiya, there were eighty-four thousand gems, with the gem treasure as the foremost. While I was that king, monk … there were eighty-four thousand women, with Lady Subhaddā as the foremost. While I was that king, monk … there were eighty-four thousand khattiyas as attendants, with the wheel-turning gem as the foremost. While I was that king, monk … there were eighty-four thousand cows, with milk pails and bronze vessels. While I was that king, monk … there were eighty-four hundred thousand garments, of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, and fine cotton. While I was that king, monk … there were eighty-four thousand serving dishes; morning and evening meals were served.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Blessed One, taking up a little bit of dust on the tip of his fingernail, said to that monk: "Even this much, monk, of form is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will not remain the same forever. If, monk, even this much of form were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this holy life would not be discerned for the complete destruction of suffering. But because, monk, even this much of form is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the holy life is discerned for the complete destruction of suffering."
translations.sn35.101:4: Suppose, monks, whatever grass, sticks, branches, and leaves there are in this Jeta's Grove, people were to carry them away, burn them, or do with them as they see fit—would it occur to you: 'People are carrying us away, burning us, or doing with us as they see fit'?
translations.sn35.116:2: Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: "This Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow monks. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief teaching given by the Blessed One, the meaning not yet analyzed in detail. What if we were to approach Venerable Ānanda and ask him about this matter?"
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those bhikkhus approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. After exchanging polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn35.116:5: "Just as, friend, a man in search of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, might pass by the root of a great tree standing with heartwood, might pass by the trunk, and think that heartwood should be sought in the branches and foliage; so it is with you venerable ones, having passed by the Teacher face-to-face, thinking that you should ask us about this matter. For, friends, the Blessed One knows, he sees—he has become vision, he has become knowledge, he has become the Dhamma, he has become Brahma, the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. And this was the proper time for you to ask the Blessed One about this matter. As the Blessed One would have explained it to you, so you should remember it."
translations.sn35.116:6: "Surely, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One knows, he sees—he has become vision, he has become knowledge, he has become the Dhamma, he has become Brahma, the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. And this was the proper time for us to ask the Blessed One about this matter. As the Blessed One would have explained it to us, so we would remember it. But Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow monks. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief teaching given by the Blessed One, the meaning not yet analyzed in detail. Let Venerable Ānanda analyze it, not making it difficult."
translations.sn35.116:7: "Then, friends, listen, attend well, I will speak." "Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: "Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Ānanda, and having risen from their seats, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.117:1: "Before my awakening, bhikkhus, when I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, this occurred to me: 'Whatever five cords of sensual pleasure have been touched by the mind in the past, ceased, changed, my mind might often go there rather than to present or future ones.' Then, bhikkhus, this occurred to me: 'Whatever five cords of sensual pleasure have been touched by the mind in the past, ceased, changed, there proper heedfulness, mindfulness, and protection of the mind should be practiced by me.' Therefore, bhikkhus, you too, whatever five cords of sensual pleasure have been touched by the mind in the past, ceased, changed, your minds might often go there rather than to present or future ones. Therefore, bhikkhus, you too, whatever five cords of sensual pleasure have been touched by the mind in the past, ceased, changed, there proper heedfulness, mindfulness, and protection of the mind should be practiced by you. Therefore, bhikkhus, that base should be understood where the eye ceases and perception of forms ceases, that base should be understood …pe… where the tongue ceases and perception of tastes ceases, that base should be understood …pe… where the mind ceases and perception of mental phenomena ceases, that base should be understood." Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to the Blessed One: "What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition why some beings here do attain final Nibbāna in this very life?"
translations.sn35.118:2: There are, lord of the devas, forms cognizable by the eye, desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, arousing lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains holding to them, then consciousness becomes dependent on that and clings to that. With clinging, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu does not attain final Nibbāna …pe….
translations.sn35.118:3: There are, lord of the devas, tastes cognizable by the tongue …pe… There are, lord of the devas, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, arousing lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains holding to them, then consciousness becomes dependent on that and clings to that. With clinging, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu does not attain final Nibbāna. This, lord of the devas, is the cause, this is the condition why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life.
translations.sn35.118:4: But there are, lord of the devas, forms cognizable by the eye, desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, arousing lust. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain holding to them, then consciousness does not become dependent on that, does not cling to that. Without clinging, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna …pe….
translations.sn35.127:1: At one time Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita's monastery. Then King Udena went up to Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Udena said to Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: "What is the cause, Master Bhāradvāja, what is the reason why these young monks—black-haired, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, never having played the games of sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure spiritual life for their entire lives, and also extend their lifespan?" "This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha: 'Come, monks, you should establish a mother's mind towards your motherly women, a sister's mind towards your sisterly women, a daughter's mind towards your daughterly women.' This, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks—black-haired, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, never having played the games of sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure spiritual life for their entire lives, and also extend their lifespan."
translations.sn35.127:2: "The mind is restless, Master Bhāradvāja. Sometimes greedy thoughts arise even towards motherly women, towards sisterly women, towards daughterly women. Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, another cause, another reason why these young monks—black-haired … and also extend their lifespan?"
translations.sn35.127:3: "This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha: 'Come, monks, you should examine this very body, from the soles of the feet up, from the tips of the hairs down, enclosed by skin, full of many kinds of impurity: In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.' This too, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks—black-haired … and also extend their lifespan." "For those monks, Master Bhāradvāja, who have developed the body, developed ethics, developed the mind, developed wisdom, this is easy. But for those monks, Master Bhāradvāja, who have not developed the body, not developed ethics, not developed the mind, not developed wisdom, this is difficult. Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, when one intends to attend to the unattractive, the attractive comes. Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, another cause, another reason why these young monks—black-haired … and also extend their lifespan?"
translations.sn35.127:4: "This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha: 'Come, monks, you should live with sense doors guarded. Seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its sign or its features. Since, if you lived with the eye faculty unguarded, bad unwholesome qualities of covetousness and displeasure would flow in, practice for its restraint; guard the eye faculty; achieve restraint of the eye faculty. Hearing a sound with the ear … Smelling an odor with the nose … Tasting a flavor with the tongue … Touching a tangible with the body … Knowing a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its sign or its features. Since, if you lived with the mind faculty unguarded, bad unwholesome qualities of covetousness and displeasure would flow in, practice for its restraint; guard the mind faculty; achieve restraint of the mind faculty.' This too, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks—black-haired, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, never having played the games of sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure spiritual life for their entire lives, and also extend their lifespan."
translations.sn35.136:2: Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, touches, and mental phenomena as well; agreeable, pleasing, and delightful, are called 'as far as they go'.
translations.sn35.136:3: These are agreed upon as happiness by the world with its devas; where these cease, that is agreed upon as suffering by them.
translations.sn35.136:4: The noble ones have seen as happiness the cessation of identity; this is contrary to what is seen by all the world.
translations.sn35.136:5: What others call happiness, that the noble ones call suffering; what others call suffering, that the noble ones, the wise, know as happiness.
translations.sn35.136:6: See this Dhamma hard to understand, where the foolish are confused; for those who are covered there is darkness, for those who do not see.
translations.sn35.136:7: For the wise there is light, like light for those who see; those unskilled in the path of Dhamma do not understand what is near.
translations.sn35.136:8: By those obsessed with lust for existence, by those following lust for existence, by those come under Māra's power, this Dhamma is not well understood.
translations.sn35.63:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Migajāla …pe… sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Migajāla said to the Blessed One: "'One who lives alone, one who lives alone,' venerable sir, is said. How, venerable sir, is one a 'one who lives alone,' and how, venerable sir, is one a 'one who lives with a second'?"
translations.sn35.69:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Upasena were staying near Rājagaha in the Cool Wood, at the Snake's Hood Grotto. Now at that time a viper had fallen on Venerable Upasena's body. Then Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: "Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a stretcher and carry it outside. Before this body breaks up right here, like a handful of chaff."
translations.sn35.74:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk went up to the Blessed One …pe… sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: "In such and such a dwelling, venerable sir, a certain monk is new, unknown, sick, suffering, seriously ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would go to that monk out of compassion."
translations.sn35.74:12: "Good, good, monk. It is good that you, monk, understand the Dhamma taught by me as for the fading away of lust. For the Dhamma is taught by me, monk, as for the fading away of lust. What do you think, monk, is the eye permanent or impermanent?"
translations.sn35.74:18: But what is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change, is it fitting to regard that as: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard both the new monk's statement and the sick monk's statement, knowing "The monks do not know this one," approached that monk. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he lay down on his couch. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: "Enough, monk, do not lie down on your couch. There are seats prepared here; I will sit there." The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to that monk: "Is it tolerable for you, monk? Is it bearable? Are painful feelings subsiding, not increasing? Is there subsiding evident, not increase?"
translations.sn35.74:3: "It is not tolerable for me, venerable sir, not bearable; my painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; increase is evident, not subsidence."
translations.sn35.75:7: "I understand, venerable sir, that the Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One for the purpose of Nibbāna through non-clinging."
translations.sn35.75:8: "Good, good, monk. It is good that you understand, monk, that the Dhamma has been taught by me for the purpose of Nibbāna through non-clinging. For the Dhamma has been taught by me, monk, for the purpose of Nibbāna through non-clinging."
translations.sn35.88:1: Then Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached …pe… seated to one side, Venerable Puṇṇa said to the Blessed One: "It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute."
translations.sn35.88:12: "If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta strike me with a stick, then this will occur to me: 'These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed excellent, in that they do not strike me with a sword.' Thus it will be here, Blessed One; thus it will be here, Fortunate One."
translations.sn35.88:14: "If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta strike me with a sword, then this will occur to me: 'These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed excellent, in that they do not take my life with a sharp sword.' Thus it will be here, Blessed One; thus it will be here, Fortunate One."
translations.sn35.88:16: "If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta take my life with a sharp sword, then this will occur to me: 'There are disciples of that Blessed One who, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted with body and life, seek a weapon-bearer; this weapon-bearer has been obtained by me without seeking.' Thus it will be here, Blessed One; thus it will be here, Fortunate One."
translations.sn35.88:17: "Good, good, Puṇṇa. You will be able, Puṇṇa, endowed with this self-taming, to dwell in the country of Sunāparanta. Now, Puṇṇa, when you think it is the right time."
translations.sn35.88:18: Then Venerable Puṇṇa, having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping his right side towards him, packed up his lodgings, took his bowl and robe, and set out on a walking tour towards the country of Sunāparanta. Walking by stages, he arrived at the country of Sunāparanta. There Venerable Puṇṇa dwelt in the country of Sunāparanta. Then within that rainy season, Venerable Puṇṇa established five hundred male lay followers. Within that rainy season, he established five hundred female lay followers. Within that rainy season, he realized the three true knowledges. Within that rainy season, he attained final Nibbāna.
translations.sn35.88:19: Then several monks approached the Blessed One …pe… seated to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: "That clansman named Puṇṇa, venerable sir, who was instructed by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has died. What is his destination? What is his future state?"
translations.sn35.88:4: "In which country will you dwell, Puṇṇa, being instructed by me with this brief exhortation?" "There is, venerable sir, a country called Sunāparanta; there I will dwell."
translations.sn35.88:5: "The people of Sunāparanta are fierce, Puṇṇa; the people of Sunāparanta are rough. If, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile you, what will occur to you there?"
translations.sn35.88:6: "If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, then this will occur to me: 'These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed excellent, in that they do not strike me with their fists.' Thus it will be here, Blessed One; thus it will be here, Fortunate One."
translations.sn35.88:8: "If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta strike me with their fists, then this will occur to me: 'These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed excellent, in that they do not strike me with clods.' Thus it will be here, Blessed One; thus it will be here, Fortunate One."
translations.sn35.95:1: Then Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approached the Blessed One …pe… seated to one side, Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One: "It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute."
translations.sn35.95:10: "And here, Māluṅkyaputta, in regard to things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, in the cognized merely the cognized. When, Māluṅkyaputta, in regard to things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there is merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, in the cognized merely the cognized; then, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not 'by that.' When, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not 'by that'; then, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not 'therein.' When, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not 'therein'; then, Māluṅkyaputta, you are neither here nor beyond nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering."
