translations.sn35.95:12: Having seen a form with mindfulness lost, Attending to the pleasing sign; With mind attached one feels it, And remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:13: His feelings increase, Many born of form; Greed and aversion too, His mind is struck down; Thus accumulating suffering, Far from Nibbāna is it said.
translations.sn35.95:14: Having heard a sound with mindfulness lost, Attending to the pleasing sign; With mind attached one feels it, And remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:16: Having smelled an odor with mindfulness lost, Attending to the pleasing sign; With mind attached one feels it, And remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, mindfulness is lost, Attending to a pleasing sign; With a mind full of passion one feels it, And remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:2: “What shall we say to you now, Mālukyaputta, young monks? For here you, monk, being old, aged, advanced in years, come to the end of life, ask for a brief exhortation.”
translations.sn35.95:20: Having contacted a contact, mindfulness is lost, Attending to a pleasing sign; With a mind full of passion one feels it, And remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having known a mental phenomenon, mindfulness is lost, Attending to a pleasing sign; With a mind full of passion one feels it, And remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:24: One does not delight in forms, Seeing a form with mindfulness; With a detached mind one feels it, And does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:25: As one sees a form, And experiences a feeling; It is exhausted, not accumulated, Thus one lives mindfully; Thus eliminating suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:26: One does not delight in sounds, Hearing a sound with mindfulness; With a detached mind one feels it, And does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:27: As one hears a sound, And experiences a feeling; It is exhausted, not accumulated, Thus one lives mindfully; Thus eliminating suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:28: One does not delight in smells, Smelling a smell with mindfulness; With a detached mind one feels it, And does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:3: “Although, venerable sir, I am old, aged, advanced in years, come to the end of life. Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, let the Fortunate One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that I might understand the meaning of what the Blessed One says. So that I might become an heir to what the Blessed One says.”
translations.sn35.95:30: One does not delight in tastes, Tasting a taste with mindfulness; With a detached mind one feels it, And does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:35: As one knows a mental phenomenon, And experiences a feeling; It is exhausted, not accumulated, Thus one lives mindfully; Thus eliminating suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.’
translations.sn35.95:36: This, venerable sir, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One.” “Good, good, Mālukyaputta. Good that you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by me:
translations.sn35.95:4: “What do you think, Mālukyaputta, as to those forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen, that you have never seen before, that you do not see, and that it is not your intention to see—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn35.95:9: “As to those mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that you have not known, that you have never known before, that you do not know, and that it is not your intention to know—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn36.19:12: And what, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. This, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness. Those who say: ‘This is the ultimate, this is the supreme, that we experience this peaceful happiness and joy’—I do not concede this to them. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:15: And what, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the complete surmounting of the base of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:7: And what, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness. Those who say: ‘This is the ultimate, this is the supreme, that we experience this peaceful happiness and joy’—I do not concede this to them. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:8: And what, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness. Those who say: ‘This is the ultimate, this is the supreme, that we experience this peaceful happiness and joy’—I do not concede this to them. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:9: And what, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware, and experiences happiness with the body; that which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily,’ he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Ānanda, is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness. Those who say: ‘This is the ultimate, this is the supreme, that we experience this peaceful happiness and joy’—I do not concede this to them. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness that is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.21:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. Then Moḷiyasīvaka the wanderer approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging courteous and amiable greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Moḷiyasīvaka the wanderer said to the Blessed One: “There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who are of such a view and such an opinion: ‘Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is due to previous action.’ What does Master Gotama say about this?”
translations.sn36.21:2: “Bile-born feelings also, Sīvaka, arise here. This too, Sīvaka, should be personally known as it is, that bile-born feelings arise here. This too, Sīvaka, is agreed upon by the world as true, that bile-born feelings arise here. Therein, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and such a belief: ‘Whatever this person feels, whether pleasure or pain or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is due to previous actions.’ They go beyond what is personally known, and they go beyond what is agreed upon by the world as true. Therefore I say of those ascetics and brahmins that they are wrong.”
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! … Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth, for life.”
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the practice leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?”
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual rapture? Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This is called, bhikkhus, spiritual rapture.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, bhikkhus, is more spiritual than spiritual rapture? That rapture which arises in a bhikkhu who is a taintless one, when he reviews that his mind is liberated from lust, reviews that his mind is liberated from hatred, reviews that his mind is liberated from delusion—this is called, bhikkhus, more spiritual than spiritual rapture.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual happiness? Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware, and he experiences happiness with the body; that which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily,’ he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This is called, bhikkhus, spiritual happiness.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, bhikkhus, is more spiritual than spiritual happiness? That happiness and joy which arises in a bhikkhu who is a taintless one, when he reviews that his mind is liberated from lust, reviews that his mind is liberated from hatred, reviews that his mind is liberated from delusion—this is called, bhikkhus, more spiritual than spiritual happiness.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual equanimity? Here, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and dejection, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This is called, bhikkhus, spiritual equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, bhikkhus, is more spiritual than spiritual equanimity? That equanimity which arises in a bhikkhu who is a taintless one, when he reviews that his mind is liberated from lust, reviews that his mind is liberated from hatred, reviews that his mind is liberated from delusion—this is called, bhikkhus, more spiritual than spiritual equanimity.
translations.sn36.4:2: Whoever does not endure these, arisen painful feelings, bodily, life-threatening, by which one is afflicted and trembles.
translations.sn36.4:3: He cries out and wails, weak and lacking strength; he has not risen from the lower depths, nor has he gained a foothold.
translations.sn36.6:2: But, bhikkhus, when the instructed noble disciple is touched by painful feeling, he does not sorrow, grieve, or lament; he does not weep beating his breast and become distraught. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise one, learned, does not feel the feeling; pleasure and pain, even though learned; this is the great difference of the skilled one from the ordinary person.
translations.sn36.6:5: For one of trained nature, learned, seeing this world and the next; agreeable things do not obsess his mind, nor does disagreeableness provoke resistance.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating mind in mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection in regard to the world. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu fully aware? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu acts with full awareness when going forward and returning, when looking ahead and looking aside, when bending and stretching, when wearing the robes and carrying the bowl, when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, when defecating and urinating, when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu acts with full awareness. Mindful, bhikkhus, and fully aware, a bhikkhu should await his time. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: If, monks, while that monk dwells thus mindful, fully aware, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: 'This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. It is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. How could a pleasant feeling arisen in dependence on an impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen body be permanent?' He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, he dwells contemplating fading away, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, as he dwells contemplating fading away, as he dwells contemplating cessation, as he dwells contemplating relinquishment, the underlying tendency to lust in regard to the body and the pleasant feeling is abandoned.
translations.sn36.7:8: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent, as not clung to, as not delighted in; if he feels a painful feeling ... if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent, as not clung to, as not delighted in. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached; if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached; if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. Feeling a feeling limited to the body, he understands 'I feel a feeling limited to the body'; feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands 'I feel a feeling limited to life'. He understands: 'With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, right here all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool.'
translations.sn4.13:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi deer park. Now on that occasion the Blessed One's foot had been cut by a stone splinter, and sharp pains were occurring in the Blessed One—bodily feelings that were painful, severe, acute, harsh, disagreeable, displeasing. The Blessed One, mindful and fully aware, bore them without being distressed. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: 'Do you sleep out of dullness, or is it poetic conceit? Don't you have abundant aims? Alone in a secluded bed and seat, why do you sleep with mouth agape?'
translations.sn4.13:3: 'I do not sleep out of dullness, nor is it poetic conceit; Having reached the goal, I am without sorrow; Alone in a secluded bed and seat, I sleep, compassionate towards all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: Those in whom a dart has entered the chest, Piercing the heart again and again; Even they here obtain sleep with the dart in them, Therefore I do not sleep, one with dart removed.
translations.sn4.13:5: I do not think of wakefulness, nor am I afraid of sleep; Days and nights do not torment me; I see no decline anywhere in the world, Therefore I sleep, compassionate towards all beings.'
translations.sn4.18:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans in the brahmin village of Pañcasālā. Now on that occasion the young women of Pañcasālā brahmin village had guests. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Pañcasālā brahmin village for alms. Now on that occasion the brahmins and householders of Pañcasālā had been possessed by Māra the Evil One: 'May the ascetic Gotama not get alms.'
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One entered Pañcasālā brahmin village for alms with a clean bowl and departed with a clean bowl. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: 'Did you get alms, ascetic?' 'Did you do such a thing, Evil One, that I would not get alms?' 'Then, sir, let the Blessed One enter Pañcasālā brahmin village for alms a second time. I will do such a thing that the Blessed One will get alms.'
translations.sn4.19:4: 'What they call mine, what they call me, If your mind is in this, Ascetic, you will not escape from me.'
translations.sn4.19:5: 'What they call is not mine, What they call me I am not; Thus know, Evil One, You will not even see my path.'
translations.sn4.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the root of the Ajapāla banyan tree, just after becoming fully enlightened. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'I am freed from that ascetic practice. Good that I am freed from that useless ascetic practice. Good that I, freed, have attained awakening.'
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, having known with his mind the reflection in the Blessed One's mind, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: 'Having turned away from ascetic practice, By which young men purify themselves; Impure you think yourself pure, Fallen away from the path of purity.'
translations.sn4.1:6: Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, The path developing awakening; I have attained supreme purity, You are defeated, End-maker.'
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One, knowing 'The Blessed One knows me, the Fortunate One knows me,' sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the Kosalan country in the Himalayan region in a forest hut. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'Is it possible to rule justly, without killing or causing to kill, without conquering or causing to conquer, without sorrowing or causing to sorrow?'
translations.sn4.20:3: 'A whole mountain of gold, Of pure born gold; Would not be enough for one, Knowing this, one should live restrained.
translations.sn4.20:4: Having seen the origin of suffering, How would a person incline towards sensual pleasures; Knowing acquisition as a bond in the world, Let a person train for its removal.'
translations.sn4.21:1: So have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Silāvatiya. Now at that time several monks were dwelling near the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Then Māra the Evil One, having assumed the form of a brahmin, with a great matted mass of hair, wearing an antelope hide, old, bent like a roof beam, breathing heavily, taking a staff of udumbara wood, approached those monks; having approached, he said to those monks: "You are young renunciants, with black hair, endowed with the prime of youth, in the first stage of life, not delighting in sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, sirs. Do not abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what takes time." "We do not, brahmin, abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what takes time. We, brahmin, abandon what takes time to pursue what is visible here and now. For sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to take time, full of suffering, full of trouble, with greater danger here. This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, onward leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves." When this was said, Māra the Evil One shook his head, lolled his tongue, raised three wrinkles on his forehead, leaned on his staff, and departed.
translations.sn4.24:1: So have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Ajapāla banyan tree. Now at that time Māra the Evil One had been following the Blessed One for seven years, seeking an opportunity but not finding one. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: Finding no satisfaction there, the crow left; like a crow attacking a rock, we have grown weary, Gotama."
translations.sn4.24:2: "Are you overwhelmed with grief, meditating in the forest? Have you lost your wealth, or do you desire some? Did you commit some offense in the village? Why do you not make friends with people? No friendship is formed with you by anyone."
translations.sn4.24:3: "Having dug up the root of grief entirely, I meditate without grieving; having cut off all craving for existence and longing, I meditate, free of taints, having broken the bonds of negligence."
translations.sn4.24:6: "If you have discovered the path, secure, leading to the deathless; go away alone, why do you instruct others?"
translations.sn4.24:7: "Those people who ask about what is beyond death's domain, who have gone to the far shore; asked by them I declare what is true, without attachment."
translations.sn4.24:8: "Just as, sir, there is a pond near a village or town. There is a crab in it. Then, sir, several boys or girls, having left that village or town, would approach that pond; having approached, they would lift that crab out of the water and place it on dry land. Whatever limb, sir, that crab would stretch out, that very limb those boys or girls would break, crush, and smash with a stick or a potsherd. Thus, sir, that crab, with all its limbs broken, crushed, and smashed, would be unable to enter that pond. So too, sir, whatever contortions, writhings, and tremblings there were, all of them have been broken, crushed, and smashed by the Blessed One. I am now unable, sir, to approach the Blessed One again, seeking an opportunity." Then Māra the Evil One, in the presence of the Blessed One, recited these verses of disappointment:
translations.sn4.24:9: "A crow went around a stone that looked like fat; we found nothing soft here, not even a trace of satisfaction.
translations.sn4.25:10: 'The Arahant, the Fortunate One in the world, is not to be led by lust; he has gone beyond Māra's domain, therefore I grieve greatly.'"
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Craving, Māra's daughter, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: "Having attained the goal, peace of heart, having conquered the army of what is dear and pleasing; I alone meditate, having understood happiness, therefore I do not make friends with people; no friendship is formed with me by anyone."
translations.sn4.25:16: "How does a monk dwell much, O god, who has crossed the five floods and the sixth here; how does one who meditates much find sensual perceptions removed, not obtaining what one craves?"
translations.sn4.25:17: "With body calmed, well liberated in mind, not proliferating, mindful, without home; having understood the Dhamma, meditating without thought, he does not get angry, does not remember, is not sluggish.
translations.sn4.25:2: "Why are you so sad, dear? Which man do you grieve for? We will bind you with the snare of lust, like an elephant in the forest; having bound you we will bring you back, you will be under our control."
translations.sn4.25:20: "Having cut off craving, wandering in groups and assemblies, many faithful ones will certainly wander; this homeless one will lead many people, having cut them off, to the far shore of the King of Death."
translations.sn4.25:23: "Fools, pound the mountain with lotus stalks; dig the mountain with your nails, eat iron with your teeth.
translations.sn4.25:24: Strike your head against a rock, seek a foothold in the abyss; embrace a thorn-bush with your chest, grow weary of Gotama."
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said to the Blessed One: "We will attend to your feet, ascetic." Then the Blessed One did not attend to them, as he was liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of attachment.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, having withdrawn to one side, thought thus: "Men have various inclinations. What if we were to create each one hundred forms of a hundred maidens?" Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, having created each one hundred forms of a hundred maidens, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said to the Blessed One: "We will attend to your feet, ascetic." The Blessed One did not attend to that either, as he was liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of attachment.
translations.sn4.8:1: So have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn4.8:2: "One with children rejoices in children, one with cattle rejoices in cattle likewise; people rejoice in attachments, one without attachments does not rejoice."
translations.sn4.8:3: “The one with children grieves because of children, The cow woman grieves because of cows just the same; Grief for a person is because of acquisitions, But one without acquisitions does not grieve.”
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Now at that time the bhikkhunī Khemā, while wandering in the Kosalan country, had taken up residence at Toranavatthu between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, going from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, took up residence for one night at Toranavatthu between Sāketa and Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: “Come, good man, find out at Toranavatthu whether there is any ascetic or brahmin whom I could pay homage to today.”
translations.sn44.1:2: “Yes, your majesty,” that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala, and having gone all around Toranavatthu, he did not see any ascetic or brahmin whom King Pasenadi of Kosala could pay homage to. He saw the bhikkhunī Khemā who had taken up residence at Toranavatthu. Having seen her, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
translations.sn44.1:3: “There is no ascetic or brahmin at Toranavatthu, your majesty, whom your majesty could pay homage to. But there is, your majesty, a bhikkhunī named Khemā, a disciple of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And of that lady this good report has spread abroad: ‘She is wise, learned, intelligent, very learned, a good speaker, of goodly eloquence.’ Let your majesty pay homage to her.”
translations.sn44.1:6: “Well then, great king, I will ask you about this very thing. You should answer as it seems proper to you. What do you think, great king, do you have any accountant or calculator or reckoner who could count the sand in the Ganges—so many grains of sand, or so many hundreds of grains of sand, or so many thousands of grains of sand, or so many hundreds of thousands of grains of sand?” “No, venerable lady.” “But do you have any accountant or calculator or reckoner who could count the water in the great ocean—so many buckets of water, or so many hundreds of buckets of water, or so many thousands of buckets of water, or so many hundreds of thousands of buckets of water?” “No, venerable lady.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom.” “So too, great king, that form by which one describing the Tathāgata might describe him—that form has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, unable to arise again in the future. Released from reckoning by form, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—like the great ocean. ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply, ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply, ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply, ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.
translations.sn44.1:9: That consciousness by which one describing the Tathāgata might describe him—that consciousness has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, unable to arise again in the future. Released from reckoning by consciousness, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—like the great ocean. ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply, ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply, ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply, ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having approved and agreed with what the bhikkhunī Khemā said, rose from his seat, paid homage to the bhikkhunī Khemā, circumambulated her keeping his right side towards her, and departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: “Ignorance, bhikkhus, is the forerunner in the entry upon unwholesome states, with shamelessness and lack of fear of wrongdoing following along. For one who is ignorant, bhikkhus, of wrong understanding, wrong view arises; for one of wrong view, wrong intention arises; for one of wrong intention, wrong speech arises; for one of wrong speech, wrong action arises; for one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; for one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; for one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; for one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
translations.sn45.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in the Sakyan town named Nagaraka. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Half of this holy life, venerable sir, is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.”
translations.sn45.2:2: “Do not say so, Ānanda, do not say so, Ānanda. It is the whole of this holy life, Ānanda, this good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. Of a bhikkhu who is a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, Ānanda, it is to be expected that he will develop and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
translations.sn45.2:3: And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who is a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade develop and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view dependent on seclusion, dependent on fading away, dependent on cessation, maturing in release; he develops right intention dependent on seclusion …pe… he develops right speech …pe… he develops right action …pe… he develops right livelihood …pe… he develops right effort …pe… he develops right mindfulness …pe… he develops right concentration dependent on seclusion, dependent on fading away, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. Thus, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who is a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path.
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi leaving Sāvatthī in an all-white mule-chariot. The mules harnessed to it were white, the decorations were white, the chariot was white, the attendants were white, the reins were white, the goad was white, the umbrella was white, the turban was white, the clothes were white, the sandals were white, and he was fanned with a white yak-tail fan. When people saw him, they said: "Indeed, sir, a brahma-vehicle! Indeed, sir, a vehicle worthy of Brahmā!"
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will and non-cruelty, seclusion is his weapon; patience is his armor of hide, leading to security from bondage.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms-round after the meal, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: "It is possible, Ānanda," the Blessed One said. "For this is a designation for this noble eightfold path: 'brahma-vehicle' or 'dhamma-vehicle' or 'unsurpassed victory in battle'."
translations.sn45.4:8: He whose faith and wisdom are always yoked as the pole; conscience is the hook, mind the yoke-tie, mindfulness the charioteer.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot with virtue as its equipment, jhāna as its axle, energy as its wheel; equanimity as the yoke and concentration, non-desire as its covering.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. "Monks, I will teach and analyze for you the noble eightfold path. Listen to this, attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, monks, is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this is called right view, monks.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, monks, is right intention? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of non-cruelty—this is called right intention, monks.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, monks, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this is called right speech, monks.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, monks, is right action? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is called right action, monks.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, monks, is right livelihood? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes a living by right livelihood—this is called right livelihood, monks.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states... for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states—this is called right effort, monks.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, monks, is right mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world—this is called right mindfulness, monks.
translations.sn46.11:1: "Just as, monks, whatever living beings make use of the four postures—walking at times, standing at times, sitting at times, lying down at times—all of them do so depending on the earth, established on the earth; so too, monks, depending on virtue, established on virtue, a monk develops the seven factors of enlightenment, makes much of the seven factors of enlightenment.
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. At that time Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling in the Pepper Cave, sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: "I hope, Kassapa, that you are bearing up, I hope that you are getting better? I hope that your painful feelings are subsiding, not increasing; that their subsiding is evident, not their increase?" "I am not bearing up, venerable sir, I am not getting better. My painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is evident, not their subsiding."
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness depending on seclusion... the enlightenment factor of equanimity depending on seclusion, depending on fading away, depending on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. Thus developed, monks, thus made much of, the seven factors of enlightenment lead to the abandoning of things that are fetters.
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas in a Sumbhan town named Setaka. Then Venerable Udāyī went to the Blessed One... Having sat down to one side, Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: “It is wonderful, sir, it is marvelous, sir. How much I have done, sir, and how much love, respect, conscience, and prudence I have for the Blessed One. For, sir, when I was previously a householder, I was not much given to the Dhamma, not much given to the Sangha. But seeing love and respect and conscience and prudence for the Blessed One, I went forth from the household life into homelessness. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such as volitional formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’
translations.sn46.30:3: Then, sir, having gone to an empty hut, turning over and over these five aggregates subject to clinging, I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ The Dhamma has been realized by me, sir, and the path has been obtained; which, when developed and cultivated, will lead me to such a state of being that I will understand: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’
translations.sn46.38:1: In whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having made a bone [of contention], having attended mentally, having applied the whole mind, having set up mindfulness, listens to the Dhamma, on that occasion these five hindrances are not present for him. The seven factors of enlightenment on that occasion go to the fulfillment of development.
translations.sn46.3:1: “Those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation, seeing, I say, bhikkhus, is of great value for those bhikkhus; listening, I say, bhikkhus, is of great value for those bhikkhus; approaching, I say, bhikkhus, is of great value for those bhikkhus; attending, I say, bhikkhus, is of great value for those bhikkhus; recollection, I say, bhikkhus, is of great value for those bhikkhus; going forth after, I say, bhikkhus, is of great value for those bhikkhus. What is the reason for that? Because, bhikkhus, having heard the Dhamma from bhikkhus of such a sort, one dwells withdrawn by twofold withdrawal—by bodily withdrawal and by mental withdrawal. He, dwelling thus withdrawn, recollects and thinks over that Dhamma.
translations.sn46.3:2: In whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, dwelling thus withdrawn, recollects and thinks over that Dhamma, on that occasion the mindfulness enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor; on that occasion the mindfulness enlightenment factor in the bhikkhu goes to the fulfillment of development. He, dwelling thus mindful, examines, investigates, and scrutinizes that Dhamma with wisdom.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the energy enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the energy enlightenment factor that has arisen? There is, bhikkhus, the element of arousal, the element of endeavor, the element of exertion. Frequent attention to that—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the energy enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the energy enlightenment factor that has arisen.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the rapture enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the rapture enlightenment factor that has arisen? There are, bhikkhus, states that are a basis for the rapture enlightenment factor. Frequent attention to that—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the rapture enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the rapture enlightenment factor that has arisen.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the tranquility enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the tranquility enlightenment factor that has arisen? There is, bhikkhus, bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Frequent attention to that—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the tranquility enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the tranquility enlightenment factor that has arisen.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the concentration enlightenment factor that has arisen? There is, bhikkhus, the sign of serenity, the sign of non-distraction. Frequent attention to that—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor that has not arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the concentration enlightenment factor that has arisen.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then several bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: “It is too early yet to walk for alms in Sāvatthī. What if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.52:10: And what, bhikkhus, is the method by which, having relied on that method, the seven enlightenment factors become fourteen? Whatever, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of internal phenomena, that too is the mindfulness enlightenment factor; whatever is mindfulness of external phenomena, that too is the mindfulness enlightenment factor. ‘Mindfulness enlightenment factor’—thus this is the designation. By this method too this is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:11: Whatever, bhikkhus, is examination with wisdom of internal phenomena, investigation, scrutiny, that too is the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor; whatever is examination with wisdom of external phenomena, investigation, scrutiny, that too is the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor. ‘Investigation-of-states enlightenment factor’—thus this is the designation. By this method too this is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:12: Whatever, bhikkhus, is bodily energy, that too is the energy enlightenment factor; whatever is mental energy, that too is the energy enlightenment factor. ‘Energy enlightenment factor’—thus this is the designation. By this method too this is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:13: Whatever, bhikkhus, is rapture with thought and examination, that too is the rapture enlightenment factor; whatever is rapture without thought and examination, that too is the rapture enlightenment factor. ‘Rapture enlightenment factor’—thus this is the designation. By this method too this is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:14: Whatever, bhikkhus, is bodily tranquility, that too is the tranquility enlightenment factor; whatever is mental tranquility, that too is the tranquility enlightenment factor. ‘Tranquility enlightenment factor’—thus this is the designation. By this method too this is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:15: Whatever, monks, is concentration with thought and examination, that too is the awakening factor of concentration; whatever is concentration without thought and examination, that too is the awakening factor of concentration. 'Awakening factor of concentration' is the designation that goes in this way. By this method too this is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those monks went to the park of those wanderers of other sects; having gone, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. When they had sat down to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to those monks:
translations.sn46.52:3: 'The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches his disciples thus: "Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind, weakeners of wisdom, develop the seven awakening factors as they really are." We too, friends, teach our disciples thus: "Come, friends, having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind, weakeners of wisdom, develop the seven awakening factors as they really are." What, friends, is the distinction here, what is the difference, what is the distinction between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, in the teaching of the Dhamma or in the instruction?'
translations.sn46.52:4: Then those monks neither approved nor disapproved of what those wanderers of other sects said; without approving, without disapproving, they rose from their seats and departed: 'We will understand the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.' Then those monks, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the almsround after the meal, went to the Blessed One; having gone, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. When they had sat down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:8: 'When wanderers of other sects speak thus, monks, they should be spoken to thus: "Is there, friends, a method by which, having come to that method, the five hindrances become ten, the seven awakening factors become fourteen?" When asked thus, monks, wanderers of other sects will neither be able to respond nor will they fall into further distress. Why is that? Because, monks, it is outside their domain. I do not see, monks, in this world with its devas, with its Māras, with its Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind with an explanation of these questions, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one having heard it from here.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what, monks, is the method by which, having come to that method, the five hindrances become ten? Whatever, monks, is sensual desire internally, that too is a hindrance; whatever is sensual desire externally, that too is a hindrance. 'Hindrance of sensual desire' is the designation that goes in this way. By this method too this is twofold. Whatever, monks, is ill will internally, that too is a hindrance; whatever is ill will externally, that too is a hindrance. 'Hindrance of ill will' is the designation that goes in this way. By this method too this is twofold. Whatever, monks, is dullness, that too is a hindrance; whatever is drowsiness, that too is a hindrance. 'Hindrance of dullness and drowsiness' is the designation that goes in this way. By this method too this is twofold. Whatever, monks, is restlessness, that too is a hindrance; whatever is remorse, that too is a hindrance. 'Hindrance of restlessness and remorse' is the designation that goes in this way. By this method too this is twofold. Whatever, monks, is doubt about things internally, that too is a hindrance; whatever is doubt about things externally, that too is a hindrance. 'Hindrance of doubt' is the designation that goes in this way. By this method too this is twofold. This, monks, is the method by which, having come to that method, the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: When, monks, the mind is restless, it is not the time at that time for the development of the awakening factor of investigation of states, not the time for the development of the awakening factor of energy, not the time for the development of the awakening factor of rapture. Why is that? Because, monks, a restless mind is difficult to calm down with these things.
translations.sn46.53:11: Just as, monks, a man might want to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw dry grass on it, throw dry cow dung on it, throw dry sticks on it, blow on it with his mouth, and not cover it with dust; would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn46.53:13: But when, monks, the mind is restless, it is the time at that time for the development of the awakening factor of tranquility, the time for the development of the awakening factor of concentration, the time for the development of the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because, monks, a restless mind is easy to calm down with these things.
translations.sn46.53:14: Just as, monks, a man might want to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw wet grass on it, throw wet cow dung on it, throw wet sticks on it, blow on it with water, and cover it with dust; would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?' 'Yes, venerable sir.'
translations.sn46.53:2: 'When wanderers of other sects speak thus, monks, they should be spoken to thus: "When, friends, the mind is sluggish, at that time which awakening factors are not the time for development, which awakening factors are the time for development? And when, friends, the mind is restless, at that time which awakening factors are not the time for development, which awakening factors are the time for development?" When asked thus, monks, wanderers of other sects will neither be able to respond nor will they fall into further distress. Why is that? Because, monks, it is outside their domain.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see, monks, in this world with its devas, with its Māras, with its Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind with an explanation of these questions, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one having heard it from here.
translations.sn46.53:4: Bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, it is not the right time to develop the awakening factor of tranquility, it is not the right time to develop the awakening factor of concentration, it is not the right time to develop the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, a sluggish mind is difficult to rouse up by those things.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. He would put wet grass there, wet cow dung there, wet sticks there, give a blast of wind, and cover it with dust. Would that man be able to kindle a small fire? No, venerable sir.
translations.sn46.53:7: But, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, it is the right time to develop the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, it is the right time to develop the awakening factor of energy, it is the right time to develop the awakening factor of rapture. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, a sluggish mind is easy to rouse up by those things.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. He would put dry grass there, dry cow dung there, dry sticks there, give a mouth-blast of wind, and not cover it with dust. Would that man be able to kindle a small fire? Yes, venerable sir.
translations.sn46.54:1: Now at that time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Koliyans in a Koliyan town named Haliddavasana. Then several bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: It is too early yet to walk for alms in Haliddavasana. What if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?
translations.sn46.54:11: Bhikkhus, when the wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be answered thus: But friends, how is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? How is the liberation of mind by compassion developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? How is the liberation of mind by altruistic joy developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? How is the liberation of mind by equanimity developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? Bhikkhus, when thus asked, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to respond and will furthermore fall into distress. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, it is not their domain. I do not see anyone, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, with its Māra, with its Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness ... he develops the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes: May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive, he dwells there perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes: May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive, he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes: May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, he dwells there perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes: May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive, he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes: Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, or else he enters and dwells in the liberation of the beautiful. I say, bhikkhus, that the liberation of mind by loving-kindness has the beautiful as its peak, for a wise bhikkhu who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by compassion developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by compassion ... he develops the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by compassion, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes: May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive, he dwells there perceiving the repulsive ... if he wishes: Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Or else, having completely transcended perceptions of forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that space is infinite, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. I say, bhikkhus, that the liberation of mind by compassion has the base of infinite space as its peak, for a wise bhikkhu who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by altruistic joy developed, what is its destination, what is its peak, what is its fruit, what is its culmination? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by altruistic joy ... he develops the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by altruistic joy, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes: May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive, he dwells there perceiving the repulsive ... if he wishes: Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Or else, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, aware that consciousness is infinite, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. I say, bhikkhus, that the liberation of mind by altruistic joy has the base of infinite consciousness as its peak, for a wise bhikkhu who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:3: “The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches his disciples thus: ‘Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances, mental corruptions that weaken wisdom, dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every respect, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every respect, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every respect, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every respect, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will.’”
translations.sn46.8:1: On one occasion Venerable Upavāṇa and Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then in the evening Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Upavāṇa; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Upavāṇa. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Upavāṇa:
translations.sn46.8:2: “Could a monk know, friend Upavāṇa, ‘Through my own wise attention thus well undertaken, these seven factors of enlightenment lead to a pleasant dwelling’?” “A monk could know, friend Sāriputta, ‘Through my own wise attention thus well undertaken, these seven factors of enlightenment lead to a pleasant dwelling.’”
translations.sn47.10:1: Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking bowl and robe, approached a certain nuns’ quarters; having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then several nuns approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Those nuns, seated to one side, said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: “Here, Venerable Ānanda, several nuns dwell with minds well established in the four establishments of mindfulness and perceive a supreme distinction between before and after.” “So it is, sisters, so it is, sisters. For whoever, sisters, a monk or nun dwells with mind well established in the four establishments of mindfulness, it may be expected of him or her: ‘They will perceive a supreme distinction between before and after.’”
translations.sn47.10:7: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena …pe… in the mind …pe… ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating phenomena in phenomena, bodily fever or mental sluggishness arises, or the mind is distracted externally. Then, Ānanda, the monk should direct the mind towards some inspiring sign. When the monk directs the mind towards some inspiring sign, gladness is born. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, one feels pleasure. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. He then reflects thus: ‘The purpose for which I directed my mind has been achieved. Now let me withdraw it.’ So he withdraws it and does not think or examine. He understands: ‘Without thought and examination, internally mindful, I am happy.’ Thus, Ānanda, there is development by directing.
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, development by directing has been taught by me, development without directing has been taught. Whatever, Ānanda, should be done by a teacher out of compassion for his disciples, seeking their welfare, that has been done by me for you. These, Ānanda, are the roots of trees, these are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda, do not be negligent, lest you regret it later. This is our instruction to you.”
translations.sn47.13:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Now on that occasion Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans in the village of Nālaka, sick, afflicted, gravely ill. And the novice Cunda was attending on Venerable Sāriputta.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then Venerable Sāriputta attained final Nibbāna through that very illness. Then the novice Cunda, taking Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robe, went to Sāvatthī, to Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, to Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. The novice Cunda, seated to one side, said to Venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna, venerable sir. This is his bowl and robe.”
translations.sn47.13:3: “There is this matter to be reported to the Blessed One, friend Cunda. Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, let us report this matter to the Blessed One.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the novice Cunda replied to Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Venerable Ānanda, seated to one side, said to the Blessed One: “This novice Cunda says thus, venerable sir: ‘Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna, venerable sir; this is his bowl and robe.’ Moreover, venerable sir, my body seems to have become as if drugged, directions are not clear to me, and teachings do not occur to me on hearing that ‘Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna.’”
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas in a Sumbhan town called Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Once, monks, a bamboo acrobat, having set up a bamboo pole, addressed his apprentice Medakathālikā: 'Come, my dear Medakathālikā, climb the bamboo pole and stand on my shoulders.' 'Yes, teacher,' replied the apprentice Medakathālikā to the bamboo acrobat, and having climbed the bamboo pole, she stood on the teacher's shoulders. Then the bamboo acrobat addressed his apprentice Medakathālikā: 'You protect me, my dear Medakathālikā, and I will protect you. Thus protected by each other, guarding each other, we will show our skills, get our earnings, and descend safely from the bamboo pole.' When this was said, monks, the apprentice Medakathālikā addressed the bamboo acrobat: 'No, teacher, it will not be so. You, teacher, protect yourself, and I will protect myself. Thus protected by ourselves, guarding ourselves, we will show our skills, get our earnings, and descend safely from the bamboo pole."
translations.sn47.19:2: "That is the proper course there," said the Blessed One, "as the apprentice Medakathālikā spoke to the teacher. 'I will protect myself,' monks, should be the basis for establishing mindfulness; 'I will protect another,' monks, should be the basis for establishing mindfulness. By protecting oneself, monks, one protects another; by protecting another, one protects oneself.
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas in a Sumbhan town called Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn47.20:2: "Suppose, monks, 'country's beauty, country's beauty,' a great crowd would gather. And if that country's beauty were highly skilled in dancing, highly skilled in singing, and 'the country's beauty dances and sings,' monks, an even greater crowd would gather. Then a man would come who loves life, fears death, desires happiness, and is averse to suffering. Someone would say to him: 'Good man, you must carry around this bowl of oil full to the brim between the great crowd and the country's beauty. And a man with a drawn sword will follow right behind you. Wherever you spill even a little, there he will cut off your head.' What do you think, monks, would that man, without attending to that bowl of oil, be careless outside?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging polite conversation and courteous remarks, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: "What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why the true Dhamma does not last long after the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna? And what is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why the true Dhamma lasts long after the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna?"
translations.sn47.25:2: Through non-development and non-cultivation of the four establishments of mindfulness, brahmin, the true Dhamma does not last long after the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna. Through development and cultivation of the four establishments of mindfulness, brahmin, the true Dhamma lasts long after the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna.
translations.sn47.29:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha; having approached, he sat down on a prepared seat. Sitting down, Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: "Is it manageable for you, householder? Is it sustainable? Do painful feelings subside rather than increase? Is their subsiding evident, not their increase?" "It is not manageable for me, venerable sir, it is not sustainable. Strong painful feelings increase for me, they do not subside; their increase is evident, not their subsidence."
translations.sn47.29:3: "Therefore, householder, you should train thus: 'I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; in feelings ... in mind ... I will dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.' Thus, householder, should you train."
translations.sn47.33:1: For whoever, monks, the four establishments of mindfulness are undeveloped, the noble path going to the complete destruction of suffering is undeveloped for them. For whoever, monks, the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, the noble path going to the complete destruction of suffering is developed for them.
translations.sn47.37:1: Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating the body in the body, desire in regard to the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless has been realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, desire in regard to feelings is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless has been realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating mind in mind, desire in regard to mind is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless has been realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the deathless has been realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the deathless has been realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: One dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating mind in mind, the mind is fully understood. With the mind fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: “Mendicants, I will teach you mindfulness meditation, the development of mindfulness meditation, and the path that leads to the development of mindfulness meditation. Listen to this. And what, mendicants, is mindfulness meditation? Here, mendicants, a mendicant dwells contemplating body in body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… they dwell contemplating mind in mind …pe… they dwell contemplating principles in principles, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called, mendicants, mindfulness meditation.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what, mendicants, is the development of mindfulness meditation? Here, mendicants, a mendicant dwells contemplating the origin of phenomena in the body, they dwell contemplating the passing away of phenomena in the body, they dwell contemplating the origin and passing away of phenomena in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. They dwell contemplating the origin of phenomena in feelings …pe… they dwell contemplating the origin of phenomena in mind …pe… they dwell contemplating the origin of phenomena in principles, they dwell contemplating the passing away of phenomena in principles, they dwell contemplating the origin and passing away of phenomena in principles, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called, mendicants, the development of mindfulness meditation.
translations.sn47.4:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in the brahmin village of Sālā. There the Blessed One addressed the mendicants …pe… and said:
translations.sn47.4:2: “Those mendicants who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this Dhamma and Discipline, you should encourage, settle, and establish those mendicants in the development of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. Which four? Come, friends, dwell contemplating body in body, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing the body as it really is; dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing feelings as they really are; dwell contemplating mind in mind, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing the mind as it really is; dwell contemplating principles in principles, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing principles as they really are.
translations.sn47.4:3: And those mendicants who are trainees, who have not attained their mind's ideal, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, they too dwell contemplating body in body, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of fully understanding the body; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of fully understanding feelings; they dwell contemplating mind in mind, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of fully understanding the mind; they dwell contemplating principles in principles, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of fully understanding principles.
translations.sn47.4:4: And those mendicants who are perfected ones, with defilements ended, who have completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge, they too dwell contemplating body in body, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, detached from the body; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, detached from feelings; they dwell contemplating mind in mind, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, detached from the mind; they dwell contemplating principles in principles, ardent, fully aware, with unified mind, with purified mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, detached from principles.
translations.sn47.6:1: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, mendicants, the quail, being carried away by the hawk, lamented thus: ‘We are so unfortunate, we are so lacking in merit, that we have wandered into what is not our domain, into another's territory. If only today we had wandered in our own domain, in our own paternal territory, this hawk would not have been a match for me, that is, in battle.’ ‘But quail, what is your domain, your own paternal territory?’ ‘That is, the ploughed field with clods of earth turned up by the plough.’ Then, mendicants, the hawk, not yielding to its own strength, not acknowledging its own strength, released the quail: ‘Go then, quail, but even going there you will not escape me.’
translations.sn47.6:2: Then, mendicants, the quail, having gone to the ploughed field with clods of earth turned up by the plough, having climbed up on a large clod, stood challenging the hawk: ‘Come now to me, hawk, come now to me, hawk.’ Then, mendicants, that hawk, not yielding to its own strength, not acknowledging its own strength, folding both wings, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When, mendicants, the quail knew ‘This hawk has come at me in full force,’ then it slipped inside that very clod. Then, mendicants, the hawk shattered its breast right there. So it is, mendicants, for one who wanders into what is not their domain, into another's territory.
translations.sn47.6:3: Therefore, mendicants, do not wander into what is not your domain, into another's territory. For one who wanders into what is not their domain, mendicants, into another's territory, Māra will find an opening, Māra will find a foothold. And what, mendicants, is not a mendicant's domain but another's territory? That is, the five kinds of sensual stimulation. What five? Sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasing, sensual, and arousing; sounds known by the ear …pe… smells known by the nose …pe… tastes known by the tongue …pe… touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasing, sensual, and arousing—this, mendicants, is not a mendicant's domain but another's territory.
translations.sn47.7:1: “There are, mendicants, in the Himalayas, king of mountains, rugged and uneven regions where neither monkeys nor humans can go. There are, mendicants, in the Himalayas, king of mountains, rugged and uneven regions where monkeys can go, but not humans. There are, mendicants, in the Himalayas, king of mountains, level and delightful regions where both monkeys and humans can go. There, mendicants, hunters set lime on monkey paths to catch the monkeys.
translations.sn47.8:2: That foolish, incompetent, unskilled cook, monks, does not pick up on the sign of his own master: 'This is what my master likes in soup today, or he takes to this, or he takes a lot of this, or he praises this. Sour is what my master likes in soup today, or he takes to sour, or he takes a lot of sour, or he praises sour.
