Bitter is what my master likes today ... pungent is what my master likes today ... sweet is what my master likes today ... salty is what my master likes today ... unsalty is what my master likes today, or he takes to unsalty, or he takes a lot of unsalty, or he praises unsalty.'
translations.sn47.8:4: That foolish, incompetent, unskilled monk, monks, is not one who attains pleasant dwellings in this very life, nor is he one who attains mindfulness and full awareness. Why is that? Because, monks, that foolish, incompetent, unskilled monk does not pick up on the sign of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Just as, monks, a wise, competent, skilled cook would attend upon a king or royal minister with various kinds of soups—sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, salty, and unsalty.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā, having dressed in the morning and taking bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the almsround after the meal, she went to the Blind Men's Grove for the day's abiding. Having entered the Blind Men's Grove, she sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the bhikkhunī Vajirā, wanting to make her fall away from samādhi, approached the bhikkhunī Vajirā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Vajirā in verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: 'By whom is this being created? Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen? Where does the being cease?'
translations.sn5.10:3: Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vajirā: 'Who is this, a human or non-human, speaking verse?' Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vajirā: 'This is Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in me, wanting to make me fall away from samādhi, speaking verse.' Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā, having understood 'This is Māra the Evil One,' replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
translations.sn5.10:4: 'Why do you assume a being, Māra? Is that your view? This is a heap of mere formations; here no being is found.
translations.sn5.10:5: For just as, with an assemblage of parts, the word 'chariot' is used, so too, when the aggregates exist, the convention 'being' is used.
translations.sn5.10:6: For only suffering arises, suffering persists and passes away; nothing but suffering arises, nothing but suffering ceases.'
translations.sn5.1:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, having dressed in the morning and taking bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the almsround after the meal, she went to the Blind Men's Grove, desiring seclusion. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, wanting to make her fall away from seclusion, approached the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā in verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: 'There is no escape in the world; what will you do with seclusion? Enjoy sensual pleasures; don't be one who regrets later.'
translations.sn5.1:3: Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā: 'Who is this, a human or non-human, speaking verse?' Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā: 'This is Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in me, wanting to make me fall away from seclusion, speaking verse.' Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, having understood 'This is Māra the Evil One,' replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
translations.sn5.1:4: 'There is an escape in the world, well touched by me with wisdom; kinsman of the negligent, evil one, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures are like swords and spears, the aggregates their chopping block; what you call sensual delight, for me that has become discontent.'
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking 'The bhikkhunī Āḷavikā knows me,' sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: 'That which is to be attained by seers, a state hard to achieve; with the wisdom of a two-finger measure, a woman is not able to reach it.'
translations.sn5.2:4: 'What can womanhood do, when the mind is well concentrated; when knowledge is functioning, when one rightly sees the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.2:5: For one to whom it might occur, 'I am a woman' or 'I am a man,' or 'I am anything else'—that is worthy for Māra to address.'
translations.sn5.3:2: 'Why do you sit alone with tearful face, like one whose son is dead? Having gone alone into the forest, are you seeking a man?'
translations.sn5.3:3: Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī: 'Who is this, a human or non-human, speaking verse?' Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī: 'This is Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in me, wanting to make me fall away from samādhi, speaking verse.'
translations.sn5.3:5: 'I have completely finished with sons, with men the end has come; I do not grieve, I do not weep, and I do not fear you, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Delight is destroyed everywhere, the mass of darkness is shattered; having conquered the army of Death, I dwell without defilements.'
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking 'The bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī knows me,' sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Vijayā, having dressed in the morning ... she sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the bhikkhunī Vijayā, wanting to make her fall away from samādhi, approached the bhikkhunī Vijayā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Vijayā in verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: 'You are young and beautiful, and I too am young; with fivefold music, come let us enjoy ourselves.'
translations.sn5.4:4: 'Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and tactile objects that are delightful—I offer them all to you, Māra, I have no need of that.'
translations.sn5.4:5: With this putrid body, fragile and breakable; I am disenchanted and ashamed, sensual craving is destroyed.
translations.sn5.4:6: Whatever beings are form-attained, and those who dwell in the formless; and whatever peaceful attainments, darkness is destroyed in all of them.
translations.sn5.5:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, having dressed in the morning... stood at the root of a certain fully blossomed sāla tree. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and hair-raising in the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, wanting to drive her out of concentration, approached the nun Uppalavaṇṇā; having approached, he addressed the nun Uppalavaṇṇā with a verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: Having approached a fully blossomed tree, nun, you stand alone at the root of a sāla tree; there is no second of your beauty, fool, aren't you afraid of ruffians?
translations.sn5.5:4: Even a hundred thousand ruffians, such as these might come here; I do not stir a hair, I am not terrified, Māra, I am not afraid of you even alone.
translations.sn5.5:6: I am one who has mastery over the mind, the bases of psychic power are well developed; I am released from all bonds, I am not afraid of you, friend.
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Māra the Evil One, knowing "The nun Uppalavaṇṇā knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: Why do you not delight in birth? One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures; who persuaded you of this, that you should not delight in birth, nun?
translations.sn5.6:3: For one who is born there is death, one who is born experiences pains; bondage, killing, and trouble, therefore I do not delight in birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma, the transcendence of birth; for the abandoning of all suffering, he established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: Whatever beings are form-attained, and those who dwell in the formless; not understanding cessation, they are returners to renewed existence.
translations.sn5.7:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Upacālā, having dressed in the morning... sat down for the day's abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Evil One approached the nun Upacālā; having approached, he said to the nun Upacālā: "Where do you wish to be reborn, nun?" "I do not wish to be reborn anywhere, friend."
translations.sn5.7:2: The Tāvatiṃsa and Yāma, and also the Tusitā devas; the Nimmānaratino devas, and the devas who are Vasavattino; direct your mind there, you will enjoy delight.
translations.sn5.7:3: The Tāvatiṃsa and Yāma, and also the Tusitā devas; the Nimmānaratino devas, and the devas who are Vasavattino; they are bound by the bond of sensual pleasure, they come under Māra's control again.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is blazing, the whole world is smoking; the whole world is burning, the whole world is trembling.
translations.sn5.7:5: Unshaken, unburned, not frequented by ordinary people; where Māra has no access, there my mind delights.
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Māra the Evil One, knowing "The nun Upacālā knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Sīsupacālā, having dressed in the morning... sat down for the day's abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Evil One approached the nun Sīsupacālā; having approached, he said to the nun Sīsupacālā: "Whose sect do you approve of, nun?" "I do not approve of anyone's sect, friend."
translations.sn5.8:2: On account of whom are you shaven-headed, you appear like an ascetic; and you do not approve of any sect, what are you doing, confused one?
translations.sn5.8:3: Outside of here are sects, they have confidence in views; I do not approve of their Dhamma, they are unskilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Released everywhere, unattached, the seer sees everything; one who has reached the end of all kamma, liberated in the destruction of attachments; he is my Blessed One, my teacher, his instruction I approve.
translations.sn5.9:2: By whom was this image made, where is the maker of the image; where has the image arisen, where does the image cease?
translations.sn5.9:4: This image was not made by oneself, nor was this misery made by another; arisen from a cause, it ceases with the breaking of the cause.
translations.sn5.9:6: Thus aggregates and elements, and these six sense bases; arisen from a cause, they cease with the breaking of the cause.
translations.sn56.11:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
translations.sn56.11:10: But, monks, when my knowledge and vision of these Four Noble Truths in this three-round, twelve-mode manner was truly purified, then, monks, in the world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, I declared 'Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is awakened by me.' And this knowledge and vision arose in me: 'My liberation is unshakeable, this is my last birth, there is now no renewed existence.' This is what the Blessed One said. The group of five monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose for Venerable Koṇḍañña: 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.'
translations.sn56.11:13: And in that instant, in that moment, in that second, a cry went up as far as the Brahma-world. And this ten-thousand-world-system trembled, quaked, and shook, and an immeasurable, magnificent light appeared in the world, surpassing the divine majesty of the devas.
translations.sn56.11:2: These two extremes, monks, should not be practiced by one who has gone forth. What two? This pursuit of sensual pleasure in sensual pleasures, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and this pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Not approaching either of these extremes, monks, the middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to calm, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata that produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to calm, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbāna? It is just this noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata that produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to calm, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:4: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; union with what is displeasing is suffering; separation from what is pleasing is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there, that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: it is this noble eightfold path, that is, right view …pe… right concentration.
translations.sn56.11:5: This is the noble truth of suffering: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before. This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood: such, monks, …pe… arose in me. This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before.
translations.sn56.11:6: This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before. This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned: such, monks, …pe… arose in me. This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before.
translations.sn56.11:7: This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before. This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized: such, monks, …pe… arose in me. This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before.
translations.sn56.11:8: This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before. This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed: such, monks, …pe… arose in me. This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed: such, monks, was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me regarding things not heard before.
translations.sn56.11:9: And, monks, as long as my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
translations.sn56.20:1: Monks, these four things are actual, unerring, not otherwise. What four? This is suffering, monks, is actual, unerring, not otherwise; this is the origin of suffering is actual, unerring, not otherwise; this is the cessation of suffering is actual, unerring, not otherwise; this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering is actual, unerring, not otherwise—these, monks, are the four things that are actual, unerring, not otherwise.
translations.sn56.26:1: Monks, whatever you have compassion for, whether friends or companions, relatives or blood relations, they should be encouraged, settled, and established in true comprehension of these four noble truths.
translations.sn56.26:2: Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Monks, whatever you have compassion for, whether friends or companions, relatives or blood relations, they should be encouraged, settled, and established in true comprehension of these four noble truths.
translations.sn56.27:1: Monks, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—these, monks, are the four noble truths that are actual, unerring, not otherwise; therefore they are called noble truths.
translations.sn56.28:1: Monks, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The Tathāgata is noble in the world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; therefore they are called noble truths.
translations.sn56.30:1: On one occasion several elder monks were dwelling at Ceti in Sahañcanika. Now on that occasion, after several elder monks had returned from their alms round and had finished their meal, they sat down in the circular pavilion and this discussion arose among them: Friends, one who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, also sees the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambi in the Siṁsapā grove. Then the Blessed One, having taken a few Siṁsapā leaves in his hand, addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more numerous—the few Siṁsapā leaves that I have taken in my hand or those up in the Siṁsapā grove?” “The few Siṁsapā leaves that the Blessed One has taken in his hand are few, sir; those up in the Siṁsapā grove are more numerous.” “So too, bhikkhus, the things that I have directly known but have not taught you are more numerous. And why, bhikkhus, have I not taught them? Because they are unbeneficial, irrelevant to the fundamentals of the holy life, and do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; therefore I have not taught them.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, have I taught? ‘This is suffering,’ bhikkhus, I have taught; ‘this is the origin of suffering’ I have taught; ‘this is the cessation of suffering’ I have taught; ‘this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’ I have taught.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why, bhikkhus, have I taught this? Because this is beneficial, this is relevant to the fundamentals of the holy life, this leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; therefore I have taught this.
translations.sn56.35:1: “Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a man with a lifespan of a hundred years, living a hundred years. Someone might say to him: ‘Come, good man, in the morning they will strike you with a hundred spears, at noon they will strike you with a hundred spears, in the evening they will strike you with a hundred spears. And you, good man, being struck with three hundred spears day after day, with a lifespan of a hundred years, living a hundred years, at the end of a hundred years you will realize the four noble truths that you had not realized.’
translations.sn56.35:2: It would be fitting, bhikkhus, for a clansman intent on the goal to accept this. For what reason? Because this saṁsāra is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned of blows from spears, blows from swords, blows from arrows, blows from axes. Even if that were so, bhikkhus, I do not say that the realization of the four noble truths is accompanied by suffering or displeasure; but I say that the realization of the four noble truths is accompanied by pleasure and joy. Which four? The noble truth of suffering … the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man would cut up all the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage in this Jambudīpa and collect them together into one heap; having collected them together, he would make stakes. Having made stakes, he would impale the large creatures in the great ocean on the large stakes, the medium creatures in the great ocean on the medium stakes, and the small creatures in the great ocean on the small stakes. And the gross creatures in the great ocean would not be exhausted.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage in this Jambudīpa would be used up and exhausted. For even more numerous, bhikkhus, are the small creatures in the great ocean that are not easy to impale on stakes. For what reason? Because of the subtlety of their bodies. So vast, bhikkhus, is the plane of misery. So vast is the plane of misery from which a person accomplished in view is liberated, who truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Come, bhikkhus, let us go to Paṭibhānakūṭa for the day's abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One went to Paṭibhānakūṭa together with a number of bhikkhus. A certain bhikkhu saw a great chasm at Paṭibhānakūṭa. Having seen it, he said to the Blessed One: “This chasm is truly great, venerable sir, fearful and terrifying, venerable sir. Is there, venerable sir, another chasm greater and more fearful and terrifying than this one?” “There is, bhikkhu, another chasm greater and more fearful and terrifying than this one.”
translations.sn56.42:2: “But what, venerable sir, is the chasm greater and more fearful and terrifying than this one?” “Those ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, who do not truly understand: ‘This is suffering,’ who do not truly understand: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ who do not truly understand: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ who do not truly understand: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they delight in volitional formations that lead to birth, they delight in volitional formations that lead to aging, they delight in volitional formations that lead to death, they delight in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Delighting in volitional formations that lead to birth, delighting in volitional formations that lead to aging, delighting in volitional formations that lead to death, delighting in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, they generate volitional formations that lead to birth, they generate volitional formations that lead to aging, they generate volitional formations that lead to death, they generate volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Having generated volitional formations that lead to birth, having generated volitional formations that lead to aging, having generated volitional formations that lead to death, having generated volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, they fall into the chasm of birth, they fall into the chasm of aging, they fall into the chasm of death, they fall into the chasm of sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. They are not liberated from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. ‘They are not liberated from suffering,’ I say.
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw a number of Licchavi youths shooting arrows from a distance through a small keyhole, hitting the target without missing shot after shot. Seeing this, it occurred to him: "These Licchavi youths are trained, indeed well trained, in that they can shoot arrows from a distance through a small keyhole, hitting the target without missing shot after shot."
translations.sn56.45:3: "What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and challenging—to shoot arrows from a distance through a small keyhole, hitting the target without missing shot after shot, or to pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with the tip of another hair?" "This is more difficult and challenging, sir, to pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with the tip of another hair." "But, Ānanda, those who pierce what is even more difficult to pierce—they who pierce 'This is suffering' as it really is … 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is."
translations.sn56.46:1: "There are, bhikkhus, interstitial spaces, impenetrable and unilluminated, of blinding darkness, where the light of these moons and suns, so powerful and mighty, does not reach."
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "That is great darkness indeed, sir, that is very great darkness indeed. Is there, sir, any other darkness greater and more terrifying than this?" "There is, bhikkhu, another darkness greater and more terrifying than this."
translations.sn56.48:1: "Suppose, bhikkhus, this great earth were entirely covered with water. A man would throw a yoke with a single hole into it. The east wind would carry it west, the west wind would carry it east, the north wind would carry it south, and the south wind would carry it north. There would be a blind turtle. It would surface once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, put its neck into that yoke with a single hole?" "It is a matter of chance, sir, that the blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, would put its neck into that yoke with a single hole."
translations.sn56.48:2: "So too, bhikkhus, it is a matter of chance that one obtains the human state. So too, bhikkhus, it is a matter of chance that a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. So too, bhikkhus, it is a matter of chance that the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world. Now, bhikkhus, this human state has been obtained, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world."
translations.mn82:12: Then Raṭṭhapāla the clansman got up, gathered his strength, and went to the Buddha. Having approached, he paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla the clansman said to the Buddha: "Venerable sir, I have been permitted by my parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness. May the Buddha ordain me."
